- **Filesystem storage no longer reports a write as complete when its last buffered write failed, which could make a correct chunked `docker push` fail with `DIGEST_INVALID`** (#4646). `put` and `put_stream` called `sync_all` without `flush` first. tokio's `sync_all` waits for the last in-flight write but does not return its error, so if that write failed (for example disk full on the storage volume) the short temp file was still renamed into place, and the call returned the length and SHA-256 of the full input. For an OCI chunked upload, the PATCH was accepted with the right `Range`, and the commit later read the short part and refused the push with a digest that matched nothing the client sent. Both writes now flush before syncing, so the failed write returns an error and nothing is published. The OCI commit also now checks each stored part against the length recorded at PATCH time. A mismatch is reported as a 500 naming the part instead of `DIGEST_INVALID`. Digest mismatches log the session's part keys and sizes, the assembled length, and both digests.

- **Every login response now says how long the session lasts, and the short login lifetime is documented** (#4648). `POST /api/v1/auth/login` already returned `expires_in` and `token_type`, but LDAP login (`POST /api/v1/auth/sso/ldap/{id}/login`) and the SSO exchange (`POST /api/v1/auth/sso/exchange`) returned no `expires_in` and set the access cookie for one hour while the token itself expires after `JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRY_MINUTES` (30 by default). Both now return `expires_in` in seconds and size the cookie to the token's real lifetime. `.env.example` and `docs/api-token-expiration-policy.md` now state that login sessions are short-lived, that `JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRY_MINUTES` sets the lifetime (the uncommented `JWT_EXPIRATION_SECS=86400` there suggested a 24-hour session but no token lifetime reads it), and that scripts and CI should mint an API token with `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens` instead of logging in. The default lifetime is unchanged.

- **Migrating a Debian repository from Artifactory or Nexus now imports its packages, not just its files** (#4657). The importer copied each `.deb` but registered none of them: no control document, no `packages`/`package_versions` row, so the Packages tab stayed empty and the rendered `Packages` index had file-name-only entries (or none, for a `.deb` outside `pool/<component>/`). It also copied the source's own `dists/` tree (`Release`, `InRelease`, `by-hash/...`), signed with the source's key, as ordinary artifacts. Each migrated `.deb` is now parsed and recorded the way a native `PUT /debian/<repo>/pool/...` records it: control document, catalog row with description, maintainer-script analysis and repository bump. A `.deb` outside `pool/<component>/`, such as Artifactory's "Set Me Up" path `pool/<file>.deb`, is filed under `pool/main/`, and `dists/` is skipped because Artifact Keeper renders and signs its own index. Debian therefore moves from "file copy only" to fully supported in the migration assessment.

  To repair a repository migrated before this fix, re-run the migration job: a `.deb` that is already present but unregistered is re-imported in place instead of being skipped as a duplicate, and a copy an earlier run left outside `pool/<component>/` is retired once it is re-filed under `pool/main/`. The copied `dists/` files from the earlier run stay in the artifact list and can be deleted.

- **A file uploaded again to the same path now reaches push and mirror peers instead of the peers keeping the first upload** (#4658). A re-upload to a versioning-enabled Generic or ML model repository, and an upload after a delete, keep the artifact id, so the upload only raised the priority of the peer's push task, which had already completed, and the new content was never sent. Such a push is now queued again with a fresh retry budget, a push that finishes after the artifact changed under it is queued again, a push waits for an undelivered delete of the same artifact, and a second delete of a re-uploaded artifact is sent again. Other uploads that keep the id, such as a Maven snapshot redeploy, are not re-sent, because the peer would answer 409.

- **A virtual repository's REST listings now explain an empty result when the caller holds read on the virtual but on none of its members** (#4690). A grant on a virtual repository does not grant its members: reading through a virtual needs read on each member the caller should see, and a grant on the virtual alone yields an empty channel. That is unchanged. Before, a user granted only the virtual (for example through a group rule) got an empty member list, an empty artifact listing and 404s from the format routes, and the only explanation was the server log line `virtual member walk narrowed by caller authorization`. `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/members` and `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts` now add an `X-AK-Virtual-Members-Notice` header in that case saying a grant on the virtual does not include its members. The header depends only on the caller being able to read no member, so a virtual with no members answers the same and private members are not revealed. Format routes such as `/maven/<virtual>/...` still answer 404. `docs/repository-visibility.md` documents the rule with a group-grant example.

- **A Maven or Gradle repository migrated from Nexus or Artifactory now lists its packages on the Packages tab** (#4691). Since #2676 the importer registers migrated artifacts in the package catalog (`packages` / `package_versions`, which the Packages tab reads), but it skipped the whole Maven family. A migrated Maven repository therefore stored every file, yet showed "No packages in this repository yet". The importer now catalogues each Maven file as `groupId:artifactId` at its directory version, the same entry a live `mvn deploy` and the catalog backfill write. Checksum sidecars and `maven-metadata.xml` are skipped. A repository imported before this fix keeps its empty catalog until an admin runs the existing backfill once per repository: `curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN_TOKEN" "https://<host>/api/v1/admin/packages/backfill?repository_key=<repo-key>"`. Re-running the migration job does not rebuild the catalog, because already-imported files are skipped.

- **A tarball already in a Remote npm repository's proxy cache is now served without reading the package's packument** (#4692). Every tarball GET read the whole raw upstream packument from storage and parsed it into a generic JSON tree just to pick `dist.integrity` and the tarball URL for one file, so a `yarn install` with an empty client cache read several times more packument bytes than it served and left the allocator holding hundreds of MB per run for documents like `@prisma/client` (68 MB) or `next` (31 MB). With scan-on-proxy or a download age gate configured the packument is still read on every GET, and there, on a cache miss and through a Virtual repository the tarball lookup now keeps only `versions.*.dist.{tarball,integrity,shasum}` (plus the name and version fields the GitHub Packages layout from #3785 needs) in memory, and a malformed value in any other field no longer disables the integrity check.

- **The same Conan recipe or package revision can be uploaded to more than one Conan repository on S3, GCS or Azure storage** (#4694). Conan files were written to the flat key `conan/{name}/{version}/{user}/{channel}/...`, which every repository on a shared object-storage namespace shares, so uploading a revision another Conan repository already held was refused with `409 ... already owned by another repository; refusing cross-repository overwrite`, on every retry. New recipe and package files on a cloud backend are written under the repository-scoped key `conan/{repository_id}/...` (the #2624 scheme npm and Maven already use), so each repository keeps its own copy. Existing files stay where they are and keep serving from the key their artifact row records; filesystem storage and `STORAGE_KEY_SCHEME=flat` keep the flat key.

- **OIDC sign-in with Microsoft Entra ID no longer fails with `Token response missing id_token`** (#4699). The authorization-code exchange now sends the provider's configured scopes (`scope`, default `openid profile email`) on the token request as well as on the login redirect; Entra's v2 token endpoint only returns an `id_token` when the token request itself carries `openid`, and RFC 6749 lets every other IdP accept it. When an IdP still answers without an `id_token`, the callback now returns `502` with code `OIDC_NO_ID_TOKEN` and a message naming the provider (and the IdP's OAuth `error` code, when it sent one) instead of an opaque `500 INTERNAL_ERROR`.

- **Remote and virtual conda channels serve real `current_repodata.json`, `run_exports.json` and `repodata.json.sig`, and `patch_instructions.json` is proxied or 404 instead of an empty stub** (#4708). `repodata.json` branched on the repository type, but its four sibling documents did not: they were always built from the repository's own package rows, which a remote or virtual repository does not have. conda (classic solver and libmamba) requests `current_repodata.json` first and only falls back to `repodata.json` on a 404, so it took the empty 200 as an empty channel and resolved nothing while pixi and rattler worked; `run_exports.json` was silently empty for conda-build and rattler-build; and a virtual's `repodata.json.sig` was a valid signature over a document the client never downloads, bypassing the allowlist and name-ownership merge. A remote channel now proxies its upstream's `current_repodata.json`, `run_exports.json`, `patch_instructions.json` and `repodata.json.sig` through the same capped, budgeted fetch as `repodata.json`, passing an upstream 404 through as 404, and never signs upstream content with its own key. A virtual channel derives `current_repodata.json` from the merged `repodata.json` it serves (the newest version of each package plus the newest builds that satisfy dependencies the kept records leave unmet, as conda-index does), merges `run_exports.json` over its members under the same allowlist and hosted-name ownership rules, signs the merged `repodata.json` bytes with its own key, and applies the existing member-failure policy (502, or a partial document when the virtual allows one) to all three. Hosted channels are unchanged except for one behaviour change: `patch_instructions.json` on hosted and virtual channels now answers 404 instead of an empty 200, which falsely asserted that the channel has no patches. The `/t/<token>/` routes share the same handlers.

- **The conda channel policy predicates are documented as failing closed, which is what they do** (#4711). The `CondaPolicyPredicates` documentation, and the OpenAPI description generated from it, said that `conda.allowed_channels` and `conda.denied_channels` fall back to the owning repository's key when a package records no channel of origin. That fallback never existed: since 1.11.0 an unknown channel is an unknown origin, so a non-empty `allowed_channels` refuses the package and `denied_channels` cannot match it. Only the documentation changes; a test now pins the documentation and the evaluation together.

- **Audit retention runs on a schedule, as the documentation said it did** (#4718). `docs/audit-events.md` described `audit_log` retention as applied by a cleanup job, but the only code that deleted old rows was `POST /api/v1/admin/cleanup`, so an operator who set `audit_retention_days` still got unbounded growth until someone ran the cleanup by hand. An hourly scheduler job now deletes rows older than the configured period, oldest first in batches of 5,000, on one replica at a time, and logs one summary line per run; the period in force is logged at startup. The setting is read on every run, so a change applies within the hour. A period must be saved explicitly before anything is deleted: `0`, or a setting that was never saved, leaves retention off, and `GET /api/v1/admin/settings` now reports `audit_retention_days: 0` in that case instead of a `90` that was never applied, so upgrading deletes no audit rows. The manual cleanup endpoint stays; with the period at `0` or unsaved it now deletes no audit rows (at `0` it used to delete all of them, and unsaved it used 90 days).

- **A database outage while checking a credential now returns a retryable 503, not a 401** (#4750). Previously the auth middleware returned 503 only when the connection pool timed out or the password-hashing concurrency limit was reached. Other database failures returned 401 "Invalid or expired token": a closed pool, a lost or refused connection, a statement or lock timeout, a server shutting down. For a signed JWT, the failed live-user lookup fell through to the API-token lookup and also ended in 401. The `/v2` OCI registry and its `/v2/token` exchange returned 401 for every such failure, including an exhausted pool. Docker, twine, cargo and CI runners abort or ask for a login again on 401, but retry on 503. These failures now return 503 with `Retry-After: 1` on the auth middleware, the format-endpoint resolver, every `/v2` verb, `/v2/` and `/v2/token`. An unknown, wrong, expired or revoked credential still returns 401. So does a database error caused by the request's own bytes, such as a NUL in a Basic-auth username.

- **Login and other API requests now return a retryable 503 during a database outage, not a 500** (#4756). With the database unreachable, `POST /api/v1/auth/login` returned `500 DATABASE_ERROR` for correct and wrong credentials alike, because the user lookup cannot run. The same happened to any handler whose own query hit the outage, for example `GET /api/v1/auth/me` with an API token served from the token cache. Clients that treat a 5xx other than 503 as a server bug gave up instead of retrying. A lost, refused or closed database connection, a statement or lock timeout, and a server that is shutting down or recovering now return `503` with code `DATABASE_UNAVAILABLE` and `Retry-After: 1`, using the same classification as #4750. A pool-acquire timeout still returns `503 POOL_EXHAUSTED`, and query or data errors still return `500 DATABASE_ERROR`.

- **A proxy-cache entry whose body no longer has the size its sidecar records is refetched on filesystem storage too, instead of being served as `Content-Length: N` over a short body** (#4758, #4630). The #4630 read-side guard recognized a poisoned entry by the storage ETag its sidecar pinned, and the filesystem backend (the default) pins none, so an emptied or truncated `__content__` under an intact `__cache_meta__.json` still answered `200` with the sidecar's length and no body, without contacting upstream, on every request.

  When a sidecar pins no storage ETag, the streaming hit path and the stale-if-error fallback now compare the stored object's size with the size the sidecar records. On a mismatch the entry is evicted (body and sidecar), a warn names the cache key and both sizes, and the request falls through to the upstream fetch, which republishes the entry. Entries that do pin an ETag keep the existing checks and pay no extra storage call.

- **A Remote whose upstream promises a `Content-Length` and sends no body now answers `502 UPSTREAM_SHORT_BODY` instead of dropping the client connection with no status** (#4759). The streaming proxy returned the upstream's `200` and `Content-Length` before reading any of the body, so when the body never came the only thing left to do was close the connection (curl: "Empty reply from server").

  The streaming path now waits for the first body byte before it answers. If the upstream body ends (or fails) before that byte, the client gets a `502` with code `UPSTREAM_SHORT_BODY` and a message naming the repository and the expected and received byte counts, or the stale cached copy when stale-if-error has one. Once bytes have been forwarded the response is committed, so a body that ends short after that point still closes the connection, which is the only honest signal left; a warn now names the cache key with the expected and received counts. In both cases nothing is cached, as before.

- **Every audit row written while handling a request now records the client IP, including `REPOSITORY_CREATED` and `USER_CREATED`** (#4762). Only login, the other authentication events and the #4710 rows asked for the client IP, so repository and user creation, update and deletion, role changes, password and TOTP changes, token mint and revoke, settings and policy changes, curation, trash restore, SBOM, storage integrity and the other older writers stored an empty `ip_address` (and a `null` `source_ip` in the audit stream). An audit entry now takes the request's verified client IP by default, the same address login records: the TCP peer, or the forwarded address only behind a trusted proxy with `XFF_TRUSTED_FOR_AUTHZ=true`. Rows written by background jobs, or behind a trusted proxy without that setting, still record no IP rather than an unverified one. `docs/audit-events.md` describes the column.

- **npm, OCI, Git LFS and the other format endpoints now answer a database outage with a retryable 503, not a 500** (#4765). Format handlers that build their own protocol error body classified only a saturated connection pool as transient, so with the database unreachable an `npm install`, a `docker pull` past the credential check or a Git LFS batch got a non-retryable `500`. A closed pool, a lost or refused connection, a statement or lock timeout, and a server that is shutting down or recovering (the classification from #4750) now return `503` with `Retry-After: 1` in each format's own error shape: npm `{"error": ...}`, Git LFS `{"message": ...}`, OCI code `UNAVAILABLE` and protobuf Connect code `unavailable` (both also used now for a saturated pool, which said `INTERNAL_ERROR` / `internal` before). The Swift, Maven metadata and Pub virtual-member error responses also gained the `Retry-After` header on a 503. Query and data errors still return `500`.

### Security

- **quick-xml 0.39 is gone from the dependency graph, and the two cargo-audit ignores that covered it are removed** (#2158). The direct quick-xml dependency has been 0.41 since the RUSTSEC-2026-0194/0195 XML-parser DoS fixes. But `object_store` 0.13.2, which backs S3 storage, still pulled in a vulnerable quick-xml 0.39.2 to parse S3 responses. That instance only ever parsed responses from the operator's own storage endpoint, so the DoS was not reachable there, and it was ignored in `.cargo/audit.toml`. `object_store` is now 0.14.2, which depends on quick-xml ^0.41. `cargo tree -i quick-xml` shows a single 0.41.0 instance, and `cargo audit` passes without the ignores. The upgrade also drops the second reqwest (0.12) from the build. S3 TLS keeps the same trust rules: the system trust store, plus any `S3_CA_CERT_PATH` certificates. The three SigV4 signing calls move to `try_authorize`, so a signing failure on the AWS upstream-auth and S3 REST fallback paths now returns an error instead of panicking.

- **The backend image's bundled `grype` moves to upstream v0.120.1, which pins `golang.org/x/crypto` v0.57.0 and `google.golang.org/grpc` v1.83.2 itself** (#3698). `golang.org/x/crypto` below v0.56.0 carries CVE-2026-56855 and CVE-2026-78662 (`x/crypto/ssh` denial of service). Trivy still rates both UNKNOWN, so they had not failed Docker Publish's `CRITICAL,HIGH` gate. The 1.11.0 `x/net` override already moved `x/crypto` to v0.57.0, but only as a side effect. With this release that version comes from upstream's own `go.mod`, and the build now fails if the compiled binary's Go build info records `x/crypto` below v0.56.0. The source pin moves from v0.118.0 to **v0.120.1** (commit `6f8d854a`) in `docker/Dockerfile.backend{,.alpine}`. Because v0.120.1 pins grpc v1.83.2, the gRPC override from #3655 and #3790 has reached its removal condition and is deleted. The `golang.org/x/net` v0.60.0 override for CVE-2026-78669 stays, because v0.120.1 still pins v0.59.0. It now starts from v0.59.0 and moves exactly one module. The five `github.com/docker/docker` entries in `.trivyignore` stay live: v0.120.1 still pins v28.5.2, and an override to v29.3.1 still fails to resolve. `grype --version` now prints `0.120.1`. The image is still built on go1.27.2 or newer.

- **Reloading a git-sourced WASM plugin now runs the same outbound-URL check that install does before re-cloning its stored source** (#4757, GHSA-r8fc-5fvw-rvh4). `POST /api/v1/plugins/{id}/reload` re-cloned the plugin's stored `source_url` with no SSRF validation, so a source whose host had since moved to, or started resolving to, a private or internal address was fetched from anyway. Every git re-fetch now validates the stored URL first and refuses a blocked source with the same `400` install returns, naming `AK_SSRF_ALLOW_PRIVATE_CIDRS` for an address an operator can admit, before any clone is attempted. Reload is admin-only. Thanks to @vadim-belous for the report.

## [1.11.1] - 2026-10-17

### Sponsors

Thank you to our sponsors for supporting ongoing development of Artifact Keeper.

**Backers**

- **Advailo, SIA** ([@advailo](https://github.com/advailo))
- **stringke** ([@StringKe](https://github.com/StringKe))
- **Ash A.** ([@dragonpaw](https://github.com/dragonpaw))
- **Mike** ([@huylv95](https://github.com/huylv95))
- **Gabriel Rodriguez** ([@injectedfusion](https://github.com/injectedfusion))
- **Narek Engibaryan** ([@narek01](https://github.com/narek01))
- and one sponsor who chose to stay private

[Become a sponsor](https://github.com/sponsors/artifact-keeper) to support the project and get your name listed here.
### Thank You

- **[@mymarche](https://github.com/mymarche)**: reporting that a CI OIDC provider could be given a Kubernetes API server's audience, so every pod's default ServiceAccount token was accepted (#4133).
- **[@axi92](https://github.com/axi92)**: reporting that `wget` and Maven, given a service-account token, got `404` from the generic download route instead of the file (#4593, fixed by #4654).

### Fixed

- **PyPI attestations published before about May 2026 verify again instead of failing as a signature/certificate-chain error** (#4082). Rekor records a DSSE entry's `envelopeHash` over the envelope exactly as it was submitted, and PyPI's publishing tooling submitted Python's default spaced JSON (`{"payload": ...}`) until it switched to compact JSON around 2026-05. `sigstore-rs` re-serializes the envelope compactly before comparing, so every attestation from the first ~18 months of PEP 740 failed its transparency-log consistency check although the signature, certificate chain and log entry were all genuine. Verification now accepts the recorded `envelopeHash` when it matches either the compact or the spaced serialization of the bundle's own envelope; the Rekor SET and inclusion proof are still checked against the unmodified log entry.

  A Rekor entry that disagrees with its bundle is now reported as `transparency log entry mismatch` (naming the envelopeHash it recorded and both hashes it was compared with) rather than `signature/certificate chain`, which sent operators auditing certificates, keys and clock skew that were never wrong. This covers conda CEP-27 attestations too, which share the same verification core.

- **The generic download route now challenges anonymous callers with 401 and accepts an API token as the Basic-auth password** (#4654, #4593). `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/download/{path}` answered a request with no credential on a private repository with the existence-hiding 404 and no `WWW-Authenticate` challenge. Clients that only send credentials after a challenge (wget, curl without pre-auth, Maven, most CI fetch helpers) therefore never sent the token they were given, and the user saw a 404 for a file they were entitled to. On top of that, the route sat under the `/api/v1` Basic-auth boundary (#2809), so `username:<api_token>` was refused even when a client did send it; a service account has no password, so for it no Basic credential worked there at all. The route now takes the format routes' contract instead: no credential on a non-public or nonexistent repository answers `401` with the Basic and Bearer challenges (the two cases are byte-identical, so the status is not an existence oracle, as #1808 established for `/maven`, `/npm` and the other package-manager routes), and an API token presented as the Basic password resolves to the token owner with its scopes and repository ceiling intact. A valid credential that is not entitled still gets the existence-hiding 404, a `?ticket=` still rescues a browser download, and a browser navigation still gets the `Bearer` challenge only so the web UI's login flow appears rather than the native Basic dialog. The rest of `/api/v1/*` is unchanged: `/api/v1/auth/me`, `/api/v1/repositories` and every other management route keep refusing the token-as-Basic-password. This matches how Artifactory, GitLab, Nexus and Cloudsmith treat a token on their download URLs while keeping it off their management and identity APIs. No release ever accepted the fallback on this route (#2798 and #2809 both landed before 1.7.0), so this is a deliberate loosening for one data-plane route, not a revert.

- **A login refused with 429 now reports the login limiter's `X-RateLimit-Limit` and `X-RateLimit-Remaining`, not the general API bucket's** (#4664). The login limiter (10 attempts per 900 s per username and source IP) sits inside the general API limiter, and the outer limiter, which had allowed the request, overwrote the headers of the inner limiter's 429 with its own (`X-RateLimit-Limit: 10000`) while `Retry-After` still came from the login bucket. Clients and dashboards reading the headers concluded the API limiter had fired. An outer limiter now leaves a 429 that already describes its limiter untouched, so the headers and `Retry-After` describe the same bucket. The same applies to any limiter nested inside the API limiter.

- **A client that trickles its request headers, or connects and sends nothing, is now disconnected after `HTTP_HEADER_READ_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default 10)** (#4665). The API and metrics listeners were served with `axum::serve`, which builds hyper connections without a timer, so hyper applied no header-read timeout at all: a slow-loris client held a socket and a task for as long as it kept trickling bytes, and nothing recorded it. The listeners now run an equivalent accept loop (same `ConnectInfo` peer wiring, HTTP/1 with upgrades, HTTP/2 prior knowledge, graceful shutdown) that sets hyper's HTTP/1 `header_read_timeout` and applies the same deadline to the protocol-detection read hyper does before it. Each connection closed with a request head outstanding increments the new counter `ak_http_header_read_timeouts_total`. The same timer also closes an idle HTTP/1 keep-alive connection after the interval (not counted), so a reverse proxy that pools upstream connections to the backend should use an upstream idle timeout below this value. `0` disables the timeout. HTTP/2 and gRPC are unchanged.

- **`storage-scrub` no longer flags every OCI manifest as corrupt** (#4666). Since #3601 an OCI manifest's `artifacts.size_bytes` holds the image size (config plus layers), not the length of the stored manifest body, and the scrub compared that against the object it read, so every manifest reported a size mismatch and real corruption was buried in the noise. The scrub now checks a manifest's length against `oci_manifests.size_bytes`, the recorded body length, and verifies a manifest with no such record yet by its SHA-256 alone; a finding's expected size is that body length. Blobs and every other artifact are checked as before, and a truncated or altered manifest is still reported corrupt.

- **`POST /api/v1/security/findings/external` refuses a NUL byte with 400 and never leaves an orphaned `completed` scan behind** (#4667). A `\0` in any string field of a submission reached the `scan_findings` insert and answered 500 `DATABASE_ERROR`, and because the `scan_results` row had already been committed `completed` in a separate statement, the failed import left a clean-looking verdict with no findings under it. Every string field of `IngestExternalFindingsRequest` and `ExternalFindingInput` now goes through the NUL-refusing deserializer (400 `VALIDATION_ERROR`, as #3713 did for the other body carriers), and the scan row and its findings are written in one transaction.

- **Concurrent scans of the same artifact no longer share one scan workspace** (#4668). The Trivy and Grype filesystem scanners, OpenSCAP and Grype's OCI layout all extracted into a directory named only by the artifact id, so two scans of one artifact running at once (a re-scan during a scan, a repository rescan, a scan flood) deleted or overwrote each other's tree and one of them failed. Each scan job now gets its own directory (`<artifact_id>-<job>`), which its guard still removes on completion, failure and cancellation (#3565).

- **The dependency scanner asks OSV about the scanned package itself, not only its dependencies** (#4669). A leaf package with no dependencies, such as `lodash@4.17.20`, put nothing in the advisory batch and graded `complete` with 0 findings and `live:osv` provenance without a single OSV request. The package's own pinned identity (npm, PyPI sdist, RubyGems, Cargo, NuGet and Maven coordinates, the same pin the CVE engines grade) now joins the batch, so its own advisories are reported; it is queried once even when the manifest also names it, and is not added to the dependency inventory.

- **`POST /api/v1/sbom/environment` has a bounded response and can render one platform at a time** (#4670). The route built one document per (environment, platform) graph whole in memory, so a 31 MiB lockfile produced a 162 MB buffered response. The body is now serialized graph by graph into a buffer capped at 64 MiB; a response past the cap is refused with 422 `UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY` naming the lockfile's graphs, and the new `platform` and `environment` query parameters select which graphs to render. A filter that matches no graph is a 400 that lists the graphs there are.

- **`POST /api/v1/plugins/install/local` answers 501 `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` instead of 500** (#4671). The route is a known, intentional gap, but it resolved the caller's path on the server and then failed with an alert-generating 500 from a placeholder. It now returns 501 with the stable error code `NOT_IMPLEMENTED` without touching the filesystem, logs at info rather than error, and the OpenAPI document describes the 501.

- **Starting an OCI blob upload with an over-limit `Content-Length` is refused with 413 at once** (#4672). `POST /v2/<name>/blobs/uploads/`, both the session-create form with a body and the monolithic `?digest=` form, streamed the body until it crossed `MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE` before answering 413, and a client that declared more than it sent was only reaped by the 408 stall watchdog; over HTTP/2 through a gateway the client could see a `PROTOCOL_ERROR` stream reset instead of a status. The declared length is now checked before anything is registered or a body byte is read, exactly as `PATCH` already did, so the 413 is answered before the request stream is reset.

### Security

- **A CI OIDC provider can no longer be given a Kubernetes API server's audience** (#4133). A provider whose `audience` is `https://kubernetes.default.svc` or `https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local` accepts every pod's default ServiceAccount token, and a token presented to Artifact Keeper is then also valid against the API server. Creating or updating a provider with such an audience now fails with 400 naming it, for every provider type, and nothing is written. Providers that already carry one are kept, and named in a `security` warning at each startup so they can be changed.

- **A repository-restricted token keeps its restriction when it is refreshed** (#4261). The refresh token was signed without the access token's repository allow-list, and `POST /api/v1/auth/refresh` re-mints the access token from the refresh token's claims, so a restricted session came back unrestricted after one rotation. Refresh tokens now carry the allow-list along with the action-scope ceiling they already carried, on the interactive refresh path and on the OCI registry offline-token path alike. Refresh tokens issued before this release still carry no allow-list and refresh as before until they expire.

- **Repository-scoped admin tokens are refused on `/api/v1/admin/downloads*` and `/api/v1/admin/stats`** (#4550). An admin's API token or JWT restricted to some repositories could list download attribution (client IPs, users, paths) and instance-wide statistics for every repository, while `/api/v1/admin/holds/*` already refused it. These endpoints now apply the same rule, that token scope binds ahead of admin, and return 403 for such tokens. Unrestricted admin tokens are unaffected.

- **A public Remote no longer silently spends its upstream credentials for anonymous callers** (#4662). A Remote could be created or updated with `is_public: true` (or `visibility: public`) and an upstream bearer token, basic credentials, AWS upstream auth or userinfo in `upstream_url`; every anonymous request through it then went upstream carrying those credentials, with nothing at configuration time to say so. Moving a repository into that state is now refused with `400 PUBLIC_REMOTE_UPSTREAM_CREDENTIALS` on all three paths that can do it: creating the repository, updating it (making a credentialed repository public, or adding userinfo to a public one's `upstream_url`), and `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/upstream-auth`.

  An administrator who means it sends `allow_public_with_upstream_credentials: true` on the same request. The acceptance is stored with the repository, logged at `WARN` and recorded in the audit log (`allow_public_with_upstream_credentials: true` in the `REPOSITORY_CREATED` / `REPOSITORY_UPDATED` details); sending `false` withdraws it. Repository responses report `public_with_upstream_credentials` and `allow_public_with_upstream_credentials` so the UI can flag such a repository. A repository already public with credentials before this release is not refused on unrelated updates (a Terraform apply that re-sends `is_public: true` keeps working), but now reports `public_with_upstream_credentials: true`.

- **An expired CI OIDC assertion no longer buys a session, and Artifact Keeper's own tokens get no expiry leeway** (#4663). `POST /api/v1/auth/ci/token` accepts an assertion up to 60 s past its `exp` for clock skew, and capped the minted token at that already-passed `exp`, so it answered `expires_in: 0` with a token that session validation then accepted for its own 60 s leeway. The exchange now refuses with 401 when less than one second of the assertion's validity remains, and never returns `expires_in: 0`. Tokens this server signs (sessions, refresh tokens, TOTP tickets, on HTTP and gRPC) are now validated without leeway, since issuer and verifier share a clock; they expire exactly at their `exp`. The assertion-side leeway is unchanged.

- **A `.vsix` whose archive entries carry traversal or absolute paths is refused at publish** (#4673). The server only inspects a VSIX (bounded manifest reads, #3961) and never extracts it, but it stored and served such an archive verbatim, so any client that unzipped it naively could be made to write outside its target directory (`../../etc/passwd`, `/tmp/x`). Publishing now walks the zip's central directory, names only, and refuses an entry with a `..` segment or an absolute, backslash-rooted or drive-qualified name with `400 VALIDATION_ERROR`, before anything is stored. This applies to any zip body on the publish route, including one published under the legacy `x-*` headers.

- **Download tickets and other URL-carried credentials are redacted from the `uri` recorded on every request span** (#4675). The `http_request` span already replaced `token`, `key`, `api_key`, `password` and `secret` query values with `[REDACTED]` (#544), but not `ticket`, so every `?ticket=` download put a live single-use ticket into the trace and log pipeline. The list now also covers `ticket`, the OAuth2 / OCI `/v2/token` style `access_token`, `refresh_token`, `id_token` and `client_secret`, the OIDC callback's authorization `code`, and presigned-URL signatures (`X-Amz-Signature`, `X-Amz-Credential`, `X-Amz-Security-Token`, `X-Goog-Signature`, `X-Goog-Credential`, `Signature`, `sig`). Parameter names are matched case-insensitively after percent-decoding, so `%74icket=` is caught too; other parameters are logged unchanged.

- **`quinn-proto` bumped 0.11.15 -> 0.11.19 for RUSTSEC-2026-0338, -0339, -0340, -0341 and -0342** (#4679). The QUIC implementation under `reqwest`'s HTTP/3 support could be driven into unbounded memory growth through stream reassembly, pending connection-ID retirements and zero-length DATAGRAM frames. Lockfile-only; the registry does not negotiate HTTP/3 today, so there is no behaviour change.

- **`rustls` 0.23.45 -> 0.23.46 for RUSTSEC-2026-0346, -0347, -0348 and -0349** (#4679). `rustls` is the TLS stack under every outbound connection the registry makes (`reqwest`, `hyper-rustls`, `redis`, `sqlx`'s `tls-rustls`, the Prometheus exporter and the backend's own dependency). 0.23.45 could leak TLS secrets through `Debug` output, send buffered application data to the outer server after an ECH rejection, allocate up to 1 GiB decompressing a Brotli certificate before authenticating the peer, and let an unauthenticated ServerHello downgrade later connections to classical key exchange. Lockfile-only; `backend/Cargo.toml` already allowed `0.23` with a caret.

- **WASM plugin runtime updated to wasmtime 36.0.18** (#4679; RUSTSEC-2026-0352, RUSTSEC-2026-0363). A WASM plugin guest could escape its filesystem sandbox by renaming a symlink with a trailing slash, and component-model handle tables were capped only per instance and charged to no limiter, so a guest could grow host memory past its store limits. Both are fixed upstream in 36.0.18; both workspace pins (`wasmtime`, `wasmtime-wasi`) move together as in #4361 and #4332, and no configuration change is needed.

- **IP-conditioned permission rules and audit-row client IPs no longer trust an X-Forwarded-For address the backend cannot verify** (#4681, GHSA-59x8-r6jj-x95h). For a request whose TCP peer is inside `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`, the client IP resolved from `X-Forwarded-For` was used for `allowed_cidrs` permission conditions (#1849) and for the client IP recorded in audit rows. That address is only reliable when every trusted proxy appends the peer it received the request from, which the backend cannot check. The new `XFF_TRUSTED_FOR_AUTHZ` setting (default `false`) decides whether it may be used for these purposes. With it unset, a request through a trusted proxy has an unknown client IP for authorization and audit: IP-conditioned grants do not match it and are denied, unconditioned grants are unaffected, and audit rows record no IP. A request whose TCP peer is not a trusted proxy still uses that peer. Rate limiting, the upload guard and download telemetry keep resolving the client from `X-Forwarded-For` as before. Startup logs a warning when `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` is set and `XFF_TRUSTED_FOR_AUTHZ` is not. **Deployments behind reverse proxies that use `allowed_cidrs` conditions or rely on audit-row client IPs should set `XFF_TRUSTED_FOR_AUTHZ=true`, but only after confirming that every proxy in the trusted ranges appends or overwrites `X-Forwarded-For` with its own peer address.** Behind SNAT that hides the client address before the first proxy, no setting recovers the client IP, and a condition covering the proxy, node or pod ranges matches every proxied request. See `.env.example`.

- **`zip` 8.6.0 -> 9.0.4 and the rattler crates to the 0.57 line for RUSTSEC-2026-0367, -0368 and -0369** (#4705). The advisories cover `ZipArchive::extract()`: SUID/SGID bits preserved on extraction, symlinks created with targets outside the destination directory, and Unix permissions applied through symlinks. The backend never calls `extract()` (it reads archive entries by index and writes with `ZipWriter`), so no shipped behaviour was affected and none changes; `rattler_package_streaming` moves to 0.27.15 and `rattler_conda_types` to 0.57.1 because the newer streaming crate is the one built on zip 9. The one pre-9 instance left in the lockfile, zip 2.4.2, is a build-time-only dependency of `utoipa-swagger-ui` 8.1.0 that unpacks the vendored swagger-ui distribution during the build and is not linked into the binary; it is recorded in `.cargo/audit.toml` with that rationale until utoipa-swagger-ui builds with zip 9.

- **The scanner adapter's bundled trivy is rebuilt as 0.74.0-r5 with containerd 2.3.4 for CVE-2026-95837; published as scanner-adapter 1.4.2** (#4713). The HIGH advisory (containerd's CRI checkpoint restore bypassing the destination security context) was published against the containerd 2.3.3 that trivy 0.74.0 links for its containerd image source, and it failed the image publish gate on every build from 2026-10-17 without a byte of this repository changing. Trivy itself runs no CRI plugin, so no scan behaviour changes; the rebuild clears the gate. Upstream trivy fixes it by moving to containerd 2.4.1 in 0.75.0 and 0.76.0, which the adapter cannot take alone because it requires the trivy server sidecar to report the same version as the bundled client; the coordinated move of both to 0.76.0 is #4712.

## [1.11.0] - 2026-10-11

### Added

- **Guest (anonymous) access can be turned on or off at runtime by an administrator, without a restart** (#867). New admin endpoints `GET` / `PATCH /api/v1/admin/settings/system` (body `{"guest_access_enabled": false}`) store the setting in `system_settings` (`security.guest_access_enabled`). The replica that serves the `PATCH` enforces the new value on its next request and other replicas within 5 seconds (in-process cache). The guest-access guard, `/api/v1/system/config`, the public-repository refusal and the anonymous `/v2/token` mint all read the same runtime value. Every write is audited as `SETTING_CHANGED` with the old and new effective value and its source.

  **Precedence: `AK_GUEST_ACCESS_ENABLED` still wins when set explicitly** to `true`, `1`, `false` or `0`. It stays the offline break-glass, the same model as `TOTP_POLICY`. While it pins the value, the `GET` response reports `guest_access_source: "environment"` and `guest_access_editable: false`. A `PATCH` is still stored and reported as `guest_access_stored`, and takes over once the variable is unset. To move an instance that runs with `AK_GUEST_ACCESS_ENABLED=false` to UI management without reopening anonymous access, first `PATCH` `false`, then remove the variable. Unset, empty or other values do not pin, and behave as before (guests enabled) until an administrator stores a value. Without a pin the setting fails closed: a stored row that is not a boolean, or a database that cannot be read before any value has been resolved, refuses guests; startup refuses to begin if the first read fails. The web UI toggle is a follow-up in artifact-keeper-web.

- **npm publishes and dist-tag writes addressed at a virtual repository are routed to its deployment target** (#968). A publish to a virtual repository was rejected with 400 "Cannot publish to a virtual repository", forcing clients to bypass the single entry point and publish to the hosted repository directly. The write now lands in the first hosted (local/staging) member, in the virtual's flattened resolution order, that accepts direct uploads and that the caller may write — the same caller-relative composition the read side uses, so routing through a virtual can never publish where a direct publish would have been refused. A virtual with no writable hosted member still answers 400.

- **Kubernetes clusters can pull images with a pod's ServiceAccount token instead of an `imagePullSecret`** (#1246). Since Kubernetes 1.34 the kubelet can hand an image credential provider a pod-bound ServiceAccount token, and the CI OIDC exchange (`POST /api/v1/auth/ci/token`) now serves as the server side of that. Three additions make it work for real clusters. A CI OIDC provider can carry a **static JWKS** (`key_source: static`, `static_jwks`) and then verifies only against it, never contacting the issuer, so on-prem clusters (kubeadm's `https://kubernetes.default.svc.cluster.local`) and AKS without `--enable-oidc-issuer` work although Artifact Keeper cannot reach them; existing providers become `key_source: discovery` and behave exactly as before. A `claim_filters` key starting with `/` is a **JSON Pointer** into nested claims, so `{"/kubernetes.io/namespace": "payments"}` admits every ServiceAccount of a namespace; keys without a leading `/` keep their meaning, and a malformed pointer is refused with 400 when the mapping is saved. And a new provider type, **`kubernetes`**, changes what an exchange mints. See the Kubernetes section of `docs/ci-oidc.md` for issuers per platform, key rotation and an example CronJob that keeps a static JWKS current.

  Security-relevant behaviour: a **`kubernetes` exchange mints a pull-only credential** (`read:artifacts`, `read:repositories`, whatever the account's groups allow) **and no refresh token**, because the kubelet caches it on a node where root can read it and a leaked push-capable token could replace images for every consumer; the ceiling is fixed by type and cannot be configured wider. Its `security` log line records the pulling workload's namespace, ServiceAccount, pod and node. A **static JWKS is a hand-entered trust anchor**: it accepts public RSA/EC keys only (private members are refused with 400), at most 16 keys and 64 KiB, requires unique `kid`s, refuses a token whose `kid` is not in the set with 401 naming the missing `kid` (no fall-back to another key; the `security` warning for it is written at most once a minute per provider), and every change to a provider's key source or JWKS is written to the `security` log with the acting admin and the resulting `kid`s. Use a dedicated provider audience, never the API server's own; that is documented, not yet enforced (#4133). `provider_type` is matched case-insensitively and an unknown value (such as `k8s`) is refused with 400 on create or when changing a provider's type, so a typo cannot silently yield a push-capable provider (an update that sends a provider's stored pre-upgrade value back unchanged is still accepted); changing a provider's type is written to the `security` log. The `gitlab`, `github` and `generic` provider types still mint action-unrestricted tokens with a refresh token; action scopes for them are tracked in #4132. Migration 257 adds `key_source` and `static_jwks` to `ci_oidc_providers` with safe defaults. Rolling back leaves the columns unused and makes `kubernetes` providers act as `generic` (unrestricted, renewable tokens), so disable them before rolling back.

- **OpenPGP signing keys can now be Ed25519: `key_type = gpg` with `algorithm = ed25519`** (#1326). `POST /api/v1/signing/keys` used to generate RSA for every OpenPGP key. An Ed25519 key is generated as a v4 EdDSA key, the form `gpg --quick-gen-key ... ed25519` produces and that apt/gpgv/sqv on Debian bookworm and trixie and Ubuntu noble verify. It signs InRelease, Release.gpg and repomd.xml.asc with SHA-512, and its fingerprint is the usual 40-hex-digit v4 fingerprint. RSA OpenPGP keys still sign with SHA-256 as before. The web UI's key-type select lives in artifact-keeper-web.

- **Rotating a Debian/RPM signing key no longer breaks clients that still trust the old key: both keys sign metadata during an overlap window** (#1329). apt and dnf verify against a static keyring, so after `POST /api/v1/signing/keys/{id}/rotate` every client that had not yet imported the new key failed `apt update` with a signature error. Now, for `SIGNING_KEY_ROTATION_OVERLAP_SECS` after a rotation (default 14 days, `0` turns it off), InRelease, Release.gpg and repomd.xml.asc carry one signature from the new key and one from the old key. `gpg-key.asc` and `repomd.xml.key` serve both public keys in one armored block. apt, gpgv and sqv accept the metadata if any one signature verifies, so clients holding either key keep working while operators roll out the new one. The old key's `expires_at` records when its overlap ends, and the rotation audit entry includes it as `overlap_ends_at`. A key that cannot co-sign, such as a pre-OpenPGP `gpg` row holding PEM material, retires immediately, and the audit entry says why. Revoking the old key ends its overlap at once, and so does rotating its successor with the overlap off. **If you rotate because a key is compromised, revoke the old key right after rotating**, or it stays published and co-signing for the whole window. Keys rotated before this release are unaffected. Published RPM `@N` snapshots keep the key they were frozen with.

- **Startup now warns about every signing key that cannot sign the Debian/RPM metadata it is configured for, and can replace them automatically** (#1331). A key created before OpenPGP signing existed, or any `key_type = rsa` key, holds X.509/PKCS#8 material, and a Debian or RPM repository bound to one fails every InRelease, Release.gpg and repomd.xml.asc request. On every boot the backend now logs one WARN per such key with its id and the repositories it is bound to. With `SIGNING_AUTO_MIGRATE_LEGACY_KEYS=true` it also generates a fresh `key_type = gpg` key for each one, repoints those repositories at it, and audits the old key as `auto_migrated`. A key that is also bound to a raw-RSA format such as Alpine stays active for that repository. A key whose material cannot be decrypted, usually because `JWT_SECRET` changed, is only reported and never replaced. Clients must import the new public key after a migration. Rotating an `rsa` key is not a fix, because rotation keeps the key type.

- **Admins can register "ghost" artifacts left in storage without a database row** (#1570). `POST /api/v1/admin/repositories/{key}/reindex-storage` (admin-only, body `{"dry_run": <bool>}` required, optional `limit`) lists the objects in a Maven or Gradle repository's own storage namespace. It covers the filesystem repository root and the repo-scoped `maven/{repository_id}/` prefix on S3 and GCS (#2624). For every artifact object with no row, it records a row with the object's real SHA-256 and size. It also reports live rows whose object is missing. The response is `{scanned, registered, skipped, skipped_recent, skipped_unknown_age, missing_objects, truncated, …}`. Objects modified in the last 5 minutes are left for their in-flight upload (`skipped_recent`), and so are objects whose listing reports no modification time (`skipped_unknown_age`). The S3 REST listing fallback used for endpoints such as Alibaba OSS now reads `<LastModified>`. Registered rows record SHA-256, SHA-1, and MD5, as a Maven upload does. It is safe on a live repository and idempotent. Paths that already have a row, live or soft-deleted, are never touched. Checksum sidecars and `maven-metadata.xml` are skipped. Legacy flat cloud keys, which every repository shares, are not attributed. Backends that cannot list objects (Azure) answer 422. Runs are audit-logged (`STORAGE_REINDEX_RUN`), including refused and failed ones.

- **Artifacts now show whether and where they were last promoted** (#1758). Artifact responses (the repository artifact listing, `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{path}` and `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}`) carry `last_promotion: {target_repo_key, promoted_at, status}`, taken from the newest `promotion_history` row with status `promoted`. Rejected and pending attempts never count, and the field is `null` for an artifact that was never promoted. The Maven-component and Docker-tag groupings carry the same field, so the signal is there for Maven and Docker staging repositories too. `target_repo_key` is `null` when the caller cannot read the target repository, so a staging listing does not reveal the name of a private release repository.

- **Permission rules now support request-IP conditions, including anonymous-download grants restricted by CIDR** (#1849). `POST /api/v1/permissions` accepts an optional `conditions` object — today `{"allowed_cidrs": ["10.0.0.0/8", ...]}` — that makes the rule apply only when the request's client IP (resolved from the TCP peer, with `X-Forwarded-For` believed under the `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` trusted-proxy policy) falls inside one of the ranges; an unknown IP matches nothing, so conditioned rules fail closed. A new `principal_type: "anonymous"` grants unauthenticated callers `read` on a repository or project — the CI-runner use case: keep a repository private to the world while letting runners inside your CIDRs pull without credentials. Anonymous rules are read-only, and a caller outside the ranges gets the same existence-hiding denial as a rules-less repository. Conditions are enforced at the canonical permission choke-point (native-format, OCI, and REST read/write gates) and in repository/search/webhook visibility listings.

  Note on interplay with role assignments: conditions narrow when the RULE applies, per rule — a principal whose conditioned rule does not match the request IP falls back to whatever its role assignments grant unconditionally, exactly as if the rule did not exist for that request. To confine a principal to a CIDR, grant it only through the conditioned rule.

- **Lifecycle policies can keep the newest N versions under an age rule and can be scoped to a path prefix** (#2024). `max_age_days` accepts an optional `min_keep` (`{"days": 14, "min_keep": 5}`): the newest five artifacts of each package or image, grouped and ordered exactly as `max_versions` groups them, survive even when they are older than the window, and excluded tags do not take one of those slots. Every policy type also accepts `"match": {"path_prefix": "..."}`, which limits it to artifacts whose repository-relative path starts with that literal string. Both are compiled into the same SQL as the dry-run preview, so a preview reports exactly what the run deletes. Other `match` selectors and the composite `conditions` list from the request are still rejected by name until they are implemented.

- **Soft-deleted artifacts can now be kept in a trash for a configurable number of days and restored by an admin** (#2072). Storage GC used to hard-delete a soft-deleted artifact on its next pass, so a developer who noticed an artifact had been removed (by hand or by a lifecycle policy) had no recourse short of a backup restore. A new `GC_TRASH_RETENTION_DAYS` setting holds soft-deleted artifacts back from GC for that many days; it defaults to `0`, which keeps the previous behaviour exactly, so an upgrade does not change how much storage GC reclaims. Migration 261 adds `artifacts.deleted_at`, stamped by a trigger whenever an artifact is soft-deleted and cleared when it comes back, so every delete path records it. Two admin endpoints expose the trash: `GET /api/v1/admin/trash` lists trashed artifacts (optionally for one repository, paged with `page`/`per_page`) with the time each becomes eligible for GC, and `POST /api/v1/admin/trash/{id}/restore` restores one. Restore returns 409 for OCI manifests and blobs (their tags were already removed and their layers are reclaimed by blob GC, so re-push the image instead), for legacy proxy-cache rows (the proxy cache owns and expires those objects; they are re-fetched from upstream), when another live artifact holds the path, or when the stored object is already gone. GC's hard-delete of trashed rows is now scoped to the same storage backend (and, on filesystem, the same storage root) as its locked re-check, so reclaiming one repository's copy of shared content never removes another repository's trash entry.

- **System-wide maintenance and downtime banners** (#2155). Administrators can create, update and delete banners through `/api/v1/admin/banners`. Each banner has a title, a message, a severity (`info`, `warning`, `critical`), a target (`all`, `ui`, `api`), an optional `http(s)` link, an optional `starts_at` / `ends_at` window and an enabled flag. Every change is audited. The new public `GET /api/v1/banners` (`?target=ui|api`) returns the banners active now, most severe first. A banner expires on its own when its window ends, so no cleanup job is needed. The endpoint needs no authentication and stays reachable when `AK_GUEST_ACCESS_ENABLED=false`, so the login page can show it. Adds migration `258_system_banners`, which creates a new, empty table. Rendering banners in the web UI and the CLI are follow-ups in those repositories.

- **The gRPC and metrics listeners can bind a specific IP via `GRPC_BIND_IP` and `METRICS_BIND_IP`** (#2161). Both listeners hard-coded `0.0.0.0`, so a deployment that must bind everything to loopback (for example Nomad behind a Consul service mesh, where another allocation on the same node could otherwise bypass the mesh) had no way to do it for these two ports. Both variables default to `0.0.0.0`, so nothing changes unless they are set; IPv6 literals (`::1`, or `[::1]`) are accepted, and an invalid value now fails startup rather than silently binding every interface.

- **Project admins can manage their own project's membership and create repositories in it** (#2473). A principal holding `admin` in a project grant (`POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/members` with `actions: ["admin","read","write","delete"]`, directly, as a service account, or through a group) may now `GET`/`PUT /api/v1/projects/{id}` and list, add and remove that project's members, which previously required a global admin. Listing, creating and deleting projects, changing a project's `quota_bytes`, and the global `/api/v1/permissions` API stay global-admin-only, and a credential restricted to a repository allowlist is never treated as a project admin. `POST /api/v1/repositories` now accepts a project admin when the request assigns the repository to that same project; repository data-plane access for the project's admins comes from project inheritance. A repository created through project admin alone records its creator but does not give them the `repository-owner` role, so removing someone from the project removes their access to the repositories they created there; global and system-level repository admins keep the owner auto-grant as before. Because permission actions match exactly, the role needs all four actions: `admin` alone gates management but grants no read or write.

  Repository keys may follow the optional `<project.key>-<name>` convention. A repository assigned to a project whose key starts with another project's `<key>-` prefix is rejected with 400 on create and on a rename or reassignment (this applies to every caller, including administrators), so a project admin cannot mint names in another project's namespace; keys that use no project's prefix are unaffected, and keys and URLs stay flat. Reassigning a repository to a different project through `PATCH /api/v1/repositories/{key}` now requires a global admin, a system-level repository admin, or project admin on the destination project; repository admin alone is no longer enough. A reassignment also drops the local permission cache immediately.

- **Project storage quotas are now enforced across every repository in the project** (#2474, #2475). `projects.quota_bytes` was stored but ignored, so a project cap could be evaded by spreading uploads across its repositories. Upload admission now also checks the project's aggregate usage, summed from the per-repository usage ledger (hosted artifacts, proxy-cache entries and OCI blobs) over every repository assigned to the project, in addition to the repository's own `quota_bytes`. The authoritative check locks the project row, so concurrent uploads into sibling repositories cannot both pass against the same total. A rejected upload returns `507 QUOTA_EXCEEDED` with `Project storage quota exceeded`. An unset or non-positive project quota means unlimited, as it does for repositories.

  `npm publish` now runs the same repository and project quota admission. Before this it skipped quota checks entirely. A publish addressed to a virtual repository (#968) is charged to the hosted member it resolves to, so the member's project quota applies and the virtual's does not.

- **R/CRAN repositories can be migrated from Artifactory and Nexus** (#2525). Nexus `r` and Artifactory `cran` repositories migrate into native CRAN repositories: source packages land at the native path and are listed in `src/contrib/PACKAGES`, and the source's own `PACKAGES*` index files are skipped. Binary packages are copied at their source path but are not yet listed in a binary `PACKAGES` index.

- **Bazel repositories now speak the Bazel module registry (Bzlmod / BCR) protocol at `/bazel/{repo}`** (#2858). Point Bazel at `--registry=https://<host>/bazel/<repo>` and it resolves modules through Artifact Keeper instead of a generic repository behind a rewrite. Hosted repositories accept `PUT /bazel/{repo}/modules/{name}/{version}/{file}` (MODULE.bazel, source.json, patches, overlays and source archives) and generate each module's `metadata.json` from the published versions; published files cannot be overwritten. Remote repositories proxy an upstream registry such as `https://bcr.bazel.build`, caching versioned files permanently and revalidating `bazel_registry.json` and `metadata.json` on the mutable TTL. Virtual repositories merge `metadata.json` across their members and resolve files by member priority; a module that a hosted member publishes shadows the same module name on remote members. Source archives referenced by a proxied `source.json` are still downloaded by Bazel from their original URLs.

- **OCI/Docker blob pulls can be served by a presigned-URL redirect** (#2894). With `PRESIGNED_DOWNLOADS_ENABLED=true` and a storage backend that signs URLs (S3 with redirect downloads, GCS, Azure, CloudFront), `GET /v2/<name>/blobs/<digest>` now answers `307 Temporary Redirect` to the object store instead of streaming the layer through the backend, so a layer is no longer transferred twice (object store to backend, then backend to client). This covers hosted repositories, local members of a virtual repository, and remote repositories whose proxy cache already holds the layer. Range requests are redirected too (object stores honour `Range` on a presigned GET). `HEAD` is never redirected, and every authorization and vulnerable-image re-block check still runs before the redirect is issued. Proxy-cache entries stored with an upstream `Content-Encoding` or inside a Package Age Policy hold keep streaming.

- **The OCI blob GC's minimum blob age is configurable through `BLOB_GC_MIN_AGE_SECS`** (#2906). The 24-hour grace that shields an in-flight push from blob garbage collection was a compile-time constant, so a short-lived environment such as the release gate could never observe a pushed blob being reclaimed. The default stays 86400 seconds; the value is clamped to between 60 seconds and 7 days and a value under one hour is logged as a warning at startup. The grace window on objects recorded for GC by a repository delete (#3733) guards the same push-time hazard and now follows the same setting, so the two windows cannot drift apart.

- **Findings are now classified as `vulnerability`, `malicious` or `policy`, and known-malicious packages from OSV are flagged `malicious`** (#3013). Every finding used to be the same kind of row, so a known weakness and a known-hostile package were indistinguishable to any policy. `scan_findings` gains `finding_class` (migration 260, default `vulnerability`); the dependency scanner marks OSV `MAL-*` advisories (the ossf/malicious-packages feed) as `malicious` and grades them `Critical` (they usually carry no severity and previously defaulted to `Medium`, below a typical `max_severity = high` gate), external findings with a `MAL-*` id are classified the same way, OpenSCAP rule failures are classed `policy`, and the class is returned on every finding and filterable with `GET /api/v1/security/scans/{id}/findings?finding_class=malicious`. This is the first slice of malware detection; policy treatment of malicious findings and a signature-based scanner are follow-ups.

- **Scan results now record which vulnerability database the scan ran against, not only which scanner binary** (#3014). `scanner_version` named the binary (`trivy-0.71.2`), but the same binary returns different answers about identical bytes depending on how old its database is, so a scan against a stale database was indistinguishable from a fresh one and a reused (dedup) verdict silently inherited an unknown vintage. `scan_results` gains `vuln_db_version` and `vuln_db_published_at` (migration 259), returned on the scan API: grype reports `grype-db-<schema>` and its build time from `grype db status`, trivy reports `trivy-db-v<schema>` and its `UpdatedAt` through the scanner-adapter, and the dependency scanner, which queries live advisory APIs, reports `live:osv` (or `live:osv+ghsa`) stamped with the query time. A reused scan carries its source scan's database provenance. Both fields are NULL ("unknown", never "fresh") for scan types without a database, for scans recorded before this release, and for trivy until the scanner-adapter is upgraded to a release that reports its database metadata.

- **Search results now report each artifact's quarantine state** (#3066). `SearchResultItem` gains `quarantine_status` (always present, `not_quarantined` when the artifact carries no state) and `quarantine_until` (timed holds only), with the same contract as the artifact listing; the quarantine reason stays behind `GET /api/v1/quarantine/{artifact_id}`. Quick, advanced, trending and recent search all carry the fields. On the OpenSearch path the values are read from PostgreSQL for each hit rather than from the index, so they are current without a reindex.

- **Admins can read the npm upstream change-feed status over the API** (#3069). `GET /api/v1/admin/npm/upstream-feed/status` reports whether the feed is enabled, the feed URL (credentials removed), the persisted cursor and when it last moved, whether the answering replica runs the consumer and holds leadership, whether any replica holds the feed lock cluster-wide, the leadership term, and the most recent feed error. The response names the replica that answered (`replica_id`, `<POD_NAME or HOSTNAME>:<pid>:<boot-uuid>`), because the consumer, leadership and last-error fields describe that replica only and a load balancer may route successive calls to different replicas. Configuration stays environment-only (`NPM_UPSTREAM_FEED_ENABLED`, `NPM_UPSTREAM_FEED_URL`).

- **Repository responses now carry `format_key` for WASM-plugin-backed repositories** (#3070). A plugin repository is stored as `format: "generic"` plus a plugin key, and until now no read path returned that key, so API consumers could not tell a plugin repository from a plain generic one after creating it. Create, get, update and the repository listing now include `format_key` whenever the stored key names a handler other than the built-in one for `format`; plain repositories omit the field.

- **New guide for using a Hugging Face repository as a proxy of huggingface.co: `docs/huggingface.md`** (#3135). It covers creating a Remote repository with upstream `https://huggingface.co` (no routing rules needed), pointing `huggingface_hub` at it with `HF_ENDPOINT=https://<host>/huggingface/<repo_key>`, and using an Artifact Keeper API token as `HF_TOKEN`. It also explains how to give the Remote its own Hub token for gated models, the upload route for Local repositories, and what is not supported (datasets and Spaces, Hub search, the commit API, model info through Virtual repositories).

- **Hosted Arch Linux package repositories for pacman** (#3343). A `pacman` repository accepts `makepkg` packages (`.pkg.tar.zst`/`.xz`/`.gz`/`.bz2`) under `/pacman/{repo}/`, reads `.PKGINFO` and the file list from each upload, and serves `{repo}.db` and `{repo}.files` rendered on demand in the same layout `repo-add` writes, so `pacman -Sy`, `-S` and `-F` work against it with no index step. Uploaded package signatures are served as `.sig` and embedded as `%PGPSIG%`, and a repository with a gpg signing key attached serves detached `.db.sig`/`.files.sig` signatures, so clients can run with `SigLevel = Required`. Packages are deleted with `DELETE /pacman/{repo}/{arch}/{package}` or the regular artifact API. Remote and virtual pacman repositories are not supported yet (#4407). See `docs/pacman.md`.

- **Remote OCI/Docker repositories can trust specific cross-origin Bearer token realms** (#3591). Since GHSA-78h6-3wp8-2542, a remote only sent its configured upstream credentials to a token `realm` on the upstream's own origin. Registries that issue tokens from another host, such as Docker Hub (`registry-1.docker.io` to `auth.docker.io`) and GitLab with a separate registry hostname, could therefore not authenticate: private images failed, and Docker Hub pulls fell back to anonymous rate limits. The new per-repository `oci_trusted_bearer_realms` list, accepted on create and update and returned on the repository API, names the exact `https://host[:port]` origins that may also receive the credentials. Entries are validated when written: https only, an origin with no path or userinfo, no wildcards, and SSRF-checked like upstream URLs. Nothing is trusted by default, including Docker Hub. **A credentialed Docker Hub remote (`upstream_url: https://registry-1.docker.io`) must add `"oci_trusted_bearer_realms": ["https://auth.docker.io"]` to pull private images or use its account rate limits.** An unlisted cross-origin realm still gets an anonymous token request. When the remote has credentials, the security warning now names the setting. Credentials sent to a trusted realm are logged at INFO on the `security` target. See `docs/oci-trusted-bearer-realms.md`.

- **Proxy scanning can now record findings without blocking pulls: `proxy_scan_action = record_only`** (#3645, #3868). Until now, scanning proxied artifacts and blocking them were one switch, and the default `block_on_policy_violation = false` meant "block on any finding", so a repository could not get vulnerability visibility on proxied packages without also failing builds. Setting `proxy_scan_action` to `record_only` through `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/security` scans and records every proxied pull exactly as enforcement does (the `proxy_scan_results` verdict, per-CVE findings and SBOM inventory), but never withholds one. A vulnerable artifact is served on every pull with `X-AK-Scan: recorded`, a first pull is served `X-AK-Scan: pending` while the scan runs in the background, and an object over the scan byte cap or a scan that cannot finish is served pending rather than answered with 423. `record_only` overrides `block_on_policy_violation` and `severity_threshold`, and switching back to `fail_open` or `fail_closed` changes only whether pulls are blocked, not what was recorded. It applies to every format that enforces scan-on-proxy, including the OCI manifest gate and its layer blobs. On a virtual repository the result is `record_only` only when every side with proxy scanning enabled chose it, so an enforcing member is never relaxed by a record-only virtual, and a record-only member behind an enforcing virtual follows the virtual's threshold. An unrecognised `proxy_scan_action` (for example `record-only` or `fail-closed`) is now rejected with 400 instead of silently becoming `fail_open`. Every change to a repository's scan configuration (scanning on or off, `block_on_policy_violation`, `severity_threshold`, or `proxy_scan_action`) is audited as `REPOSITORY_UPDATED` with the configuration before and after the change and the names of the fields that changed. Migration 256 adds `record_only` to the column's allowed values.

  The reporter of #3868 ran with `severity_threshold = critical` and `block_on_policy_violation = false` and expected nothing below critical to be blocked. That configuration blocks by design: `block_on_policy_violation = false` does not mean "don't block". It means the threshold is off, so the gate blocks on any finding. Set `block_on_policy_violation = true` to enforce the threshold, or use `record_only` to stop blocking altogether.

- **GitHub release downloads can be mirrored through dedicated github, mise and aqua formats** (#3657). The formats share the generic handler and `/general` route, with a seven-day finite release-asset cache lifetime and existing revalidation and TTL overrides. Ordinary generic cache and write behaviour is unchanged. Documents private token-backed mirrors and mise lockfiles; GitHub API caching remains unchanged (#3658), and standalone aqua CLI integration is not provided. Nothing in the code prevents a mirror from combining `is_public: true` with an upstream token, so any anonymous caller could spend that token against GitHub; operators must keep token-bearing mirrors private. The mise `url_replacements` recipe puts the Artifact Keeper token in the URL userinfo (`https://USER:TOKEN@host/...`), so it can surface in mise's logs, shell history or proxy logs; treat that token as exposed wherever the mise config is readable.

- **GitHub-Releases mirroring for mise's aqua backend, documented and cached properly** (#3656) (docs/mise-aqua.md). aqua packages are plain downloads from `github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/download/<tag>/<asset>`, and mise ≥ v2025.9.3 can rewrite those URLs to a mirror via `settings.url_replacements` — so a `generic` remote repository with `upstream_url: https://github.com` already serves as the mirror; no new format was needed. What was missing: the cache classifier had no rule for the shape, so every release asset was cached under the conservative 5-minute mutable TTL and revalidated against GitHub on a schedule, which is exactly the traffic a mirror exists to absorb. `classify()` now recognises the tag-pinned `{owner}/{repo}/releases/download/{tag}/{asset}` shape on `generic` repositories as immutable (cache forever, never revalidate); everything else generic keeps the mutable default, and generic coordinates remain swap-protected (`is_explicitly_mutable_index` is unchanged). The github.com → `objects.githubusercontent.com` redirect hop this flow depends on is now pinned by a regression test: reqwest must keep stripping `Authorization` on the cross-origin hop, so a repository-configured GitHub PAT reaches github.com but never the S3 host (which would reject the request — and must not see the token). Ships with `scripts/native-tests/test-mise.sh`, an end-to-end check that creates the repository, verifies a checksummed asset download through the proxy, and runs a real pinned `mise install aqua:jqlang/jq@1.7.1` through `url_replacements`.

- **Lifecycle policies assigned to a Remote repository now reclaim its proxy cache** (#3734). Until now the lifecycle executors only looked at `artifacts`, while a Remote repository records what it proxies in `proxy_cache_artifacts`. Storage GC leaves `proxy-cache/*` objects alone, so a long-lived Remote repository's cache grew without bound. When a `max_age_days` or `no_downloads_days` policy is explicitly assigned to a Remote repository, `max_age_days` evicts cache entries whose `cached_at` is older than the window, and `no_downloads_days` evicts entries that were cached before the window and have not been served or downloaded inside it. Each eviction deletes the `__content__` body and the `__cache_meta__.json` sidecar, then removes the catalogue row. If a storage delete fails, or the row records a key outside the repository's cache (for example after a repository rename), the row stays and the entry is reported in `errors`. `match.path_prefix` applies to the cached path. Preview and execute report cache entries in a new `proxy_cache` object on the result (`entries_matched`, `entries_removed`, `bytes_matched`, `bytes_freed`, `skipped_reason`), separate from the artifact counters. `last_run_items_removed` counts both.

  **Global (`applies_to_all`) policies do not reach Remote caches.** This keeps upgrades safe: a global policy written for hosted cleanup does not start evicting every Remote cache, which may hold the only copy of content that is gone upstream. Such a run names the reason in `proxy_cache.skipped_reason`. To reclaim a Remote cache, assign the policy to the repository explicitly, and run a preview first: `max_age_days` evicts by cache age regardless of how often an entry is used.

- **npm virtual repositories can opt into an isolate mode where a hosted package name never resolves from upstream** (#3767). A virtual npm repository merges every member's packument, so an upstream version of a name a hosted member owns (an attacker's `internal@1.0.1` next to your `internal@1.0.0`) is advertised and served. Setting `npm_virtual_isolate_hosted_names: true` on the virtual (create or update repository) serves a name owned by any hosted member exclusively from the members: upstream versions of that name are dropped from the merged packument and refused on the tarball route, so resolution and download agree, matching the PyPI virtual's isolation. Names no hosted member owns still federate from upstream, and the default stays the existing union behaviour.

- **Lifecycle policies are now scoped by explicit repository assignments: a policy applies to all repositories, to a chosen list of repositories, or to none, and one policy can be reused across repositories** (#3794). Previously a policy's scope was a single nullable `repository_id`, where null meant every repository, so a policy could not be shared by a subset of repositories and a forgotten field silently widened a destructive policy to the whole instance. Policies now carry `applies_to_all` plus `repository_ids`, stored in a new `lifecycle_policy_repositories` join table (migration 233). `PUT`/`DELETE /api/v1/admin/lifecycle/{id}/repositories/{repository_id}` attach and detach one repository idempotently, `GET /api/v1/admin/lifecycle?repository_id=` lists the global and assigned policies for a repository, and `GET /api/v1/admin/lifecycle/capabilities` lets clients confirm the backend supports explicit assignment before they write scope. Every policy type now runs per resolved repository, so `max_versions` and `size_quota_bytes` also work under global scope, evaluated independently in each repository. Scheduled runs and execute-all skip policies with no assignment. The migration preserves existing behaviour: a policy with a null `repository_id` becomes `applies_to_all = true`, and a single-repository policy gets one assignment. The deprecated `repository_id` field is still returned, but only as a projection: it holds a UUID when the policy has exactly one assignment and is null otherwise, so null no longer means global. See `docs/lifecycle-policy-assignments.md`.
  **Upgrade note: stop every old backend replica and lifecycle scheduler before running migration 233. Do not do a rolling or mixed-version deploy.** Older binaries treat any policy that has no single `repository_id` as GLOBAL. That includes an unassigned policy and a policy assigned to two or more repositories. An old replica or scheduler still running during the upgrade could therefore delete artifacts across every repository.
