Helm upgrades are rolling updates by default, so scale the backend to zero (or otherwise stop all old pods) before upgrading. Downgrading to an older binary is unsafe unless you first reconcile policy scopes by hand. **Two API behaviour changes:** (1) creating a policy without `repository_id` (omitted or null) now creates a dormant policy that deletes nothing, not a global one; CLI, Terraform and other API clients that relied on the old default must send `applies_to_all: true`. (2) Deleting a repository no longer deletes its single-repository policies; it removes the assignment and leaves the policy dormant.

- **Repositories have a visibility axis: `public`, `internal`, or `private`** (#3813, #3812). Access was a single boolean, `repositories.is_public`, which could express "anyone including anonymous" or "grant holders only" and nothing in between — leaving no way to say "readable by every authenticated principal", the state most repositories on a corporate instance actually need. `visibility` is now the authoritative field, persisted independently of any server-wide flag. `internal` grants a READ baseline to any resolved principal and confers no write, delete, or administrative capability — including filing a promotion-approval request, which still needs an explicit grant on the source repository; it is invisible to anonymous callers on every surface (REST, native protocols, OCI `/v2`, listing, search). For every decision other than read authorization it behaves exactly as `private`, including the repository-scoped-token ceiling: a token whose allow-list excludes an internal repository is still refused, because an anonymous caller gets nothing from one and so there is no credential-free baseline for a scoped credential to have fallen below.

  The API is additive. `visibility` is the new field on the create, update and read shapes; `is_public` and its alias `allow_anonymous_access` remain accepted and returned, and mean exactly `visibility == "public"`. A client that speaks only the boolean — the out-of-tree Terraform provider, an older SDK — keeps working unchanged and simply reads an internal repository as not-public. Supplying `visibility` and the boolean with contradictory values is rejected with a 400 rather than silently resolving to one of them. With guest access disabled, a request for `public` is still refused with a 400 (#3855); a request for `internal` is accepted, since it never asks for anonymous access.

  Blast radius reports a fourth access scope, `internal` (#2386): `classify_access_scope` had only `public`, `restricted_acl` and `restricted_roles`, so an internal repository would have been reported as restricted — telling an operator triaging a CVE that a vulnerable artifact reached a handful of grantees when every principal on the instance could pull it. The accessible-users endpoint likewise reports `exposure: everyone` for an internal repository instead of enumerating the whole user table. The audit log's `RepositoryDetails.visibility` now records the authoritative state rather than deriving `"public"`/`"private"` from the boolean, which would have recorded internal repositories as private.

  **Upgrade note — one manual review step.** Migration 245 backfills `is_public = true -> 'public'` and `false -> 'private'`. No repository becomes `internal` automatically and no repository's audience changes: the upgrade is exactly access-preserving in both directions. Repositories that were *meant* to be internal but were coerced to `is_public = false` by the pre-#3855 guest-access rule are indistinguishable from ordinary private ones, and that intent cannot be recovered from the data; identify them from your own records (the audit log's `RepositoryCreated`/`RepositoryUpdated` entries carry the requested value). Instances that have always run with guest access enabled need no action. Separately, to narrow a specific `public` repository to `internal`, list the candidates with `SELECT key, name, created_at FROM repositories WHERE visibility = 'public' ORDER BY key;` and change each one through the API (`PATCH /api/v1/repositories/{key}` with `{"visibility": "internal"}`) rather than a raw `UPDATE`: both propagate to every serving instance, but only the API records the change in the audit log. During a rolling deploy, pods still on the previous release serve an `internal` repository as `private` (a 404 to an authenticated caller without a grant) until they are replaced — narrower, never wider. "Any authenticated principal" includes CI workloads signing in through OIDC with no repository list on their trust mapping and just-in-time provisioned SSO users; see `docs/repository-visibility.md`.

- **Storage scrub: detect, report, and (from a verified copy) repair corrupt content-addressed objects** (#3910). `POST /api/v1/admin/storage-scrub` (admin-only, body `{"repair": <bool>}` required, optional `max_objects`, `max_bytes`, `repository`) re-reads live artifact objects (content-addressed keys and `oci-manifests/*`) and `oci-blobs/*` through the repository's storage backend, including migration-mode fallback keys, hashes them incrementally, and records every mismatch or missing object in `storage_scrub_findings`, which you can list with `GET /api/v1/admin/storage-scrub/findings`. Each run is bounded by an object budget and a byte budget. Its cursor is saved after every object, so a run cut short by the request timeout resumes where it stopped; a repository-scoped run keeps its own cursor. A cluster-wide lock allows only one scrub at a time. A mismatch is only recorded after re-reading the row, so a concurrent republish, delete, or storage-GC reap is never reported as corruption. With `repair: true`, only objects in the content-addressed layouts (`ab/cd/<sha256>`, `oci-blobs/sha256:<hex>`, `oci-manifests/sha256:<hex>`) are restored, and only from another stored copy of the same digest that re-hashes correctly; the copy is written atomically and re-verified. Path-keyed objects (for example Maven) and objects without a verified copy are reported and never overwritten. Each run is audit-logged (`STORAGE_SCRUB_RUN`) when it starts, before any object is touched, and again when it completes, fails, or is cancelled (for example by the request timeout); both entries share a `run_id`. Protobuf module commit bundles are skipped as unverifiable, because their rows record the commit digest rather than the bundle's SHA-256. Set `STORAGE_SCRUB_INTERVAL_SECS` to also run a report-only pass on a schedule (disabled by default).

- **`storage_backend` is now returned by the repository read endpoints** (#3917). The field was accepted on `POST /api/v1/repositories` and immutable from then on, but no read path echoed it back: `RepositoryResponse` had no such member, so it was absent from the `ToSchema`-generated OpenAPI document and from the live JSON of both `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}` and the `GET /api/v1/repositories` listing. The practical effect was that the one repository property an operator can never change after creation was also the one they could not ask the API about — a deployment mixing `filesystem`, `s3` and `azure` repositories had to infer placement from `STORAGE_BACKEND` and creation-time records. It is read straight off the repositories row (`VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL DEFAULT 'filesystem'`), so like `curation_enabled` it is always concrete and needs no second lookup, and it is a plain non-skipped field, so it is present on every repository in both the single-repository and listing responses. The same argument the `curation_enabled` comment already makes applies here: state that is stored and enforced but cannot be read back is its own class of problem.

- **A VS Code extension publish now reads the uploaded `.vsix` instead of trusting three request headers** (#3961). `POST /vscode/{repo}/api/extensions` took the publisher, name and version from `x-publisher` / `x-extension-name` / `x-extension-version`, never opened the archive, and stored four fields. Nothing editor-visible was recorded, which is why the catalog row from #3659 had no description, and why a gallery response cannot be built from a published extension: a client needs `engines.vscode` to decide whether it can run one, and `targetPlatform` to choose between platform-specific builds. Both manifests are now parsed into the existing `artifact_metadata.metadata` JSONB (no migration): `extension/package.json` for `displayName`, `description`, `engines.vscode`, `icon`, `categories`, `extensionDependencies` and `extensionPack`, and `extension.vsixmanifest` for `Identity/@TargetPlatform` and the pre-release property, which `package.json` does not carry. Extraction runs under `bounded_archive::with_ingest_extraction` on the shared ingest budget, and a corrupt archive, a missing manifest or a missing `engines.vscode` is a 400.

  **Upgrade note — a publish that works today keeps working.** `vsce package` output publishes with no headers at all. Headers that are sent are checked against the archive — identity casefolded, version exact — and a disagreement is refused with a 400 naming the header instead of one side being picked silently. A body that is not a VSIX at all (not a zip, or a zip with no `extension/package.json`) still publishes on the header coordinates and produces the same four-key record as before, with a log line saying so; a VSIX whose manifest is present but invalid is a 400 even when all three headers are sent, so a broken manifest cannot route around the header check. Those coordinates are now validated before they become an artifact path and a storage key; they previously reached both with no charset check.

- **A hosted `vscode` repository is now served through the VS Code gallery protocol, so a published extension can be found and installed by an editor** (#3956). Every gallery route funnelled through one gate that answered `501` for any repository type except Remote, so an extension published to a hosted repository was reachable only through AK-specific routes no editor speaks — and since an editor has exactly one `extensionsGallery.serviceUrl` (microsoft/vscode#179919), the gallery an operator configures has to serve local extensions too. `gallery_upstream` is split into the gate every route shares (repository type, public-only) and the Remote-specific upstream resolver, and `extensionquery`, the latest-version template, the manifest, the details redirect, `vspackage` and the asset route each answer from the repository's own `artifacts` rows. A version carries the `Microsoft.VisualStudio.Services.VSIXPackage` file entry that installs it, `lastUpdated`, `targetPlatform` where the build is platform-specific, and the engine and pre-release properties. `filterType` 7/4 and 10 select, `pageNumber`/`pageSize` page, `Target` and `ExcludeWithFlags` are accepted as qualifiers, and `flags` decides what each version carries; `TotalCount` counts every match, and an unmatched query is an empty page rather than a 404. Search and paging run in SQL over distinct extension ids and only the page's versions are then read, so a repository with any number of versions lists every extension (one extension's long nightly history cannot push the others off the listing); each extension lists its newest 100 versions, and an older one still installs by its exact coordinates. A version the download gate refuses — quarantined with an unexpired hold, or rejected — is left out of every listing, so an editor is never offered an install that would fail; an expired hold is listed again, as conda's repodata does (#4059).

  **Remote repositories are untouched, and hosted package bytes stay on the route that already served them.** The proxy path — composition, skeleton projection, age gate, metadata budget, URL rewriting — is not reached for a hosted repository. A hosted `vspackage`/asset request redirects to `/vscode/{repo}/extensions/{publisher}/{name}/{version}/download`, so those bytes remain quarantine-checked and download-counted by one code path and no new storage surface appears; any other asset type is a 404. Public-only is unchanged for hosted repositories, for the reason recorded in #3257. Virtual repositories still answer `501`. Two limitations: a hosted repository holds one build per version (the artifact path has no platform component, so a second platform under one version is a `409`), and icon and README assets are not served.

- **A virtual `vscode` repository now answers the gallery protocol by aggregating its members, so one `serviceUrl` can serve an organisation's own extensions and a proxied public gallery at once** (#3962). This is the configuration the single-`serviceUrl` constraint actually calls for, and until now no repository type could provide it: hosted members were not served by the gallery at all, and a remote member could only be configured as the editor's one gallery, which excludes everything internal. A virtual repository's `extensionquery` and latest-version routes now read every member the caller may see, in the operator's own priority order — hosted members from their artifact rows, paged by the client's own `pageNumber`/`pageSize` exactly as a hosted repository is, and remote members through the same plan a direct remote repository uses, so an update check (named identities with their version history) or an over-ceiling search is composed into its bounded equivalent rather than forwarded as a query Open VSX answers with tens of MiB — and merge the results, with the first member that knows an extension being the one that describes it. Putting a hosted member first is therefore how an internal extension shadows a public one of the same name. Each member's entries are rewritten onto that member's own routes, so a package or asset URL resolves through the per-member route that already serves it and the virtual repository needs no byte-serving route of its own.

  **Aggregation does not widen any member's visibility, and one bad member cannot take the page down.** Members go through `authorize_virtual_members`, the same read predicate a direct read applies (#1804) — and because a gallery client is anonymous, that means public members only, which is consistent with the gallery being public-only in the first place. A remote member that fails — no usable gallery upstream, an upstream error or timeout, a metadata-budget wait, a malformed or over-ceiling page, or an age gate that cannot be evaluated — contributes nothing and is skipped with a log line naming it and the status, while the other members' entries are still served; each remote member's own age gate and curation still apply to its own entries. One aggregation holds a permit of the gallery's composition admission bound from before the first member is read until the merged page is serialized, so anonymous callers cannot pile up unbounded multi-member pages; no byte reservation is held across the fan-out. At most eight members are read per query, since each remote member is an upstream round-trip. `TotalCount` is the sum of what the members reported, an upper bound while an extension exists in more than one of them, and the merged page is not re-sliced — members are already paged by the client's own `pageNumber`/`pageSize`, so a page may carry up to one page per member. The `vspackage` and `/asset/...` routes still answer `501` for a virtual repository, and nothing a virtual page emits points at them.

- **The trace sampler is now configurable via `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER` / `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG`** (#4029). The SDK default was hard-wired, so an operator had no way to reduce trace volume short of turning tracing off. All six values from the OpenTelemetry specification are accepted — `always_on`, `always_off`, `traceidratio`, `parentbased_always_on`, `parentbased_always_off`, `parentbased_traceidratio` — parsed case- and whitespace-insensitively. **The default is `parentbased_always_on`, which is both the specification's default and the SDK's previous behaviour, so a deployment that sets neither variable samples exactly as it did before.** An unrecognised sampler name falls back to that default rather than failing startup, and the resolved sampler is logged at boot so a typo is visible rather than silent. `OTEL_TRACES_SAMPLER_ARG` is the ratio for the two `traceidratio` forms; an absent, unparseable, out-of-range or NaN value falls back to `1.0` rather than `0.0`, because a misconfigured ratio behaving like `always_on` is a far better failure than one that silently drops all telemetry. Note the interaction with the trace-context adoption below: under the default sampler a caller's `traceparent` can only suppress its own trace, but under `parentbased_traceidratio` or `parentbased_always_off` an untrusted `sampled=01` can force export of a trace the sampler would otherwise have dropped — an operator choosing either on a publicly reachable deployment should gate trace-context extraction on their trusted-proxy range, which is a follow-up.

- **The backend now joins the caller's distributed trace instead of starting its own, and its HTTP entry span is marked `SERVER`** (#4029, part of #3954). A request arriving behind an instrumented reverse proxy produced two unrelated traces: the proxy's, and the backend's. There was no single view of a request end to end, so "how much of this latency was the edge and how much was us" could only be answered by comparing aggregate means from two separate systems. The cause was not that the `traceparent` header was ignored — `api::middleware::tracing` has read it since #2414, but only to slice out the trace-id for use as a correlation-ID string. It was never turned into an OpenTelemetry remote parent, and no `TextMapPropagator` was installed globally at all, so every `extract`/`inject` in the process was a no-op against the SDK's default no-op propagator. `init_tracing` now installs `TraceContextPropagator` on the OTel path, and the `http_request` span adopts a valid inbound context as its remote parent. The span is also now `otel.kind = "server"` rather than defaulting to `INTERNAL`, which is what trace UIs and span metrics use to tell a request entry point from a standalone operation — the same idiom the storage backends already use for their `CLIENT` spans. Extraction fails safe in every direction: a missing, unparseable, wrong-length, non-hex or unknown-version header, and a syntactically valid header carrying all-zero ids (invalid per the W3C spec), all leave the request starting a fresh trace rather than parenting it to nothing. `tracestate` rides along with `traceparent`, except that one over the W3C limits (32 members / 512 bytes) is dropped while the `traceparent` is still adopted — the SDK bounds each key and value but not the list, and copies the parent's `tracestate` onto every span of the request. The `sampled` flag is carried through unmodified. The propagator reads the headers through a local extractor over axum's `HeaderMap`, so this adds no use of the `opentelemetry-http` crate. Operators must configure their reverse proxy or ingress to forward (or originate) `traceparent` for the backend to join its trace; `.env.example` documents this alongside the sampler variables. **No behaviour changes for a deployment with no OTLP endpoint configured**, since the propagator is installed only when tracing is enabled. Under the default sampler (`parentbased_always_on`, see above) honouring a remote parent can only reduce export volume — a caller sending `sampled=00` suppresses its own trace — but under `parentbased_always_off` or `parentbased_traceidratio` an untrusted `sampled=01` can force export. Inbound trace context is currently accepted from any client; a follow-up will gate extraction on the trusted-proxy CIDRs (`rate_limit_trusted_proxy_cidrs`). The correlation-ID behaviour, its 256-byte clamp (#2414) and the single-span invariant that #2308/#2309 established are all untouched — the remote parent is set on the existing `TraceLayer` span rather than by opening a second one.

- **Package content analysis: what is actually inside an artifact, and which of it is vulnerable** (#4033, #4037, #4038, #4045, #4047, #4056, #4057). A package's metadata describes what it claims to be; for a compiled package the two barely overlap. A conda package or a Python wheel physically contains C and C++ libraries — libwebp, OpenBLAS, libjpeg-turbo — that its own metadata never names, so a scanner reading metadata alone reports it clean while the vulnerable code sits in the artifact. Ingest now reads the bytes the registry already holds and records what it finds: native libraries recovered from `info/recipe/` (conda) and from `auditwheel`/`delocate` layouts (wheels), and install-time scripts from six formats — conda `post-link`, npm `scripts.postinstall`, RPM `%post`, Debian `postinst`, Alpine hooks, and an sdist's `setup.py`. Those components are then queried against OSV and the GitHub Advisory Database, so a vendored library produces a real finding against a package that declared nothing. Served at `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}/package-analysis` and shown in an Analysis tab on the artifact.

  **The distinction the feature is built around is that "we found nothing" and "we never looked" must never render alike.** `completeness` states whether the archive was read at all, and is a required argument rather than an inference from an empty result — a caller that has not decided cannot compile. A script whose declared interpreter the rule engine cannot read (an RPM scriptlet running `<lua>`) is stored with `findings = NULL` and a reason rather than an empty list, and a database CHECK enforces the pairing. Advisories are `null` when no query was possible, `[]` only when the feeds answered and matched nothing. Vendored components carry `soname` and `abi_version` in their own columns and never in `version`: the number in `libwebp.so.7` is an ELF ABI version, and that file ships in libwebp 1.2.4, so promoting it would match the wrong advisories confidently.

  **Install scripts run as the installing user, and on RPM and Debian as root.** The rule engine reads shell text — remote code execution, network egress, credential access, writes outside the install prefix, privilege change, obfuscation, persistence — and recurses into nested interpreters (`node -e`, `python -c`, PowerShell `-EncodedCommand`). Its binding constraint is false positives, not coverage: most install scripts are a `mkdir -p $PREFIX` and a symlink, and a scanner that fires on those gets muted. Two zero-findings assertions guard it, over 16 complete benign scripts and 75 individual lines modelled on real feedstock hooks.

- **Conda version ordering, version-spec matching and MatchSpec parsing now come from the rattler crates — the same implementation the pixi/prefix.dev client tooling is built on — so registry-side decisions agree with the client by construction** (#4040). Conda semantics used to be hand-rolled in three places, and each disagreed with the client in a place that matters: the generic curation comparator (`curation_service::version_compare`, split on `.`/`-`, numeric-when-possible) ordered a pre-release *above* its release (`"0a" > "0"` lexicographically), ordered an epoch *below* every epoch-less version (`"1!2" < "2"`), and ordered `1.0+local` above `1.0` — while conda orders letters below numbers inside a segment, so `1.0a < 1.0`, `1!2.0 > 2.0` and `1.0+local < 1.0`. A version-constrained curation rule is a vulnerability/policy match, and a rule the client would match but the registry does not is a silent miss. A new `conda_semantics` module wraps `rattler_conda_types` (`Version`, `VersionSpec`, `MatchSpec`) and now serves: conda-format curation rule evaluation (the typed dispatch routes `conda`/`conda_native` pattern rules to conda's ordering; every other format keeps the generic comparator byte-for-byte), and MatchSpec name extraction in the environment lockfile parser. The `.conda` (v2) container reader (`extract_conda_v2_metadata`) is migrated to `rattler_package_streaming`'s `stream_conda_info`, with the info tar still walked by the shared bounded walk — all three #2556 ingest caps apply unchanged, and the decompressed ceiling moves from a private 100 MiB buffering cap to the shared 128 MiB streaming budget the v1 path already uses. Deliberately NOT migrated, with the reason pinned by a test: the v1 `.tar.bz2` readers stay on our `MultiBzDecoder` path because `rattler_package_streaming` decodes bzip2 single-stream and cannot read a pbzip2/lbzip2-written package whose `info/index.json` sits past the first stream boundary (#4067 — the differential test asserts the reference implementation fails on the two-stream fixture, so a future rattler release that fixes it turns the test red and the migration can be revisited); repodata.json generation stays hand-rolled JSON because it is served byte-for-byte and rattler's `PackageRecord` serialization is not byte-identical to it; `current_repodata`/latest selection keeps its created-at ordering; and `rattler_index`/`rattler_repodata_gateway`/`rattler_lock` are not adopted. The migration is guarded by a differential harness that must pass against both implementations: a version-ordering corpus (epochs, pre/post/dev releases, local segments, separator equivalence, total-order spot checks) pinning the exact points where the old comparator disagreed with the reference, a MatchSpec corpus pinning the extracted name for every spelling the old extractor documented plus the one divergence found (`numpy. >=1.0` — the old walk trimmed the trailing dot and linked the edge to `numpy`; the reference reports `numpy.` as written, which matches no real package, so the edge is now recorded unresolved instead of silently linked), a container-streaming parity test for the v2 path, and a golden served-repodata test that uploads a fixture channel (one `.tar.bz2`, one `.conda`) through the real pipeline and asserts `repodata.json` and `current_repodata.json` are byte-identical to the pre-migration output — which they are, with zero differences to explain. Both new dependencies are BSD-3-Clause and build under the pinned Rust 1.98 toolchain; `rattler_package_streaming` is taken with default features off, so its reqwest networking module is not pulled in.

- **A conda artifact's emitted and stored purl now names the build — channel, subdir and build string — instead of the whole name/version set** (#4041). `format_to_purl_type` mapped `"conda" => "conda"` and that was the entire conda identity strategy: a bare `pkg:conda/name@version` matches every build of that version on every subdir at once, even though the `linux-64` and `osx-arm64` builds are different binaries with different vendored libraries and different CVE surfaces, and grype/syft catalog the conda component with `purl: None` (#4039), so the artifact's own inventory row reached the SBOM with no identity at all. The qualified identity `CondaPurl` (introduced with #4042 for the advisory path) is now wired into the scan/SBOM pipeline: when a hosted scan of a conda artifact persists its package inventory, the scanner-reported row that names the artifact itself — matched on normalized name and exact version, never on scanner-supplied purl strings — is stamped from the artifact's own metadata (`conda_identity::artifact_purl_from_metadata`, which prefers the identity document written at ingest and falls back to the flat `name`/`version`/`build`/`subdir`/`noarch`/`package_format` keys for artifacts stored before that block existed), so `scan_packages.purl` carries `pkg:conda/name@version?build=…&channel=…&subdir=…&type=…`. The SBOM read path (`extract_dependencies_for_artifact`) restates the same identity onto purl-less rows from scans that predate the persisted value and the findings-only fallback, and both generators carry it: CycloneDX `components[].purl`, SPDX `packages[].externalRefs[referenceType=purl].referenceLocator` — the convention every other ecosystem already rides on. Two builds of one name/version on different subdirs therefore produce distinct purls, a `noarch` package produces exactly one identity (`subdir=noarch`) regardless of the subdir it was seen under — enforced by `CondaPurl::with_noarch`, the single place that invariant lives — and every qualifier value is percent-encoded, so an attacker-controlled build string carrying `?`, `&` or `@` cannot forge a qualifier. Non-conda formats, scanner-supplied purls, and rows naming anything but the artifact itself are byte-for-byte untouched; the bare `conda` type remains the documented last-resort mapping only when an artifact's own coordinates genuinely were never recorded.

- **A conda dependency is now queried for advisories as the PyPI distribution it corresponds to, and a conda package the registry cannot identify degrades the scan instead of reporting it clean** (#4042, #4088, #4089). OSV has no `conda` ecosystem and the GitHub Advisory Database does not index one — `query_github_detailed` mapped ecosystems with a `match` whose `_` arm was `continue` — so a conda dependency got **nothing** from either feed and the result was bit-for-bit indistinguishable from a clean scan. The dependency scanner now resolves each conda name through the alias graph in `conda_identity` and branches on all three coverage states, which are three different facts and are never collapsed into one: a **mapped** name is queried as that PyPI distribution (OSV `PyPI`, GitHub `pip`), which is real coverage; a name that positively ships no PyPI distribution is queried **unscoped**, exactly as a vendored native library is, which is real but weaker; and a name that *is* a Python package whose alias the registry does not know becomes a coverage gap that **degrades the scan to `partial`** rather than letting an unidentifiable package render as clean. A finding names the package the reader actually installed (`py-opencv`), with the alias it was looked up under (`opencv-python`) disclosed in the description, so nobody is sent to patch a package they never installed. `AdvisoryLookup` gains `not_queried`, deliberately distinct from `degraded`: an ecosystem GitHub does not index was never asked about, which is not the same as a feed that was asked and failed — and both differ again from asked-and-clean. Shipped with it, `analysis_degraded` is now genuinely covered in the `feeds_degraded` disjunction (#4088): the term could be deleted and the entire suite still passed, because the test that appeared to exercise it used a fixture with no declared dependencies and returned before ever reaching it.

  **Honest limit — an alias-mapped query sends the conda version string to PyPI advisory ranges verbatim.** There is no conda→PEP 440 conversion and no local comparison: the version is copied straight from the conda coordinate into a `PyPI`-ecosystem query and all range evaluation happens server-side at the feed. Where the two version lines diverge, the answer can be wrong in the over-reporting direction — conda-forge's `py-opencv 4.9.0` against PyPI `opencv-python 4.9.0.80`, a backend-scoped CVE reported against the GUI-less `matplotlib-base`, or a conda rebuild that patches a vendored library and bumps only the build string. Every such finding's description carries that caveat, but the false-positive rate is not measured and no test bounds it; read an alias-mapped conda finding as "the PyPI distribution this package corresponds to has this advisory", not as a confirmed match against the bytes on disk.

- **Vendored native components now map to candidate CPEs — with confidence and provenance — so NVD-keyed matching has something to key on** (#4043). The native libraries content analysis recovers (recipe sources, wheel auditwheel layouts) are C/C++ projects whose advisories live in NVD, which is keyed on CPE, not package names; a vendored `libwebp` was discovered and then matched against nothing. A new `cpe_candidates` module restates each component's identity as **candidate CPEs, plural**, produced by three explicit rules — `cpe-known-table-v1` (a small vendored table of well-known libraries and the vendor/product pair NVD uses, e.g. `libwebp` → `webmproject:libwebp`; **high** confidence), `cpe-source-url-vendor-v1` (the forge owner of the component's own `source_url`/`git_url`, when the repo name matches the component; **medium**), and `cpe-name-as-product-v1` (the name itself and the `<name>_project` vendor spelling, both **low** — two vendors publish the same product name often enough that offering one would be a coin flip). Every candidate carries the `rule_id` that produced it, so a wrong candidate is traceable to its rule; the name-guessing rule has a confidence floor, and a name too short or malformed to be a real upstream product (`ab`, `{{ name }}`) produces no candidate at all rather than an invented one. Ambiguity is **surfaced, never resolved**: the package-analysis API serves the full candidate set per component with confidences, rule ids and a `cpe_ambiguous` flag, while the Dependency-Track submission and the stored/on-demand SBOM stamp a component's CycloneDX `cpe` field (and SPDX `cpe23Type` SECURITY external ref, persisted to the long-dormant `sbom_components.cpe` column) **only when the top-confidence tier holds exactly one candidate** — an ambiguous identity is submitted CPE-less rather than arbitrarily picked, because DT treats `cpe` as authoritative for NVD correlation. Matching semantics are pinned offline by `match_advisories`, an evaluator for NVD-shaped `cpeMatch` criteria (version ranges included, boundary-checked both directions) tested against a fixture advisory set modelled on CVE-2023-4863; in production the NVD matching itself happens inside Dependency-Track against the submitted `cpe`, and an in-tree NVD feed sync remains future work with its evaluator ready.

- **A conda component discovered through more than one path now reports as ONE component and ONE finding per vulnerability, with every discovery path preserved as evidence** (#4044). Once a conda artifact carries both a conda and a PyPI identity (#4042) and its payload is cataloged (#4041), the same underlying component surfaced repeatedly: as the conda component itself, as the `.dist-info` inside its payload, and as the advisory finding reached through the alias — the same CVE counted two or three times, which destroys confidence in the number faster than a miss does. Dedup now happens at the component-identity layer (`component_dedup`, scoped strictly to conda artifacts at the scan persistence boundary), keyed on `(normalized name, version)` across ecosystems linked by the alias graph — same name+version via alias is the same component. The inventory merge (`merge_artifact_packages`) collapses the artifact's own rows into one: the survivor keeps the richest identity (the qualified conda purl), is renamed to the conda package the reader holds, and records EVERY discovery path in a sorted, deduplicated seen-via `source_target` — the paths are diagnostic information and are never silently dropped. Within one scan, artifact-self findings sharing a vulnerability identity merge (`merge_artifact_self_findings`), retaining maximum severity with the survivor's `source` and description carrying every path (`Also discovered via: …`). Across scans, a cataloging scanner's artifact-self finding is suppressed ONLY when the latest completed `dependency` scan of the same artifact already recorded a finding with the same `(vulnerability, component, version)` identity (`partition_covered_findings` against `latest_dependency_scan_finding_identities`), which keeps finding counts stable when a rescan catalogs MORE than the last one did; a finding the advisory path never recorded is always kept, so suppression cannot hide unique coverage, and a lookup failure fails open (a false duplicate stays). False merge is treated as strictly worse than false dup throughout: versionless rows never merge, unnormalizable names never merge, a same-named row at a different version stays (a vendored native library inside a DIFFERENT artifact is never touched, because the scope is the artifact's own identity), and cross-scan suppression only fires when the alias graph positively owns the component (`Mapped` or `NotPythonPackage`) — an `Unmapped` package is an unasked question (#4042) whose payload catalog is its only coverage. The #3442 pin-path `dedupe_findings` behavior is untouched (its tests, including the measured 21→7 lodash collapse, still pass). Vendored native components discovered by BOTH package analysis and the payload catalog, and the inline-proxy scan path, are documented in the module as deliberate follow-ups, not defects.

- **Packages with no recipe now yield their statically linked C libraries from the binaries themselves — SONAME, version banners and build-id — as visibly lower-confidence components** (#4046). Recipe-derived component recovery (#4033) covers packages whose recipe declares a source, which is most of conda-forge but not the channels that publish no recipe; that residue is statically linked code only the payload's bytes can name. Ingest now harvests ELF shared objects and executables from the conda payload walk (the same bounded walk that collects install scripts — same entry-count cap, same decompressed-byte budget, a new 32 MiB per-entry cap under which an oversized binary contributes its head) and a new `binary_catalog` service catalogs them from three signals in descending confidence order: **SONAME + version-banner agreement** (`detection_method: binary:soname+banner:<rule>`), **banner alone** (`binary:banner:<rule>`, the normal shape of a statically linked library inside an executable), and **SONAME alone** (`binary:soname`, identity without a version — the ABI tail is still never promoted into `version`). Banner rules are well-known patterns only — `banner-libwebp-v1`, `banner-openssl-v1`, `banner-zlib-v1` (the deflate/inflate banner, so a bare `1.2.13` does not match), `banner-libpng-v1` — each a named, individually tested rule in the `cpe_candidates` style, so a wrong component is traceable to the pattern that produced it. The GNU build-id is used strictly as identity: two payload files with one build-id catalog once, and it is never used for advisory matching. **The lower confidence is visible, not flattened**: binary-derived rows never rise above `inferred` (a bare SONAME is `unresolved`), the `detection_method` names the signals and the rule, and the two classes sit side by side in the same `package_vendored_components` table the Analysis tab already renders — no migration needed. Because banner matching has a real false-positive rate, it is spent only where there is nothing better: `record_analysis` suppresses `binary:` components when a parsed recipe declares sources. The false-positive rate is **measured, not assumed**: a fixture corpus of crafted ELF binaries — true positives beside truncated banners, similar-but-wrong strings (`libwebpages`), LibreSSL-vs-OpenSSL, and one deliberately counted genuine false positive (a banner embedded as data in another library) — asserts a measured precision floor of 0.90 (currently 0.909). Mach-O and PE payloads are deferred: `catalog_file` dispatches on magic bytes, so adding a format is a new parser and a new arm, not a restructure. The ELF reader is a minimal dependency-free section-table walk (SONAME from `DT_SONAME`, build-id from `.note.gnu.build-id`): the tree carries no ELF crate, and two bounded structures sit well below the complexity at which a new parsing dependency earns its `cargo audit` surface.

- **Conda artifacts now carry a publisher identity that `publisher_trust` curation rules can gate on, derived from verified CEP-27 provenance** (#4049). Conda was explicitly asserted not-applicable for publisher trust alongside maven/generic/docker — reasonable while conda had no attestation story, but stale since CEP-27 verification (#4048) and the `curation_packages.attestation_*` record (migration 195) exist. The verified path mirrors PyPI exactly: a verified CEP-27 record's cert-bound repository owner (the Fulcio certificate's GitHub org/user, issuer-checked against the OIDC allowlist) reaches the evaluator through the trusted server-side verification marker and satisfies `publisher_trust match: "attestation"` — including on re-evaluation, where the persisted record is rehydrated. The metadata fallback is the self-asserted `about.json` `maintainer` / `maintainers[]` string, always labeled `Metadata` and `verified = false`: it can satisfy only an explicit `match: "metadata"` opt-in, never a verified-publisher gate. Conda deliberately has no unverified-attestation middle tier: CEP-27 has no claimed-publisher field (which is why `Check::PublisherOwnerBound` does not exist for conda), so a stored-but-unverified attestation blob carries no honest publisher name, and its presence never upgrades a metadata identity. The ingest-time marker stripping that makes a self-asserted verification record a forgery rather than a bypass applies to conda rows unchanged.

- **Every artifact now carries an immutable record of where its bytes came from, exposed on the API and usable as a policy predicate** (#4050). Origin was the security-relevant fact most easily lost in transit: a caching proxy re-serves content under its own identity, and a lower-trust source shadowing a higher-trust one (channel/repository priority misconfiguration) was invisible once the bytes landed. `artifacts` gains an `origin` JSONB column (migration 227) holding `{v, kind, repository_key, upstream_url?}` — `hosted` for uploads into a local repo, `proxy` for fetches through a remote repo naming the normalized upstream URL that supplied the bytes, `migration` for worker imports naming the source system (Artifactory/Nexus base URL) the bytes came from. A `BEFORE INSERT` trigger derives the value from the owning repository row, so all ~40 ingest paths (every format handler, the proxy cache, OCI manifest upserts) are covered with one enforcement point, including paths written after this change; the migration worker supplies its origin explicitly because only it knows the source system. Immutability is enforced at the database layer: a `BEFORE UPDATE` trigger rejects any change to a recorded origin — a proxy re-serve or re-migration may refresh size/checksum/storage columns via upsert but can never rewrite or clear origin (the sole NULL exception exists for the one-time backfill). Rows predating the column are backfilled in batches (migration 228) from the best available fact — the owning repository's type and current `upstream_url`, the same derivation the trigger applies — and a validated CHECK (migration 229) plus a concurrent expression index on `origin->>'upstream_url'` (migration 230) make "which artifacts did this upstream supply?" an indexed query. The artifact detail endpoints (`GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}` and `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{path}`) now return the origin document. Scan policies gain a cross-format `origin` block in `scan_policies.predicates`, following the #4058 pattern but placed at the top level (origin is a fact every artifact carries, not a format's fact): `allowed_upstreams` / `denied_upstreams` over the normalized upstream URL, `allowed_repositories` / `denied_repositories` over the recording repository key, and `allowed_kinds` over the ingest kind. Allowlists fail closed when the facet is unknown — the predicate exists to prove origin, and an unknown origin proves nothing — and every violation records the fired predicate's stable token (`[origin.upstream]`, `[origin.repository]`, `[origin.kind]`). The fact load is one PK lookup and only runs when an applicable policy configures origin predicates. Surfacing origin in the web console is a follow-up in the artifact-keeper-web repository.

- **A proxied conda repodata response is now attributable to a recorded upstream repodata patch generation** (#4051). Upstream conda channels rewrite the dependency metadata of ALREADY-published packages via repodata patching: the artifact hash never changes, but resolution behavior does, so two solves months apart against the same channel and the same package hashes can produce different environments with no recorded difference to point at. When a Remote conda repository serves an index (`repodata.json` / `.bz2` / `.zst`), the registry now also fetches the upstream `{subdir}/patch_instructions.json` through the same proxy cache, content-addresses it — the generation is the BLAKE2b-256 hex of the served bytes, which works across upstreams that do not version their patch documents — records it in the new `conda_repodata_patch_generations` table (migration 225, one insert-only row per distinct generation per repository/subdir), and names it on the response in the `X-Repodata-Patch-Generation` header. A header rather than an extra top-level key: repodata.json is parsed by conda clients against the CEP schema, and a header cannot perturb the document a client solves against at all — the body is still served byte-identical to upstream, and no dependency metadata is rewritten. Identical upstream patch content maps to the same generation (`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`, so the hot serve path never becomes a per-request UPDATE), while an upstream patch revision appears as a NEW row with a later `first_seen_at` — a change that is visible as a change, not silent. Recording is best-effort by design: an upstream that serves no patch instructions (404), a transient upstream failure, or a recording failure never takes down the repodata serve — the response simply carries no attribution header. Hosted (local) and virtual channels are untouched: there is no upstream patch authority behind them, so there is nothing to attribute, no header, and no rows.

- **Environment SBOMs now carry the dependency graph — one document per platform, with dependency edges, not a flat component list collapsed across platforms** (#4053). An SBOM that only lists components answers "what is here"; the graph is what makes a finding actionable ("libwebp is vulnerable *and it is here because you asked for pillow*"), and a conda environment is N graphs, one per subdir — `depends`/`constrains` resolve differently per platform, so one document covering `linux-64` and `osx-arm64` at once is wrong for both. The new `environment_sbom` service module renders the parsed lockfile graph of #4052 (`LockedEnvironment`: per-scope packages and resolved `dependant -> dependency` edges) as SBOM documents, **one per (environment, platform) scope**, with no cross-platform edge leakage by construction: no scope's generator ever sees another scope's rows, and a package present on `linux-64` but not `osx-arm64` has no node and no edge in the osx document. CycloneDX 1.5 expresses the graph as `dependencies[].dependsOn` over bom-refs with the environment itself as `metadata.component` (type `platform`); SPDX 2.3 as `DEPENDS_ON` relationships below an `SPDXRef-Environment` package the document `DESCRIBES`. Conda components are identified by the #4041 qualified purl — `pkg:conda/name@version?build=…&channel=…&subdir=…` — which *is* the bom-ref, so two builds of one name/version on two subdirs are two components with two stable ids; pypi/npm/cargo components use their conventional purl types, and a package whose coordinates cannot form a purl (no recorded version) falls back to a ref derived from its lockfile key, with uniqueness enforced rather than assumed. Edges come only from the lockfile's resolved edges, never from re-resolving repodata: a conda `constrains` entry is carried as an `artifact-keeper:constrains` component property rather than masquerading as a dependency, and conda virtual packages (`__glibc`, `__cuda`, `__osx`) — which the parser already records as explained absences, not packages — appear in no document and leak no edges. The root layer ("you asked for pillow") is the document root depending on exactly the in-degree-zero nodes of the emitted graph, which is the recorded project package where the format has one (npm v2/v3, `uv.lock`) and the best available approximation where it does not. Served at `POST /api/v1/sbom/environment?filename=<lockfile name>&format=cyclonedx|spdx` with the raw lockfile as the body; the response carries one document per scope plus the parser's coverage summary, so "we understood 380 of 400 packages" travels with the graphs. Nothing is persisted — the lockfile parser of #4052 is a pure transformation and no stored environment model exists in this build, so documents are regenerated per request (the same shape as the proxy SBOM) and the endpoint needs authentication but no repository permission, since it reads no tenant data.

- **Stored environments and the component → environment reverse index: given a component or advisory purl, the registry now names the affected environments per platform, with the inclusion paths that pull the component in** (#4054). The incident question "what do we have to fix?" is asked against environments, not packages, but #4052's lockfile parser was a pure transformation and #4053's environment SBOM endpoint persisted nothing — so there was no stored fact to ask it against. This change adds the stored environment model: migration 226 creates `environments` (one row per `(repository_id, name)` — the repository is the unit of ACL and lifecycle, and re-ingesting the same name REPLACES the stored graph, since a re-solved environment is a new fact and stale membership would keep answering "are we exposed?" with an environment nobody runs anymore), `environment_packages` (one row per (scope, package) membership, carrying both the full #4041-qualified purl for display and its qualifier-stripped base), and `environment_edges` (one row per resolved edge, per scope). The reverse index is a btree on `environment_packages.purl_base`: the base is the identity an advisory carries (OSV/GHSA name a package and version range, not a conda build string), so a lookup reduces any qualified purl to its base and answers "which stored environments contain X" as an index scan — asserted by a DB test that seeds 300 environments and verifies the plan via EXPLAIN — while per-platform answers fall out of the scope columns every membership row carries. On a hit, the scope's stored rows are reloaded into a `LockedEnvironment` and the parser's own reverse-BFS (`LockedEnvironment::explain`) reconstructs the chains from a root down to the component, so the path answer is the same algorithm over the same data as the parse-time answer; paths are capped per hit (default 8, max 64) and hits per query at 500 (with a `truncated` flag). Served at `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/environments?filename=…&name=…` (ingest, repo `write`; 201 on first store, 200 on replace), `GET`/`DELETE` on the same nest for list/detail/delete, and `GET /api/v1/environments/lookup?purl=…&max_paths=…` for the reverse index across every repository the caller may read — visibility is rendered by the same `require_visible` predicate the repository listing uses, so a caller never learns that an environment in a repository they cannot read exists. Client telemetry (which users *ran* a component) is deliberately out of scope: this answers which stored environments contain it.

- **Stored environments are now re-evaluated when advisory data changes: a newly published advisory against an already-installed component marks the affected environments — with no artifact, lockfile, or environment row changing — and the registry reports TRANSITIONS, not steady state** (#4055). An environment scanned clean in March is not clean in June, and #4054's stored component set is exactly what makes closing that gap cheap: a re-evaluation is a match against stored rows, never a rescan of bytes. The trigger hooks the advisory DELTA rather than a timer over everything: the `AdvisoryClient`'s answer cache is where new advisory data enters this system, and a refresh whose advisory-id set differs from the previously cached answer reports an `AdvisoryDelta` for the `(ecosystem, name)` to a persisted queue (`advisory_deltas`, one upserted row per package — persisted, not an in-memory channel, so a delta detected on a replica that does not hold the scheduler lease is still processed by the one that does); a cluster-leased scheduler tick (`environment_reeval`, reusing the existing `scheduler_service` + `cluster_work` singleton-lease machinery) drains it. Processing one delta costs one index scan over the new `idx_environment_packages_identity((ecosystem, name))` — the delta package's stored versions across every environment — plus one batched feed query of that size, so cost scales with the advisory delta and a package in NO environment touches no rows (fenced by an EXPLAIN test and a touches-no-rows test). Version-range matching is the feed's, not ours: each stored version is queried through the same OSV path a scan uses, so no third semver/range evaluator exists, and a withdrawal or a fixed-version shift past the stored version renders identically — the feed stops naming the advisory for that version. The feed's answer is diffed against the new `environment_advisory_state` table (row present == affected); only the diff is recorded, in `environment_advisory_transitions` (`new-affected` / `no-longer-affected`, denormalised with the advisory's summary/severity/fixed version so the event stands alone), and published on the existing `EventBus` as repo-scoped `environment.advisory_affected` / `environment.advisory_cleared` events — two types rather than one with a payload, because the DIRECTION is the fact a subscriber pages on. A degraded feed answer records NOTHING (absence of an answer is not absence of affectedness): the delta stays pending and is retried with a bounded attempt budget, and every state/transition insert is guarded against an environment being deleted mid-evaluation. Served at `GET /api/v1/environments/advisory-transitions?advisory=…&kind=…&since=…&until=…` (visibility rendered by the same `require_visible` predicate the reverse-index lookup uses) and `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/environments/{id}/advisories` for one environment's current state. Conda-keyed and unscoped (`*`) deltas are skipped by design: no feed serves the conda ecosystem (the scan path resolves conda through the PyPI alias graph before querying, #4042), and an unscoped vendored-library query has no ecosystem to key a reverse lookup on.

- **Scan policies can now gate conda artifacts on the facts the content epic persists — channel of origin, license, install scripts, and attestation state** (#4058). `scan_policies` gains a `predicates` JSONB column (migration 224; empty object = no predicates, so every existing policy evaluates byte-for-byte as before) holding a `conda` block with seven optional predicates: `allowed_channels` / `denied_channels` over the channel recorded in the artifact's identity purl at ingest (a remote repo's upstream URL, or the owning repo's key for hosted uploads — defence against channel-priority misconfiguration and typosquatted channels, failing closed when origin is unknown), `denied_licenses` / `denied_license_families` over the `license` / `license_family` `about.json` keys `build_conda_metadata` persists (an undeclared license is not a denied license), `block_install_scripts` and `max_install_script_severity` over the `package_install_scripts` rows and their analysis findings (scripts the rule engine could not examine are covered by the presence predicate, never graded "clean" by the severity one), and `min_attestation_state` (`present` / `verified`) over the CEP-27 verification record on `curation_packages.attestation_state`, folded weakest-first across a name/version's builds. Predicates compose with the existing CVE/severity conditions in the same policy — a violation from either blocks — and every violation is recorded with the fired predicate's stable token (`[conda.channel]`, `[conda.license]`, `[conda.license_family]`, `[conda.install_scripts]`, `[conda.attestation]`) in `PolicyResult.violations`, which is what the download gate, quarantine reason and audit trail persist. The allow/deny lists are the organisation's own: the product ships the mechanism and seeds no list. Evaluation loads the fact set only when an applicable policy configures conda predicates, so predicate-free repos pay zero extra queries on the download path. A staleness predicate against the last-observed upstream version is deliberately NOT included: nothing in-tree records an upstream version observation (the npm replication feed is a cache-invalidation mechanism, not a version record), and building that pipeline is out of scope here.

- **Conda channels can now withdraw ONE package — purge-via-quarantine — with every repodata variant reflecting the withdrawal and a CEP-6 notice explaining it** (#4059). `DELETE /conda/{repo_key}/{subdir}/{filename}` withdraws a single package (malicious upload, license problem, embargoed advisory) without touching the rest of the channel. Withdrawal is deliberately not a hard delete: it applies the same auditable permanent quarantine hold the admin console applies (`quarantine_service::quarantine_now`, #2912), so the row stays in `artifacts` with the reason on it, the existing download gate refuses the package (409), and the hold is reversible through the quarantine console. The repodata gap is closed at the one place every variant is built from: `list_conda_artifacts` now filters through `is_withdrawn`, the exact blocking predicate of the download gate, so repodata.json, current_repodata.json, the bz2/zst/sig encodings, JLAP (its advertised `latest` hash), the CEP-16 shard index and individual shards, run_exports.json and channeldata.json all drop the withdrawn package on the next serve — and the pre-withdrawal content-addressed shard URL stops resolving, so no stale path serves the withdrawn version. The withdrawn package is also named in repodata's `removed` array, the CEP mechanism by which a channel tells clients to evict a package. An expired upload hold stays listed, mirroring the gate. The endpoint sits behind the shared rails rather than a parallel path: the `delete:artifacts` token scope every format-native delete route enforces (GHSA-vvc3-h39c-mrq5) plus the instance-admin gate the quarantine console uses, hosted repositories only, and a blast-radius ceiling by construction — the lookup is an exact-path equality returning at most one row, with no pattern or range form of the endpoint. Each withdrawal appends a CEP-6 channel notice (`{id, message, level, created_at, package, subdir, reason}`, level `warning`) served from `GET /conda/{repo_key}/notices.json` — previously a stub returning an empty array — persisted per repository in `repository_config` under `conda_channel_notices`, so no migration was needed.

- **Conda packages now inherit PyPI advisory coverage through a conda-to-PyPI alias graph, instead of scanning bit-for-bit identically to a clean package** (#4089). OSV has no `conda` ecosystem and the GitHub feed skipped conda silently, so a conda dependency got nothing from either advisory source and the result looked exactly like an all-clear. A scanned conda package is now resolved through the alias graph and branches on what it learns: a package with a known PyPI counterpart (`py-opencv` → `opencv-python`, `pytorch` → `torch`, `matplotlib-base` → `matplotlib`) is queried as that distribution in the `PyPI` ecosystem; a package that positively ships no PyPI distribution is queried across every ecosystem like a vendored native library; and a Python package with no known alias degrades the scan to `partial` rather than publishing an empty findings list as a clean bill. Findings name the conda package actually installed and disclose the alias the match rests on, at the package's own version line.

- **`GET /api/v1/formats` now reports whether each format enforces scan-on-proxy** (#4099). Every format handler carries `scan_on_proxy`: `enforced` when the format's proxied package downloads are scanned inline and withheld per the repository's policy (npm, PyPI, OCI and VS Code today), `accepted` when the setting is stored but proxied downloads are served unscanned, and `unsupported` for WASM plugin handlers. Clients can read this instead of keeping their own list of gated formats; the value comes from the same registration the download handlers use, and a test fails if a declared format's package routes stop reaching the scan.
  For VS Code this also closes a gap: the legacy `/extensions/{publisher}/{name}/{version}/download` route served a Remote or Virtual repository's VSIX unscanned even with scan-on-proxy on. It now applies the same scan as the gallery package route, including the stricter-of-two policy on each Virtual member.

- **Scan-on-proxy now gates every proxied Maven, Gradle and sbt download except a short allowlist of metadata files** (#4100, part of #4097). With scan-on-proxy enabled on a Remote `maven`/`gradle` repository (or an `sbt` repository on the `/ivy` route), every proxied file except POMs, `.xml` metadata, Gradle `.module`, checksums, signatures and `-sources`/`-javadoc` jars now goes through the shared inline gate. This covers `.jar`/`.war`/`.ear`, and also `.zip`, `.tar.gz`, `.aar`, `.klib`, `.so` and other native or distribution bundles, which were previously served unscanned. Under `fail_closed`, any of these files returns `423` when no scanner is available or when it is larger than the 200 MiB scan cap (large distributions included); under `fail_open` it is served with `X-AK-Scan: pending`. For gated files: a vulnerable archive is refused with `403 scan_blocked`, a clean one is served with `X-AK-Scan: clean` and its verdict reused on the next pull, and fail-open (`X-AK-Scan: pending`), fail-closed (`423`) and the severity threshold behave as they do for npm and PyPI. Virtual repositories apply the stricter of the virtual's and the member's policy per Remote member, and a member's `403`/`409`/`423` ends the walk instead of falling through to the next member. If the scan configuration cannot be read, the virtual walk fails closed with `503`. The allowlist is matched case-insensitively on the same normalised path the proxy cache uses (`-sources`/`-javadoc` jars are skipped based on the classifier in their name), and unknown extensions and odd suffixes are scanned. A `.jar`/`.war`/`.ear` that names a Maven coordinate gets an identity pin; anything else is scanned without one. Known gap: the scan workspace does not unpack `.aar`, `.hpi`/`.jpi`, `.nbm`, `.jmod`, `.rar` or `.zip`, so those are graded only from what the engine reads in the raw file. On Remote and Virtual `maven`/`gradle`/`sbt` repositories (whether or not scan-on-proxy is on), a proxied path containing `?`, `#`, `;`, `%`, a space or a control character after decoding, or ending in `.`, or one that places a metadata file under a segment named like an archive (`.../widget-1.0.jar/x.pom`), is now refused with `400`, because an upstream could read such a path as a different file than the one classified and cached. The archive's identity is taken from the request path and pinned only when the archive's own `META-INF/maven/<groupId>/<artifactId>/pom.properties` agrees; archives without one (typical of Gradle- and sbt-built jars) are scanned without the identity check. `GET /api/v1/formats` now reports `maven` and `sbt` as `scan_on_proxy: "enforced"`. The buffered path keeps the `.sha1` sidecar check: a body that disagrees with its sidecar is evicted from the proxy cache and refused with `502`, the same way Cargo handles a `cksum` mismatch. If the eviction fails twice, the pull is refused with a retryable `503` instead. A `record_only` repository (#3645) is scanned and recorded and serves every pull with `X-AK-Scan: recorded`.

- **Scan-on-proxy now gates proxied NuGet, Chocolatey and PowerShell packages** (#4102, part of #4097). With scan-on-proxy enabled on a Remote `nuget`, `chocolatey` or `powershell` repository, every `.nupkg` it proxies goes through the shared inline gate, on both the V3 flat container (`/v3/flatcontainer/{id}/{version}/{file}`) and the legacy V2 route (`/v2/package/{id}/{version}`) that Chocolatey and `nuget.exe` use, whichever protocol the upstream speaks. A vulnerable package is refused with `403 scan_blocked`. A clean one is served with `X-AK-Scan: clean`, and its verdict is reused on the next pull, from either route. Fail-open (`X-AK-Scan: pending`), fail-closed (`423`), record-only (`X-AK-Scan: recorded`) and the severity threshold behave as they do for the other enforced formats. The package's identity is taken from the requested id and version and pinned only when its own `.nuspec` agrees (ids compared case-insensitively, versions in NuGet's normalized form, so a `.nuspec` saying `1.0` matches a flat-container `1.0.0`). A package that declares a different coordinate is treated as inconclusive. The `.nuspec` manifest itself passes unscanned. A symbols package (`.snupkg`) is scanned without an identity pin, so a vulnerable one is blocked but fail-closed does not withhold it for lacking one. Against a V2 upstream, the flat container now answers only `{id}.{version}.nupkg` and returns `404` for any other file name; it used to answer a `.nuspec` request with the package bytes, which also bypassed the gate. On a Virtual repository each Remote member is scanned under the stricter of the virtual's and the member's policy, and a member's `403`/`409`/`423` ends the walk instead of falling through to the next member; a hosted member ahead of a scanning remote still serves first. A Remote package row whose stored blob is missing is repaired as follows on a scanning repository: with no recorded digest, the re-fetch goes through the gate (and the warm proxy-cache body is no longer copied into the row unscanned); with a recorded SHA-256, a stored `vulnerable` verdict for that digest refuses the pull. On Remote and Virtual NuGet repositories (whether or not scan-on-proxy is on), a package id, version or file name containing `/`, `\`, `?`, `#`, `;`, `%`, a space or a control character after decoding, ending in `.`, or equal to `..`, is now refused with `400`: such a coordinate let the version-list route fetch a `.nupkg` from upstream and serve it unscanned. `GET /api/v1/formats` now reports `nuget` as `scan_on_proxy: "enforced"`. The shared `.nuspec` reader now stops at 4 MiB, because the gate runs it on upstream bytes. It also backs validation and metadata parsing for NuGet packages uploaded through the generic upload endpoint, so such an upload with a larger `.nuspec` is now refused with `400` (`dotnet nuget push` uses its own bounded reader and is unchanged). On the proxy gate an oversized `.nuspec` leaves the package unpinned, i.e. inconclusive.

- **New `docs/security/scan-on-proxy.md` documents scan-on-proxy and which formats enforce it** (#4114, part of #4097). It covers what the gate does, the settings, the verdict cache and its freshness rules (30 days, invalidated by a scanner or vulnerability-database version change), `fail_open` / `fail_closed` / `record_only`, the stricter-of-two rule for Virtual repositories, a per-format coverage table (`enforced` / `accepted` / `unsupported`), and the known gaps, including the generic `/api/v1/repositories/{key}/download/*path` route (#4442). A unit test fails when the table disagrees with the `scan_on_proxy` capability that `GET /api/v1/formats` reports, so the two cannot drift apart.

- **A CI OIDC identity mapping can now grant its service account access directly, instead of that access living in a second, disconnected group membership.** (#4117). `allowed_repo_ids` reads like a grant in HCL but was only ever a ceiling, intersected with the account's RBAC — and a CI service account was provisioned with no RBAC of its own, so the mapping alone authenticated a pipeline but never authorized it. Making a pipeline work took an unrelated second act in a different file: create a group, grant it repository actions, add the service account to it by hand — three commits per pipeline on this project's own `test` instance. A mapping now accepts `group_binding_ids`, the set of groups its service account SHALL belong to; declare it and the account has exactly that access from the moment the mapping does, reconciled immediately on every mapping write and on every token exchange, so narrowing a binding revokes rather than merely looking like it does. Reconciliation is enforced, never skipped: a mapping write whose reconcile fails changes nothing, an exchange through a bound mapping whose reconcile fails is refused with `503` and issues no token, and every membership change a mapping write makes is recorded in the audit log as `CI_OIDC_GROUP_BINDING_RECONCILED`. `null` (omitted) and `[]` are distinct and deliberately so: a mapping created before this release, or one that simply never declares a binding, has an absent binding and behaves exactly as it always has — nothing reconciles and any hand-wired membership is left alone; `[]` is a declared assertion of "no memberships" and strips everything. A binding names groups by id, never creates one, and refuses a create or update that names a group that does not exist. `allowed_repo_ids` is unchanged and is now specified for what it always was: a ceiling that can only narrow what the binding confers, never widen it. See `docs/ci-oidc.md` for the adoption order (declare the binding, verify, then remove the hand-wired membership) and for why the mapping's `claim_filters` remain the security boundary an any-of filter and a broad binding compound.

- **Hosted RPM repositories can serve independent YUM/DNF metadata at a configured directory depth** (#4216). Set `repodata_depth` on an empty local RPM repository to preserve nested upload paths and isolate each build's packages, metadata, and signatures without creating child repositories. Depth zero preserves existing behavior; unsupported repository modes and unsafe layout changes are rejected explicitly.

- **Admin queues for hosted and proxy-cache quarantine holds** (#4516, #4281). `GET /api/v1/admin/holds/summary` and `GET /api/v1/admin/holds/quarantine` list currently-blocking `artifacts` rows and proxy-cache `quarantine_until` holds, filterable by repository and by `kind` (`active`, `expired`, `rejected`). Scan-policy blocks are stored as quarantine today, so they appear here as active hosted holds. Repository-scoped tokens are refused.

- **The scanner-adapter can run its scans as a client of a shared `trivy server`** (#4351). Every adapter downloaded and held its own copy of the trivy vulnerability DB and analyzed every image layer itself, even when several adapters run side by side. Setting `SCANNER_TRIVY_SERVER` now runs every image and filesystem scan with `--server`: the server holds the DB and does the matching, image layers already analyzed by any client are neither pulled nor re-analyzed, and the adapter skips its startup DB download. Readiness stays fail-closed: `/probe/ready` is 200 only while the server answers `/version` with a loaded DB and the same trivy release as the bundled CLI, since trivy accepts a mismatched client silently, and each scan re-checks the server info trivy embeds in its report. Because trivy's `--insecure` (on by default for plain-HTTP registry pulls) also disables TLS verification of the server, an `https` server with `SCANNER_TRIVY_INSECURE=true` keeps the adapter not-ready unless `SCANNER_TRIVY_SERVER_INSECURE=true` opts in. Because trivy keys an image layer's cached analysis by the diff ID the image config claims, without re-hashing the layer, adapters that should not trust each other's cache entries can set distinct `SCANNER_TRIVY_CACHE_PARTITION` values and still share the DB. In this mode the scan results' vulnerability-DB provenance comes from the server block of each scan's report instead of the local cache. Unset, nothing changes. The adapter is 1.4.0.

- **Remote repositories can restrict which paths they request from their upstream, and a virtual repository no longer waits on a member whose filter excludes the path** (#4399, #840). A new per-remote upstream filter (`GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /api/v1/repositories/{key}/upstream-filter`, repository admin only) takes `include_patterns` and `exclude_patterns` regexes, the same shape as a peer's `replication_filter`, matched against the path as sent upstream (anchor with `^`/`$`): for Maven, Debian, OCI and Go the layout path such as `com/acme/lib/1.0/lib-1.0.jar`; for npm the encoded `@scope%2Fname` for metadata and `@scope/name/-/...` for tarballs; for downloads from another host (PyPI files, cargo `dl` hosts, NuGet service URLs) the full URL. A path the filter refuses answers 404 without contacting the upstream, so a virtual repository skips that member for it: a fringe Maven remote that hosts a handful of groups can be limited to them, and when it goes down it no longer stalls every `maven-metadata.xml` merge until the upstream timeout. Patterns are validated on write (at most 64 per list, 512 bytes each, each list compiled to at most 64 KiB; subjects over 4 KiB are refused), and a change applies on every replica at once. The npm `/-/` passthroughs and npm audit, curation upstream sync, change feeds and the `test-upstream` probe are not filtered yet. An object already in the proxy cache for a now-filtered path is served until its cache entry expires; it is then refused with 404 like any other miss (no revalidation, no stale-if-error), and the cache invalidate endpoint removes it immediately. This is the first slice of the remote-repository policy work; package-name, size and vulnerability rules are not part of it.

- **Offline content bundles: versioned manifest format, job tables and an admin-only `/api/v1/bundles` API skeleton** (#4400, #2464). This is the first of three steps toward exporting repositories on an online instance and importing them into a disconnected one. The bundle is an uncompressed, inspectable tar with content-addressed blobs that keep their real file extension, and a versioned `manifest.json` that already reserves fields for sequenced delta sets, per-record signatures and media volume sets (DVD-R through BD-R XL). `GET /api/v1/bundles/format` describes the format, `POST /api/v1/bundles/manifest/validate` checks a manifest, and the job endpoints list export and import jobs. `POST /exports` and `POST /imports` answer 501 Not Implemented until the later steps land. The bundle reader refuses path traversal, absolute paths, links, devices, duplicate entries, compressed streams and oversized input before anything is unpacked.
  Scan results now record whether this instance's scanner produced them (`scan_results.origin`), and hash-based scan reuse only considers local scans. Scan evidence carried in a bundle is stored separately, so it can never mark future uploads of the same bytes as already scanned.

- **Webhooks can be signed with an instance Ed25519 key and verified against a public JWKS** (#4401, first slice of #921). A webhook's new `signing_mode` (`hmac`, the default; `asymmetric`; or `both`, set at create time and returned by GET/LIST) decides which tokens `X-ArtifactKeeper-Signature` carries. `asymmetric` and `both` add `v2=<kid>:<sig>`, an Ed25519 signature (base64url, no padding) over `<t>.<webhook_id>.<body>`, and send the destination in `X-ArtifactKeeper-Webhook-Id`. Receivers no longer need a shared secret: they check that the webhook id is their own and verify the signature against `GET /api/v1/webhooks/jwks`, which needs no credentials and stays reachable when guest access is disabled. The webhook id is part of the signed message because one key signs for every webhook on the instance; without it, a delivery captured at one receiver would verify at another. The `kid` is the key's RFC 7638 thumbprint. The instance key is created on first use, and its private half is encrypted at rest with `AK_WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY`, so `asymmetric`/`both` need that key set (create returns 422 without it). Existing webhooks stay `hmac`, and their headers are byte-identical to before. Receivers that only check `v1=` ignore `v2=`.

  If `AK_WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY` is changed after the signing key exists, asymmetric deliveries go out without `v2=` and asymmetric creates return a 422 that says so. Until key rotation ships, an administrator recovers with `UPDATE webhook_signing_keys SET retired_at = NOW() WHERE retired_at IS NULL;`, after which a new key is created on next use. Key rotation with an overlap window and sample receivers will follow.

- **`.safetensors` files uploaded to Mlmodel repositories now expose their tensor structure as artifact metadata** (#4402, #2382). After the upload commits, the server reads only the 8-byte header length and the JSON header (capped at 8 MiB; at most two parses run at once) through ranged storage reads, never the tensor data, and records each tensor's dtype and shape, the total and per-dtype parameter counts, and the header's `__metadata__` string map under `safetensors` in `artifact_metadata` (format `mlmodel`). The stored document stays under 1 MiB: the per-tensor listing and `__metadata__` are cut to size budgets and flagged `tensors_truncated` / `metadata_truncated`. It is returned in the `metadata` field of `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{path}` and `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}`, and by `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}/metadata`. A malformed or unreadable header never fails the upload; a short reason is recorded as `safetensors_error` instead. Applies to generic `PUT`, multipart and chunked uploads; GGUF and ONNX are not parsed yet.

- **Bulk artifact existence check and opt-in dedup at chunked-upload init, so air-gap imports transfer only new bytes** (#4405, #3427). `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts-missing` takes up to 1000 `{path, sha256}` items and returns the ones the hosted repository does not already hold with that content, each marked `not_found` or `checksum_mismatch`; more than 1000 items is a 400. It needs read access to the repository, and a caller without it gets the same 404 as for a nonexistent repository. The check reads the artifact catalogue only and does not probe storage, so an artifact whose stored file was lost still reads as present; clients should keep sending `skip_if_present` on chunked pushes, which does check storage and so lets the re-upload repair it. `POST /api/v1/uploads` accepts `skip_if_present: true`: when a live artifact already exists at the path with the declared checksum and size, and its stored object is present, the server answers 200 with `already_present: true` and the existing artifact id instead of opening a session. Clients that do not send the flag see no change.

- **Curated RPM repositories can now prune old snapshot versions automatically** (#4406, #2359). Every curated RPM snapshot (`@N`) kept its database rows, signed repodata and cached packages forever, so a nightly mirror grew by one full snapshot per night. Setting `RPM_VERSION_RETENTION_KEEP=N` (default unset: keep everything) starts an hourly pass on each replica, run by one replica at a time under a scheduler lease, that keeps each repository's N newest published versions, every unpublished version newer than the newest published one, and its active publication, deletes the other versions, and deletes the objects stored under their `@N` prefix (including objects a crashed publish or pass left behind). A pruned `@N` URL stops resolving; the active publication and the newest version are never removed, so version numbers are never reissued, and unpublished drafts never push a published snapshot out of the window.

- **`S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT` and `AZURE_STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT` set the address presigned download redirects point at** (#4417).
