Presigned redirects (including the OCI blob `307`) used the backend's own storage endpoint, so with an in-cluster `S3_ENDPOINT` such as `http://storage-minio:9000` every redirected download from outside the cluster failed. When the new variable is set, S3 presigned URLs are signed for and point at that origin (SigV4 covers the host, so the URL is signed for it rather than rewritten), and Azure SAS redirect URLs use that base; the backend's own storage calls keep the internal endpoint. Malformed values (no `http`/`https` scheme, userinfo, query, or a path for S3) stop the backend at startup when it is the primary storage backend; a secondary (per-repository) backend is skipped with a warning. CloudFront, when configured, still signs S3 redirects and the public endpoint is ignored. Unset, nothing changes.

  Operator note: do not enable `PRESIGNED_DOWNLOADS_ENABLED` while the storage endpoint is unreachable from clients and no public endpoint is set. For S3 the proxy in front of the public endpoint must keep the `Host` header and path unchanged; for Azure it must rewrite `Host` to the storage account host (or use the account's custom domain). See `docs/operations/presigned-downloads.md`.

- **New guide for Bazel module registries, `docs/bazel.md`, including how virtual repositories shadow upstream modules** (#4429). When any hosted member of a Bazel virtual repository publishes a module name, the virtual stops consulting its remote members for that name (the same dependency-confusion guard npm uses, #1217), so every BCR version of that module disappears and transitive dependencies on an upstream version fail to resolve. The guide explains the rule, shows the failure, and recommends distinct names for internal modules (or Bazel's own `single_version_override` / `archive_override` for patching a public module) instead of reusing a public name.

- **Proxy-service upstream registry requests now appear in traces as CLIENT spans that carry the trace onward, and failed storage operations mark their spans as errors** (#4434, #3954). Every upstream request the proxy service makes (artifact and metadata fetches including `fetch_upstream_direct`, conditional revalidations, and the OCI bearer-token exchange and its retry) runs in an `otel.kind = client` span named after the HTTP method, with `http.request.method`, `url.full` (credentials, query and fragment removed), `server.address`, `server.port`, `http.response.status_code` and, on failure, `error.type`. The span covers connect, TLS, redirects and the wait for response headers, so upstream latency is now attributable in a trace instead of being an untraced gap. The span's W3C `traceparent`/`tracestate` is injected into the outbound request, so an instrumented upstream continues the same trace. A 4xx or 5xx or a transport failure sets the span status to error. The exception is a `401` to a request sent without credentials, which is the bearer challenge an OCI registry sends before the token exchange. A `401` to a request that carried credentials means they were rejected, and is an error. The upstream requests made outside the proxy service are covered too, see #4455.

  Injection happens only when OpenTelemetry export is configured (`OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT`). The trace context sent upstream continues whatever inbound trace the request joined. With `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` set, only a listed proxy's `traceparent` is adopted. With the list empty (the default), any client's `traceparent` and `tracestate` are adopted and therefore forwarded to third-party upstreams such as Docker Hub or PyPI. Set the trusted-proxy list if you do not want caller-chosen trace context relayed upstream.

  The filesystem, S3, GCS and Azure storage spans now record the error of a failed operation, which sets the span status to error. The error is recorded as an INFO-level event on the span, so a routine miss (a proxy-cache lookup of an absent key) is visible in the trace without becoming an ERROR log line. Because that text now reaches INFO logs and exported span status, the filesystem backend's directory-sync errors name the storage key instead of the absolute path, and S3 errors go through the S3 error classifier with request URLs (endpoint and bucket) replaced by `<url>`. Errors from presigned S3 requests no longer include the presigned URL.

- **Traces now cover the remaining upstream calls, carry the route, status, repository and cache outcome on the request span, show the authentication, virtual-resolution and proxy-fetch phases, and can include one span per database query** (#4455, #3954). The upstream requests made outside the proxy service now run in the same `otel.kind = client` span with `traceparent` injection as the proxy service's own: the PyPI JSON publish-time lookup, the npm change-feed consumer, the npm audit and `/-/` passthroughs, the Go checksum-database proxy, and the AWS ECR/CodeArtifact token exchange.

  The `http_request` server span now records `http.route` (the matched route pattern), `http.response.status_code`, `http.response.body.size` (when the length is known up front), `artifact_keeper.repository.key` (once the key names an existing repository) and `artifact_keeper.cache.outcome`. The outcome has two vocabularies: a buffered fetch records the `ak_proxy_cache_lookups_total` `result` value (`hit`, `miss_no_metadata`, `miss_expired`, `miss_checksum_mismatch`, `miss_no_content`, `error`), and a streaming fetch records `hit`, `miss` or `negative_hit`, so match misses by the `miss` prefix. Both are recorded once, when the handler returns: when one request looks up the cache more than once (a virtual repository probing members), the attribute holds the last outcome. A 5xx response sets `error.type` and the span's error status; a 4xx does not, per the HTTP server semantic conventions. The repository key and cache outcome are span attributes only, not metric labels. Three `INTERNAL` phase spans appear under it: `authenticate` (credential validation for the format and optional-auth routes), `resolve_virtual_members` (a virtual repository's member resolution) and `proxy_fetch` (a proxy fetch: cache lookup, the upstream `CLIENT` span, cache write).

  **Stdout logs change too, with or without OTLP.** These are ordinary INFO spans, and the default `RUST_LOG` enables them, so request-scoped log lines (pretty, and the `span`/`spans` of `LOG_FORMAT=json`) now also show `http.route` on the `http_request` span, and the `authenticate`, `resolve_virtual_members` and `proxy_fetch` spans in the span chain. The repository key and cache outcome are recorded only when the handler returns, so they appear on log lines emitted after that point, not on lines logged while the handler runs.

  With OpenTelemetry export configured, each SQL statement sqlx reports becomes a `CLIENT` span named after its operation and table (for example `SELECT repositories`) with `db.system.name`, `db.operation.name`, `db.collection.name` and `db.response.returned_rows`, parented to the span the query ran under. **SQL text is never exported:** the statement is not copied onto the span, and sqlx's own per-statement log events (which carry `summary` and `db.statement`) are now kept out of the OpenTelemetry export, where they used to appear as events on the request span for every statement the log filter let through. Only the stdout log shows SQL, and only for the statements `RUST_LOG` enables. These spans follow the `sqlx::query` log filter: with the default `RUST_LOG` only statements sqlx reports as slow (over 1 s) produce one, and `sqlx::query=debug` in `RUST_LOG` produces one per statement, which also logs every statement to stdout. A query outside any request or job span produces none.

- **Lifecycle policies can combine several conditions and can be scoped to a tag or version pattern** (#4456, #2024). The new `composite` policy type takes a `conditions` list that is ANDed. For example, `{"conditions": [{"type": "max_age_days", "value": 90}, {"type": "no_downloads_days", "value": 30}]}` deletes only artifacts that are older than 90 days and also have not been downloaded in 30 days.
  - Each condition uses the same SQL as the single-condition policy of the same name.
  - `min_keep`, `match` and `exclude` work on a composite policy exactly as they do on `max_age_days`.
  - Every policy type also accepts `"match": {"version_pattern": "^sha-"}`, which limits the policy to artifacts whose version (the tag, for container images) matches the regex. It is applied before `min_keep` and `max_versions` count their kept versions, so "keep the 5 newest" counts only in-scope versions. The pattern is a PostgreSQL regular expression, checked by PostgreSQL when the policy is saved, and unanchored unless it uses `^`/`$`.
  - The preview and the live run share each definition, so a preview reports exactly what the run deletes.
  - A composite policy, or any policy with `match.version_pattern`, never evicts a Remote repository's proxy cache: cache entries have no version. Assigning one to a non-OCI Remote repository is refused with 422, and a global one skips the cache and reports why.
  - Day windows (`days`, and each condition's `value`) must now be at most 36500. A larger value used to wrap around to a much shorter window; it is now refused when the policy is saved.

- **Hosted conda repodata carries a server-set `indexed_timestamp` on every record (CEP-47)** (#4555). A record's `timestamp` is whatever the build machine's clock said, so a client cooldown such as pixi's `exclude-newer` could be defeated by any publisher. Every record served from a hosted channel (and every hosted record in a virtual channel's merge) now has `indexed_timestamp`: the moment the package entered that channel, in Unix milliseconds, taken from the artifact row's `created_at`, which is written once at upload and never rewritten, so every rebuild of `repodata.json`, its `.bz2`/`.zst` encodings, `current_repodata.json` and the CEP-16 shards reports the same value. A package promoted into a channel is indexed at its promotion time there.

- **Conda channels accept rattler's token URL layout, `/t/<TOKEN>/conda/<repo>/...`** (#4555). Conda's `.condarc` token channels put the token after the format prefix (`/conda/t/<TOKEN>/<repo>/...`), which the registry already served, but rattler and pixi (`pixi auth login <host> --conda-token`) store the token per host and insert `/t/<TOKEN>` at the front of every request path, so every such request 404'd. The same read, upload and attestation routes are now also mounted under `/t/<TOKEN>/conda/<repo>/...`, with the token resolved by the same visibility middleware. The `Authorization` header remains the recommended form, since a token in a URL can end up in logs and lockfiles.

- **Configurable trust policy for CEP-27 conda attestations, including key-based Sigstore bundles for on-premises CI** (#4556). Upload verification accepted only keyless bundles whose Fulcio certificate named the GitHub Actions issuer, which a regulated organization's own CI cannot produce. Three settings now define the policy: `CONDA_ATTESTATION_ISSUERS` (comma list of OIDC issuers accepted on keyless bundles; default the GitHub Actions issuer, so existing deployments are unchanged), `CONDA_ATTESTATION_IDENTITIES` (optional comma list of certificate identity patterns, `*` wildcard; empty accepts any identity the issuer vouches for), and `CONDA_ATTESTATION_PUBLIC_KEYS` (comma list of PEM file paths or inline PEM public keys, each optionally `name=`-prefixed). A bundle produced by `cosign attest-blob --key ... --tlog-upload=false --bundle ...` with predicate type `https://schemas.conda.org/attestations-publish-1.schema.json` verifies when its DSSE signature verifies under a configured key (ECDSA P-256/P-384/P-521, Ed25519 or RSA), its in-toto subject names the package and matches the SHA-256 the server computes from the stored bytes, and its statement passes the CEP-27 policy; no Fulcio certificate or transparency log is consulted (a bundle with no tlog entry is expected), so the configured key is the trust anchor. The in-toto Statement may be v1, as CEP-27 specifies, or the v0.1 that `cosign attest-blob` still emits; the version that verified is recorded as `statement_type`. The stored `attestation_verification` record now says how it verified: `method` is `sigstore-keyless` or `sigstore-key`, with `identity`, `issuer`, `statement_type` and, for keys, `key_fingerprint`. `GET /api/v1/attestations/policy` returns `{"require_verified", "issuers", "identities", "keys": [{"id", "name", "fingerprint", "algorithm"}]}` to any authenticated caller; it carries public material only (no key bytes or file paths).

- **Conda channels serve CEP-50 attestation sidecars and advertise them in repodata, and attestations are readable by anyone who can read the package** (#4556). A CEP-27 attestation uploaded to `PUT /conda/{repo}/{subdir}/{file}/attestation` was stored on the artifact but never served where a client looks for it, a second upload silently replaced the first, and `GET .../attestation` demanded credentials even on a public channel. Attestations are now append-only (an identical bundle is not stored twice; a different one is added beside the earlier ones), the sidecar (the JSON array of Sigstore bundles) is stored verbatim and served at `GET /conda/{repo}/{subdir}/{file}.sigs` and, immutably, at `{file}.sigs.{sha256}`, and every repodata record of an attested package carries `attestations_sha256`, so `repodata.json`, its `.bz2`/`.zst` encodings, `current_repodata.json` and the CEP-16 shards all agree. Virtual channels serve the sidecar from the member that holds the package, and remote channels proxy the upstream's. `GET .../attestation` and the sidecars follow the repository's read access: anonymous on a public channel, authenticated on a private one. `metadata.attestation` and `metadata.attestation_verification` still name the most recent upload.

- **Package allowlist on virtual conda channels** (closes #4576). `GET`/`PUT`/`DELETE /api/v1/repositories/{key}/allowlist` on a virtual conda repository (repository admin; every change is audited as `REPOSITORY_ALLOWLIST_CHANGED`) restricts what the virtual's remote members contribute to a list of `{ "name", "version", "subdirs" }` entries: `name` is an exact package name or a `*`/`?` glob, `version` an optional conda version spec evaluated with conda ordering (`2.2.3`, `2.2.*`, `>=2,<3`, `1.0|1.1`; a version that does not parse is not admitted), `subdirs` an optional platform restriction. When `enabled`, a remote record the list does not admit is left out of the virtual's `repodata.json`, `.zst` and `.bz2` and its name out of `channeldata.json`, and a download of it through the virtual answers 404 without contacting the upstream, so a client reports the package as not found instead of resolving it and failing at download. Hosted (local and staging) members are not filtered. `enabled` is required; an enabled empty list admits nothing from remotes, and `enabled: false` restores the unfiltered merge. Merged documents report the number of records the list left out in an `X-AK-Allowlist-Dropped` header.

- **Remote and virtual conda channels serve CEP-16 sharded repodata** (#4577). Sharded repodata (`repodata_shards.msgpack.zst` plus one content-addressed shard per package) was served for hosted channels only; a remote or virtual channel answered 404, so pixi and rattler-based clients fell back to the monolithic index on every solve. For the private-channel pattern, where consumers only ever read a virtual, that meant rebuilding and shipping a 74 MB merged `linux-64/repodata.json.zst` per solve instead of a half-megabyte shard index and a few hundred shards of a few KB each. A remote channel now proxies its upstream's shard index, rewritten so packages and shards resolve against the registry rather than the upstream, and proxies each shard by address through the proxy cache, where it is cached as immutable; a shard that does not hash to its address is refused with 502, never served or cached as that shard. A virtual channel merges its members' shard indexes under the rules of its `repodata.json` merge: hosted members' shards first (one shard per name across all hosted members), then each remote member's index in priority order, a name a hosted member owns never taken from a remote (#4576's ownership guard), and the allowlist applied per package name, with `X-AK-Allowlist-Dropped` counting the names left out. A shard fetched through a virtual is served only when every record in it names a package the virtual admits from a remote, so a hash a client did not learn from the merged index cannot leak a hosted-owned or non-admitted package. Both published upstream layouts work: shards beside the index (conda.anaconda.org) and under `shards/` (prefix.dev), as does an absolute shard host. The sharded endpoints now also follow the repository's read access like every other channel document; a private hosted channel used to answer them anonymously.

  Two limits follow from shards being addressed by their content. A remote package name is listed from the highest-priority remote member that publishes it, so where two remote members publish the same name the sharded view carries the first member's records only (the monolithic index merges them per file). A remote name the allowlist admits only under a version constraint is left out of the sharded view, because a shard carries every version of its package and can be admitted whole or not at all; it stays available through `repodata.json`, where records are filtered one by one. A virtual whose remote member publishes no shard index for a subdir answers 404 for its own, so clients take the documented fallback; a member whose index fetch fails is handled under the virtual's member-failure policy (#4192): 502 naming the member, or a partial index marked `X-AK-Partial-Members` and `Cache-Control: no-store` when the virtual opts in. Shards are still rebuilt per request for hosted channels; materialising them at write time remains #4173.

- **Scan-on-proxy is enforced on conda remote and virtual channels** (closes #4585, part of #4097). A `conda` or `conda_native` Remote repository with `scan_on_proxy` on now runs `.conda` and `.tar.bz2` downloads through the same inline gate as npm, PyPI, Cargo, Maven, NuGet, OCI and VS Code: digest-keyed verdicts reused across pulls, `fail_open` (served with `X-AK-Scan: pending` and scanned in the background), `fail_closed` (scanned inline; inconclusive is `423`), `record_only` (served with `X-AK-Scan: recorded`), and the severity threshold. A blocked package answers `403 {"error": "scan_blocked", "file": ..., "reason": ...}`, so the client fails the download. A Virtual channel scans each Remote member under the stricter of the virtual's and the member's policy. The `/t/<token>/` URL forms are covered, and a `.sigs` attestation sidecar is refused when its package's stored verdict blocks. Repodata, channeldata and shards are not gated. `GET /api/v1/formats` now reports `conda` and `conda_native` as `scan_on_proxy: "enforced"`, so the web UI offers the toggle for them. The identity check pins the package's `name@version` from the file name when its `info/index.json` agrees; a package the scanner catalogs nothing for (some compiled libraries) is inconclusive, so a `fail_closed` channel withholds it.

  Behaviour change: on a conda repository that scans on proxy, the generic download route (`/api/v1/repositories/{key}/download/...`) now refuses proxied files with `403 scan_on_proxy_route_required` (#4442), and a package-route path segment containing `?`, `#`, `;`, `\`, a control character, a stray `%` or a space is a `400` on Remote and Virtual conda repositories.

- **`SMTP_TLS_MODE=starttls-opportunistic` upgrades with STARTTLS when the server offers it and sends unencrypted when it does not** (#4591). This is how Forgejo's `smtp+starttls` and Nexus (JavaMail's `mail.smtp.starttls.enable`) behave, which is why the same mail server can work for them and fail for Artifact Keeper with `STARTTLS is not supported on this server`: Artifact Keeper's `starttls` mode requires STARTTLS, and still does. In the new mode a STARTTLS that is offered but fails (for example on an untrusted certificate) is an error, not a silent fallback to plaintext. Credentials sent after a fallback travel unencrypted, so prefer `starttls` or `tls` wherever the server supports them.

- **SMTP can trust a private CA, via `SMTP_TLS_CA_CERT` or the existing `CUSTOM_CA_CERT_PATH`, and `SMTP_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY` turns verification off for testing** (#4591). The SMTP transport verified the server certificate against the system trust store only, so `SMTP_TLS_MODE=starttls` or `tls` against a mail server with an internal-CA certificate (common for on-prem Exchange) failed with `tls error: ... certificate verify failed`, and the only workaround was to replace the container's CA bundle. `SMTP_TLS_CA_CERT` takes a PEM file path or the PEM text, and when it is unset the SMTP transport now also honours `CUSTOM_CA_CERT_PATH`, the CA setting the outbound HTTP clients already use. The certificates are added to the system store, not substituted for it. `SMTP_TLS_SKIP_VERIFY=true` (default `false`) accepts any certificate and hostname and logs a warning at startup. An unreadable or unparsable CA file disables email delivery with a startup warning that names the variable.

- **`/readyz` reports its dependencies, and `READYZ_REQUIRE_SEARCH` makes OpenSearch gate readiness** (#4610). `/readyz` keeps meaning "this replica can serve artifacts" (database reachable, migrations applied), but with OpenSearch stopped it answered 200 with nothing in the body to say search was down. Its response now always carries a `dependencies` object (`opensearch`, `storage`, `scanner`, `ldap`, each `healthy`, `unhealthy` or `not_configured`, with whether it is `required`), probed concurrently through the `/health` caches with a 2 second deadline each, and a `failing` list when not ready. Probe error text is only included with `EXPOSE_DETAILED_HEALTH=true`. Setting `READYZ_REQUIRE_SEARCH=true` (default false) makes an unhealthy or unconfigured OpenSearch a `503` naming `opensearch`; a database failure is a `503` either way. The endpoint stays exempt from the global concurrency limit. See `docs/operations/health-probes.md`.

- **Debian remote and virtual repositories mirror flat APT repositories (`deb <uri> /`), such as Kubernetes' pkgs.k8s.io** (#4619). A remote only spoke the `dists/<suite>` layout, so the Kubernetes and openSUSE Build Service repositories could not be proxied: `GET /debian/<repo>/InRelease` was a 404 and `dists/stable/InRelease` a 502. The flat layout is now served from the repository root (and from an exact-path suite directory): `InRelease`, `Release` and `Release.gpg` pass through byte-for-byte so apt keeps verifying the publisher's key, they revalidate on the dists TTL and drive the release epoch that invalidates the indices next to them, each `Packages`/`Sources`/`Translation` index is checked against the signed `Release` before it is served, and a package is cached only when it matches the SHA-256 its cached `Packages` records; flat-layout packages are cached as immutable. Only paths an APT flat repository contains are proxied. Point apt at `deb [signed-by=<publisher key>] <base>/debian/<repo>/ /`. Setting `debian.flat_repository = true` declares a remote flat and answers its `dists/` routes with 404 and that sources line; left unset, both layouts are served and a `dists/` request that fails against an upstream which serves a flat repository answers the same way. Each decision is logged once per repository. Closes #4619.

### Changed

- **`POST /api/v1/signing/keys` now rejects `key_type = ed25519` (and `key_type = rsa` with `algorithm = ed25519`) with 400** (#1326). `key_type = ed25519` never produced an Ed25519 key: generation fell through to RSA and stored an RSA keypair labelled `ed25519`, which could not sign Debian or RPM metadata. The 400 points at the real option, `key_type = gpg` with `algorithm = ed25519`. Existing `ed25519` rows keep loading, and rotating one now produces the `rsa` key it really holds.

- **Revoking a signing key now sets its `expires_at` to the time of revocation** (#1329). A revoked key used to keep `expires_at: null` in the signing-key API. Revocation now stamps it (an earlier expiry is kept), and that is what ends a rotated-out key's co-signing overlap immediately.

- **Storage GC and OCI blob GC now read their deletion candidates in bounded pages instead of loading the whole set at once** (#2524). The orphan storage-key scan and both blob-GC phases (mark and sweep) used to fetch every candidate into memory in one query, so a large deletion wave meant one huge result set and an unbounded memory spike. Each scan now walks the candidates 1000 at a time with a keyset cursor and still reclaims everything in a single pass. What GC deletes, and the row-lock re-check before each deletion, are unchanged.

- **A remote repository's cache TTL can now be set high enough to stop revalidation** (#2667). `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/cache-ttl` capped `cache_ttl_seconds` at 30 days. The maximum is now 315360000 seconds (about ten years), the lifetime immutable artifacts are cached for, so setting it means the remote's mutable paths (indexes, tag manifests) are never revalidated. Overrides read from the database are also clamped to that range, so a hand-edited value can no longer overflow the expiry computation. The web UI's TTL input needs the same maximum (artifact-keeper-web).

- **Hex publish rejects a tarball without a usable `CHECKSUM` member with 422** (#2904). Such a tarball used to be accepted and stored, but the registry could never describe the release (`inner_checksum` is required by `mix`), so every later `/packages/{name}` read answered 500. The check now runs before anything is stored, so a refused publish leaves no artifact or storage object behind. Tarballs built by `mix hex.build` always carry the member; releases already stored keep resolving through the existing read-path backfill.

- **GitHub API release-by-tag lookups are cached for seven days on github, mise and aqua remotes** (#3658). mise's aqua backend calls `api.github.com/repos/<owner>/<repo>/releases/tags/<tag>` even for exactly pinned versions. Through a `github`-format API mirror those responses took the five-minute default, so a cold CI runner could only resolve pinned tools for about the first hour of a GitHub outage. That exact path shape now gets the same seven-day finite lifetime as release assets and is still revalidated when it expires. The paginated release list, `releases/latest` and every other API path keep the short default. A repository TTL override still takes precedence, as it does for every mutable path. Ordinary `generic` remotes are unchanged.

- **Assigning a lifecycle policy that cannot reclaim anything in a Remote repository now returns 422** (#3734). Before, such a policy was accepted and silently matched nothing. The check runs when you create a policy, attach it, or change its config. It covers `max_versions`, `tag_pattern_*` and `size_quota_bytes`, and also `exclude` lists and `min_keep`, which match artifact versions that proxy-cache entries do not have. OCI Remote repositories (Docker, Podman, Helm OCI and the like) are exempt because pulled manifests have `artifacts` rows. Policies that were already assigned keep running and can still be renamed, disabled, or re-sent their unchanged config.

- **Creating or updating a repository as public while guest access is disabled now fails with `400 Bad Request` instead of silently rewriting the repository to private** (#3855). With `AK_GUEST_ACCESS_ENABLED=false`, a request carrying `is_public: true` (or `allow_anonymous_access: true`) contradicted a deliberate operator policy; the old coercion answered `201`/`200` for a repository the caller never asked for, which produced perpetual Terraform drift and late "why can nobody pull this anonymously" surprises. The API now rejects the request with an error naming the switch (`AK_GUEST_ACCESS_ENABLED=false`) and the two resolutions — enable guest access, or choose a non-public visibility. **Breaking change:** clients that relied on the silent coercion must stop sending `is_public: true` on guest-disabled instances.

- **A release run now dispatches the release announcement and the AMI build itself, and both can be run by hand** (#3896, #3897, #4359). Releases are created by the release workflow, and a release created that way starts no other workflow, so recent releases were never announced and had no AMI built although every release run was green. The release workflow now starts the announcement (every release) and the AMI build (stable releases only) and waits for each, so a failed one fails the release run. Both can also be dispatched by hand for a given tag or version. The announcement no longer calls a stable release "a new pre-release" or repeats the product name in its title.

- **VS Code gallery queries draw from their own buffered-metadata sub-budget, so a burst of anonymous gallery reads can no longer starve npm, PyPI, Debian or RPM metadata fetches** (#3914). Gallery reservations are now charged against a gallery share of the shared buffered-metadata budget as well as the budget itself, so the gallery can hold at most its share (default 3/8 of `AK_PROXY_METADATA_BUDGET_BYTES`, 384 MiB of the default 1 GiB, but never less than the 256 MiB one full-width composed gallery response needs unless the shared budget itself is smaller; override with `AK_VSCODE_GALLERY_METADATA_BUDGET_BYTES`) and queues and sheds (503 + `Retry-After`) against that share alone. The new `ak_proxy_metadata_sub_budget_saturation_ratio{family="vscode_gallery"}` gauge reports how full it is (0 on an idle replica). The per-query reservation is now set from measured Open VSX responses (a peak of up to 9.24x the wire size when parsed and re-serialized) at 10x the 2 MiB wire cap, replacing the estimated 6x. Capacity note for operators: at the defaults the gallery now admits 19 concurrent cap-sized queries (it was 85 against the whole shared budget) and 6 concurrent 64 MiB version-history fetches (was 16), shedding the rest with 503 + `Retry-After` after 5 s; raise `AK_VSCODE_GALLERY_METADATA_BUDGET_BYTES` on gallery-heavy deployments. The sub-budget type is family-keyed so RPM repodata can adopt it next.

- **CHANGELOG entries are now one fragment file per PR under `changes/unreleased/`, assembled into `CHANGELOG.md` only when a release is cut** (#4016). Every PR used to add its bullet at the top of the same `## [Unreleased]` subsection, so two open PRs always conflicted on `CHANGELOG.md` even though both entries were wanted: 76 % of merges to `main` touched the file, every currently conflicting PR conflicted on it, and 69 % of force-pushes landed within an hour of a merge, each one re-running the full CI pipeline for a rebase that changed nothing. A PR now adds `changes/unreleased/<issue>-<slug>.md` — `section:` and `issues:` front matter over the bullet exactly as it reads in the changelog — and no two PRs touch the same file. `scripts/release/assemble-changelog.sh` renders the fragments into the new `## [X.Y.Z] - <date>` section at the release prep, in Keep a Changelog section order and a deterministic entry order, and deletes them; `--check` previews the section. `check-changelog-unreleased.sh` validates every fragment (name, section, a non-empty `issues:` list the body cites, exactly one bullet), `check-changelog-placement.sh` validates the fragments a PR adds and no longer fails a release prep for the bullets it assembles, release preflight check 5 reconciles unassembled fragments alongside `## [Unreleased]`, and the release-hygiene exemptions and the Release-Bump Gate accept the fragment directory. The 37 entries pending under `## [Unreleased]` were moved into fragments byte for byte.

  **Transition.** A PR that still adds a bullet under `## [Unreleased]` passes CI (with a notice), and the assembler merges those bullets with the fragments at the cut, so PRs opened before this change do not need rewriting — though they will conflict once more against the emptied section.

- **Container image builds and the docker-compose E2E suites run on the self-hosted `rocky` pools instead of GitHub-hosted runners.** (#4206) The amd64 legs of the three `Docker Publish` image builds and CI's `🐳 Build Backend Image` / `🐳 Build OpenSCAP Image` now run on `ak-docker-runners`; `🔥 Smoke E2E Tests`, the `E2E Tests` native-client / stress / failure suites, the nightly E2E, the cache-correctness suite, the single-flight race and the weekly container scan run on `ak-e2e-runners`. Both are scale sets separate from `ak-ci-runners`, so none of these jobs takes a slot from the four Rust jobs. The arm64 legs stay on GitHub-hosted arm runners, and the release, signing, manifest, scan and small gate jobs stay GitHub-hosted. The "free disk space" steps that existed only for the hosted runner's ~14 GB root disk are removed: on the pools the build runs in the pod's DinD daemon, whose storage is a hostPath on the runner host. `docker/Dockerfile.backend` gains a `CARGO_BUILD_JOBS` build argument (default 8) in its two compiling stages, because cargo inside DinD sees all of the host's CPUs rather than the pod's share; the workflows pass 8 on the pools and 4 on the hosted arm64 leg, and CI's image build can use the pool's per-slot local buildx cache (`AK_BUILDKIT_CACHE_DIR`) in front of the read-only registry cache. The published image's contents do not change.

- **CI skips the four Rust jobs when nothing they read changed, and on a push whose tree a merged pull request already proved green.** (#4207) A pull request that touches only CI-only files (`.github/release-notes/`, `scripts/release/`, `docs/`, and the `scripts/ci/*.sh` gates no Rust job executes) now runs Shell Tests and Security Audit but skips Check Rust, Backend Unit Tests, Code Coverage and Backend Integration Tests, about 65 pool-minutes per run. Other workflow files, `ci.yml`, the toolchain pin and every script a Rust job runs still run them: the backend's own tests read every file under `.github/workflows/`. On a push, `scripts/ci/resolve-verified-tree.sh` skips the Rust jobs when the pushed commit's tree is identical to the head of the merged pull request, that head contained the pushed commit's parent, and its CI Complete, Check Rust and Backend Unit Tests all passed; integration is skipped only if it also passed there. Pushes that change `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock` or the toolchain still run, so `main` keeps saving the Rust cache, and any lookup error runs the jobs. CI Complete accepts those skips the way it already accepts the version-bump-only skip. `test-ci-change-classification.sh` and `test-resolve-verified-tree.sh` pin both decisions in Shell Tests. CI-only; nothing shipped changes.

- **CI builds the backend's test binaries once per run instead of three times: `🧪 Backend Unit Tests` is now also the coverage run and the integration run** (#4208, #3124). The unit, coverage and integration jobs each compiled the `artifact-keeper-backend` crate from scratch on the self-hosted pool, which no cache can hold, and the 17.5k-test unit suite ran twice -- 37 of the ~65 pool-minutes a pull-request push cost went to the three leaf-crate compiles. The unit job now builds once with `cargo llvm-cov` instrumentation (keeping the coverage job's memory guards: debuginfo off, 4-way compile parallelism, the single SIGKILL retry), runs the unit suite once, writes `lcov.info` from that run, and then runs the pure integration targets and the PostgreSQL integration suites from the same build, the latter on pushes and on backend-touching pull requests as before. The integration suites are serialized by a `kind(test)` entry in `.config/nextest.toml`'s `db-serial` test group instead of `cargo test --test-threads=1`. The 50% floor, the 70% new-code gate and the duplication gate move to a `coverage-gates` job on a GitHub-hosted runner that reads the uploaded report, still under the `📊 Code Coverage` name and still advisory. The `test-backend-integration` job and its `🔗 Backend Integration Tests` check are gone; that check was never a required context. When a runner exports `AK_PERSISTENT_TARGET_DIR`, the unit job builds there, so the dependency graph survives between runs; without it the job uses the ephemeral checkout `target/` as before. A follow-up (#4209) removed the dead `integration` change-detection output and moved `.config/nextest.toml` and `scripts/ci/run-measured-build.sh` into the backend classification, so a pull request touching only them runs the integration suites.

- **Code coverage becomes a merge gate: it measures production code only, diffs against the true merge base, and is rolled out shadow-first with a grace date and an audited maintainer override** (#4220). The coverage floor and the new-code gate counted inline `#[cfg(test)]` modules as covered code; they are 65% of the instrumented lines at ~98% hit, so the old 50% floor read 90.4% while production code sat at 76.6%, and a pull request that added well-tested test code and untested production code could pass the 70% new-code gate. `scripts/ci/coverage-gate.py` now excludes those modules (the rule `jscpd-prepare-sources.py` already applies, plus files declared by a `#[cfg(test)] mod x;`) from both gates, lists every uncovered new line in the job summary, and the floor is recalibrated to 76% of production lines. The new-code diff is taken from the merge base the compare API reports for the measured merge commit (`scripts/ci/coverage-merge-base.sh`) instead of a 200-commit shallow walk that fell back to the base tip, so branches far behind `main` no longer count other PRs' lines as their own (#1646). The duplication gate stays advisory.

  `✅ CI Complete` now decides whether a coverage failure blocks, from `.github/coverage-gate.json`: in `shadow` mode (this change) it only reports what it would do. With `"mode": "enforce"`, a floor or new-code failure, or a run that measured nothing, fails CI Complete unless the pull request was created before `enforce_after` (2026-10-08), is a draft, carries the `coverage-grace` label, or has a maintainer override: the `coverage-override` label applied by a user with admin or maintain permission plus a `/coverage-override <reason>` comment by such a user, with both names and the reason written to the job summary. A Backend Unit Tests job skipped by the existing skip rules needs no coverage; a failed one fails the gate with that reason. The workflow now also runs when a draft is marked ready for review, so the draft exemption cannot outlive the draft. CI-only; nothing shipped changes.

- **CI's per-PR backend image now builds with a lighter `ci` Cargo profile; published images are unchanged** (#4222). `🐳 Build Backend Image` spent most of its time in the release profile's thin LTO over a single codegen unit, for an image that only feeds the smoke E2E job and is never pushed. The root `Cargo.toml` gains `[profile.ci]` (inherits `release`, so the binary is still stripped, with `lto = false`, `codegen-units = 16`, `opt-level = 2`), and `docker/Dockerfile.backend` gains a `CARGO_PROFILE` build argument (default `release`) used by the `cargo chef cook` step, the `cargo build` step and the `target/<profile>/` path the runtime stage copies the binary from. Only that CI job passes `CARGO_PROFILE=ci`: measured at `-j8`, the backend compile drops from 601 s to 317 s at the same peak memory, for a 97 MiB instead of 81 MiB stripped binary. `docker-publish.yml` (the images `release.yml` certifies), `e2e.yml` and the compose files keep `release`, so what ships is built exactly as before.

- **CI runs the backend unit tests as five shards on GitHub-hosted runners, and gains scheduled whole-repo duplication, mesh and OCI-on-S3 runs** (#4234, #4260, #4247, #4243, #4194, #4383). The instrumented unit-test build peaked at 16.7 GiB in one rustc process and kept being killed on the self-hosted pool; inline test modules now carry an `ak_test_shard` gate and run as a five-leg matrix on `ubuntu-latest`, aggregated under the same required `🧪 Backend Unit Tests` check (#4234). A module without a gate now warns and runs in exactly one leg instead of failing Check Rust (#4260), and the one module that landed ungated was gated (#4247). The coverage gate warns when the report holds lines past the end of a file, the signature of stale coverage objects (#4243). Dependabot no longer proposes the hand-managed Rust toolchain pin or `x509-cert` majors that sigstore cannot build against (#4194). The scheduled workflow adds a weekly whole-repo duplication report (#1619), a nightly two-peer mesh end-to-end run that now actually syncs an artifact (#1936), and a nightly OCI push/pull against MinIO and the filesystem backend (#1529) (#4383). No shipped behaviour changes.

- **An npm virtual repository with a private member now serves its packument from the computed-packument cache, and consults its members concurrently instead of one after another** (#4240, #3951). Every virtual packument request walked its members serially — `collect_virtual_packument` awaited each member inside a `for` loop — so a virtual over N remote members cost roughly the *sum* of N upstream round trips on a cold path, and a member that did not have the package still cost a full one. On top of that, #3323 had to make every virtual with a non-public member ineligible for the #2166 cache: the merge is narrowed to the members the caller may read, the cache key carried nothing about the caller, and a shared entry would have served one caller's view to another. A virtual that aggregates anything internal has a private member by construction, so in practice those virtuals recomputed the full merge on every request, and no cache tier — including a shared `NPM_PACKUMENT_CACHE_REDIS_URL` backend — could reach them.

  **Members are now consulted concurrently, with byte-identical output.** The merge resolves contributions in priority-order batches with `join_all` — the shape #2069 already gave the other formats' aggregating walk — and folds them in priority order, so `merge_packument_into`, which lets the higher-priority member win a version or dist-tag, sees exactly the sequence it did before. The first member in priority order whose contribution errors still fails the merge, and a member miss still never does. Memory stays bounded by the #2665 metadata budget whatever the walk shape: each remote fetch reserves its cap from a process-wide budget that waits rather than failing, so concurrency cannot raise the ceiling or silently drop a member, and each member holds exactly one reservation and reserves nothing further while holding it, so the walk cannot form the hold-and-wait #4145/#4170 removed. The batch width is bounded so one request holds at most half the budget's slices — 4 concurrent member fetches on the default 1 GiB `AK_PROXY_METADATA_BUDGET_BYTES` — and a budget shrunk below two slices falls back to the serial walk, so a wide virtual cannot monopolise the budget other requests share.

  **A virtual's cache entry is keyed by the caller's authorized member list.** The merged document depends on the caller only through `authorized_virtual_members`, so it is a pure function of that ordered list: the list is resolved once per request, a digest of its ordered member ids becomes the third key segment (`{repo}:{package}:m{digest}:{variant}:{encoding}:{base}`), and the entry is computed from exactly that list rather than from a caller — which is what lets the background stale-while-revalidate refresh, which has no caller, recompute precisely the document its key names. Callers with identical visibility share one entry; callers with different visibility get different entries and cannot read each other's. Remote keys are unchanged; existing virtual entries move to the new layout once, so each all-public virtual recomputes its packuments once after upgrade and its old shared-cache entries expire with the stale window. Age-gated virtuals still bypass the cache entirely.

  **A definitive 404 now evicts only the member list that produced it.** The cache evicted the whole package whenever a compute returned 404/410, so that upstream unpublishes and takedowns propagate. With one entry per member list that was wrong — a 404 for one list says nothing about a larger list that includes a member still carrying the package — and it would have let any caller flush every other caller's entries on demand. A virtual's 404 now evicts that list's entries only, and every list still evicts on its own next refresh, so a takedown still reaches all of them. A caller who may read no member is answered with the existing not-found body before the cache is touched. To make list-scoped eviction work on the shared backend, the Redis `invalidate_prefix` now honours the contract the backend trait already documented — drop every entry whose key starts with the prefix — by filtering the package's key index; previously any prefix narrower than a whole package was silently a no-op there. Eviction for every existing caller, all of which pass whole-package prefixes, is unchanged.

- **Test suites hardened against the flakes seen during the 1.11.0 cycle** (#4255, #4310, #4354, #4360, #4006). The system-stats proxy-cache test asserts inside one repeatable-read snapshot, so concurrent writers no longer skew its deltas (#4250); the `upload_service` tests run in the serial database group, because the staging reaper they call purges every test's chunks (#4309); the OCI commit-time PATCH rejection test no longer races request authentication against a 200 ms budget (#4353). The RPM repodata handler reads a router without the auth layer as an anonymous caller instead of answering 500, which had failed the RPM metadata integration test; production always mounts that layer (#4381). The `rcgen` dev-dependency moves to 0.14 with the test OIDC issuer updated to its API (#4006). No shipped behaviour changes.

- **Creating a webhook now rejects event names that can never fire** (#4419). `POST /api/v1/webhooks` stored any string in `events`, so a plausible spelling such as `artifact.uploaded` (the internal event-bus name) was accepted while deliveries are matched on `artifact_uploaded`, and the webhook silently never fired. Every entry is now checked against the subscribable set (`artifact_uploaded`, `artifact_deleted`, `repository_created`, `repository_deleted`, `user_created`, `user_deleted`, `build_started`, `build_completed`, `build_failed`, `age_gate_queued`, `age_gate_approved`, `age_gate_rejected`, `age_gate_reopened`); an unknown name returns 400 naming the offending entries and listing the accepted ones. Webhooks already stored with an unknown name are left as they are and still never fire; recreate them with the accepted spelling.

- **The OCI registry now records every committed manifest in a first-class `oci_manifests` table, independent of its tags** (#4433, #1683). Manifest existence used to be inferred from `oci_tags`, so a manifest whose last tag was gone became invisible even though its bytes were still stored. Migration 268 adds the table (online-safe: a new, empty table); every push, proxy-cache fill and migration import writes its row in the same transaction as the tag, a delete by digest removes it once nothing (no tag, no parent index) still holds the manifest, and a background startup backfill records manifests pushed before the upgrade (reading each body from storage, idempotent, failures logged and retried on the next start). Nothing reads the table yet: moving manifest GET/HEAD/DELETE, the Referrers API and storage GC onto it follows in later releases.

- **`ak_http_request_duration_seconds` is now exported as a Prometheus histogram with buckets, not as a summary** (#4434, #3954). The Prometheus recorder had no buckets configured, so the request-latency histogram rendered as a summary: per-series `quantile="0|0.5|0.9|0.95|0.99|0.999|1"` values pre-computed over the exporter's own window, which cannot be aggregated across replicas, paths or a chosen time range. The metric now exports `ak_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{le=...}` series with bounds 0.005, 0.01, 0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2.5, 5, 10, 30 and 60 seconds (plus `+Inf`), so `histogram_quantile(0.99, sum by (le) (rate(ak_http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])))` gives a fleet-wide percentile. `_sum` and `_count` are unchanged. The labels are unchanged too, but each label set now exports 16 series instead of 9 (14 `_bucket` series plus `_sum` and `_count`, where the summary had 7 quantiles plus `_sum` and `_count`), so operators with tight series budgets should expect this metric to grow by about 78%.

  **Breaking for dashboards and alerts:** the `quantile` series of this metric are gone. A panel or rule that selects `ak_http_request_duration_seconds{quantile="0.99"}` must be rewritten with `histogram_quantile()` over the `_bucket` series. Other histograms keep their existing export.

- **Promotion `gate_results` also list every scan-policy predicate that was checked and held, with the reason** (#4556). A successful promotion reported only the scan and unscanned rules, so a UI could not show that the attestation was verified, the license allowed or the channel allowed: those predicates were evaluated but only their failures were recorded. Single and bulk promotion now add one passed `policy-predicate` entry per configured conda or origin predicate that held, its reason carrying the predicate token, for example `Policy 'release-gate' [conda.license]: license 'mit' is allowed` or `Policy 'release-gate' [conda.attestation]: attestation is verified: verified CEP-27 attestation (sigstore-key, identity ci, issuer key:...)`. Failures are reported exactly as before.

- **A token scoped to a virtual repository reads the virtual's members through it** (closes #4559). A repository token minted on a virtual repository, or a user token whose `repo_selector` names it, can now read the virtual's members on requests routed through the virtual (the format endpoints such as `/conda/<virtual>/...` and `/pypi/<virtual>/simple/...`, the `/t/<token>/` forms, and the virtual's REST member listing, artifact listing, download and storage total), without its scope naming the members. Before, such a token was refused every member and a virtual conda channel answered `404 Virtual repository has no accessible members`, so a per-repository consumer token could not be issued for the one channel URL consumers use. Each member is still checked against the token owner's grants, so a member the owner cannot read stays out of the listings and indexes and cannot be downloaded through the virtual. A request to a member's own URL with such a token is still refused (404), which keeps per-virtual policies such as the conda package allowlist (#4576) from being bypassed through the member. Writes are unchanged: deploying through a virtual still needs the token's scope to name the hosted member. Scoping a token to the members, or to the virtual and its members, keeps working.

### Deprecated

- **`POST /api/v1/users/{id}/roles` is deprecated in favour of `POST /api/v1/permissions`** (#3522). Roles assigned through it are written to `user_roles`, which is identity and SSO role-mapping metadata that no authorization gate reads, so the call never granted access to any repository (#3387). The endpoint keeps working unchanged, but it is now flagged `deprecated` in the OpenAPI spec and every successful response carries a `Deprecation: @1791244800` header (RFC 9745) and `Link: </api/v1/permissions>; rel="successor-version"`. To give a user, service account or group access, create a fine-grained grant with `POST /api/v1/permissions` (repository or project targets). No removal date has been set.

### Fixed
- **The stock Caddyfile routes rattler's `/t/<token>` conda prefix to the backend** (#4564). #4555 added the `/t/<token>/conda/<repo>/...` URL layout that `pixi auth login --conda-token` produces, and the stock compose stack's Caddy sent those requests to the web UI, which answered an HTML 404. The route is in the shipped `docker/Caddyfile`, and the CI check that every backend format mount has a `reverse_proxy` line covers it.
- **The backend image's bundled `grype` and `buildctl`, and the scanner adapter's `trivy`, are rebuilt on Go 1.27.2 / 1.26.9 with `golang.org/x/net` 0.60.0** (#4618). Three HIGH Go advisories published on 2026-10-10 against those binaries, not Artifact Keeper's code, turned the image publish gate red; nothing was added to `.trivyignore`, the binaries are rebuilt against fixed versions (details under #3579 and #3698 in Security).
- **Streaming ratchet and the stalled-LFS cap test** (#4617). The shared conda merge's own error line (never an artifact or metadata body, capped at 1 MiB) is read once so every waiting request gets the same answer, and is allowlisted in the streaming invariant as such; the stalled-upload cap test waits for admission before counting. No runtime behaviour change.
- **The live-tree fragment check accepts a release-prep tip** (#4628). `scripts/ci/test-changelog-fragments.sh` case 14 failed on a tree whose fragments the release prep had already rendered and deleted; with no fragments and no `## [Unreleased]` entries, "nothing to assemble" now passes, and an invalid fragment still fails. No runtime behaviour change.

- **Maven hosted uploads commit the artifact row and its metadata in one transaction** (#3587, #3814). The `ON CONFLICT` upsert that closed #3587 and the dependent `artifact_metadata` write ran as two autocommit statements, so a metadata failure after the row landed left a live artifact with no Maven metadata, and a concurrent republish could observe the row before its metadata existed. Both now commit together, matching the shared `ArtifactService` upload path; the quarantine upload-hold and catalog registration run after the commit as before. The #3587 regression now runs its eight racers on a multi-thread runtime so the statements genuinely overlap.

- **Quality checks now read artifacts from the repository's configured storage backend, so they work on S3, GCS and Azure** (#3736, #4090). Both ways of running checks, the automatic check after an upload and `POST /api/v1/quality/checks/trigger` for an artifact or a repository, read the artifact from the default filesystem backend, so a check of anything stored in object storage failed with "Storage key not found" even though the object existed. Checks now read from the backend the repository is configured with.

- **Proxy-cache publishes work on Google Cloud Storage's S3-compatible API** (#3737). GCS answers a PUT without `Content-Length` with `411 Length Required`, including the empty-bodied CopyObject that moves a staged proxy-cache object to its live key, so on `STORAGE_BACKEND=s3` pointed at `storage.googleapis.com` every publish failed and the cache never filled. A copy rejected with 411 is now retried as a signed CopyObject carrying `Content-Length: 0`, and the backend uses that form for every later copy; the multipart `UploadPartCopy` path sends the header too.

- **Warm Maven proxy-cache hits no longer perform synchronous PostgreSQL I/O on every GET** (#3778). The Maven resolver now reads repository metadata from the shared 60-second in-process repo cache that `repo_visibility_middleware` already maintains (the enforcement columns `promotion_only`/`age_gate_*`/`curation_*` ride the same cache entry and are covered by the fleet-wide invalidation trigger, so gates cannot go stale), and the `proxy_cache_artifacts` upsert + `proxy_download_statistics` insert are recorded from a bounded background task instead of blocking the response — falling back to inline recording when the background limiter is saturated, so download statistics stay exact under load. A warm hit is now memory lookup + cache storage read, with database latency off the critical path.

- **npm Remote repositories now rewrite and proxy tarball URLs from upstreams that do not use the npmjs `/-/` layout, such as GitHub Packages** (#3785). A packument served through a Remote whose upstream is `https://npm.pkg.github.com` kept GitHub's `/download/@scope/pkg/<version>/<hash>` tarball URLs, so clients bypassed the proxy and failed without GitHub credentials. Any tarball URL on the configured upstream's host is now rewritten to this repository's `/npm/<repo>/@scope/pkg/-/pkg-<version>.tgz` route, and the download fetches the original upstream URL with the repository's upstream credentials only when it is on the same origin (scheme, host and port; URLs carrying a username or password are rejected). Virtual repositories resolve these tarballs through the normal priority-ordered member walk, so member priority, local ownership and caching behave as before. The separate proxy-cache catalog "Artifact not found" on delete reported alongside this is tracked in #4305.

- **Local RPM repositories now publish dependency metadata in `primary.xml`, so `dnf` resolves dependencies** (#3801). Each package's `<format>` block now carries `rpm:provides`, `rpm:requires` (with `flags`/`epoch`/`ver`/`rel` and `pre="1"`), `rpm:conflicts`, `rpm:obsoletes` and the weak-dependency lists, plus `rpm:header-range`, vendor, buildhost, packager, the header's epoch, build time, installed and archive sizes, and the primary file list. `filelists.xml` now lists every file. The output follows `createrepo_c` element for element. Packages uploaded before this release are fixed automatically: the first repodata render reads each one's stored header (a ranged read, not the whole package) and records the missing metadata, so no manual backfill or re-upload is needed.
  RPM uploads whose header exceeds rpm's own header limits (more than 65,535 index entries, a data section over 32 MiB, malformed entry counts) declares more than 262,144 dependency and file entries or expands to more names and paths than its size warrants (64 KiB plus four times the header, counting 64 bytes per entry, at most 64 MiB), or whose metadata contains control characters XML cannot carry, are now rejected with `400 Bad Request`, as `createrepo_c` would refuse to index them. Stored packages in that state are marked unparseable once and served without dependency data rather than breaking the repository's metadata.

- **LDAP group memberships and admin status are now re-synced against the directory on a schedule, and users removed from the directory can be deactivated automatically** (#3830). A federated LDAP user's standing used to be re-evaluated only when they logged in, so removing someone from an Active Directory group, or deleting them, left their API tokens and sessions working indefinitely, and the documented `LDAP_SYNC_INTERVAL` was never read. A background job now runs every `LDAP_SYNC_INTERVAL` seconds (default 3600, `0` disables, minimum 60) on one replica at a time. It re-reads each active LDAP user with the service account of the provider they last logged in through, re-syncs their LDAP group memberships, and recomputes admin from the provider's admin group exactly as login does, for users whose login provider is recorded. A user removed from the admin group loses admin and their tokens are revoked. Demotions are capped like deactivations, and a pass never leaves the instance without an active admin, counting deactivations too. Membership removals are capped the same way. Local accounts are never touched.
  **Upgrade note:** deactivation is opt-in. With `LDAP_SYNC_DEACTIVATE=true`, a user whose entry is gone, or no longer matches the provider's user filter, is deactivated and their API tokens, access tokens and refresh tokens are revoked; without it such users are only logged. An entry missing from its DN is not treated as gone if a username search finds the username elsewhere. Nothing is re-synced from that other entry, because it may be a different person who reused the username. A user who has not logged in since the upgrade is treated as gone only when every enabled provider covering their DN agrees. A directory error, timeout or referral never deactivates anyone, and a pass that would deactivate more than `LDAP_SYNC_MAX_DEACTIVATE` (default 25) users of a provider, or more than one user and more than `LDAP_SYNC_MAX_DEACTIVATE_PERCENT` (default 10) percent of them, deactivates nobody of that provider and logs an error. Package-manager clients still authenticate with a personal API token; LDAP username/password Basic auth on format endpoints is not implemented.

- **Repository-management endpoints now require scopes an API token can actually carry** (#3831, #4271, #4270). Fourteen handlers (repository create/update, cache TTL and invalidation, npm scope policy, PyPI tracks, virtual members, upstream auth, egress proxy, routing rules) gated on the bare `write` scope, which is deliberately not mintable — only session auth and `admin`/`*` tokens could ever call them, and a `write:repositories` token held by a global admin got a 403. They now require `write:repositories`; the read-side handlers (`get_npm_scope_policy`, `get_egress_proxy`, `test_upstream`) require `read:repositories`, `DELETE /repositories/{key}` requires `delete:repositories`, and `DELETE /repositories/{key}/artifacts/{path}` plus the chunked-upload cancel endpoint require `delete:artifacts`, so a `write:repositories` token can drive CI automation such as evicting stale proxy-cache entries. (The Web UI's token dialog still maps its "Write" type to `write:artifacts`, which does not cover repository management; mint `write:repositories` explicitly until the dialog offers it.) All existing per-repository permission checks are unchanged, and `GET /repositories/{key}/test-upstream` — which probes the upstream with the repository's stored credentials — now requires repository admin like the other upstream-configuration reads.

- **Lowering a remote repository's cache TTL now applies to entries that are already cached** (#3832). The proxy stamped an absolute `expires_at` into each cache entry when it was written and trusted that stamp on every read, so after an operator lowered a remote's TTL (for example from 30 days to 4 hours) every mutable index cached under the old value (PyPI simple indexes, npm packuments, OCI tag manifests) kept being served without contacting upstream until its original expiry, up to 30 days later. Every freshness gate (buffered and streaming reads, the presigned-redirect probe, the key-only cache reads and the APT dists check) now uses one shared rule: a mutable entry expires at the earlier of its stamped expiry and the moment the *current* TTL has passed since it was cached or last revalidated. Immutable artifacts are unaffected. Raising a TTL takes effect from each entry's next revalidation. A `304 Not Modified` revalidation now also updates the entry's `cached_at`. The TTL override is now read through a 30-second in-process cache instead of a database query per read. A TTL change takes effect immediately on the replica that handled the request and within 30 seconds on the others.

- **OTLP `http/protobuf` never exported a span** (#3833, #3834). `opentelemetry-otlp`'s `reqwest-client` feature, added in #812, selects the *async* reqwest client, which is first in the builder's priority order. `BatchSpanProcessor` drives exports from a dedicated OS thread with no Tokio runtime, so the first flush panicked with `there is no reactor running`, killing the processor thread while the process kept serving — every later span dropped with a `BatchSpanProcessor.OnEnd.AfterShutdown` warning, one per request. The feature is removed so the crate's default `reqwest-blocking-client` supplies the client. `grpc` is unaffected.

- **NuGet V3 search, registration, autocomplete and the V2 feed report a package id with the casing its `.nuspec` declared** (#3835). A push stores the id lowercased for case-insensitive lookups, and every read surface echoed that stored name, so `Some.Package.Id` came back as `some.package.id`. Every surface now reads the id from the package's single catalog row, which keeps the first push's spelling, so a later push with different casing, a deleted version or a version without push metadata no longer changes it. V3 URLs stay lowercased as the protocol requires; the V2 feed's entry and content URLs carry the reported id, as nuget.org's V2 feed does. Packages pushed before this fix report their authored casing too, without republishing.

- **Virtual repositories whose members are themselves virtual repositories now list and resolve the nested members' content** (#3840). Member expansion was a single-level join, so a nested virtual contributed nothing: the flat listing, the Maven grouped view, the Docker tag view and every download-resolution path saw zero content through it. Expansion is now recursive — leaves are inlined at the nested virtual's slot in depth-first priority order, so listing and download resolution pick the same member for a duplicate coordinate — with an explicit cycle guard (cycle-closing edges are skipped and logged) and the same 32-level depth cap the write-time cycle check enforces. npm packument and cargo index cache invalidation now also reach every ancestor virtual, not just direct parents, so writes to a leaf no longer leave a nested virtual's cached document stale. The shared-cache gates (any private or age-gated member disables the caller-independent packument / sparse-index / Maven document cache), download attribution, the HuggingFace ETag, the PyPI PEP 708 isolation decision and the Maven `prefixes.txt` union all follow the same recursive walk. Visibility through a nested virtual is decided by the leaf's ACL alone: intermediate virtuals are transparent grouping (the convention the storage aggregate already used), so a caller who can read the top virtual and a leaf reads that leaf even without a grant on the virtual in between.

- **Concurrent pushes of one blob to different repositories no longer risk a spurious `503 BLOB_UPLOAD_INVALID`** (#3851). The OCI upload cleanup journal kept one row per storage key across the whole database, so two pushes of the same digest to different repositories shared a row: the first to commit deleted it, and if that repository was deleted before the second push committed, the second push lost its only proof that a peer (not a cleanup sweep) had removed the row and was refused. Journal rows are now unique per repository and key (migration 243), so a push's row can only be cleared by a push to the same repository, its own repository's deletion, or a sweep. Content-addressed dedup is unchanged; on backends where repositories share one object namespace a cleanup sweep no longer deletes an object while another repository has a fresh journal row for it, and registration and the sweep's tombstone serialize per key.

  On shared-namespace backends a repository delete no longer deletes journaled `oci-blobs/<digest>` objects directly (another repository may have committed the same object); it records them as OCI GC candidates, and the candidate sweep deletes each one after its 24-hour grace unless another repository references it or holds a cleanup-journal row for it.

- **CycloneDX SBOMs emit compound SPDX license expressions as `expression`, so Dependency-Track evaluates them against license policy** (#3866). A component license such as `MIT AND PSF-2.0` or `Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception` was written as a free-form `license.name`, which Dependency-Track stores as an unresolved license name: every license policy then failed on that component even when each operand was approved, and names over 255 characters were truncated. A string that parses as a compound SPDX expression (`AND`, `OR`, `WITH`, parentheses) is now emitted as `{"expression": ...}`; known single SPDX identifiers still use `license.id`, and free-form text such as `Public Domain` or `GPL v2 or later` still uses `license.name`, so arbitrary strings never reach `license.id` (#1474). Scanner-derived multi-license values (a Trivy or Grype package reporting several licenses) are now joined with `AND` instead of `OR`: the scanner's list says every one of those licenses applies, not that the consumer may pick one, and an `OR` exported as an evaluable expression would let a package carrying GPL or a proprietary `LicenseRef-` alongside MIT pass a policy that approves MIT. Scan results stored before this release keep their `OR` value until the artifact is rescanned. SBOMs already imported into Dependency-Track must be regenerated and re-imported to pick this up.

- **Creating a lifecycle policy with `"enabled": false` now creates it disabled** (#3869). `POST /api/v1/admin/lifecycle` silently dropped the `enabled` field and the row fell through to the column default, so a retention policy meant to be reviewed first was live (and eligible for the scheduled sweep) until a follow-up `PATCH` disabled it. The create request now accepts an optional `enabled`; omitting it keeps the existing enabled-by-default behaviour, and a disabled policy can still be previewed.

- **A remote NuGet repository now lets a client discover package versions it has not restored yet** (#3870). Restoring through a remote repository worked, but `dotnet list package --outdated` failed with `Object reference not set to an instance of an object` and the Visual Studio and Rider version pickers stayed empty. For a package with a long history, such as `Serilog`, the upstream registration index splits its versions into pages, and the index handed to the client pointed at `/v3/registration/{id}/page/{lower}/{upper}.json` URLs that AK answered with `404`. Those pages are now proxied and rewritten onto AK the same way the index is, through the remote repository or each remote member of a virtual repository in priority order. The package id and every path segment are validated before any upstream fetch, and the upstream URL is built from encoded path segments, so a client cannot add a query, a fragment or a `..` hop. A V2 upstream links no pages and answers `404`. The service index also advertises `RegistrationsBaseUrl/3.6.0` and a `SearchAutocompleteService`. Autocomplete answers package ids and versions from a hosted repository's rows, from a remote repository's upstream, or from both merged for a virtual repository, and honours `skip`/`take`. An upstream that advertises no autocomplete service, which includes every V2 feed, gets an empty answer instead of a `502`. A remote repository that still holds cached `artifacts` rows for a package now merges the upstream version list into them, deduplicated case-insensitively, instead of listing only the cached versions. If the upstream fails, the cached versions are returned.

- **Ansible Galaxy pagination links now stay inside the repository URL the client configured** (#3873). When `ansible-galaxy` was pointed at a Galaxy repository's generic download URL (`/api/v1/repositories/{key}/download/`), a Remote repository streamed the upstream's JSON verbatim, so `links.next` was the upstream's root-relative `/api/v3/plugin/...` path and following it left the repository (401/404). Galaxy API reads on that URL, and the collection tarballs they advertise, are now answered by the Galaxy handler itself. Every link a client follows (`href`, `versions_url`, `download_url` and the `first`/`previous`/`next`/`last` paging links) is built from the path the client requested, so it stays under whichever of `/ansible/{key}/` or the generic download URL the client was configured with. Requests without paging parameters still receive the complete list as a single page.

  Behaviour change: the collection and version lists on the `/ansible/{key}/` route now honour `limit`/`offset` as well. `ansible-galaxy` sends `?limit=100`, so a collection with more versions is now served in pages with a `next` link, where it previously came back as one unpaged list.

- **PyPI PEP 658 `.whl.metadata` now works for PyTorch remote indexes and for large local wheels such as `torch`** (#3886). Remote resolution compared the upstream index's percent-encoded hrefs (`torch-2.12.0%2Bcpu-...whl`) against the decoded request filename, so every local-version wheel missed and fell back to a reconstructed `{upstream}/{project}/{file}` URL that PyTorch's flat layout does not serve (403 on `download.pytorch.org`, reported as 502; 404 on `download-r2.pytorch.org`). Hrefs are now matched on their decoded basename too, so the advertised URL is used verbatim, and an upstream 403 on the sidecar falls back to extracting METADATA from the wheel just as a 404 does (ordinary downloads still surface 403 as 502). Locally, METADATA extraction was refused for wheels with more than 10,000 entries (`torch` has 12,704), so the advertised sidecar 404'd while the wheel downloaded; the lookup now allows large wheels and reads only the root `*.dist-info/METADATA`, never a vendored copy. The wheel that the sidecar fallback reads is now fetched without touching the proxy cache and is checked against the index's `#sha256=` before METADATA is extracted; previously it was cached, unverified, under the same key wheel downloads are served from. Upload validation now checks the same root `*.dist-info/METADATA` the sidecar serves.

- **Conan v2 API now answers 404 for a missing recipe, revision or package instead of an empty 200** (#3887). The recipe revisions list, a revision's file list, the package search for a revision, the package revisions list and a package revision's file list returned `200` with an empty body when the reference did not exist, so the Conan client treated the remote as authoritative and stopped instead of falling through to the next remote. They now return `404` with the official Conan server's wording (`Recipe not found: '<ref>'`, `Binary package not found: '<ref>:<package_id>'`). A package search on an existing revision with no binaries still returns `200 {}`. Private repositories still answer `401` before the lookup, and virtual repositories only consult members the caller can read, so the 404 reveals nothing about content the caller cannot see.

- **Authentication audit events now record the client IP address** (#3888). Login, logout, token-refresh, SSO (OIDC/SAML/LDAP), and TOTP second-factor events were written to `audit_log` with `ip_address = NULL`. A new request-scoped client-IP context, resolved from the TCP peer with `X-Forwarded-For` believed only when the peer is inside a configured `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` range (the same trusted-proxy policy the rate limiter keys on), is now attached to every authentication audit entry. Events emitted outside a request (background jobs) still record NULL rather than a sentinel.

- **A failed remote NuGet resolution now logs which step failed, the upstream and the status** (#3899). The reported failure (a paginated registration page such as `registration/serilog/page/0.1.6/1.2.47.json` answering 404, which `dotnet` surfaces as "Object reference not set to an instance of an object") was fixed in 1.9.0 by #3871, which added the registration page route. A remote NuGet failure still reached the log only as the request's final status; service-index discovery, registration index and page fetches, and flat-container version-list and package fetches now each record the step, the redacted upstream and fetch URLs, and the status (INFO for an upstream 404, WARN otherwise).

- **The `LDAP_*` environment bootstrap no longer undoes admin-API changes to the env-managed LDAP provider on every restart** (#3904). The per-boot reconcile used to write every field it derived and force `is_enabled`, `priority` and (with `LDAP_USE_STARTTLS` unset) `use_starttls` back to hard-coded values, so disabling the provider, raising its priority or enabling STARTTLS through the admin API silently reverted on the next boot. It now follows the same ownership rule as the OIDC bootstrap (#3507): a field an `LDAP_*` variable sets is written, a field the environment set on the previous boot and no longer sets is reset to its default, and every other field keeps its stored value. `is_enabled`, `priority` and the per-provider TLS options are never touched after the provider is created. `LDAP_ADMIN_GROUP_DN` stays env-definitive, like `OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP`: unsetting it clears the admin group. A field changed through the admin API stops being env-owned, so removing its variable later keeps the admin's value. Every stored value a boot overwrites or removes is logged at WARN, with a dedicated warning when STARTTLS is being turned off. Clearing the admin group does not demote users already granted admin. Ownership is recorded in the new `ldap_configs.env_owned_fields` column (migration 255).

- **Quarantine on proxy repositories now honours the release-date window on the streaming download path, and held proxied artifacts can be released individually** (#3912). Package downloads stream, and the streaming leader previously refused to open the upstream fetch at all while the Package Age Policy was enabled — a 2015 release was held exactly like today's. The leader now reads `Last-Modified` from the streaming response headers and applies the same release-date computation the buffered path uses: a package older than the configured window is served on first fetch, while a fresh one is cached under its hold and answered 409 until the window elapses (polls no longer re-fetch upstream). `proxy_cache_artifacts` gains `quarantine_until` / `quarantine_released_at` columns, and a held entry can be released without disabling the policy via `POST /api/v1/quarantine/proxy-cache/{repo_key}/release` (admin only, keyed on repository + path). Enabling quarantine on a remote repository is allowed again; virtual repositories remain refused because they carry no cache of their own — enable the policy on the member remotes.

- **Raw `PUT` uploads into S3-, GCS- and Azure-backed repositories no longer spool to local disk** (#3916). Every upload was written to a scratch file under `STORAGE_PATH` before reaching the repository's object storage, so each replica needed local disk proportional to concurrent upload volume. `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{path}` into an object-storage repository now streams the body into a staging object (`generic-upload-staging/<uuid>`) on that repository's own backend (bounded-memory multipart/block upload, digests and the size limit computed on the fly), then promotes it to the content-addressed key with a backend copy and deletes the staging object. Each staging object is tracked in a new `generic_upload_staging` table (migration 248), and the hourly upload cleanup deletes any left more than 24 hours old by an upload that was killed mid-flight. Filesystem repositories, RPM packages (header parse) and repositories with a WASM format plugin keep the local spool, as do the multipart, format-native and chunked upload paths.

- **Chunked (resumable) uploads work behind more than one backend replica** (#3918). Upload sessions assembled their bytes in `$STORAGE_PATH/.uploads/<session_id>` on whichever replica served `POST /api/v1/uploads`, so with per-pod storage a `PATCH` or `PUT .../complete` routed to another replica failed with `I/O error` or produced a corrupt object. Each chunk is now staged as its own object in the repository's storage backend and session state stays in the database, so any replica can accept any chunk and complete the session; completion reassembles the chunks into a request-scoped scratch file on the completing replica, verifies size and SHA256, and removes it afterwards.
