A chunk must now cover exactly its placeholder's byte range (`chunk_index * chunk_size`, full chunk length except the last), which every client that follows the returned `chunk_size` already does. Sessions created by an earlier server version cannot be continued after the upgrade and are refused with a clear message; restart those uploads.

  **Upgrade notes.** `PATCH /api/v1/uploads/{id}` now requires each chunk to cover exactly its placeholder range (offset `chunk_index * chunk_size`, full `chunk_size` bytes except the last chunk); a misaligned chunk gets 400. Upload sessions started before the upgrade cannot be continued and get `410 Gone` (status, PATCH and complete), which the web UI and CLI already answer by starting a new session. During a rolling upgrade, older pods cannot serve sessions created by upgraded pods, so finish the rollout promptly (or drain in-flight chunked uploads first). A peer-replication retry that replaces a stale replication session for the same path now also deletes that session's staged chunks in shared storage, whichever replica staged them (previously it only reached the local file on the replica handling the retry).

- **A corrupted stored artifact is no longer served as a complete `200` under its original `X-Checksum-Sha256`** (#3919). The generic download route (`GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/download/{path}`, including `?version=` revisions) now hashes the body incrementally while streaming it, holding back only the final chunk; if the bytes or length no longer match the recorded SHA-256, the response is aborted before that chunk and the corruption is logged with the repository and path, so no client receives a full body that contradicts the digest header. A `Range` request that covers the whole object (`bytes=0-`, a suffix at least as long as the object) is verified the same way. Memory use stays at one chunk. Proper sub-ranges and presigned redirects are not verified.

  A stored object longer than its recorded size is refused the same way instead of being served as a clean prefix. Protobuf module commit bundles are exempt, because their rows record the commit digest rather than the bundle's own SHA-256.

  **Upgrade note:** verification is on by default and costs one SHA-256 pass per full download. Some pre-existing races that used to serve bytes not matching the row now abort the download instead. These include a Maven SNAPSHOT redeployed while it is being downloaded, a promotion that failed with 409 after overwriting the target object, a backup restore over existing objects, and a NuGet or PyPI object being re-materialized during a download. Clients see a failed transfer they can retry instead of silently mismatched bytes. Set `DOWNLOAD_VERIFY_CHECKSUMS=false` to turn verification off and leave integrity checking to clients.

- **Concurrent uploads of byte-identical content no longer fail with 500 on the Azure backend** (#3920). Two uploads of the same content stream blocks to the same content-addressed blob; Azure keeps one uncommitted block list per blob, so when the first upload committed, the second's staged blocks were discarded and its Put Block List failed with `400 InvalidBlockList`, surfacing as `500 STORAGE_ERROR`. A commit that fails this way now checks the blob the other writer committed and, when it is byte-for-byte what this upload streamed (same size and SHA-256), treats the upload as successful. A commit that lost to different content still fails.

- **Failed, cancelled and abandoned chunked uploads no longer leave staged data behind** (#3922). A completion that failed (for example an Azure `InvalidBlockList` error, a checksum mismatch or a quota rejection) left the assembled multi-GiB session file on the pod's disk with nothing to reclaim it, which filled emptyDir volumes and got pods evicted. The completion's scratch copy is now removed on every path, a terminally failed or cancelled session's staged chunks are deleted immediately, and the hourly upload reaper deletes the staged chunks of any failed, cancelled, completed or expired session that still has them (recorded in the new `upload_sessions.staging_purged_at` column), on whichever replica runs it.

  Staged chunks of sessions removed by a repository or user deletion are recorded (`upload_staging_orphans`) and purged by the same reaper. A completion that fails on a transient database error before the artifact is recorded now releases the session for retry instead of failing it, so clients can re-issue the completion without re-uploading.

- **An Azure default storage backend no longer refuses to start once a remote repository exists** (#3923). The proxy cache has no Azure support, and the startup check that guarded that gap looked only at `STORAGE_BACKEND`: creating any remote repository succeeded, and the next restart exited with a fatal config error, taking the whole instance down. On a default without proxy-cache support the proxy cache now runs on the local filesystem under `STORAGE_PATH`: a remote repository created without `storage_backend` is placed on `filesystem`, served alongside Azure-backed hosted repositories, and one that explicitly names a backend the proxy cache cannot use is rejected up front with a 400 that says which `storage_backend` to use. Pre-existing ones are reported at error level at startup instead of blocking it (startup still fails closed if the filesystem proxy cache itself cannot be initialized while remote repositories exist). The messages no longer cite the unrelated #1555.

  **Multi-replica deployments:** with an Azure default, the proxy cache lives under each replica's `STORAGE_PATH` while its cache records are shared in the database, so `STORAGE_PATH` must be shared storage (for example a ReadWriteMany volume) when more than one replica serves remote repositories; otherwise purges, quarantine and scans reach only one replica's copy. The backend logs a warning at startup when remote repositories exist on such a deployment.

- **The OpenAPI description of `PUT /api/v1/uploads/{session_id}/complete` now documents both of its 409 responses, not only the checksum mismatch** (#3924, #4210). Since completion was put behind the immutable-path check, a 409 from this endpoint can also mean "Artifact version already exists and is immutable", but the spec still described every 409 as "Checksum mismatch", so clients built from it (the web UI among them) reported a checksum error for an occupied path. The two cases are only distinguishable by the response body, and they need different handling: a checksum mismatch fails the session (re-upload in a new one) and answers `{"error": "checksum mismatch: ..."}`, while an immutability conflict writes nothing, leaves the session open for a retry once the occupying artifact is deleted, and answers `{"code": "CONFLICT", "message": "Artifact version already exists and is immutable"}`. The 409 description now spells out both causes, both body shapes and what to do about each.

- **Migrated RPM repositories are indexed natively** (#3925). The importer now records each `.rpm` header's metadata exactly as an upload does, so the repodata served for a migrated RPM/YUM repository carries summaries and dependencies, and RPM is no longer reported as a file-copy-only format. A package whose header exceeds the repodata indexing limits is still migrated and listed from its filename. Conan, Conda and Debian repositories still migrate as file copies with the empty-index warning shown in the assessment and report.

- **Artifactory migrations no longer fail artifacts that take longer than 30 seconds to download** (#3926). The Artifactory source client used a 30 s whole-request timeout that also covered the response body, so every artifact larger than about 30 s of source bandwidth failed with "error decoding response body". Streamed downloads are now bounded by a connect timeout and a read-idle timeout (a stalled source is still cut off), while the buffered API calls and connection tests keep a whole-request ceiling (300 s). All three are tunable for Artifactory and Nexus sources with `MIGRATION_SOURCE_READ_TIMEOUT_SECS`, `MIGRATION_SOURCE_CONNECT_TIMEOUT_SECS` and `MIGRATION_SOURCE_BUFFERED_TIMEOUT_SECS`.

- **Migrated Maven repositories now serve `maven-metadata.xml`** (#3927). The importer stored Maven files without the coordinate metadata that `maven-metadata.xml` generation reads, so `LATEST`/`RELEASE` resolution fell through to another repository. Each migrated Maven file now records its groupId/artifactId/version, and re-running the migration job repairs repositories migrated before this fix without re-transferring anything.

- **The pre-migration assessment reports real artifact counts** (#3928). It read a one-row listing page's `range.total` as the repository size, which neither Artifactory nor Nexus provides, so every repository counted as at most one artifact and the job's denominator was seeded from that. Repositories are now counted by a bounded listing walk; the assessment flags counts that are only a lower bound (`artifact_count_exact` / `total_artifacts_exact`), and the job's total is seeded only from an exact count.

- **Concurrent publishes of the same package version no longer fail the catalog upsert with a `size_bytes` NOT NULL violation** (#3931). Two racing publishers could hit a statement-snapshot race in the `package_versions` upsert CTE that wrote `COALESCE(NULL, NULL)` into `packages.size_bytes`; the statement now retries on exactly that 23502 race with a fresh snapshot. The publish itself was never affected — the symptom was a missing catalog row plus an error log.

- **A Cargo virtual member whose sparse-index body is stored content-encoded now contributes its versions to the merged index instead of silently dropping them** (#3937). The ungated Virtual member index fetch used the coding-blind `proxy_fetch_capped`, so a gzip-stored member body parsed as zero NDJSON lines and the member contributed nothing to the merged sparse index with no error — cargo then could not resolve versions the upstream plainly published. The fetch now goes through the encoding-aware `proxy_fetch_capped_encoded` plus the same decode step the age-gated member path already used.

- **`artifact.uploaded` webhooks now fire for CRAN, Hex, Ansible, Puppet and RubyGems publishes, promotions, approved promotions, Git LFS uploads and chunked uploads** (#3939). These paths wrote their `artifacts` row directly and never produced the event, so a webhook or email subscription on `artifact.uploaded` heard nothing for them. Each now emits exactly one event, carrying the new artifact's id, its repository and the uploader, the same shape the generic upload API sends; a promotion's event belongs to the target repository. CRAN, Hex, Ansible, Puppet and RubyGems publishes also now appear on the Packages page, like the other native formats. A test now fails the build when a handler writes `artifacts` without producing the event.

- **npm virtual repositories with a private member no longer re-fetch a member's definitive 404 on every packument request, and buffered proxy-cache hits no longer read the same `__cache_meta__.json` twice** (#3951). The virtual member walk now keeps a short-lived in-process negative cache per (member, package) — the mechanism #3527 added for OCI — absorbing repeated misses within `NPM_VIRTUAL_NEGATIVE_CACHE_TTL_MS` (default 5 s, clamped to the proxy layer's 45 s negative window; `NPM_VIRTUAL_NEGATIVE_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES`, default 4096, bounds memory; 0 disables). Only a definitive upstream 404 is recorded — throttling and 5xx are never pinned as absences. Separately, the buffered cache-read path reuses the metadata sidecar its freshness evaluation already loaded instead of bypassing the in-process sidecar LRU for a second storage read.

- **Cargo virtual repositories now resolve each Remote member's `dl` download template from that member's own `config.json`, so crates download from the member's download host instead of 404ing against its index host** (#3952). The Virtual download route built `api/v1/crates/{name}/{version}/download` against the member's `upstream_url` — the index host — so a virtual over a crates.io-backed remote (index at `index.crates.io`, bodies at `static.crates.io`) only served crates already cached through some other route. Each member's template is now resolved and SSRF-validated per member (a hostile `dl` falls that member back to its index host rather than failing the virtual), the canonical path stays the proxy-cache key, and the `dl` template markers `{prefix}` / `{lowerprefix}` from the cargo registry spec are expanded instead of left literal.

- **A hosted crate name in a Cargo virtual repository no longer shadows every upstream version of that name — only the exact locally-held name@version is shadowed** (#3953). The Virtual download ownership guard fired on the crate name alone, so one internally-published version of a crates.io name made every other version 404 through the virtual while the merged sparse index kept advertising it, failing `cargo build`. The guard now fires on the exact name@version (the npm fix from #3646 / PR #3743 applied to cargo), so upstream versions resolve through the Remote member while the dependency-confusion protection on the locally-owned coordinate is unchanged.

- **npm virtual repositories no longer fail `npm install` with EINTEGRITY when a hosted member holds the same `name@version` as a higher-priority remote member** (#3955). The packument merge honours member priority (the highest-priority member's `dist.integrity` wins per version) but the tarball route's dependency-confusion guard suppressed every Remote member whenever any non-Remote member owned the exact version, so the advertised integrity and the served bytes came from different members. Following the priority rule PyPI adopted in #2311, the guard now suppresses a Remote member only when an owning non-Remote member outranks it; the name-only fail-safe for unparseable tarball filenames is unchanged.

- **A quality gate configured to `warn` now reports its violations on a successful promotion instead of nothing at all** (#3977). `promote_artifact` collected warn-level gate violations into a local vector, but `build_success_response` took only `(source, target, promotion_id)` and hardcoded `policy_violations: vec![]`, so the collected violations were dropped on the way out and every successful promotion returned an empty list no matter what the gate found. A gate set to `warn` was therefore silent to the API, the web UI and `ak`: it recorded an evaluation server-side and told the caller nothing. The builder now takes the accumulated violations and both the single and bulk success paths pass them, so a warning gate is visible where it was meant to be. Blocking gates are unchanged -- they never reached this path.

- **The promotion endpoints document `400` for a validation refusal, which is the status they have always returned** (#3977). Every `#[utoipa::path]` on the promotion handlers listed `422 Unprocessable Entity` for repository-shape, package-format, release-link and not-a-staging-repository refusals, while `AppError::Validation` maps to `400 Bad Request` throughout the API. The OpenAPI document is the input to the SDKs that `artifact-keeper-web` and `artifact-keeper-cli` consume, so a client branching on the documented code never matched the response it actually got. The five annotations are corrected to `400`; **runtime behaviour is unchanged** and no request that works today changes its status. A downstream consumer that coded against the published `422` for these five operations should re-generate its SDK and expect `400`.

- **Maven proxy GETs no longer pay two sequential proxy-cache round-trips per artifact** (#3982). `serve_artifact` awaited the upstream `.sha1` sidecar fetch to completion before even starting the content fetch, doubling the per-request storage latency of resolve-heavy Maven builds on network-attached storage (NFS). The sidecar digest now resolves concurrently with the body stream and is only awaited at cache-commit time: a warm hit never touches the sidecar at all (one round-trip total), and a cold miss overlaps the two fetches while gating the cache commit on both results exactly as before (GHSA-qxv7-p3mq-88fv posture unchanged — a digest mismatch is still served-but-never-cached).

- **A CI OIDC identity mapping now authenticates every branch, tag and matched project as one service account, instead of only the first ref that ever ran** (#4031). `POST /api/v1/auth/ci/token` derived the service-account username from the identity mapping (`ci-<8 hex of the mapping id>`) but looked the account up by the token's `sub`. GitLab's `sub` embeds the ref (`project_path:group/app:ref_type:branch:ref:main`), so the first pipeline to run created the account, and every other branch and every tag failed with **`409 Conflict "Username already exists"`**. A tag-triggered release pipeline broke as soon as a `main` build had run, and the error named neither the mapping nor the cause. The same mismatch had three other effects. Array (any-of) `claim_filters` could never admit a second project. Two mappings whose UUIDs shared their first 8 hex characters could not both have an account. And the account only existed after a successful exchange, so operators had to run the pipeline, let it fail, copy `ci-xxxxxxxx` out of the job log, grant it, and apply their configuration a second time. The account is now keyed on the mapping (`users.external_id = ci:<provider_id>:<mapping_id>`), and the subject is kept only in the display name and the exchange's `security` log line. The account is created in the same transaction as its mapping. `service_account_id` and `service_account_username` are returned on every mapping create, read, list, update and toggle, so the account can be granted access before any pipeline runs. New accounts are named `ci-<12 hex>`. If that name is already taken, mapping creation fails with a `409` that names the conflicting account; previously a pipeline would have hit the collision at run time. Deleting a mapping, or a provider with its mappings, now deactivates its account rather than leaving it active, and revokes its refresh tokens. The account row is kept so its audit history stays attributable. Deactivation now sticks: an exchange for a deactivated CI account is refused with `401`, where the federated sync previously set `is_active = true` again on every exchange, so the next pipeline silently undid an administrator's deactivation. Keying on the mapping also separates principals the old `sub` lookup merged: the same subject presented through two providers, or matched by two mappings, now authenticates as two accounts rather than one shared row. `docs/ci-oidc.md` is the first operator documentation for the feature. It covers setup, the one-mapping-one-principal model, granting access, the `.gitlab-ci.yml` shape, and the security boundary: a mapping whose any-of filter admits a fork trusts that fork exactly as much as the upstream.

  **Upgrade note — existing CI accounts keep their `users.id`, and with it their group memberships, permissions and audit history.** Migration 232 rewrites `external_id` in place on existing `auth_provider = 'ci'` rows. It resolves `ci-<8 hex>` to the one mapping whose UUID starts with those characters, and rewrites the row only when exactly one mapping matches. Rows whose mapping was deleted, and rows whose prefix two mappings share, are left untouched. The first exchange through their mapping adopts them when exactly one mapping carries the prefix, and refuses when several do. A unique 8-hex match is effectively, not provably, the original mapping: if that mapping was deleted and a later one happens to share its prefix (about 1 in 2^32 per pair), the row binds to the later mapping. Every decision, including later adoptions, is recorded with the previous key in `ci_oidc_service_account_rekey_log`, which is the migration's report and the input to the rollback statement in the migration header and in `docs/ci-oidc.md`. Existing `ci-<8 hex>` names are not renamed. Anything that parses a CI username as exactly 8 hex characters must accept 12 for mappings created from now on. **During a rolling upgrade, CI token exchange served by a replica still on the old version fails with the old 409 for any account that has already been re-keyed. Re-running the job after rollout completes succeeds.** In the same window, an old replica serving a mapping created by the new version does not find its `ci:`-keyed account and creates a stray `ci-<8 hex>` account keyed on the token subject. It has no grants and the new version never uses it; deactivate it after rollout. Mappings created before the upgrade report `service_account_id: null` until their account has been re-keyed or adopted.

- **A hosted package archive whose contents a scanner could not catalog at all is no longer graded 100 / A** (#4036). `parse_cyclonedx_catalog` deliberately distinguishes `None` ("this scanner reports no catalog") from `Some(vec![])` ("the engine ran and cataloged nothing"), but the hosted scan path discarded the signal: a package archive grype cannot read — a conda `.tar.bz2` is the canonical case — completed with zero findings and was scored as a complete clean, and with zero packages persisted its `inventory_status` stayed at the `'complete'` default. The hosted path now folds an empty catalog from a catalog-reporting scanner into a new `scan_completeness` value, `not_cataloged`, gated by `format_expects_catalog` so it applies only to package-archive artifacts (conda `.tar.bz2`/`.conda`, npm `.tgz`, PyPI sdist/wheel, `.gem`, `.crate`, `.nupkg`, `.jar`, `.deb`, `.rpm`) — a plain file in a generic repository legitimately catalogs nothing and keeps its grade, and a scanner that reports no catalog at all (`None`; the trivy family, OCI registry mode) never triggers it. The scan row still completes normally with its real counts and a persisted `scan_completeness_reason` naming the scanner, but `inventory_status` is marked `partial`, and `recalculate_score` floors the repository grade to F with a new persisted `repo_security_scores.has_uncataloged_scan` flag (mirroring the #2167 `has_failed_scan` gate, also exposed on the score API) until a superseding completed scan clears it. `not_cataloged` is deliberately distinct from `partial`: pin-downgraded and lockfile-unparseable scans still graded real content and remain gradeable.

- **A conda package carrying the legacy list spelling of `run_exports` is now served back as the CEP-12 dict, not the bare list** (#4038). A recipe may declare `run_exports` as a bare list of specs — conda-build's own `write_run_exports` defines that spelling as weak exports (`{"weak": [...]}`) — and packages built before conda-build normalised it carry the list verbatim in `info/run_exports.json`. CEP-12 requires the per-package member of a channel's `run_exports.json` to be a dict, so the bare list was served to clients in a shape they cannot parse as run exports. Ingest now normalises the list to `{"weak": [...]}` on the way into `artifact_metadata`, exactly as conda-build does when writing the package, and the `run_exports.json` read path applies the same rule, so packages already hosted with the list spelling are corrected without a republish. The dict spelling passes through untouched, and a package with no run exports still serves `{}`.

- **Conda is no longer aliased to the PyPI handler, so a hosted conda artifact whose bytes do not back its registry coordinate is now graded `partial` instead of `complete`** (#4039). `RepositoryFormat::handler_key()` mapped `Poetry | Conda | Jupyter => "pypi"`, and the security subsystem believed it: the hosted-upload pin selector (`pinned_ecosystem`) resolves conda to `"pypi"`, whose PyPI-sdist gate (`.tar.gz`/`.zip`) never matches a conda package, so `format_expects_pin` was always false for conda and the #3604 `pin_downgraded` completeness escape hatch could never fire — a text file named `numpy-1.26.0-py311_0.tar.bz2` scanned "0 findings, complete". Conda now has its own handler key, routed to the conda-native handler in both dispatch tables (`get_core_handler` / `get_handler_for_format`) and listed in the compiled-in handler registry (which also gives conda its own enablement row in `format_handlers` — previously a `conda` repository was gated on the *pypi* row, so disabling PyPI silently disabled conda repository creation). A new `ComponentEcosystem::Conda` pins `.conda`/`.tar.bz2` artifacts under both `conda` and `conda_native`, cross-checked against the package's own `info/index.json` (read through the shared bounded-archive helpers for both containers) before it is trusted. The pin is deliberately **not materialized** into the scan workspace: measured on the bundled engines, grype 0.113.0 catalogs a `conda-meta/*.json` record but has no conda matcher or conda-keyed advisory data (a pinned `urllib3@1.25.9` matches zero vulnerabilities) and trivy 0.69.3 does not read the layout at all, so a written record would fill the catalog while grading nothing and suppress #4036's `not_cataloged` fail-closed signal. The two predicates therefore stack: an untrustworthy conda coordinate is `partial` (pin), a cataloged-nothing scan stays `not_cataloged` (#4036, which keeps precedence). The same wrong-alias class in the migration worker's filename parser (`artifact_metadata.rs` routed `conda` through the PyPI sdist grammar) is fixed with a conda arm using the native handler's `<name>-<version>-<build>` parser, so migrated conda artifacts get the coordinates a natively published one has. Poetry and Jupyter were audited and stay on the pypi key: both genuinely speak the PyPI protocol (PEP 503 simple index, sdist/wheel uploads), which `age_gate_spec` and the on-demand curation family already model independently of `handler_key()`.

- **Conda v1 packages compressed with a parallel bzip2 (pbzip2, lbzip2) now yield their metadata instead of silently reading as empty** (#4067). Such a package is one tar encoded as a sequence of independent bzip2 streams, but `read_metadata_from_tar_bz2_limited` decoded it with the single-stream `bzip2::read::BzDecoder`, which stops at the first stream boundary — so when `info/index.json` sat past that boundary the upload produced no metadata at all. The scan-workspace extractor was switched to `MultiBzDecoder` for exactly this reason in #4066, leaving the two paths disagreeing about the same format. The ingest reader now uses `MultiBzDecoder` too (size ceilings unchanged), and the three other in-tree conda v1 readers — the upload-time structure validation, `extract_conda_v1_metadata`, and the install-script harvest — make the same switch, so a valid multi-stream package is no longer rejected as "missing info/index.json" either. The Debian `control.tar.bz2` readers deliberately keep the single-stream decoder: `dpkg-deb` writes single-stream members and no parallel-bzip2 toolchain produces `.deb` payloads.

- **A vulnerability found in one dependency is no longer cached against — and reported for — every other dependency scanned alongside it** (#4079). `AdvisoryClient::query_osv` batches up to 1000 dependencies into a single OSV.dev `querybatch` call, and OSV answers **positionally**: `results[i]` belongs to `queries[i]`. The response was instead flattened into one list and then written back into the cache under *every* dependency's key — the filter that was supposed to select each dependency's own matches was literally `true`, under a comment asserting the positional contract it did not implement. Scanning an artifact whose batch contained `pillow` and `requests` therefore cached pillow's advisory under `PyPI:requests:2.31.0` for the full 1-hour TTL, and the next artifact that merely depended on `requests` inherited a **fabricated finding** — same severity, same CVE alias, same source URL, indistinguishable at every surface from a real one. The blast radius is the batch: one genuinely vulnerable dependency contaminated every other dependency scanned with it, and quarantine policy, SBOM generation and the CVE-mapping lookup all consumed the result as fact. `parse_osv_grouped` now keeps one match list per query and `query_osv_detailed` writes each list under its own dependency's key. A surplus result that belongs to no dependency is given a slot past the end rather than folded into a neighbour's, and is not reported.

- **An advisory-feed outage is no longer recorded as a completed clean scan** (#4080). `query_osv` and `query_github` logged a `warn!` and returned an empty result on transport error, non-2xx status and parse failure alike; `DependencyScanner::scan` then set `scan_completeness: Complete` unconditionally. A feed outage was therefore bit-for-bit indistinguishable from a genuinely clean package. Both feeds now report whether they answered (`query_osv_detailed` / `query_github_detailed`, added alongside the existing methods, which remain as flattening wrappers), and the scan is graded `Partial` when either did not. The distinction the fix turns on is "asked and refused" versus "not applicable": a GitHub **403** — a rate limit or a rejected token — degrades the scan, while an ecosystem the GitHub Advisory Database does not index and a deployment with no GitHub token configured do not, because in both of those nothing was ever asked.

  Two narrower false-cleans are closed with it, both of which a 200 could survive for the full hour-long cache TTL. An OSV response carrying **no `results` array at all** was read as a batch of empty results and cached as clean for every dependency in the chunk; it is now treated as unanswered. A response covering only a **prefix** of the batch left the remaining queries unanswered, and padding them with empty slots would cache "clean" for dependencies the feed never spoke about; those slots are now left unrecorded and uncached, and the lookup is degraded. (Failed lookups — transport error, non-2xx, unparseable body — never reached the cache even before this change; the issue text saying otherwise is wrong.)

  **Operator note — scans will start reporting `partial` during feed outages.** This is the intended behaviour and it is visible fleet-wide, so it is worth reading before upgrading rather than discovering in a dashboard. Before this release, an OSV.dev or GitHub Advisory outage produced `scan_completeness: complete` with zero findings on every dependency scan that ran during it. After it, those same scans are graded `partial`, which is persisted to `scan_results.scan_completeness` and surfaced in the SBOM document's completeness field and anywhere downstream attestation tooling reads it. Nothing about **findings** changes — a partial scan still reports everything the feeds did return — and no scan fails; what changes is that "we could not reach the feed" is now recorded as a distinct fact from "we asked and there was nothing". Expect a correlated burst of `partial` results during any OSV.dev incident, and note that alerting or gating keyed on `scan_completeness = complete` will now see those scans. A deployment with no GitHub token configured is unaffected: not consulting the GitHub feed is not an outage.

- **A finding now names the dependency it is actually about, instead of whichever dependency happened to be first in the manifest** (#4081). Every `RawFinding` the dependency scanner emitted set `affected_component: Some(deps.first()…unwrap_or_default())`. `GET /api/v1/…/sbom` joins on `COALESCE(sf.affected_component, sf.title)` to name a component, so the wrong name propagated into generated SBOM documents — which consumers treat as authoritative — and into the finding dedup key, where two advisories against two different packages could collapse into one. The symptom was documented in-tree (a comment telling readers to treat the field as absent) but the cause was never fixed. `DependencyScanner::scan` now walks the lookup's per-dependency slots and files each finding against the dependency whose slot produced it.

- **The API now advertises a repository format string that the API itself will accept back** (#4083, #4085). `repo_to_response` built the `format` field with `format!("{:?}", …).to_lowercase()`, which drops the underscore in multi-word variants, so three formats were served under names `parse_format_str` rejects: `conda_native` as `condanative`, `wasm_oci` as `wasmoci`, and `helm_oci` as `helmoci`. Found on a running deployment with two user-visible symptoms — the repository **renders as `GENERIC` in the UI**, because the client cannot match the format string and falls back, and feeding the API its own output is refused (`POST /api/v1/repositories {"format":"condanative"}` → `400 VALIDATION_ERROR: Invalid format: condanative`). The database was correct throughout; only the response value was wrong. Nine call sites now use the canonical `RepositoryFormat::as_key()` / `RepositoryType::as_str()` spellings that already existed, and a round-trip test over **every** `RepositoryFormat::ALL` variant — not just the three that happen to be multi-word today — keeps a future multi-word format from reintroducing it. **Clients string-matching `condanative`, `wasmoci` or `helmoci` must move to `conda_native`, `wasm_oci` and `helm_oci`**: the response schema is unchanged, but the value of an existing string field is corrected from one the API rejects to one it accepts.

- **The #4036 empty-catalog fail-closed path now actually sees a zero-catalog scan, and no longer fires on artifacts that merely contain no libraries** (#4094). End-to-end verification on a live deployment with real conda-forge packages proved the original fix wrong on both sides. The miss: when grype catalogs *literally* nothing — any `.conda` package, verified against grype 0.118 — syft's cyclonedx-json presenter OMITS the `components` key entirely, and `parse_cyclonedx_catalog` returned `None` for a missing key, so the never-read case the fix was built for was still recorded `complete`; a valid grype-produced BOM without a `components` array now parses as `Some(vec![])` ("the engine ran and cataloged nothing"), with `None` kept strictly for unparseable BOM bytes. The false positive: `Some(vec![])` also fires when the BOM has components but no `type: "library"` ones — xz (`.tar.bz2`) cataloged 1 component with 2 real vulnerabilities, openssl (`.conda`) 1 component with 0 findings, and both were floored to F — so the hosted `not_cataloged` downgrade now additionally requires zero findings AND zero packages corroborating that nothing was read; an empty library catalog alongside real findings or a real inventory means "no libraries", not "never read", and keeps its scanner-reported completeness and grade. The knock-on is deliberate: the #3003 inline-proxy identity gate keys on `Some(cataloged)`, so a proxy scan where grype catalogs literally nothing now reaches the gate's empty-catalog inconclusive path (fail-closed 423) instead of skipping the gate as "no signal" — the gate's designed semantics finally firing. `parse_cyclonedx_packages` inventory semantics are unchanged: a missing `components` key there still means "no signal" and falls back to the match-derived rows.

- **The proxy-cache SBOM and package-analysis endpoints are now in the OpenAPI spec** (#4095). `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/security/proxy-sbom` and `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}/package-analysis` were annotated and routed but never registered in the merged spec, so the exported spec and every generated SDK omitted them. A new test fails whenever an annotated handler is missing from the spec.

- **The proxy-cache SBOM now marks a partially read inventory** (#4096). `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/security/proxy-sbom` always rendered its regenerated SBOM as complete, because the inline proxy scan never recorded whether the scanner could read every target. The completeness is now stored with the verdict (migration 252) and emitted as the CycloneDX `artifact-keeper:scan-completeness` property or the SPDX creation comment, so a client can tell a partial inventory from an authoritative one.

- **Scan-on-proxy now gates `.crate` downloads from Cargo Remote and Virtual repositories** (#4101, part of #4097). Cargo repositories accepted `scan_on_proxy` but streamed every proxied crate unscanned. With the toggle on, a Remote crate download (from the upstream's `config.json` `dl` host) now goes through the shared inline scan-and-block gate: a vulnerable crate is refused with 403 `scan_blocked`, a clean one is served with `X-AK-Scan: clean`, the verdict is reused for the same digest, and fail-open (serve `X-AK-Scan: pending`, scan in the background) and fail-closed (423 until a verdict exists, including crates over the scan size cap) behave as they do for npm and PyPI. The scan grades the crate the client asked for: the name and version from the request must match the crate's own `Cargo.toml`, or the scan is treated as inconclusive. A Virtual repository applies the stricter of its own and each Remote member's policy, fetches from that member's own download host, and a member's block, quarantine hold or fail-closed lock is final rather than falling through to the next member. A crate whose bytes disagree with the sparse index `cksum` (the member's own index, on Virtual) is refused with 502 and evicted from the proxy cache, never served as clean. Sparse index and `config.json` responses are unchanged, and `GET /api/v1/formats` now reports Cargo as `scan_on_proxy: "enforced"`.

- **Real NuGet packages' `.nuspec` manifests now parse; the XML declaration used to make them unreadable** (#4102, #3603). The shared `.nuspec` reader tried to skip the `<?xml ...?>` declaration by searching a trimmed copy of the text and slicing the original at that offset. That handed the XML parser `?>` plus the rest of the file for every manifest that has a declaration, which is every one `nuget pack` / `dotnet pack` writes, with or without a byte-order mark. Two things depend on this reader. Hosted scans of NuGet packages, however they were uploaded, lost their identity pin (#3603) and graded as partial. NuGet scan-on-proxy (#4102) could not establish what a real package was, so it withheld every one under fail-closed and never scanned under fail-open. The reader now hands the whole document to the parser, which skips the declaration itself, after cutting only a leading byte-order mark or whitespace.

- **Remote Go repositories cache module versions instead of revalidating them upstream every five minutes** (#4120). Every `goproxy` fetch handed the cache classifier the `Generic` stand-in format, and the classifier had no Go arm, so a module version's `@v/<version>.info`, `.mod` and `.zip` — pinned by the checksum database and never changed upstream — were stamped with the 5-minute mutable TTL and re-fetched from the upstream proxy on the next request after it. The Go handler now carries the real format, and a canonical `vMAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[-pre][+build]` version (pseudo-versions and `+incompatible` included) under `@v/` classifies immutable; `@v/list`, `@latest` and a non-canonical query such as `@v/master.info` stay mutable.

- **Eight concurrent anonymous conda repodata requests no longer deadlock the buffered-metadata proxy path for every format** (#4145, #4129). Serving a proxied `repodata.json` reserves 128 MiB (`LARGE_METADATA_MAX_BYTES`) from the process-wide buffered-metadata byte budget and holds that reservation until the response is built; the #4051 patch-generation attribution added in that PR then fetched `{subdir}/patch_instructions.json` through the same budgeted helper, taking a SECOND, untimed 8 MiB reservation from the SAME budget while the first was still held. The shipped default budget is 1 GiB — exactly eight worst-case repodata buffers — so eight concurrent requests reserved all of it and then each waited for bytes only the others could release, until the 120 s global request timeout or a client disconnect dropped them: an unauthenticated, eight-request stall of the *shared* buffered-metadata path (RPM repodata, npm packuments, the PyPI simple index, Debian `dists`), not just conda, that any caller could repeat at will and that a lowered `AK_PROXY_METADATA_BUDGET_BYTES` made cheaper still. The reservation is taken before the proxy cache lookup, so neither a cache hit nor a negative-cached 404 avoided it. The attribution fetch now runs BEFORE the repodata reservation exists rather than underneath it, so a request holds at most one permit from the budget at a time and its peak reservation falls from 136 MiB to 128 MiB; the attribution, the recorded rows and the `X-Repodata-Patch-Generation` header are unchanged, and the only cost of the order is one extra cached 8 MiB-capped attribution lookup when the repodata fetch itself then fails. A source pin keeps the two calls in that order and a budget model test proves that N nested reservations never complete while N sequenced ones do.

- **Conda's `notices.json` was the one conda read surface with no visibility check of its own, and concurrent withdrawals silently lost notices** (#4146, #4059). Every other conda read path — `channeldata.json`, each `repodata` variant and encoding, `run_exports.json`, package download — resolves the repository and then calls `check_read_access`. `notices.json` never did. While it returned a hard-coded `{"notices": []}` the omission cost nothing; since per-package withdrawal landed it carries data, one notice per withdrawn package naming the filename and quoting the administrator's reason verbatim, which is the embargoed-advisory and vendor-reported-malware text the feature exists to publish. The handler now takes the same gate in the same position, before any notice is read, and the token-URL form (`/conda/t/{token}/{repo}/notices.json`) binds the auth extension it previously did not take.

  **No disclosure was reachable on a deployed instance, and no action is needed on upgrade.** Every conda route, token URLs included, is mounted under `repo_visibility_middleware`, which resolves the repository and decides the read before any handler runs. Measured through the production router against the pre-fix handler on a private channel holding a withdrawal notice: an anonymous caller received `401 Authentication required` and an authenticated principal with no role assignment on the repository received `404 Repository not found` — byte-identical to what `channeldata.json` returned to those same two callers, and with neither the reason nor the withdrawn filename in the body. Only a repository member read the notice, which is the intended behaviour. What changes is that the endpoint no longer depends solely on the middleware for a decision the rest of the channel makes twice, so it cannot answer differently from its siblings if it is ever reached by a route mounted outside that layer.

  **Appending a notice was an unguarded read-modify-write**, spread across three statements on separate pooled connections, and this one was reachable: two withdrawals in flight at once — a vendor advisory naming a batch of packages is exactly that case — kept only the later writer's notice, silently, while both requests returned 200 with their own `notice_id`. Eight concurrent withdrawals against the pre-fix code left six notices. The append is now one transaction that takes a row lock on the `repository_config` row before reading it, appends, and writes back. The lock is taken by an upsert whose conflict arm rewrites the existing value rather than by a bare `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, because on a channel's first withdrawal there is no row to lock yet and two first withdrawals would otherwise still race on the INSERT. The stored CEP-6 notice shape is unchanged, the `value` column stays `TEXT` so no migration is required, and a missing or corrupt blob is still tolerated as an empty list rather than becoming a 500 on a client-facing endpoint.

- **The conda channel allowlist now actually fails closed on an unknown channel of origin** (#4147, #4160, #4058). `load_conda_facts` resolved the artifact's channel from its identity purl and then chained `.or(Some(row.repo_key))`, so a conda artifact whose identity declares no channel — a pre-identity upload, or a purl carrying no `channel` qualifier — was attributed to the **key of the repository it happens to be stored in** rather than to "unknown". Operators allowlist their own repository keys as a matter of course, so such an artifact silently **passed** an allowlist it should have been blocked by, and the `[conda.channel]` "channel of origin is unknown" branch the code comment, the PR body and this changelog all advertised was unreachable in production — exercised only by hand-built fact structs in unit tests. That allowlist is #4058's main defence against channel-priority misconfiguration and typosquatted channels, so the one predicate documented as fail-closed was the one that failed open. The fallback is removed: an absent channel is `None` and takes the deny branch.

  **The same issue turned out to be wider than the fallback.** Verified against a live deployment: a policy scoped to the source repository carrying `predicates.conda.allowed_channels` promoted its artifact with `policy_violations: []`, and so did `denied_channels`, `denied_licenses` and `origin.allowed_kinds` — while the same policy's `max_severity` blocked correctly, proving the gate itself ran. The cause is that promotion is evaluated by `PromotionPolicyService`, a second gate that reads the same `scan_policies` rows for `max_severity`, `block_unscanned`, the age gates and `require_signature` but never read `predicates` at all — so **the entire predicate block, conda and origin, was inert on the enforced promotion path**, and a channel allowlist that blocked a download waved the same artifact through the operation that raises its trust level. Both gates now evaluate the predicates through one shared entry point, `PolicyService::evaluate_predicates`, so they cannot disagree again; a predicate violation is reported on the promotion response as a `policy-predicate` rule at `high` severity, which blocks, and carries the same `[conda.channel]` / `[origin.kind]` token the download gate records. Predicates are evaluated across every applicable policy (repository-scoped and global), matching the download gate, where promotion's own severity gate takes only the single most specific policy — deliberate, and in the fail-closed direction.

  Five DB-backed tests pin all of it: an artifact with no declared channel is denied by an allowlist that contains its own repository key; a hosted artifact is evaluated on the channel its identity declares rather than on the repository key; and three drive `PromotionPolicyService::evaluate_artifact` — the exact call the promote handler makes with `skip_policy_check: false` — for the allowlist, the denylist and the predicate-free control. **Operator note:** a policy using `allowed_channels` will now block conda artifacts that carry no channel in their identity purl, where before it let them through; that is the intended behaviour, and anything that must be served needs a channel recorded at ingest or an explicit allowlist entry it genuinely matches.

- **A remote conda repository can now serve the uncompressed `repodata.json` for every conda-forge subdir instead of answering 502** (#4149). The proxied fetch buffered upstream metadata under the 128 MiB `LARGE_METADATA_MAX_BYTES` ceiling, and conda-forge's plain `repodata.json` runs 160-200 MiB on every major subdir (linux-64, noarch, osx-arm64, linux-ppc64le), so any client requesting the uncompressed document — older conda releases and tooling without zstd support — got a bare 502 while the compressed `.zst`/`.bz2` variants proxied fine. The ceiling abort is now distinguished from a genuine upstream failure and the document is served through the streaming path instead: teed from upstream to the client and into the proxy cache without ever being buffered whole, exactly as oversized `.deb` and npm tarballs already were. Once the stream commits the cache entry, subsequent requests are served warm with no upstream round trip.

- **OSV-sourced findings now carry their CVE id, fixed version and title** (#4150). OSV's batch query endpoint answers with only an advisory id per vulnerability, so every finding from the dependency, vendored-component and conda-alias lookups was stored with no CVE, no fix and the title "Vulnerability <id>", and could not be deduplicated against the cataloging scanner's rows. The scanner now fetches each advisory's full record (once per id, within a bounded time budget, `OSV_RECORD_FETCH_BUDGET_SECS`, default 5) and takes the CVE from its aliases, the fix from the entry and version interval that match the installed package, and the title from its summary. The same CVE in two different packages is now reported for each, and duplicate advisories for one CVE keep the higher severity.

- **A `noarch` conda package in an environment SBOM now carries `subdir=noarch`, the identity its own artifact has, instead of the platform of the scope it was resolved into** (#4151). `environment_sbom::package_purl` built every conda member's #4041 qualified purl with `CondaPurl::from_index(name, version, build, scope.platform)` — the fourth argument is the package's *subdir*, and `LockedPackage` carried no subdir at all, so the scope's platform was the only thing available to pass. A `noarch` build resolved into a `linux-64` environment was therefore emitted as `…?subdir=linux-64` while the same build ingested as an artifact gets `subdir=noarch` from its `info/index.json`, so the environment membership and the artifact it names never joined, and one `noarch` build appearing in N platform scopes became N distinct bom-refs. `LockedPackage` now carries the package's own `subdir`, recorded by both conda lockfile parsers: `pixi.lock` from its `subdir`/`platform` field or, for the v6 schema that has neither, from the channel URL; `conda-lock.yml` from the channel URL, deliberately *not* from its per-entry `platform`, which names the graph the entry belongs to rather than the subdir it was built for. A subdir inferred from a URL is accepted only when it is a recognised conda subdir, so a package installed from a local directory contributes none. The scope platform remains the fallback for a lockfile that records no subdir — and for one that records a subdir `CondaPurl` rejects, so a malformed field costs a component no identity it had before. The identity rules in `conda_identity` are unchanged; the two derivations now agree by construction.

- **Content imported by the Artifactory / Nexus migration tooling before origin tracking existed is now recorded as `migration`, not `hosted`** (#4153). The origin backfill (migration 228) derived every older row from its repository, so imported artifacts were frozen as hosted uploads by the immutability trigger. Migration 270 re-stamps a row as `{"kind":"migration","upstream_url":<source system URL>}` only when all of these hold: a completed, non-dry-run migration item for the same target repository (resolved through the job's `repo_mappings`) carries the row's SHA-256; the row already existed when the item completed; the path is one the importer writes for that item; and only one source system claims it. Anything ambiguous stays `hosted`, and so does an upload that merely shares bytes and file name with an item whose own row exists. While the migration runs, the immutability trigger's function admits exactly this one rewrite, and only on a connection that sets the transaction-local `ak.origin_rewrite` GUC. The strict function is restored at the end. No table lock is taken on `artifacts`. The re-stamp runs in 5000-row batches with a 5-second `lock_timeout` per batch and retries. It reports how many rows it planned and re-stamped, how many rows it left `hosted` because two source systems claim them, and how many items it skipped because their file name matched more than one row. The online-migration gate now requires `lock_timeout` in any new migration that backfills or adds a trigger to a large table, and refuses `DISABLE`/`ENABLE TRIGGER` on one.

  Operator note: no action is needed. To see what changed, compare `SELECT count(*) FROM artifacts WHERE origin->>'kind' = 'migration'` before and after the upgrade. The `migration 270` NOTICE lines are logged under `sqlx::postgres::notice` at INFO, so they appear with the shipped images' `RUST_LOG=info` but not with the built-in default filter.

- **An artifact that no scanner could inventory is reported as not cataloged even when grype is absent, including archives in generic repositories** (#4154). The "cataloged nothing" signal came only from grype, so on a deployment without it, or for an archive in a generic repository, a scan that assessed nothing completed as clean. The decision is now made over the whole set of scanners: when none of them found a finding, a package or a component, the scan is `not_cataloged` with a reason and the repository reports `has_uncataloged_scan`. The repository grade letter is floored to F only for packages, as before: every package in a typed repository and package-shaped archives (`.whl`, `.jar`, `.war`, `.ear`, `.gem`, `.crate`, `.nupkg`, `.egg`, `.conda`) in a generic one. A plain `.zip`, `.tar.gz`, `.tgz` or `.tar.bz2` in a generic repository (documentation bundles, build outputs, installers) is flagged without changing the grade. A not-cataloged result is never reused for another upload of the same bytes, and a reused scan now carries its source's completeness. Scan results in the API now include `scan_completeness` and `scan_completeness_reason`, so a flagged or floored repository shows why.

- **A repository with no quality gate configured no longer logs a WARN on every successful promotion** (#4156). `evaluate_gate_once` logged "Quality gate evaluation failed for artifact …" at WARN for every `Err` out of `evaluate_quality_gate`, including the two states that are simply the default: the repository has no enabled quality gate, and the artifact has no health score yet. Both come back as `AppError::NotFound`, so every promotion on an ungated repository — the out-of-the-box configuration — read as an error to log-based alerting while the promotion itself succeeded. Those two outcomes are now classified as a no-op and logged at DEBUG, matched on the error variant rather than on the message text; a genuine evaluation failure (a database error, say) keeps the WARN it had.

- **Two API-surface warts on the generic format: `PUT /general/{repo}/{path}` answered with the web UI's HTML 404 page, and `repo_type: "hosted"` was rejected on repository creation** (#4157). The `/general` router is download-only, so a write verb fell through to the application-wide method fallback and a client that guessed the upload URL got an HTML document back from an API path, with no hint of where uploads actually go. The route now answers a non-download verb with a JSON `405` carrying `Allow: GET, HEAD` and a message naming the real upload route, `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{path}`. Separately, `POST /api/v1/repositories` rejected `{"repo_type":"hosted"}` with `400 Invalid repo type: hosted` while the docs, the conda write guards and this changelog all call a local repository "hosted"; `parse_repo_type` now accepts `hosted` as an alias of `local` and normalises it at the API boundary, so nothing downstream sees a second spelling and `RepositoryType::from_db_str` stays strict. The rejection message now lists the accepted values.

- **A conda package pushed through the native `PUT /conda/{repo}/{subdir}/{filename}` route is now scanned on upload, instead of being stored ungraded until someone remembered to trigger a repository scan** (#4159). The generic upload path gets its scan-on-upload trigger from `ArtifactService::finalize_upload`, which reads the repository's `scan_configs` row and spawns the scan after the artifact row commits. `store_conda_package` never constructs an `ArtifactService` — it writes the `artifacts` row with raw SQL and returns 201 — so a repository with `scan_enabled` and `scan_on_upload` both true produced no `scan_results` row for a natively published conda package, and its repository score stayed null. The purpose-built helper for exactly this, `scanner_service::spawn_scan_on_upload`, had a single production caller (the Incus finalizer) carrying a comment that format-native paths must mirror it; conda now does, with the same config gate, the same non-blocking spawn and the same warn-on-failure logging, placed immediately after the row is committed and the upload hold applied. All four native conda upload entry points (`PUT`, `POST /upload`, and the two token-bearing variants) funnel through that helper, so all four are covered. The download-time policy gate is unaffected — `block_unscanned` already handled the never-scanned artifact — but the grade and the security dashboard now reflect a pushed package without operator action.

- **`scan_on_upload` now scans packages pushed through every format's native client, not only generic, PyPI, NuGet, Debian, Incus and conda uploads** (#4166). Thirty format-native upload handlers (npm, Maven, Cargo, Go, docker push, Composer, Conan, Helm, RubyGems, RPM, Alpine, Hex, CRAN, Ansible, Puppet, Hugging Face, Swift, Terraform, VS Code, JetBrains, Pub, SBT, Chef, CocoaPods, Git LFS, Protobuf and the chunked upload API) wrote the artifact row themselves and never started the scan, so a repository with scan-on-upload enabled stayed unscanned until someone ran a repository scan by hand. Every handler now goes through one shared trigger, and a source-scan test fails the build if a new upload path inserts an artifact without it.

- **The Packages catalog backfill no longer advertises artifacts the registry refuses to serve, and can now reconstruct Maven and Gradle coordinates** (#4168, #4169). `POST /api/v1/admin/packages/backfill` walked every live artifact regardless of `quarantine_status`, so one run listed a `quarantined` or `rejected` artifact on the Packages page as an available package while every download of it stayed refused — and because nothing rewrites a catalog row when a verdict changes, it stayed listed. The walk now applies the same listability test the download paths use (`quarantine_status NOT IN ('quarantined', 'rejected')`, including the escape hatch for a timed quarantine whose `quarantine_until` has elapsed). Separately, `maven` and `gradle` were absent from `BACKFILL_FORMATS`, which made the endpoint a no-op for them: unlike the formats already listed, Maven's `artifacts.name` holds the bare `artifactId` and the `groupId` lives only in the path, so the default coordinate arm would have registered a group-less row beside the handler's `groupId:artifactId` (#2723) for every module — the duplicate-row shape #3978 fixed for NuGet. Both formats are now backfilled through `MavenHandler::parse_coordinates`, which yields the same `groupId:artifactId` at the same directory version (#3064) that the handler registers, collapses every asset of one release (jar, pom, classified jars) onto that single version, and rejects non-package paths such as `maven-metadata.xml` instead of inventing a row. `docker`/`oci`, `npm`, `pypi`, `nuget` and `generic` stay out of the walk, with the reasons recorded on the constant.

- **Go module catalog entries no longer report the `go.mod` sidecar's size after a backfill** (#4191). The catalog backfill did not exclude sidecar rows, so a module's reported size flipped between the archive's and the go.mod's depending on row order; `.mod`/`.info` (Go) and `.prov` (Helm) rows are now excluded from the candidate set and the archive row always registers the version.

- **Helm, CRAN, Hex and Bazel virtual repositories no longer serve a merged index that silently lacks a member whose metadata failed** (closes #4192). The shared member merge (`collect_virtual_metadata`) logged a member it could not fetch or parse at `warn` and merged the rest, so a client got a 200 index missing that member's packages, and concluded they do not exist or resolved a name present in two members to the lower-priority one. Conda's virtual merge already failed loudly (#4603, #4611, #4614); the shared merge behind Helm `index.yaml`, CRAN `PACKAGES` / `PACKAGES.gz`, Hex `/names` and `/versions` and Bazel module metadata now follows the same policy: by default any member that fails to fetch or whose document does not parse fails the request with 502 naming the member and the cause. A virtual with `virtual_metadata_partial` set (the same repository setting conda honours) instead gets the merge of the members that succeeded, with `X-AK-Partial-Members` naming the missing ones, `Cache-Control: no-store` and `Warning: 199`. Each failure counts in `ak_virtual_member_metadata_failures_total{format,virtual_repo,member,reason}` in both modes. A member that answers 404 publishes no such document and is not a failure, and members the caller may not read are still left out without being reported. A Hex Remote member whose upstream is `repo.hex.pm` serves the signed protobuf registry, not the JSON `/names` and `/versions` merge, so it publishes no such document either: it contributes nothing, like a 404, and is logged at `info` rather than failing the merge (#4629).

- **Held uploads no longer appear on the Packages page, rejection delists a published package, and release from quarantine re-lists it** (#4196). The catalog liveness check filtered on `is_deleted` alone, so the twenty-one format handlers that apply the upload hold and then register the package left a held artifact listed from publish time, a later rejection never delisted it, and an older artifact released from quarantine stayed off the page until the backfill re-ran. The read-side predicate now applies the same quarantine rule the download path and the backfill use — held or rejected artifacts are not live, released or elapsed-hold artifacts are — so all three gaps close with no per-handler change.

- **Maven `maven-metadata.xml` and checksum/signature sidecar uploads no longer register bogus package catalog rows** (#4197). The generic finalize path (replication, migration, generic push) applied no metadata skip: `parse_coordinates` read the artifactId directory as a version and registered `groupId:artifactId` at a nonsense version. Publish time now applies the same skip predicate as the catalog backfill, so the two paths can never disagree.

- **A restricted CI OIDC identity mapping can be reset to all repositories via the admin API** (#4198). `PUT /api/v1/admin/ci-oidc/{id}/mappings/{mid}` treated an omitted `allowed_repo_ids` and an explicit `null` identically ("leave unchanged"), so once a mapping had any repository restriction no API call could clear it — the only way back to unrestricted was deleting and recreating the mapping, which changed its service-account identity. The field is now tri-state: omit it to leave the restriction unchanged, send `"allowed_repo_ids": null` to clear it (all repositories), and send an array to restrict (`[]` still denies every repository).

- **An image build's log no longer loses the builder's last stderr lines** (#4201). The image builder closed its output channel as soon as `buildctl` exited, so a reader task that had not yet forwarded what was still in the stderr pipe had its sends rejected and those lines were dropped. That is where BuildKit reports progress and the reason a build failed, and it made the image-builds integration test fail about one run in four. The builder now keeps reading until both stdout and stderr reach EOF (bounded by the build timeout) before it writes the last log chunk and marks the build finished.

- **`skip_policy_check` on the promotion endpoints is honoured for admins only** (#4203). Any non-admin API token with the `promote:artifacts` scope could set the flag and switch off the quality gate, the CVE/licence policy and the promotion rules on both the single and the bulk promote route. A non-admin caller that passes the flag now gets 403 naming it, and when an admin does use the override the `promotion_history` audit record carries a `policy_check_skipped` marker instead of reading like a policy that ran and passed.

- **A quality-gate evaluation error now fails the promotion closed instead of letting it through** (#4204). On both promote routes, a genuine gate-evaluation failure (a database error, for example) was logged and treated as "not evaluated", so the artifact was promoted without the gate having run. The single route now answers a retryable 503 and the bulk route fails just that item; the unchanged "no enabled gate / no health score yet" defaults still proceed as before.

- **A hex `JWT_SECRET` is no longer rejected as low entropy just because it happens to miss one of the sixteen hex digits** (#4211). Since 1.7.0 the startup check has refused any secret with fewer than 16 distinct characters, in every environment. A hex secret can contain at most 16, and a random 64-character one (`openssl rand -hex 32`, 256 bits) misses at least one digit about 23% of the time, so roughly one deployment in four with a freshly generated hex secret refused to start with `JWT_SECRET is unsuitable: it has low entropy`. The distinct-character count is replaced by an entropy estimate from the character classes the secret uses (4 bits per character for hex, 6 for base64 or base64url, up to log2(95) for printable ASCII), and a secret must reach 128 estimated bits, so 32 hex characters is the minimum hex secret. A string drawn from only a few symbols is still judged by the symbols it actually uses, so 40 characters from five letters remain rejected. The 32-character minimum, the placeholder and weak-substring lists, and the monotonic-sequence check are unchanged, and a short unit repeated (`abab…`, `0123456789abcdef` four times) is now rejected even when it has 16 distinct characters. The error still recommends `openssl rand -base64 48` and now says a 64-character hex secret is accepted too.

- **Curation rule create and update reject an unknown rule action and an invalid publisher-trust config with a 400** (#4245, #4246). The top-level `action` was passed straight to the database, so any value other than `allow` or `block` (such as `flag`, the old web form default) failed the column's CHECK constraint and came back as a 500. It is now checked in the handler, and the 400 lists the accepted values. A `publisher_trust` rule's `config` was only checked for being a JSON object, so a missing or empty `trusted_publishers` list (including one whose names are all blank), an unknown `match`, or an unknown `action` was stored with a 201 and then flagged every applicable package as misconfigured. Create and update now reject these with a 400 naming the field and its accepted values. The handler and the evaluator share one config parser, so the two cannot disagree; rules stored before this fix still fail safe to a review flag at evaluation time.

- **Publisher-trust curation rules now apply to `conda_native` repositories** (#4251). The publisher-trust evaluator only recognized the `conda` format, so a rule on a `conda_native` staging or proxy repository evaluated to "not applicable": it saved and looked active, but checked nothing. `conda_native` now maps to the same publisher family as `conda`. Its packages are judged the same way: on the cert-bound owner of a verified CEP-27 attestation, or on the self-asserted `about.json` maintainer under `match: metadata`. An untrusted publisher is flagged or blocked, and a trusted one is allowed.

- **`conda_native` packages get the same scanner-component dedup as `conda` packages** (closes #4254). `ComponentDedup` only built a dedup scope when the repository format was exactly `conda`, so a package in a `conda_native` repository did not fold its scanner components against the PyPI distribution it vendors and could report the same component twice. The check now uses the shared conda-format test (`conda` or `conda_native`), as publisher trust already does.

- **A local (hosted) Debian/APT repository can be created from the web UI again** (#4258). The create dialog attaches `debian: {distribution_paths: [], components: [], architectures: []}` to every Debian-format create request — local, staging and virtual included — and the handler rejected any present `debian` object on a repository that is not a Debian Remote ("debian filter config is only valid for Debian remote (proxy) repositories"), so an untouched form made creating a local Debian repository impossible. An all-default payload configures nothing, so it is now skipped on those targets; a payload that sets something is still rejected (#2460), and an all-`None` patch (`"debian": {}`) is treated the same way on update. Mirrors the npm scope-policy fix (#3299).

- **A Maven artifact served through a virtual repository from one of its hosted members is now counted as a download** (#4267). Pulling your own artifacts with `mvn` or Gradle through a virtual repository that groups a hosted repository never showed up on the admin Downloads page or in the artifact's download count, while the same file fetched from the hosted repository directly did. Maven resolves virtual repositories with its own member loop (for its SNAPSHOT-alias and legacy-layout lookups) rather than the shared resolver that records the winning local member (#2260). Its lookups already reported which artifact row served the bytes, but the handler dropped that before streaming. The winning hosted member's artifact is now recorded exactly once, and a HEAD probe still counts nothing. Two cases deliberately stay uncounted: a Remote member reached through the virtual, which remains an open decision about the two-phase member fan-out, and row-less legacy companion files served by the storage fallback, which a direct hosted fetch does not count either.

- **RubyGems remote and virtual specs indexes no longer come back empty when the upstream serves gzipped Marshal** (#4280, #4272). rubygems.org's `specs.4.8.gz`, `latest_specs.4.8.gz` and `prerelease_specs.4.8.gz` are gzipped Ruby Marshal, not JSON. A remote repository rebuilt them from cached gems only, and a virtual repository JSON-parsed the upstream body, failed and silently dropped the member, so `gem` and `bundler` saw an empty (~24-byte) index. A remote repository now passes the upstream index through unchanged. A virtual repository decodes each remote member's Marshal index and merges it with its hosted members' gems; a hosted member keeps precedence for every gem name it owns, and a remote member whose index cannot be fetched or decoded now fails the request with 502 naming the member instead of being left out. Thanks to @vvs9896 for the original fix.

- **The same npm package version can be published to more than one npm repository on S3, GCS or Azure storage** (#4293). npm tarballs were written to the flat key `npm/{package}/{version}/{file}`, which every repository on a shared object-storage namespace shares, so the second repository's publish was refused with `409 ... already owned by another repository; refusing cross-repository overwrite`. New tarballs on a cloud backend are written under the repository-scoped key `npm/{repository_id}/{package}/{version}/{file}` (the #2624 scheme Maven already uses), so each repository keeps its own copy. Existing tarballs stay where they are and keep serving from the key their artifact row records; filesystem storage and `STORAGE_KEY_SCHEME=flat` keep the flat key.

- **A request that arrives while an expired proxy-cache entry is being refilled no longer sends a duplicate upstream request** (#4298). The in-process metadata cache could still hold the expired sidecar for a moment after the refill had written the fresh one to storage, so a second request in that window treated the entry as stale and fetched it from upstream again (a duplicate GET, or a duplicate conditional HEAD when a validator exists). An expired sidecar now waits for an in-flight publish of the same key, as a missing sidecar already did, and then reloads the fresh metadata. Fresh cache hits are unaffected.

- **Incus chunked image uploads work behind more than one backend replica** (#4302). A chunked upload appended its chunks to a file on the local disk of the replica that served the start, so a chunk or the completion routed to another replica found nothing and the upload failed. Each chunk is now staged as an object on the repository's storage backend and recorded on the session in commit order, so any replica can take any chunk; the completing replica copies the chunks into its own staging file and finalizes as before. Chunk objects are deleted when the session completes, fails or is cancelled, and the hourly upload-staging sweep reclaims those of an abandoned session.

  Limits: the completion reads the whole image back from the storage backend before hashing it, so it takes one extra read of the image and the completing replica's staging disk must still hold it; each chunk costs one extra object write. A session started before the upgrade keeps the local-file path and still needs session affinity to finish. Moving the staging itself off local disk is a separate change.

- **An npm Remote's cached packuments no longer appear in its cached-artifact listing as if they were packages** (closes #4305). The proxy cache stores each packument under the bare package name (`@scope/name`, `name`) next to the tarballs (`@scope/name/-/name-1.0.0.tgz`), and the listing showed it as an artifact: about 1.9 MB of `application/json` that could be downloaded and its cache entry invalidated, while deleting it answered `Artifact not found`. For the npm family (npm, yarn, pnpm, bower), a cached path without the registry's `/-/` tarball segment is now treated as metadata, like a PyPI index page: it is left out of the listing and its count and out of the proxy-scans view (where it was a permanent `not_scanned` entry), and stays in the cache and in storage accounting. Tarballs are listed as before.

- **Concurrent RPM curated snapshot creates for one repository no longer fail with a serialization error** (#4307). Two `create_version` calls for the same repository ran as competing SERIALIZABLE transactions with an identical, deterministic retry backoff, so they could abort each other with `40001` on every attempt and surface a 500 once the retries ran out. Creates for one repository are now serialized by a per-repository advisory lock taken at the start of the transaction (which runs at READ COMMITTED so the waiter sees the winner's version number), the `UNIQUE(repository_id, version_number)` constraint remains the backstop, and the retry backoff is jittered.

- **A database failure while authorizing a virtual repository's members now answers a retryable 503 instead of a 404 that Gradle caches** (#4308). The Maven virtual checksum walk and the two shared virtual download resolvers used the infallible member authorization, which turned a failed query (for example a pool timeout under load) into an empty member set and answered `404 Virtual repository has no accessible members`. Gradle recorded the artifact as missing and failed every later build until its cache was cleared. These paths now use the fallible form, so a pool timeout answers `503 POOL_EXHAUSTED` with `Retry-After` (any other database error a 500), while a caller who really has no readable member still gets the same 404.

- **The quickstart no longer leaves a first-time user without a working admin password** (#4313). `ADMIN_PASSWORD` only sets the password when the admin account is created, and the backend creates it on the first boot even when a later startup check stops it, so editing the variable afterwards changed nothing and every login failed with no explanation. The backend now logs a warning when `ADMIN_PASSWORD` is set but does not match the existing account, saying it is ignored and how to recover. The installer (`scripts/install.sh`) now defaults to the compose file's ports 30080/30443 (port 80 cannot be published by rootless Podman, and the docs used 30080), falls back to Podman when the docker CLI cannot reach a daemon, sets `DEPENDENCY_TRACK_ENABLED=true` only together with `COMPOSE_PROFILES=dtrack` (opt-in with `AK_DTRACK=1`), documents that its options go on the `bash` side of `curl ... | bash`, and says where the password is and that it applies on the first start only; `docker-compose.yml` and `.env.example` say the same. `scripts/ci/check-installer-quickstart.sh` pins the installer's output. Closes #4313.

- **Remote Debian pool downloads no longer list the whole proxy cache on every request** (#4315). The Tier B checksum lookup found cached `Packages` indexes by listing storage, so every `.deb` got slower as the cache grew; it now reads the index paths from the proxy cache catalog.

- **A V2 remote member of a virtual NuGet repository no longer disappears when its upstream answers `index.json` with an error** (#4327). Many V2 servers answer `/index.json` with 400, 401, 403 or 5xx rather than 404. A standalone V2 remote already kept working in that case (#4126), but the same upstream as a virtual repository's member was dropped: its packages were missing from the virtual's V2 feed, and a V2 download through the virtual returned 404. Both now follow the standalone rule: only a positive V3 answer switches to V3, and otherwise the member's own V2 feed is used. The standalone and member downloads share one function, so they cannot drift apart again. Member downloads retain scan-on-proxy enforcement, including a virtual repository's stricter policy; a scan refusal stops the member walk rather than serving the package from a later member. The V3 surface still refuses to fall back to V2 on a probe error, so a transient failure of a real V3 feed is never answered from paths it does not serve.

  A member whose probe fails SLOWLY is still skipped, as before, and its upstream is not asked a second time. The proxy reports "never answered" the same way as "answered 403" and waits 60 seconds before giving up, and members are asked one after another, so falling back after a timeout would double that wait for every V2 request through the virtual repository. That would push a feed past a NuGet client's own timeout where it used to answer, only without the dead member. A failed probe therefore counts as an answer only if it came back within 5 seconds; a real error answer takes milliseconds. This limit applies to virtual members only: a standalone V2 remote keeps falling back after any probe error, as it has since #4126.

- **An interrupted Conan upload no longer leaves a corrupted package on the server, and re-running the upload completes it** (#4329). The Conan client uploads a revision's files one at a time, archives first and `conanmanifest.txt` last, and carries on after a file fails. When `conan_package.tgz` failed (here because the router-wide request timeout, 120 s by default, cut a 3.5 GB upload off mid-body and the reverse proxy reported a 502), `conaninfo.txt` and `conanmanifest.txt` still landed and the package revision was listed without its archive: consumers got `corrupted in the server, it doesn't contain a conan_package.t file`, and re-running the upload skipped it as already in the server. Three changes:

  - A revision is now published by its manifest.
