Files uploaded before the manifest are stored but not listed by `/latest`, `/revisions`, `/search`, `/files` or recipe search; `conanmanifest.txt` is accepted only once the files the client's own integrity checks need are stored (`conaninfo.txt` and `conan_package.t*` for a binary; `conanfile.py`, plus `conan_export.t*` / `conan_sources.t*` when the manifest names exported or export-source files, for a recipe), and is otherwise refused with `409` and nothing stored. The manifest and the publication of the revision are one transaction, and each file's artifact row and metadata are now written together.
  - Conan file transfers (`.../files/<name>`) are byte-transfer routes, exempt from `GLOBAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECS` like OCI blobs and LFS objects; a stalled body is still bounded by the upload progress deadline.
  - Conan uploads receive their body through the same complete-body extractor as the archive-parsing formats (#4609): a body shorter than its `Content-Length` is `408` and nothing is stored, and the buffer is charged to `UPLOAD_MEMORY_BUDGET_BYTES`.

- **`conan remove` works against a local Conan repository** (#4333). The Conan router registered no DELETE routes, so removing a recipe or a binary that had just been uploaded and installed answered 404, which the client reports as `Recipe not found` / `Binary package not found`, and the package stayed. The four routes the Conan 2 client deletes are now served: a whole recipe, a recipe revision (with its binaries), every binary of a recipe revision, and a single package revision. Removal needs the `delete:artifacts` token scope and the repository's `delete` permission, is refused on remote (405) and virtual (400) repositories, and answers 404 when nothing matched. Removed files are soft-deleted like every other delete path, so storage GC reclaims them.

- **Conan package search on a local repository returns each binary's configuration, so `conan list -p` and `conan download -p` filter correctly** (#4334). The hosted package search answered every package id with an empty object, so a settings filter such as `-p "os=Linux"` matched no binary: `conan list` reported none, and `conan download` exited 0 having downloaded nothing. Each package id now carries its stored `conaninfo.txt` as `{"content": ...}`, the shape conan_server returns and the Conan 2 client parses, for local repositories and for the local members of a virtual. `?list_only=True` still answers with the ids alone, without reading the files.

- **Conan recipe and package `/latest` report the revision's stored time** (#4335). Both endpoints built their `time` from the clock at request time, so the same revision showed a new time on every read, and that time did not match the revision's entry in `/revisions`. `/latest` now returns the first entry of the same revision-history query `/revisions` uses, with the same time, so repeated reads are stable and agree with the history. For a remote repository answering from its upstream, the upstream's own `time` is passed through.

- **Severity counts agree across the Overview dashboard, the security dashboard, the per-repository scores and the artifact view** (#4338). The same data gave three different critical counts: the security tiles and repository scores counted finding rows, so one CVE found in two packages, or by two scanners, counted twice; the repository scores were only recomputed after a scan, so acknowledging a finding changed the tiles but not the repository row; and the Overview summary counted every CVE ever recorded, including ones a rescan no longer reports, with acknowledged ones in its severity buckets. All of them now use one definition (`services/open_findings.rs`): for each artifact the latest completed scan of each scan type, one vulnerability per (artifact, advisory) where the advisory is the CVE id or the finding title, at its highest reported severity, with open vulnerabilities in the severity counts and acknowledged ones counted separately. Acknowledging or un-acknowledging a finding recomputes its repository's score, and an artifact's CVE history marks a CVE its latest scans no longer report as `fixed`. Repository scores and grades can change on upgrade because duplicates no longer count; `total_findings` on a repository score is now its open vulnerabilities, as on the dashboard. Closes #4338.

- **A Cargo pull-through now downloads crates whose canonical name has an uppercase letter, such as `Inflector`** (#4339). The Remote and Virtual download paths built the upstream `.crate` URL from the lowercased crate name, and crates.io stopped serving non-canonical spellings in December 2023, so every such crate answered 404 and `cargo fetch` failed on the first one. The upstream is now asked for the name exactly as the client requested it (cargo always uses the canonical spelling from the index), both for a registry's `dl` template (`{crate}` and `{prefix}`) and for the plain `api/v1/crates/{name}/{version}/download` path; the proxy cache key, the catalog and the index lookups stay lowercase, so every spelling shares one cache entry.

- **npm tarball downloads served directly from a Remote repository without scan-on-proxy are counted again** (closes #4341). The unscanned direct-Remote tarball path streamed the package without recording a proxy download, so download statistics, and the popularity and curation signals built on them, undercounted npm proxy traffic; the same tarball served through a Virtual, or with scan-on-proxy enabled, was counted. That path now records one download per GET under the canonical tarball path (never on HEAD), off the response path like Maven's. A last-known-good tarball a Virtual serves from an age-gated member is counted under that member too. The proxy-download recording check (#3446) now sees npm's direct-Remote streaming call, and no longer accepts a serve path as recorded only because the same function also calls the scan-on-proxy wrapper, which records its own serve and nothing else.

- **Maven `.meta/prefixes.txt` no longer lists nested groupIds, which made Maven 4 deny artifacts the repository serves** (#4367). Entries whose parent prefix is already listed are now left out.

- **`ansible-galaxy collection install` resolves collections through a Virtual Ansible repository** (#4379). The Galaxy metadata routes built their documents from the repository's own artifacts, which a Virtual never has, so `versions/` answered an empty list and the collection and version detail routes answered 404 while `download/` already served the members' tarballs; the install failed with "Could not satisfy the following requirements". On a Virtual these routes now read the members the caller may read, in priority order: the version list and the collection list are the members' union, the detail documents come from the first member that has them (a Remote member answers from its upstream as before), and every `href` and `download_url` points back at the Virtual. A member's upstream outage is reported as that error rather than as an empty list when no other member has versions.

- **A layer shared with an image blocked by scan policy no longer blocks every other image that uses it** (#4380). On a Docker/OCI remote repository with scan-on-proxy, one image with a blocking verdict made `GET /v2/<name>/blobs/<digest>` answer `403 blob belongs to an image blocked by scan policy` for any layer it shared with other images, under every image name in the repository, so clean images that shared a base or empty layer with it could not be pulled. A blob carries no image identity, so the blob check now refuses a blob only when no image in the repository that references it would be served by the manifest gate; the blocked image itself is still refused at its manifest, and its config and its own layers stay refused by digest. An image without a verdict yet counts as served under `fail_open` (the manifest gate serves it pending) and not under `fail_closed`. The security dashboard's `policy_violations_blocked`, previously always `0`, now counts proxied content currently refused by scan policy plus hosted artifacts in the `rejected` quarantine state.

- **Incus images and Debian packages uploaded through the chunked upload API now get the same metadata and index entries as the native upload routes** (#4403, #1846). `PUT /api/v1/uploads/{id}/complete` wrote a bare artifact row with no format processing, so an Incus image pushed that way was named after its file (its `images.json` download URL pointed at a product that does not exist) and had no arch/os/release, and a `.deb` was named after its file, versioned by its pool directory, and listed in `Packages` with "No description available" and no `Depends`. Completion now dispatches to the native finalize for incus/lxc repositories (`<product>/<version>/<file>` image paths) and Debian repositories (`pool/<component>/.../*.deb`): the row takes the product/package name and version, the `artifact_metadata` row (image `metadata.yaml`, or the control file) and the catalog row are written, and Debian maintainer scripts are analysed. A `.deb` whose control file disagrees with its file name is refused with 400 before anything is stored, as the native route refuses it. Other formats are unchanged, and the completion stays synchronous for Incus.

- **Multipart uploads into S3-, GCS- and Azure-backed repositories no longer spool to local disk** (#4404, #3916). The multipart `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts` and `.../artifacts/{path}` routes still wrote the file field to a scratch file under `STORAGE_PATH` before it reached the repository's object storage; they now stream it into a `generic-upload-staging/<uuid>` object on the repository's backend and promote it, as the raw `PUT` route does since #4321. Filesystem repositories and repositories with a WASM format plugin keep the local spool. In RPM repositories, `.rpm` packages keep it (their header parse reads the file), and so does every file sent to `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts`, whose form can name the path after the file field. A new operations page, `docs/operations/upload-scratch-disk.md`, lists which upload paths still use local scratch and how to size it.

- **Rotating a signing key created without a `repository_id` now repoints the Debian and RPM repositories bound to it** (#4416). Rotation only updated the signing config of the repository named on the key itself, so a key created unscoped and bound through `POST /api/v1/signing/repositories/{id}/config` left those configs on the retired key, and InRelease, Release.gpg and the public key returned 404 "No signing key configured for this repository" after rotation. Rotation now moves every signing config bound to the old key to its successor, in the same transaction; the old key still co-signs during the rotation overlap window.

- **Two concurrent publishes of the same RPM curation version no longer interleave their repodata writes** (#4421). Both requests passed the "already published" check and wrote the same immutable `@N` repodata keys, so `repomd.xml` and `repomd.xml.asc` could come from different writers and fail verification. A publish now holds a per-version lock for its whole run and re-checks immutability under it; the second request gets 409 Conflict before it writes anything. Marking the version published also requires `published_at IS NULL`, and a lost race at that point returns 409 without deleting the winner's repodata.

- **Repository and project storage quotas now apply to every native format publish, not only the generic upload API, chunked uploads and npm** (#4422). Until now most native publish handlers wrote their artifact rows directly and skipped the check: Alpine, Ansible, Bazel, Cargo, Chef, CocoaPods, Composer, Conan, Conda, CRAN, Git LFS, Go, Helm, Hex, Hugging Face, Incus, JetBrains, Maven, OCI/Docker, Pacman, Protobuf (BSR), Pub, Puppet, RPM, RubyGems, sbt, Swift, Terraform and VS Code. (PyPI, NuGet and Debian already went through the generic upload path.) Their bytes counted toward `quota_bytes` but an upload was never refused, so a repository or project could grow past its cap. Each of these publishes now runs the same two-step admission as the generic route: a preflight before the bytes are written, and the authoritative locked check in the transaction that records the artifact. A refused publish answers `507 QUOTA_EXCEEDED` with `Repository storage quota exceeded` or `Project storage quota exceeded`, and leaves no artifact row.

  Format-specific details: a `docker push` is checked on each blob upload (monolithic and chunked) and on cross-repository blob mounts, and a refusal uses the registry error envelope (`507`, code `DENIED`). A manifest is never refused for quota: its row records the image size, whose bytes were already admitted blob by blob, so it is charged nothing (#4545). A manifest whose descriptors declare a negative or absurd size is now rejected with `400 MANIFEST_INVALID`. A Protobuf (BSR) upload answers a Connect `resource_exhausted` error with status 507. An Incus image upload refuses synchronously when the preflight already fails. When a concurrent upload uses up the remaining space after that preflight, the background finalize marks the upload session `failed` with the quota message. Every other format, including Cargo, Git LFS and Swift, answers the generic JSON body `{"code":"QUOTA_EXCEEDED","message":...}` rather than a format-native error shape. A publish that adds no bytes is always admitted, for example a re-push of a blob the repository already holds or an overwrite with identical or smaller content. Unlimited repositories and projects behave as before. Promotions, migration imports, peer replication and proxy-cache fills are still not checked against the target's quota.

  **Upgrade note.** Before this release only the generic upload API, chunked uploads and npm enforced quotas, so a repository or project could already have grown past its `quota_bytes` through any other format. After upgrading, every publish that adds bytes to such a repository or project is refused with `507` until usage drops below the cap or the quota is raised. Check repository and project usage against their quotas before upgrading. Docker usage counts each manifest's image size on top of the blobs that hold those bytes, and counts it again for every additional tag of the same image (#4545). A capped Docker repository therefore refuses new blobs well before its real bytes reach the cap. Size Docker quotas with that in mind until #4545 lands.

- **Virtual repositories no longer report their members' bytes as their own `storage_used_bytes`** (#4423). Since #2785 a virtual repository's `storage_used_bytes` in `GET /api/v1/repositories` and `GET`/`PATCH /api/v1/repositories/{key}` was the sum of its members, so any per-project or instance total that added up repositories counted those bytes twice. A virtual repository now reports `storage_used_bytes: 0`, and the member total moves to a new `member_storage_used_bytes` field (still scoped to the members the caller can see; `null` for non-virtual repositories). The project quota rollup also skips virtual repositories explicitly. Clients that display a virtual repository's size should read `member_storage_used_bytes`.

  **Upgrade note — deliberate behaviour change for virtual repositories.** Before this release a virtual repository's `storage_used_bytes` was the combined size of its members (#2785); it is now always `0`, and that combined size is in `member_storage_used_bytes` (list, detail, create and PATCH responses). Clients that show a virtual repository's size, including the web UI and the CLI until their follow-up releases ship, will show 0 for every virtual repository until they read `member_storage_used_bytes`. Totals that sum `storage_used_bytes` across repositories need no change: they are now correct.

- **pacman `.db` requests no longer read every package's file list, and `.files` is rendered once per repository state** (#4424). Hosted pacman repositories kept each package's file list (up to 500,000 names) inside its `artifact_metadata` document, so every `pacman -Sy`, anonymous on a public repository, made PostgreSQL detoast all of them only to strip them again, and every `pacman -Fy` re-read and re-gzipped them all. File lists now live in their own `pacman_file_lists` table that the `.db` query never touches, and the rendered `.files` database is cached in memory per repository and package set (whatever architecture name the request uses, with one render in flight per repository), so a publish, delete or signature upload is picked up on the next request without explicit invalidation. Migration 276 creates the table and moves existing lists out of `artifact_metadata` in resumable batches of 100 rows.

- **Hash-based scan reuse now copies only from a scan that actually ran, never from another reused copy** (#4425). When an artifact's scan was reused from an identical artifact, the reused row was stamped with the time of the copy, so it became the newest match and later uploads of the same bytes copied from the copy. Copies chained onto copies, and each hop restarted the reuse window, so a verdict could stay reusable long after the scan behind it had expired. Reuse now requires an original scan (`source_scan_id IS NULL`), which keeps every reused row one hop from a real scan and bounds reuse by that scan's age. An artifact whose own scan is a reused copy is still treated as already scanned, so a rescan of it does not add a second completed scan.

- **The scan reuse index now covers only scans this instance ran itself** (#4426). The partial index behind hash-based scan reuse gains `origin = 'local_scan'` in its predicate, matching the filter the reuse query already applies, so scan evidence imported from a bundle is never indexed as a reuse candidate. The index is rebuilt online by migrations 273 to 275 (`CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` under a new name, `idx_scan_results_dedup_local`, then `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY` of the old one), so the upgrade does not block scan writes. The build reads `scan_results` twice and needs disk space for the new index next to the old one until the drop. If the concurrent build is interrupted, for example by a lock timeout behind a long transaction, the next startup drops the INVALID leftover index before migrations run, so the retry rebuilds it and the old index is never dropped while the new one is unusable.

- **RPM curation sync now ingests zstd, xz and bzip2 compressed `primary.xml`, and a sync that ingests nothing reports failure** (#4427). Before this fix, the sync only gunzipped a `.gz` primary and read every other href as plain text. An upstream whose `repomd.xml` lists `primary.xml.zst` therefore parsed as 0 packages, while the manual sync still returned `succeeded: true`. That is the createrepo_c default, common on Fedora and EL9 mirrors, so the staging repository was silently emptied.

  What changed:
  - The primary is decoded by its magic bytes (gzip, zstd, xz, bzip2 or plain), and every codec is held to the existing ingest decompression budget (`MAX_INGEST_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES`, 128 MiB by default). Note that a Fedora 44 Everything x86_64 primary decodes to about 177 MiB, so mirroring it requires raising that variable.
  - A plain `primary.xml` must now be valid UTF-8, as the format requires; it is no longer read lossily.
  - These cases now fail that staging repository's sync (manual trigger: `succeeded: false`; the repository retries on the next tick) instead of reporting success:
    - a primary that declares packages but yields none
    - a compressed href whose bytes are not that codec
    - a primary that cannot be decoded
    - a repomd or primary fetch failure
    - a GPG refusal (no trusted key without `curation_allow_unverified`, missing `.asc`, or a failed verification)
    - a checksum-chain mismatch
  - A failing repository no longer aborts the scheduled sweep for the remaining repositories. Repositories are now swept least-recently-synced first.

- **`WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS=true` now takes effect when `AK_SSRF_ALLOW_PRIVATE_CIDRS` is also set** (#4428). Configuring the shared private-CIDR allowlist (usually to narrow the upstream/proxy surface) made it the only rule for webhook targets too, so an explicit webhook toggle was silently ignored and a private webhook receiver outside the listed CIDRs was refused at create and at delivery. For webhook targets the two knobs are now additive: the toggle admits every private address, and without it the CIDR list still applies. Upstream and SSO behaviour is unchanged (a configured CIDR list stays authoritative there), and cloud-metadata, loopback and link-local addresses remain blocked in every case.

- **The bundled `docker/init-dtrack.sh` grants `VIEW_POLICY_VIOLATION` to the Automation team, so Dependency-Track policy violations load** (#4430). Reading a project's policy violations (`GET /api/v1/violation/project/{uuid}`) needs that permission, which the script did not grant, so every request answered `502 Bad gateway` with Dependency-Track's `403 Forbidden` underneath. A Dependency-Track instance or API key you provisioned yourself must grant it to the key's team too; the permission hint in the error message and `.env.example` now list it with the other five.

- **An npm package that mixes numeric and hash prerelease versions no longer panics its packument request through an age-gated repository** (#4431). `confusing-browser-globals` publishes `2.0.0-next.74`, `-next.103` and `-next.2150693d`, and the version comparator ordered them `74 < 103 < 2150693d < 74`: numeric between two numbers, lexical otherwise. `sort_by` panicked on that cycle, the connection dropped, and every request for the package failed. Version segments are now compared in natural order: leading digits by value, then the rest lexically. npm prerelease identifiers follow SemVer 2.0.0 §11.4.3, where a numeric identifier ranks below an alphanumeric one. The curation comparator behind the Hex, NuGet and package version listings had the same cycle and uses the same natural order.

- **The age gate keeps an npm package's own `latest` tag instead of re-pointing it to the newest allowed version** (#4432). Every gated packument had `latest` set to the newest version that passed the gate, prereleases included, so `npm install typescript` resolved to a nightly build and `next` to a canary. A `latest` the gate allows is now kept. When the gate blocks it, `latest` moves to the newest allowed release at or below it, then the newest allowed release, then the newest allowed version of any kind.

- **Deleting the last tag of an OCI image pushed only by tag now also removes its `oci_manifests` record** (#4449). After the delete the manifest is no longer pullable by digest, but the record introduced in #4441 stayed and claimed it still existed. The record now goes when the delete removed the last tag and no live manifest row for the digest and no live parent index still references it. An image that was also pushed by digest, or a child manifest still listed by another tagged index, stays pullable and keeps its record.

- **An OCI Remote whose upstream token service rejects its credentials now reports an upstream authentication failure instead of "manifest unknown"** (#4453). A 401 or 403 from the upstream's bearer token endpoint was logged as `Storage error` and the client got `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN`, so wrong upstream credentials looked like a missing image. When the Remote's credentials were actually sent to the token service, the pull now fails with `502` and the OCI error code `DENIED` ("upstream registry authentication failed"). The backend also logs a warning on the `security` target naming the token service (redacted, no credentials), at most once a minute per Remote, with a count of the warnings suppressed in between. A refusal of an anonymous token request still reports `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` and is logged at INFO. That covers a Remote without credentials, and one whose credentials were withheld from an untrusted cross-origin realm (#4527). Other token-endpoint failures are unchanged.

- **Every lifecycle policy regex is now validated by PostgreSQL, the engine that runs it, and `\b` / `\B` are refused** (#4461). `exclude.version_patterns` and the `pattern` of `tag_pattern_keep` / `tag_pattern_delete` were only checked with the Rust `regex` crate, but PostgreSQL executes them and the two dialects differ. A protective exclusion such as `\bstable\b` validated, then matched nothing in PostgreSQL (where `\b` means backspace), so the versions it was written to protect were deleted; `\z`, `\pL`, `(?P<name>...)` or a mid-pattern `(?i)` validated and then failed every run. Creating or updating a policy now compiles each of these patterns with PostgreSQL (on its own connection, with a 2-second limit, before any lock is taken) and returns 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR` for one it rejects or cannot compile in time. It also refuses `\b` / `\B` with a hint to use `\y` / `\Y` (as #4459 already did for `match.version_pattern`), back-references, patterns over 512 bytes and more than 64 `exclude.version_patterns`. The Rust-crate check, which wrongly rejected valid PostgreSQL syntax such as `\y`, is gone. Stored policies are not changed. The backend logs one WARN per offending policy at startup, and a preview lists the problems in `errors` (stopping with zero matches when a pattern cannot compile or a `match.version_pattern` or `tag_pattern_delete` pattern uses `\b` / `\B`). A live run refuses a policy whose exclusion or `tag_pattern_keep` pattern would fail open, or whose `match.version_pattern` or `tag_pattern_delete` pattern uses `\b` / `\B`, until it is fixed. The patterns are documented as PostgreSQL regular expressions, unanchored unless they use `^` / `$`.

- **The OCI migration reindex only repairs manifests the migration worker imported, so an image pushed by tag and deleted by digest before 1.11.0 stays deleted after the upgrade** (#4465). The startup repair treated any live manifest row without a tag as a never-indexed migrated manifest. An image pushed only by tag (`skopeo copy --all` pushes an index that way) and deleted by digest on an older release, or by a not-yet-upgraded replica during the rollout, leaves exactly that, so the upgrade restart re-registered it (#4450). The candidate scan now also requires `artifacts.origin` to record a migration import (`kind = migration`: stamped by the worker since #4050 and by migration 270 for older imports matched to their migration items). A row written by `docker push` carries the hosted origin and is never repaired. Migrated, never-indexed images are still repaired as before. One case remains: a migrated image pushed only by tag and deleted by digest on an older release still looks like an unindexed import and is re-registered; delete it again after the upgrade.

- **`PATCH /api/v1/repositories/{key}` now applies `upstream_url` instead of returning 200 and ignoring it** (#4467). Rotating credentials embedded in a Remote's upstream URL, or repointing a Remote, silently did nothing, and since #4462 redacts the URL in responses a client could not tell. The new URL is validated exactly as on create (SSRF guard, scheme and host checks, per-format rules), and the response redacts userinfo and sets `upstream_url_has_credentials`. Moving the URL to a different origin (scheme, host or port) while upstream-auth credentials are configured is refused with 409, so stored credentials are never sent to a host they were not configured for: remove them (`PUT .../upstream-auth` with `auth_type: "none"`), change the URL, then configure credentials for the new upstream. The audit entry for the update records the previous and new upstream URL (userinfo redacted) and whether the embedded credentials changed. The age gate no longer counts credentials embedded in the URL as part of the upstream's identity, so rotating them keeps first-seen times and review decisions; first-seen times and approvals recorded under a credentialed URL by earlier releases are moved to the new identity at startup (and again before a PATCH changes the URL). Changing the host or path still starts the age gate afresh, as a repoint should. Content already cached from the old upstream stays cached and is served until it expires or is purged.

- **The runtime images now ship `unsquashfs`, which the Incus scanner needs to extract SquashFS rootfs images** (#4469). The scanner runs `unsquashfs` on both its local Trivy path and its scanner-adapter path, but neither `Dockerfile.backend` nor `Dockerfile.backend.alpine` installed it, so every SquashFS Incus image scanned by a published image failed at extraction. The Alpine image installs `squashfs-tools`. The UBI image builds `unsquashfs` from the pinned squashfs-tools 4.7.5 release (sha256-verified and built hardened), because the UBI 9 repositories do not carry squashfs-tools; its GPL-2.0 licence text and the exact source tarball it is built from ship under `/licenses/squashfs-tools/`, and the rootfs gains `libzstd`, which it links. The UBI build reads gzip, xz and zstd SquashFS images; LZO and LZ4 images extract only on the Alpine image, whose distro package has all five codecs (see `docs/incus-image-scanning.md`). Extraction as the image's non-root user of images that carry `security.*` xattrs or device nodes is fixed separately (#4470).

- **Incus SquashFS scans no longer fail on images with extended attributes or device nodes** (#4470). The backend runs as a non-root user, and `unsquashfs` exits 2 on such an image because it cannot write `security.*` xattrs or create device nodes, which most real rootfs images carry; the scanner treated that as a failed extraction. `unsquashfs` now runs with `-no-xattrs`, and exit 2 (device nodes, timestamp, mode and symlink errors) is a logged warning, unless it reports a full disk or quota. Write, decompression and metadata errors (exit 1, such as an unsupported compressor) still fail the scan, as does an extraction that leaves no regular file. Unified tarballs extracted with GNU `tar` (the UBI image) get the same treatment: a `Cannot mknod` on a device node is a warning, and any other `tar` error still fails. The Alpine image extracts with busybox `tar`, which is unchanged.

- **`SSO_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS=true` now takes effect when `AK_SSRF_ALLOW_PRIVATE_CIDRS` is also set** (#4474). As with the webhook toggle (#4428), configuring the shared private-CIDR allowlist made it the only rule for OIDC/SSO endpoints, so an explicit SSO toggle was silently ignored and a private identity provider outside the listed CIDRs was refused, both when its URL was validated and at connect time. For SSO the two knobs are now additive: the toggle admits every private address, and without it the CIDR list still applies. Upstream behaviour is unchanged (a configured CIDR list stays authoritative there), and cloud-metadata, loopback and link-local addresses remain blocked. `.env.example` now documents `WEBHOOK_ALLOW_PRIVATE_IPS` and this rule for both surfaces.

- **SAML login now DEFLATE-encodes the AuthnRequest on the HTTP-Redirect binding** (#4475). The `SAMLRequest` parameter carried base64 of the bare XML, which SAML 2.0 Bindings §3.4.4.1 does not allow; IdPs that enforce the binding, such as Microsoft Entra ID (`AADSTS750055`) and Shibboleth/CAS, rejected every SP-initiated login. The request is now raw-DEFLATE compressed before base64 encoding.

- **Redeploying a Maven snapshot artifact to the same timestamped path is accepted again instead of failing with 409** (#4476). A build that deploys the same attached artifact twice in one `mvn deploy` uploads the same timestamped file (`object-1.0-20261006.124037-3-clear.jar`) twice. Up to 1.8.0 the second upload replaced the first; since #3839 (1.10.0) the upload path treated a resolved unique snapshot as immutable and refused it, which failed the build. Snapshots are documented as overwritable, so every file under a `-SNAPSHOT` version directory, unique or not, is republished in place again. Release coordinates still answer 409, a version that only contains the token (`1.0-SNAPSHOT-rc1`) is still a release, and the proxy cache's classification of unique snapshots is unchanged.

- **The stock `docker-compose.yml` and `.env.example` no longer ship secret values the backend refuses at startup** (#4478, #4313, #1350). Compose defaulted `JWT_SECRET` to `change-me-in-production-please` and `AK_WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY` to an intentionally invalid placeholder, and `.env.example` carried `JWT_SECRET=change-this-in-production-use-at-least-32-bytes`. The backend rejects all three, so `docker compose up -d` gave a backend that restarted forever while the web UI looked healthy, and operators had to find and fix two variables over two restart cycles. `JWT_SECRET` now has no default: unset, the backend exits once with its existing error naming the variable and `openssl rand -base64 48`. `AK_WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY` is passed through only when it is defined, so an unset key starts the backend with a warning (webhook create and rotate-secret return HTTP 500 until it is set) instead of stopping it. `.env.example` leaves `JWT_SECRET=` empty and documents both `openssl rand` commands, and `scripts/install.sh` now generates `AK_WEBHOOK_SECRET_KEY` alongside `JWT_SECRET`.

- **Every image in the stock `docker-compose.yml` now names its registry** (#4479). `postgres:18-alpine`, `alpine:3.24`, `caddy:2-alpine`, `opensearchproject/opensearch` and the two Dependency-Track images were short names, which the container engine resolves per host: under podman's default `short-name-mode = "enforcing"` the `db` service ran a locally cached `ghcr.io/artifact-keeper/ci-mirror/postgres:18-alpine` instead of Docker Hub's image, and hosts with several unqualified search registries need an alias or a TTY prompt that compose does not have. They are now `docker.io/library/...` and `docker.io/<namespace>/...` with unchanged tags, so every host pulls the same image.

- **`ARTIFACT_KEEPER_VERSION` now pins the openscap image too, and the web image has its own `ARTIFACT_KEEPER_WEB_VERSION` pin** (#4481, #2708). The stock `docker-compose.yml` documented `ARTIFACT_KEEPER_VERSION` as the way to pin a release, but only the backend honoured it: `artifact-keeper-openscap`, which every backend release publishes with the same tag, and `artifact-keeper-web` were hardcoded to `:latest`, so a "pinned" stack still pulled whatever `latest` was for two of its images. openscap now uses `${ARTIFACT_KEEPER_VERSION:-latest}`. Because web releases are decoupled from backend releases (#2708), web gets a separate `ARTIFACT_KEEPER_WEB_VERSION` (default `latest`). Both are documented in `.env.example`.

- **The stock Caddyfile now routes `/general`, `/pacman`, `/bazel` and `/lxc` to the backend** (#4482, #1772). `docker/Caddyfile` sends each native format prefix straight to the backend and lets everything else fall through to the web UI, but it was missing four prefixes the backend mounts. Behind the stock compose stack `/pacman/*` and `/bazel/*` returned the web UI's HTML 404, `/general/*` (the generic download route reported in #1772) worked only with web code that is not released yet, and `/lxc/*` worked only because the web middleware proxies it. All four are now routed directly, and a CI check derives the prefix list from `format_routes` in `backend/src/api/routes.rs` so a newly mounted format cannot be left out again.

- **Docker/OCI repository usage and storage quotas count each layer once** (#4483, #4545). An OCI manifest's `artifacts` row records the image size (config plus layers, #3601), and those same bytes are counted through `oci_blobs`, so `storage_used_bytes` (the repository header and list), `GET /repositories/{key}` and the usage ledger behind quotas counted every image at least twice, and once more for every extra tag: one reported repository held 1.10 GB of blobs and showed 4.69 GB used, and a capped Docker repository refused pushes well before its real bytes reached the cap. Usage and the ledger now leave out rows stored under `oci-manifests/` (the rule the storage panel already used, #3286); `artifacts.size_bytes` keeps the image size, so the tag listing, the packages catalog and the UI are unchanged. A manifest row is admitted at 0 bytes on push, which is now exactly what it adds to the ledger. The manifest documents themselves (a few KB each) are no longer counted toward usage.

  Migration 288 replaces the ledger trigger function and recomputes `hosted_bytes` for every repository that holds OCI manifest rows, so existing deployments are corrected on upgrade. The background reconciler and `POST /api/v1/admin/storage/ledger/backfill` use the same rule.

- **A lifecycle preview of a stored policy whose `match.version_pattern` uses `\b` / `\B` now lists the problem in `errors` instead of failing with 400** (#4502). The preview stopped at the `\b` refusal `match.version_pattern` has had since #4459 and returned `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` without its `errors` list, while the documentation said such a policy is reported and still runs. The preview now returns 200 with the problem in `errors` and zero matches, and a live run refuses the policy with 400 before it touches any repository. It is still refused rather than run, because a `\b` that matches nothing does not make a scope safe: inside a negative lookahead such as `^(?!.*\bstable)` it widens the scope to every version. The same applies to the `pattern` of a `tag_pattern_delete` policy, which used to run with `\b` (`^(?!.*\bkeep)` deletes every tag) and is now reported by the preview and refused by a live run in the same way. The documentation now says so. Nothing stored is changed; fix the pattern (use `\y` / `\Y`) with `PATCH /api/v1/admin/lifecycle/{id}`.

- **A live run of a lifecycle policy with a stored pattern PostgreSQL cannot compile now returns 400 naming the field instead of 500 `DATABASE_ERROR`** (#4504). A policy stored before create/update validated its patterns with PostgreSQL (or written to the database directly) could carry a `match.version_pattern` or `pattern` such as `foo\z`. The preview already listed it in `errors`, but `POST /api/v1/admin/lifecycle/{id}/execute` and scheduled runs sent it to PostgreSQL and failed with a 500. The live run now runs the same check as the preview first and refuses the policy with `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` ("... is not a valid PostgreSQL regular expression"). Nothing was deleted before and nothing is now; fix the pattern with `PATCH /api/v1/admin/lifecycle/{id}`.

- **Creating a virtual repository whose members already hold content reports their total in the create response** (Closes #4505). `POST /api/v1/repositories` for a virtual repository with `member_repos` returned `member_storage_used_bytes: 0` even when the members held data, while the next `GET` and any `PATCH` reported the real total. The create response now computes the member total after attaching the members, scoped to the members the caller can see, as `GET` does.

- **Curation version constraints and version ordering now honour Debian/RPM and PEP 440 epochs** (Closes #4507). `version_compare` split versions on `.` and `-` and left an epoch glued to the first segment, so `1:2.0-1` compared as lower than `10.0-1` and `1:1.0` as lower than `2.0`. It now parses a leading `N:` (Debian/RPM) or `N!` (PEP 440 / conda) epoch, treats a missing epoch as 0, compares epochs numerically first and the rest in the existing natural order. This changes curation rule matches for epoch-bearing deb and rpm versions: a block rule `< 10.0` no longer matches `1:2.0-1`, and an allow rule `>= 10.0` now does. Listings ordered by this comparator (Hex, NuGet, the packages API) order epoch-bearing versions the same way.

- **A virtual repository member whose upstream is down no longer stalls every metadata miss until the reverse proxy gives up** (closes #4508). When one Remote member of a virtual stopped answering (connections blackholed rather than refused), every metadata lookup that reached it waited for the upstream client's 60 second connect or read timeout, longer than a typical reverse proxy allows a request, so clients saw `504 Gateway Timeout` and builds slowed to a crawl (reported on Maven `maven-metadata.xml`). Each Remote member's metadata fetch is now bounded by a member deadline, `AK_VIRTUAL_MEMBER_METADATA_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default 20): a member that misses it fails the request promptly with a 502 that names the member, consistent with the loud member-failure policy (#4192), instead of being waited on or silently skipped. It applies to the Maven virtual `maven-metadata.xml` merges (release, plugin-prefix and SNAPSHOT) and `.meta/prefixes.txt`, to the shared first-hit metadata walk, and to the merged indexes of Helm, CRAN, Hex and Bazel virtuals, where a late member counts as a failed member (`reason="timeout"`) and is reported in `X-AK-Partial-Members` when the virtual allows partial merges. New metric: `ak_virtual_member_metadata_timeouts_total{member}`. Artifact downloads are not bounded by it.

- **An OCI Remote whose upstream registry refuses its credentials on the manifest request itself now reports an upstream authentication failure instead of "manifest unknown"** (#4518). #4453 covered a 401/403 from the upstream's token service. A 401/403 from the registry on the manifest request itself was still reported as `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN`. That happened after a successful token exchange whose token the registry then refused, and for an upstream that uses plain Basic auth and rejects the credentials. When the Remote's upstream credentials were actually sent, a direct Remote manifest GET or HEAD now fails with `502` and the OCI error code `DENIED`. The backend also logs a warning on the `security` target naming the upstream URL (redacted, no credentials), at most once a minute per Remote, with a count of the warnings suppressed in between. When no credentials were sent, the refusal keeps `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` and is logged at INFO. That covers a Remote without credentials, and a token obtained anonymously because the realm is not trusted (#4527). The reason: an anonymous refusal usually means the image does not exist or is private (Docker Hub answers 401 for a repository that does not exist). Generic proxy formats are unchanged.

- **`GET` / `HEAD /v2/<name>/manifests/<digest>` on a hosted repository now resolve the digest under `<name>`, not repository-wide** (#4525). After `DELETE <repo>/xa@<digest>` (scoped to the image name since #4466), the same digest was still served as `xa@<digest>` while another image name in the repository (`xb:v1`) tagged it. On Local and Staging repositories a digest reference now resolves through a tag (or by-digest push) of the requested image name, or, for a manifest that is no longer tagged under it (an overwritten tag, #1681), through the repository's manifest records unless every manifest row that image name had for that digest is in the trash. A digest deleted under one image name therefore answers `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` under that name and keeps resolving under the others. `DELETE` by digest uses the same resolution, so repeating a delete under the deleted name is a `404`. Remote and Virtual repositories are unchanged.

- **A credentialed OCI Remote whose bearer realm is not trusted reports a missing image as `MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` again, not as rejected credentials** (#4527). Such a Remote never sends its credentials to the cross-origin token service (#3591), so the token is anonymous, and the registry refusing it (Docker Hub answers 401 for an image that does not exist) said nothing about the credentials. Since #4453 / #4518 it was nevertheless reported as `502 DENIED` with a `security` warning. Now `502 DENIED` and the warning apply only when credentials were actually sent to the token service or the registry; otherwise the pull answers `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` and the refusal is logged at INFO. The `security` warning that credentials were withheld from an untrusted realm (#3591), which fired on every pull, is now logged at most once a minute per Remote with a count of the suppressed ones.

- **A NuGet Remote's flat-container download no longer 404s when the client spells the file name in mixed case** (#4528). The proxy lowercased only the package id segment of the upstream flat-container path and forwarded the version and the `.nupkg` file name as sent, so `GET .../flatcontainer/Newtonsoft.Json/13.0.3/Newtonsoft.Json.13.0.3.nupkg` asked nuget.org for a path it does not serve. The NuGet V3 flat container defines the whole path as lowercase, so the id, the version and the file name are now all lowercased: every spelling reaches the same upstream URL and the same cache entry, and a scan-blocked version answers 403 under any spelling. Real NuGet clients already send lowercase and see no change.

- **With `PROXY_SINGLEFLIGHT_ADVISORY_LOCKS_ENABLED=true`, a cold streamed object is fetched upstream once cluster-wide instead of once per request** (#4532, #4013). Before, every request contended for the cross-replica lock, including requests in the leader's own replica. The losers gave up after about 1.6 s and fetched upstream themselves: 200 concurrent GETs of a 256 MiB object across 3 replicas made 94-100 upstream fetches, and the mock upstream answered many of them with 502. Now requests coalesce in-process first, and only one request per replica contends for the lock. A replica that loses waits for the leader to finish and then serves the object, with its waiting requests, from the cache. The leader releases the lock only after its cache entry is published. A woken replica also drops the cache miss it remembered for up to 30 s, so it finds the new entry instead of fetching the object a second time. If the leader is still downloading after `PROXY_SINGLEFLIGHT_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECS` (default 65), each waiting replica fetches the object once itself. That keeps the worst case at one upstream fetch per replica, not one per request. Each waiting replica holds one database connection per cold object while it waits. `PROXY_SINGLEFLIGHT_MAX_LOCK_WAITERS` caps those waits (default 32 per replica; past the cap a replica fetches at once). Keep `PROXY_SINGLEFLIGHT_LOCK_WAIT_TIMEOUT_SECS` below your ingress read timeout. If the leading replica's node is lost mid-download (for example a force-deleted pod), Postgres detects the dead connection through TCP keepalives on the lock session within about 30 s. It then releases the lock, and the waiting replicas re-elect a new leader at once instead of waiting out the full timeout.

- **A download served through a virtual repository by one of its Remote members is now counted** (#4535, #3844). Both virtual-download resolvers recorded only a hosted (Local/Staging) member that won, so a virtual download answered by a Remote member (a presigned redirect, a proxy-cache hit or an upstream fetch) was missing from both `download_statistics` and `proxy_download_statistics`, and an all-proxy deployment fronted by a virtual repository reported no downloads at all. The winning Remote member is now recorded once in `proxy_download_statistics` under the member's own repository and path, the same row a direct download from that Remote writes. Members that were probed but lost to a higher-priority member are not counted, and a `HEAD` is never counted. The row is written off the response path, as for Maven's direct Remote downloads. Applies to every format whose Virtual download goes through the shared resolvers, with two deliberate exceptions that keep parity with their direct Remote routes, which do not count these either: Go `.mod` files and protobuf commit bundles. The formats with their own member walk (NuGet, PyPI, Helm) already recorded their Remote serves and are unchanged.

- **Proxy download history now survives cache eviction, and the admin download report covers proxy serves** (#4539, #3844). Proxy download rows were deleted together with their cache entry (`proxy_download_statistics.proxy_cache_id` cascaded from `proxy_cache_artifacts`), so every lifecycle eviction or cache purge erased the download history of what it removed, and per-path counts restarted from zero after a re-cache. Rows are now also keyed on the Remote repository and path they were served from; evicting an entry only detaches its rows (`ON DELETE SET NULL`), deleting the repository still deletes them, and the per-path and per-repository proxy counts read the new key. Migrations 277-283 add and backfill the key online (batched, no table rewrite) and build its index, and an IP index for the by-IP listing, concurrently.

  The admin download listing (`GET /api/v1/admin/downloads`, `/downloads/by-ip/{ip}`, `/downloads/by-user/{user_id}`) now returns proxy pull-through serves alongside hosted downloads. Each row carries `source` (`hosted` or `proxy`), `repository_id` and `path`; `artifact_id` is `null` for a proxy serve, which has no artifact row. New `source` and `repository_id` query filters select between them. `GET /api/v1/admin/stats` `total_downloads` now includes proxy serves, with the new `proxy_download_count` as its breakdown, so an all-proxy deployment no longer reports zero downloads.

  **Upgrade note: deliberate API behaviour change.** Two admin responses change meaning for existing clients. (1) `/api/v1/admin/downloads` and its `by-ip` / `by-user` variants now include proxy serves by default, and `DownloadRecord.artifact_id` is nullable (`null` on a proxy row); a client generated from the 1.10 spec that types `artifact_id` as required will fail to read a page containing a proxy row. Pass `source=hosted` to get the previous hosted-only listing. (2) `/api/v1/admin/stats` `total_downloads` now counts hosted and proxy downloads; the previous hosted-only figure is `total_downloads - proxy_download_count`. The `/api/v1/analytics` snapshots are unchanged: their `total_downloads` stays hosted-only, with `proxy_download_count` reported separately. The web UI and SDK updates are tracked in artifact-keeper/artifact-keeper-web#960 and artifact-keeper/artifact-keeper-api#42.

- **A Remote download larger than the repository quota no longer leaves a 0-byte "cached" entry** (#4551). Such an object is streamed to the client without any proxy-cache write (#4543), but recording the download still inserted the `proxy_cache_artifacts` placeholder a cache miss gets, and with no cache write to fill it in, the catalog listed a 0-byte cached object that was never stored. The serve now marks the object as not cached for its own download recorder, which records the download against `(repository_id, path)` (#4539) without creating a catalog row, and links it to an existing row only when one is already there. Downloads of over-quota objects are still counted.

- **The stock Caddyfile routes rattler's `/t/<token>/conda/<repo>/...` URLs to the backend** (#4555, #4482). The conda token-in-URL mount under `/t` was added without a matching `reverse_proxy /t/* backend:8080` line, so behind the stock stack those requests fell through to the web UI and got its HTML 404, and the Caddyfile route gate (`scripts/ci/check-caddy-format-routes.sh`) failed on `main`.

- **Hosted conda channels serve CEP-16 shard indexes and shards in the encoding the spec and rattler expect** (#4555, #4173). The shard index carried each shard's SHA-256 as a 64-character hex string, because it was built as a `serde_json::Value` (which has no byte type) and then written as msgpack; the shards carried each record's `sha256` and `md5` as hex strings for the same reason; and both responses declared `Content-Encoding: zstd` although the zstd frame is part of the `.msgpack.zst` document, which invites an HTTP client to strip it before the CEP-16 reader sees the bytes. The index and shards are now written with msgpack `bin` digests and map-keyed structs, served without a `Content-Encoding`, and a test decodes both with `rattler_conda_types`' own `ShardedRepodata` and `Shard`. This is the encoding half of #4173; materialising the shard set at write time is still open.

- **The `unknown` conda subdir is served as an empty index instead of 400, and a virtual channel's remote member that does not publish a subdir contributes nothing instead of failing the merge** (#4555). rattler and pixi request `unknown/repodata.json` when no platform is given (`pixi search` without `-p`), and the registry's subdir validation answered 400, which aborted the client's whole query. `unknown` is now a valid subdir on read paths (uploads still refuse it) and is served as an empty `repodata.json`. In a virtual channel, a remote member whose upstream answers 404 for every encoding of a subdir's repodata (conda-forge has no `unknown/`, most channels lack most platforms) now contributes no records rather than turning the request into a 502; any other member failure still fails the request.

- **A conda upload whose subdir disagrees with the package's own `info/index.json` is refused, and a POST without `X-Conda-Subdir` files the package under its own subdir** (#4555). The upload took the subdir from the PUT path or the `X-Conda-Subdir` header (defaulting to `noarch`) and never compared it with the package, so a `linux-64` build POSTed without the header was published as `noarch`, offered to every platform, and broke on the ones it was not built for. The package's `index.json` subdir is now authoritative: a PUT path or header that names a different subdir gets `400` naming both values, and a POST without the header uses the package's subdir. A package whose `index.json` declares no subdir keeps the previous behaviour.

- **A virtual conda channel fetches its remote members compressed and capped, and merges hosted members first** (#4555, #4180). `build_virtual_repodata` asked each remote member for the plain `repodata.json` through the uncapped buffered proxy path, parsed the whole document into a JSON tree and re-serialised it on every request: for a conda-forge subdir that is a few hundred MiB of JSON per member per request, with no ceiling at all. Remote members are now fetched as `repodata.json.zst`, then `.bz2`, then `.json` (each only if the previous one is 404), through the same budgeted path and the same 128 MiB default ceiling as a single remote channel (`CONDA_VIRTUAL_MEMBER_MAX_BYTES`); the decoded document has its own ceiling, enforced while the streaming decoder runs (`CONDA_VIRTUAL_MEMBER_MAX_DECODED_BYTES`, default 1 GiB). Members are fetched one at a time so a request never holds one budget reservation while waiting for another, and records are merged as raw JSON on a blocking thread instead of as `Value` trees. The merge order is now hosted (local and staging) members first, then remote members, each in priority order, first writer wins per filename. `channeldata.json` for a virtual channel takes the same capped, hosted-first path.

- **A virtual conda channel whose member cannot be fetched or parsed now fails with 502 naming the member instead of serving a smaller index** (#4555, #4192). The merge logged the failure at `warn` and served the members that did answer with 200, so a client saw a valid-looking `repodata.json` with an entire member missing, concluded those packages did not exist, or resolved a name present in two members to the lower-priority one. Conda virtual `repodata.json` (every encoding) and `channeldata.json` now answer `502 Bad Gateway` with a body naming each failed member and the cause (fetch error, size ceiling, decode or parse error). An operator can opt a virtual repository into degraded merges with `PATCH /api/v1/repositories/{key}` `{"virtual_metadata_partial": true}`: the merge of the healthy members is then served with `X-AK-Partial-Members: <member keys>`, `Cache-Control: no-store` and a `Warning: 199`. Every member failure increments `ak_virtual_member_metadata_failures_total{format,virtual_repo,member,reason}` under either policy. Members the caller may not read are not failures. The shared `collect_virtual_metadata` helper used by the other formats is unchanged here.

- **A verified CEP-27 attestation on a hosted conda package now satisfies `min_attestation_state` and the promotion `require_signature` gate, and promotion responses report every gate rule** (#4556). The policy predicate read the attestation state only from `curation_packages`, which is written for packages curated from a remote, so a package published to a local or staging channel with a verified attestation stayed `absent` and `min_attestation_state: verified` could never pass for it; and `require_signature` (both the scan-policy gate and the per-pair promotion rule) only recognised the repository signing key's audit entries. The predicate now also reads the verdict stored on the artifact by the attestation upload (`artifact_metadata.attestation_verification`), folded with any curation record to the weaker of the two, and `require_signature` passes for an artifact whose stored verdict is `verified`. `POST /api/v1/promotion/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{id}/promote` adds `gate_results: [{"rule", "passed", "reason"}]` listing every rule the promotion was evaluated against, passed or failed, beside the existing `policy_violations`; failed per-pair promotion rules appear there too (bulk promotion items carry them for rule failures).

- **Bulk promotion reports the same per-rule `gate_results` as single-artifact promotion, passed rules included** (#4557). An item that a scan-policy predicate refused came back from `POST .../promote` (bulk) with `"gate_results": []`, while promoting the same artifact on its own listed the failing `policy-predicate` rule, so a UI showing the gate decision had nothing to show for bulk promotions. Every bulk item now carries every evaluated rule with `passed` and `reason`: items refused by the scan policy, items refused by a per-pair promotion rule (policy results followed by the failing rules), items refused by the quality gate (as `quality-gate`), and items that were promoted.

- **Promoting an artifact now copies its format metadata, so a promoted conda package keeps its dependencies and attestation** (#4557). Promotion (single and bulk) inserted a new `artifacts` row in the target repository but no `artifact_metadata` row, and everything a format serves about a package is read from that document: a conda channel built the promoted package's repodata record with empty `depends` and `constrains`, an empty `md5` and license, and no `attestations_sha256`, so a client could install it without its dependencies and the attestation verified in staging was gone. The metadata document is now copied onto the promoted row.

- **An upload into a staging repository, and every copy promoted from it, records its origin as `hosted` instead of `virtual`** (#4557, #4152). The origin derivation mapped `local` to `hosted`, `remote` to `proxy` and every other repository type to `virtual`, so a package published to a staging repository was stamped `virtual`, and promotion, which carries the source origin over to the copy, then showed the promoted package in the release repository as "stored in a virtual repository", and an `allowed_kinds: ["hosted"]` origin predicate refused it. Migration 284 maps `staging` to `hosted` and re-stamps the rows already recorded wrongly: any origin of kind `virtual` that names a repository that is not virtual becomes `hosted`, with every other key unchanged. It runs in 5000-row batches, admits only that one rewrite through the immutability trigger while it runs, and restores the strict trigger at the end.

- **A second scan policy with the same name on the same repository is refused with 409** (#4558). Creating or renaming a repository-scoped scan policy accepted a name already used on that repository, so a re-run setup script silently stacked identical policies that the UI and promotion refusals (which name the policy) could not tell apart. `POST /api/v1/security/policies` and the policy update now answer `409 Conflict` when another policy on the same repository has the same name, compared case-insensitively. The same name on a different repository, and unscoped policies, are unaffected.

- **OCI `/v2/token` credential exchanges have their own per-user rate-limit bucket instead of spending the ten-per-fifteen-minutes login budget** (#4558, #4020). Since #4020 the token exchange drew from the same per-(username, IP) bucket as `/api/v1/auth/login`, but a container client exchanges credentials once per repository scope and per tool, so an ordinary `podman push` followed by `cosign sign` and `cosign verify` ran out of budget and got `429`. `/v2/token` now has a separate per-(username, IP) bucket, `RATE_LIMIT_TOKEN_EXCHANGE_PER_WINDOW` (default 300) per `RATE_LIMIT_LOGIN_WINDOW_SECS`, while the global login backstop and the per-IP failed-verification budget stay shared with the login endpoint, so the two surfaces together still bound total password verification.

- **Conda token-channel URLs no longer write the token to request logs and traces** (#4565, #4555, #544). The `http_request` span's `uri` field redacted secret query parameters but kept the path as sent, so the bearer token in `/conda/t/<token>/<repo>/...` and in rattler's `/t/<token>/conda/<repo>/...` (pixi `--conda-token`) was logged in clear. That path segment is now recorded as `[REDACTED]`; the rest of the path is kept. Only paths that start with one of those two prefixes are changed. Rotate any token that was used through these URLs if your logs or trace backend may have been read by someone who should not hold it.

- **An anonymous OCI manifest PUT now gets 401 with the push challenge instead of a 500** (#4568). The manifest `PUT` read the whole request body before it checked any credentials, so the retry `crane tag` / `crane copy` sends after a token exchange (it reuses the spent request: `Content-Length` set, 0 bytes written) failed the body read and answered `500 BLOB_UPLOAD_UNKNOWN` (502 behind Caddy) instead of the `401` and `WWW-Authenticate` challenge. The handler now authenticates, checks the push scope, repository write access and the repository-type and promotion-only gates first, and reads the body only after them, the order the blob upload handlers already used. An unauthenticated client can also no longer make the server buffer up to `max_upload_size_bytes` of manifest before it is refused.

- **`git lfs pull` from a private Git LFS repository no longer hangs** (Closes #4570). The batch API marked every download action `"authenticated": true` but gave it an empty `header`. git-lfs trusts an authenticated action and sends the object GET with the action's headers only, so the GET carried no credentials, got a 401, and git-lfs retried forever. Download actions now carry the caller's `Authorization` header, as upload and verify actions already did, and an action is marked `authenticated` only when it carries one. Batch responses are sent with `Cache-Control: no-store`, since they can now echo a credential.

- **Promoting a Docker/OCI image now makes it pullable from the target repository** (#4578). Promotion copied only the tag's `artifacts` row and its top-level manifest object, so a pull from the target answered `MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` and `tags/list` answered `NAME_UNKNOWN`, while the API reported `promoted: true`. This left `promotion_only` docker repositories with no way to receive a working image. The single, bulk and approval promotion paths now walk the promoted manifest in the source repository (an image index, its child manifests, and every config and layer blob), copy the missing objects into the target storage, and record the tag, the child manifests, the manifest references and the `oci_blobs` rows for the target in the same transaction as the promoted `artifacts` row. A source image with a missing manifest or blob fails the promotion instead of producing an empty tag.

- **Conda repodata and CEP-16 shard indexes resolve packages against the URL that served them, so mirror-configured clients, clients behind a proxy and token channels download from the right place** (closes #4580). Hosted and virtual `repodata.json` (and its `.zst`/`.bz2`, `current_repodata.json` and JLAP forms) carried `info.base_url = "/conda/<repo>/<subdir>/"`, and every shard index (hosted, remote and virtual) carried the same host-relative path. rattler resolves `base_url` against the channel's canonical URL before applying a `[mirrors]` rewrite, so with the standard enterprise mirror `"https://conda.anaconda.org/conda-forge" = ["https://ak.internal/conda/conda-forge"]` every `pixi exec` and `rattler-build -c conda-forge` environment creation requested `https://conda.anaconda.org/conda/conda-forge/<subdir>/<pkg>` and failed with 404, with no client-side escape (rattler-build ignores `disable-sharded`). A proxy in front of the registry (Nexus) passed the path through, so a client using the proxy's channel URL resolved packages against the proxy host at the registry's path, and a `.condarc` token channel (`/conda/t/<token>/<repo>`) lost its token on every package URL. `repodata.json` now omits `base_url`, so CEP-15's default (the document's own directory) applies, and shard indexes carry `base_url: "./"` and `shards_base_url: "./shards/"`, the values rattler's own indexer writes. The documents no longer depend on the request at all: an absolute URL built from `Host`/`X-Forwarded-*` would have pointed past a proxy that sets no forwarded headers, written token-channel tokens into the body, and made the cached bytes and `ETag` depend on a client-supplied header. The red-team workarounds (`disable-sharded` for the forge mirror, `-c https://ak.internal/conda/conda-forge` in place of `-c conda-forge` for rattler-build) are no longer needed.

- **The dashboard's `policy_violations_blocked` counts only what the proxy scan gate refuses** (#4582). Since #4380 it counted proxied content with a blocking verdict under the repository's scan policy without checking that the format runs the gate, so a format that stores `scan_on_proxy` but serves its proxied bytes unscanned (rpm, Go, generic and the others reported as `accepted` by `GET /api/v1/formats`) showed a package as blocked while serving it. The count now uses the same format predicate as the handlers, so it changes automatically as formats adopt the gate. Conda is gated as of #4585.

- **`terraform init` and `tofu init` install hosted Terraform modules** (closes #4590). A module's `.../download` answered `204` with an `X-Terraform-Get` location that named no archive type, so the client's getter fetched it as an HTML page looking for a `terraform-get` meta tag and failed on the archive bytes (`XML syntax error ... illegal character code U+0003`). The archive type is now detected from the bytes at upload (ZIP or gzip-compressed tar), recorded in the module's metadata, and advertised as `.../archive?archive=zip` or `?archive=tar.gz`. The archive is served with the matching filename and `Content-Type` instead of always `.tar.gz`. Modules uploaded before this release carry no recorded type, so theirs is read from the stored bytes on download, and they install without being uploaded again.

  An upload that is not a ZIP or a gzip-compressed tar is refused with `400` and the reason. That includes an uncompressed tar, which neither client can install (their module getter has no plain-tar support). Remote Terraform repositories now answer `.../download` with the same `204` + `X-Terraform-Get` pointing at their own `/archive`, which streams the upstream archive through the proxy cache. The hint comes from the upstream location's `archive=` parameter or extension, or from the bytes. Before, the upstream `204` body was relayed as an empty `200` without its header, which no client can use. A source the proxy does not fetch (a `git::` or `s3::` address, or an archive type other than ZIP and tar.gz) is passed to the client unchanged. A new native test, `scripts/native-tests/test-terraform-modules.sh` (e2e profile `terraform-modules`), runs the real CLI against a hosted ZIP module and a hosted tar.gz module through a host-level discovery rewrite.

- **A failed SMTP test now tells the administrator what the server offered and what to change, and a mail server that never answers no longer hangs a send** (#4591). `POST /api/v1/admin/smtp/test` answered every delivery failure with a bare `500 Internal server error`, so the reason (`535 5.7.3 Authentication unsuccessful`, `STARTTLS is not supported on this server`, `No compatible authentication mechanism was found`) was only in the backend log, and it never said why. The endpoint now returns `502` with lettre's error, what the server advertised in EHLO before and after STARTTLS (from a separate probe that sends no credentials, so mechanisms lettre ignores, such as NTLM and GSSAPI, are listed), and a one-line hint. For example, a server offering only NTLM/GSSAPI in plaintext and LOGIN/PLAIN after STARTTLS (the Exchange default) gets "set SMTP_TLS_MODE=starttls"; a 535 gets a note about SMTP AUTH being disabled on the mailbox or connector and the `DOMAIN\user` / UPN username forms; a missing STARTTLS names the port and the `tls` and `starttls-opportunistic` alternatives; an untrusted certificate points to `SMTP_TLS_CA_CERT`. Mail sent by notifications carries the same hint in its log line, without the probe. Separately, lettre's tokio transport bounds only the TCP connect, so a plaintext client on an implicit-TLS port (or any server that accepts and stays silent) waited indefinitely, and the test endpoint gave up with `503 Server overloaded, please retry: request timed out`. Each delivery is now limited to 60 seconds and fails with "no SMTP reply within 60s" and a hint about matching `SMTP_TLS_MODE` to the port. An invalid recipient address on the test endpoint is now a `400` instead of a `500`.

- **A `fail_closed` conda channel no longer locks packages the scanner catalogs nothing for** (closes #4594, follow-up to #4585). The scan-on-proxy gate treated a completed scan that cataloged nothing for the requested `name@version` as inconclusive. That is right for npm, PyPI, RubyGems, Cargo, NuGet and Maven, where the scanner catalogs the package itself, but no bundled scanner catalogs a conda package as a conda component, so for compiled libraries and data packages (`tzdata`, `ca-certificates`) it was the normal result: `fail_closed` answered `423 Locked` for most of conda-forge, and `fail_open` served them `pending` forever without recording a verdict. For `conda` and `conda_native`, a scan that ran to completion over the unpacked archive and cataloged nothing is now graded on its findings (none is `clean`, any is `vulnerable`), stored, and reused like any other verdict, so `fail_closed` serves it with `X-AK-Scan: clean` and `fail_open` serves the next pull `clean`. A scan that could not run is still inconclusive, a package whose `info/index.json` disagrees with its file name is still withheld, and a scan that cataloged a different `name@version` is still inconclusive. Other formats are unchanged.

  Each proxy verdict now records `components_cataloged` (migration 287), returned on `clean` and `vulnerable` items of `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/security/proxy-scans`. `0` means the verdict was graded on file contents only; `null` means the scanner reported no catalog, or the verdict predates 1.11.0.

- **`terraform init` / `tofu init` install modules through a virtual Terraform repository** (#4598). A virtual answered a module `/download` by streaming the resolving member's archive as a `200`, which no client can use, and listed no versions for a module, so the client stopped at "Module not found". A virtual now answers `/download` the way its member does: a `204` whose `X-Terraform-Get` points at the virtual's own `/archive` with the archive hint (`?archive=zip` / `?archive=tar.gz`), or a remote member's `git::` / `s3::` source handed through unchanged; the virtual's `/archive` streams the same member's archive (a hosted member's stored bytes, with quarantine and scan policy enforced, or a remote member's upstream archive through its proxy cache). `/versions` on a virtual lists the union of its members' versions, and on a remote repository the upstream's versions, which it did not list before either. `scripts/native-tests/test-terraform-modules.sh` now installs a hosted and a proxied module through a virtual.

- **Compiled conda packages that the scanner catalogs under a vendored upstream name are graded on their findings instead of staying inconclusive** (closes #4600). The proxy scan gate required the scanner's catalog to contain the conda package's own `name@version`, and for compiled packages it rarely does: `libzlib-1.3.1` is cataloged as `zlib 1.3.1`, `pillow` with its vendored `libjpeg-turbo`. Those scans completed and could carry real findings, but were withheld: 423 under `fail_closed`, `pending` under `fail_open`, with nothing recorded. Following #4594, a completed conda scan whose catalog names other components is now graded on its findings (`clean` with none, `vulnerable` and blocked by the policy with one), and the verdict records how many components it cataloged (`components_cataloged` in the proxy-scans view). The served identity is still checked against the package's own `info/index.json` before the scan, so bytes that disagree with their file name stay withheld. Other ecosystems keep the catalog identity check.

- **A virtual conda channel's `channeldata.json` no longer fails with 502 when one remote member's upstream publishes no channeldata** (closes #4601). The merge treated a member's 404 for `channeldata.json` as a member failure, so the whole virtual's channeldata answered 502 even though every other member answered and `repodata.json` for the same virtual merged fine; tools that index a channel from its channeldata (ProGet) could not index it at all. A 404 now means that member contributes no entries, logged at `info`, exactly as a missing subdir already did for `repodata.json`. A member that answers 5xx, times out, is over the size cap or does not parse still fails the request loudly with 502 naming it, or is reported in `X-AK-Partial-Members` when the virtual opted into partial merges.

- **A virtual conda channel serves every shard its CEP-16 index lists; a cold sharded solve that reaches `cuda-nvcc_linux-64` no longer fails with 404** (closes #4607). The virtual's merged shard index listed conda-forge's `noarch` shard for `cuda-nvcc_linux-64`, and a request for that shard through the virtual answered 404 while the member served it. The shard is 90 bytes: conda-forge removed the package's only `noarch` build, so its shard holds no records and one `removed` entry. The download path decided admission by decoding the shard and required at least one record whose name the virtual admits, so it refused the empty shard, and it answered a shard it could not decode with the same 404. pixi and rattler treat a 404 for a listed shard as fatal, so every cold sharded solve through a virtual whose closure touches `cuda-nvcc_linux-64` (pytorch, jax and much of the scientific stack) failed. Admission is now decided from the merged index itself: a shard request through a virtual rebuilds the same merge the index is served from and is answered from the source that merge took the name from (a hosted member's shard, or the remote member whose index listed it first), so the set of shards served is exactly the set listed. The record-name check stays only as a defence against a shard whose records name a package the virtual does not take from remotes (owned by a hosted member, or outside the allowlist); it now streams the shard and keeps only the names, so it cannot fail on a real shard's size. Outcomes are told apart: a shard refused by policy is 404 `Shard not found` (logged at `info`, or `warn` when a listed shard's records smuggle in a refused name); a listed shard the member cannot produce (does not decode, upstream fetch failure or 404, over the size ceiling) is 502 naming the member, and an unlisted shard while a member failed to merge is 502 too, never a 404 that tells the client the package does not exist. The ceiling on one upstream shard is raised from 8 MiB to 16 MiB, separately from the shard index's: the largest conda-forge shards measured are `linux-64/awscli` (848 KB compressed, 6.2 MB decoded) and conda-pypi's `noarch/boto3-stubs` is 713 KB compressed but 51 MB decoded, and conda 26.7.0/26.7.1 reject shards that decode past 16 MiB (conda/conda#16575). The red-team workaround (`disable-sharded` for the virtual) is no longer needed.

- **Concurrent solves against a virtual conda channel no longer drive the backend out of memory** (closes #4608). Every request for a virtual channel's `repodata.json` (any encoding), `channeldata.json` or CEP-16 shard index ran its own merge: it decoded each remote member's document (about 455 MB of JSON for conda-forge `linux-64`), merged it with the hosted records and encoded the result, and none of that was counted against the buffered-metadata budget. Memory grew with the number of concurrent solves: 20 concurrent `repodata.json.zst` requests took the backend to 20.8 GB, and at a 12 GiB limit it was OOM-killed. Requests for the same merged document now share one merge, and its encoded result is kept for `CONDA_VIRTUAL_MERGE_CACHE_TTL_SECS` (default 300, `0` disables) under one `ETag`, so revalidation answers 304; it is reused only while the caller-visible member set, the hosted records, the names hosted members own, the allowlist and each remote member's proxy-cache entry (by checksum, and only while fresh) are unchanged, a merge with a failed member is never kept, and the member-failure policy still applies to each response. Shard requests through a virtual are routed from the kept shard index merge instead of re-reading every member's index. At most `CONDA_VIRTUAL_MAX_CONCURRENT_MERGES` merges run at once (default: the buffered-metadata budget divided by the member fetch and decoded ceilings, at least 2); a merge that cannot start within `CONDA_VIRTUAL_MERGE_QUEUE_SECS` (default 60) answers 503 with `Retry-After`. Each merge reserves its fetch buffer, decoded member documents, working set and output from `AK_PROXY_METADATA_BUDGET_BYTES` before it starts (sized from the previous merge of the same document, or the whole budget the first time) and never waits for budget while holding some. The compressed encodings are serialized straight into the compressor. With the change, 20 concurrent requests peak at 0.7 GB, and a 40-way cold-cache `pixi install` stampede completes under an 8 GiB limit with the backend below 1 GB. New metrics: `ak_conda_virtual_merge_inflight`, `ak_conda_virtual_merge_cache_hits_total`, `ak_conda_virtual_merge_cache_misses_total`, `ak_conda_virtual_merge_rejected_total` and `ak_conda_virtual_merge_bytes_reserved`; sizing and restart alerting are in `docs/operations/conda-virtual-merge-memory.md`.

- **An upload the server could not receive in full is no longer reported as an invalid package** (#4609). The archive-parsing publish routes (conda, RubyGems, npm, Cargo, Composer, Hex, VS Code, Go modules, Alpine, Pacman, CRAN, RPM) took the body through axum's `Bytes` extractor, which answered every receive failure with `400 Failed to buffer the request body` and buffered each body at about twice its size: two concurrent 1.5 GB conda uploads OOM-killed a 4 GiB replica. These routes now receive the body into one buffer of its declared size, charged to a process-wide budget (`UPLOAD_MEMORY_BUDGET_BYTES`, default half the cgroup memory limit), check the received length against `Content-Length`, and only then parse it.
