A body cut short is `408` with code `incomplete_body`; a full budget or failed allocation is `503` with `Retry-After`; a full scratch or storage disk is `507` with `Retry-After` (previously a bare `500`); other server-side receive or spool failures are `503` with `Retry-After`, logged at `error` with the cause. A `400` now always means the complete package was received and is itself invalid. The shared spooling helpers used by PyPI, NuGet, Maven, Terraform, Swift, Chef and Pub apply the same rules. See `docs/operations/upload-scratch-disk.md`.

- **A remote conda channel whose upstream publishes a CEP-16 shard index larger than 8 MiB now serves it instead of answering 502** (closes #4612). The shard index fetched from an upstream was capped at the 8 MiB general metadata tier, and conda-pypi's noarch index is 28.6 MB compressed, so a remote pointed at conda-pypi answered 502 for its shard index (and for every shard, which reads the index to find the upstream's shard location). An index past 8 MiB is now read again under its own 64 MiB ceiling, reserved from the buffered-metadata budget only for that second read, so channels with ordinary indexes (conda-forge's largest is about 1 MiB) keep the small reservation; the decoded ceiling is 128 MiB. An index past 64 MiB is treated as the upstream publishing no usable shard index: the reason is logged at `warn`, the remote answers 404 and so does a virtual over it, and clients fall back to `repodata.json`.

### Security

- **LDAP login no longer reveals through its response time whether a username exists in the directory** (#3505). #3371 made an absent username and a wrong password return the same response body, but on the search-then-bind path an absent username still returned right after the directory search, while an existing one paid a second connection and a bind. With a remote directory, STARTTLS, or an Active Directory that delays rejected binds, that extra round-trip could rebuild the enumeration oracle. A search miss now binds against a random DN that cannot exist, using the submitted password, so both cases perform the same directory operations in the same order and fail with the same error. The miss still always fails, whatever the directory answers to the decoy bind. A sweep of absent usernames now costs the directory one bind per attempt, the same as a sweep of existing usernames or wrong passwords already did.

- **The scanner adapter is rebuilt on hardened trivy 0.74.0-r4 and its Go toolchain floor guards again at go1.27.2, clearing Go's October security release from the gate; published as 1.4.1** (#3579). `docker/Dockerfile.scanner-adapter` asserts a `GO_MIN_PATCH` floor so a stale builder or a lagging mirror fails the build instead of shipping a vulnerable standard library. #3579 moved the build image from `golang:1.26-alpine` to `golang:1.27-alpine` and left the floor at 1.26.6, which every 1.27.x satisfies, so the check could no longer fail; the backend Dockerfiles had the same gap and #3655 closed it there. The floor now names go1.27.2, Go's October security release (CVE-2026-78667, CVE-2026-78669, CVE-2026-97031, all HIGH). The adapter binary itself scanned clean in the run that failed on those advisories, because the floating tag had already served go1.27.2; the floor makes that a guarantee. The adapter is standard-library only, so there is no `golang.org/x/net` in it to bump. The bundled trivy is repointed at `artifact-keeper/trivy` 0.74.0-r4: the same upstream v0.74.0, rebuilt on go1.26.9 with `golang.org/x/net` overridden to v0.60.0, which clears the four HIGH findings that failed the gate against the r3 binary (CVE-2026-78669 against `x/net` v0.58.0; CVE-2026-78667, -78669 and -97031 against its go1.26.7 standard library).

- **The backend image's bundled `grype` and `buildctl` are rebuilt on go1.27.2 with `golang.org/x/net` v0.60.0, clearing the Go October security release from Docker Publish's gate** (#3698). From 2026-10-10 the `Security Scan` job failed on every `main` build, so no `:main` image was published and 1.11.0 could not be cut. Trivy reported CVE-2026-78669 (HIGH; HTTP/2 denial of service via excessive SETTINGS frames, fixed in `x/net` v0.60.0) against `usr/local/bin/grype` and `usr/local/bin/buildctl`, both at `x/net` v0.58.0, and three HIGH standard-library advisories (CVE-2026-78667 in `net/http`, CVE-2026-78669 in the bundled HTTP/2 stack, CVE-2026-97031 in `crypto/tls`; fixed in go1.26.9 / go1.27.2) against `buildctl`, which was copied out of `moby/buildkit:v0.33.0` and compiled by Docker on go1.26.8. No grype or BuildKit release carries `x/net` v0.60.0 yet (grype v0.120.1, BuildKit v0.34.0 and both projects' `main` pin v0.59.0), so a version bump could not fix either. `buildctl` is now built from source at the same v0.33.0 tag (commit `dddd5621`), the way grype has been since #3352, so its compiler is ours too; both stages raise the `GO_MIN_PATCH` floor to 1.27.2 and apply an `x/net` v0.60.0 override with the same three build-time guards as grype's gRPC override: the pinned source still requires v0.58.0, `go get` moves exactly the declared set of seven `golang.org/x` modules, and the compiled binary's Go build info records v0.60.0. Every module the override drags along lands on the version grype v0.120.1 already ships, and the `x/crypto` v0.57.0 it brings also clears the two `x/crypto/ssh` advisories #3698 was waiting on. Nothing is added to `.trivyignore`: each finding had a fixed version to build against. `grype --version` still prints `0.118.0` and `buildctl --version` still reports v0.33.0, so nothing operator-facing changes. The scanner-adapter image fails the same gate on its bundled trivy; that half is fixed in `artifact-keeper/trivy` and repointed here separately.

- **Webhook fetch-by-id now requires the same read-carrying grant as the webhook listing, and repository-scoped tokens confine admins consistently** (#3901, #4271, #4270). `GET /api/v1/webhooks/{id}` and its deliveries endpoint admitted any non-empty fine-grained grant, so a `{write}`-only grantee refused the webhook in the listing was still served its URL, headers and secret metadata by id; the by-id path now asks for `RepoAccess::READ`, and the listing's role arm carries the same `read` capability, so a custom role without `read`/`admin` neither lists nor fetches the webhook (built-in roles all carry `read`). Webhook reads (`GET /webhooks`, `GET /webhooks/{id}`, its deliveries) now also require the `read:repositories` token scope, and the custom `headers` in every read response have their values redacted to `***` — they usually carry the receiver's bearer token, and the signing secret was already digest-only. Separately, the packages listing and the repository listing evaluated `is_admin` before the token's repository scope, letting an admin with a repository-scoped token enumerate everything; the scope now binds first, matching search and the webhook reads.

- **The detailed health payload no longer echoes the raw filesystem storage error** (#3907). When the storage path could not be resolved or the probe write failed, the storage check's message interpolated the underlying I/O error (`Storage path not accessible: {e}`, `Storage write failed: {e}`), which carries the OS error text tied to the configured storage path. The message is now the fixed text alone (`Storage path not accessible` / `Storage write failed`) and the raw error is logged server-side at warn. Both phrasings join the raw-error-body gate (#3718) so they cannot return.

- **Completing a chunked upload onto an occupied immutable path is now refused with 409, instead of silently replacing the artifact** (#3924). `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{path}` has always answered `409 CONFLICT` ("Artifact version already exists and is immutable") for a write to a taken coordinate, but `PUT /api/v1/uploads/{id}/complete` answered `200 OK` and overwrote the stored content — so the same logical write was rejected or accepted purely according to which upload API the client happened to use, and a chunked client could destroy a released artifact without ever seeing an error. `ArtifactService::preflight_upload` documents itself as "the single chokepoint every service-backed upload path flows through" and carries both immutability rules; the chunked completion handler was simply never on it, and committed the artifact through a bare `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (repository_id, path) DO UPDATE` that unconditionally replaced `checksum_sha256` and `storage_key`. Both rules — the live-overwrite check and the tombstone-aware release-immutability backstop, which together are what stop a soft-delete followed by different bytes at the same released coordinate — now live in one shared `enforce_path_immutability`, called by `preflight_upload` and by the completion handler, so the two paths cannot drift apart again. The gate runs before the storage copy, so a rejected completion writes no bytes, and it *releases* the commit lease rather than failing the session: a 409 here becomes a legal write the moment the occupying artifact is deleted, so the client retries the session instead of re-uploading every chunk. It is applied unconditionally, matching the direct-write paths, which exempt replication from quota admission but never from immutability — a replica pushing identical bytes passes on the checksum comparison anyway, so what gets refused is a replication that would change the bytes under a released coordinate.

- **A multipart publish whose envelope exceeds `MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE` is now refused with `413 Payload Too Large`, not `400`** (#4023). The JetBrains plugin upload and the Swift publish parse their `multipart/form-data` body with `multer` under a `whole_stream` ceiling equal to `max_upload_size_bytes`. That ceiling always trips before the staging primitive's own per-part byte count can -- it measures the envelope, the stager measures one part -- and `multer`'s size-limit error was reported as a "malformed multipart" `400`: straight from the parser when a small body arrived in one piece, or through the stager's read-failure mapping when a chunked body crossed the ceiling mid-part. A raw (non-multipart) upload of the same size answers `413`, which is also what both handlers' comments promised. `multer`'s size-limit error is now mapped to `413` by a shared helper on both surfaces, including when it surfaces inside `stage_stream_content_addressed`; regression tests cover both delivery shapes. Follow-up to the #3848 fix in #3942, which also gains a byte-level pin of the raw `X-Plugin-Name` upload path and a database-free binary-fixture check of the multipart parser.

- **Bulk promotion now applies the quality gate and the CVE/licence policy per item, which it previously skipped entirely** (#3977). `POST /api/v1/promotion/repositories/{key}/promote` evaluated only the per-pair `promotion_rules` for each artifact: it never called the quality-gate evaluation and never called the promotion policy engine, both of which `POST .../artifacts/{artifact_id}/promote` has always run. An artifact the single-artifact route refuses with `409` on a blocking quality gate, or answers with `promoted: false` on a CVE/licence policy block -- including the `scan_policies.block_unscanned` gate that stops artifacts with no completed security scan (#1643) -- was promoted into the release repository by the bulk route regardless, and an array of one element was enough to take that path. The two evaluations now run per item in the same order the single route uses (gate, then policy, then rules, then the approval consume) and honour the same `skip_policy_check` admin override. A gate or policy block fails **that item** and the batch continues, where the single route refuses the whole request, because a bulk promotion reports per-artifact outcomes so a partial result stays distinguishable from a wholesale refusal; the blocked item carries the gate's message or the policy violations in its own result. Nothing that was promotable before becomes unpromotable unless a gate or policy was already configured to stop it -- an instance with neither configured is unaffected, because both evaluations are no-ops there. Each promoted item's `promotion_history.policy_result` now records the evaluation that ran, in the same shape the single route records, instead of a fixed `{"passed": true, "violations": []}`; and a policy or rule evaluation that errors reports a generic `Policy evaluation failed` / `Rule evaluation failed` reason on that item rather than the raw database error text.

- **The OCI `/v2/token` credential exchange is now rate limited with the same budget as `/api/v1/auth/login`** (#4020). The endpoint is unauthenticated by design and was mounted outside the API rate-limit layers, so password guessing against it was bounded only by account lockout. The Basic-auth and OAuth2 password-grant exits now draw from the login limiter's per-(username, IP) budget (default 10 attempts / 15 minutes) and global backstop — shared with `/api/v1/auth/login`, so a guess against either endpoint spends the same budget — answering excess attempts with `429` and `Retry-After`. The refresh-grant, bearer-swap, and anonymous-mint exits, which present an already-issued credential or no credential, are deliberately not limited.

- **CI OIDC token exchange no longer merges principals across issuers or mappings, and no longer reactivates a deactivated CI account** (#4031). See the CI OIDC entry under Fixed.

- **A quarantine hold on one member of a virtual repository is no longer bypassed by serving the same file from a lower-priority member** (#4098, #4343). When a virtual npm, PyPI or VS Code repository walked its members for a proxied package, a member that answered with a quarantine hold (409) was skipped and the walk went on to the next member, which could serve the very file the hold was withholding. The walk now stops at the hold, as the shared virtual resolver already did.

- **A NuGet repository now answers on both protocol surfaces whatever its upstream speaks, so a Chocolatey feed is reachable from `dotnet` and nuget.org is reachable from `choco`** (#4122). Each surface required the upstream to match it. Every V3 leg resolved through the service index and failed on anything that was not one, so a remote repository with a `/api/v2` upstream answered `502` on registration, flat container and search — and the same repository as a **member of a virtual** was skipped silently, because the member loops read the discovery error as "this member does not have it". In the other direction the V2 OData verbs were proxied verbatim to an upstream that serves no OData, so every `FindPackagesById()`, `Search()` and `Packages(...)` against a V3-backed remote repository 404'd. The protocol is now probed once per upstream (memoized through the proxy-cache entry discovery already uses) and translated both ways: a V2 feed answers the V3 version list and registration index from `FindPackagesById()` and the search page from `Search()`; a V3 feed answers the V2 verbs from the flat container and the search service. Downloads resolve through one protocol-aware target, so a V2 and a V3 client share a single cached body instead of storing it twice, and every synthesized URL points back at AK.

  **A transient upstream failure is never read as "this feed is V2".** Only a definitive signal downgrades the protocol — a 404 on the service index, a body that is not JSON, or one advertising neither `RegistrationsBaseUrl` nor `PackageBaseAddress`; a 5xx or a timeout propagates as an error, because guessing V2 during a brief outage would 404 every package on a working V3 feed. The V2 surface translates only on a positive V3 answer: when the probe errors — a Chocolatey-style server that answers `index.json` with 400, 401, 403 or 5xx — the V2 verbs and `package/{id}/{version}` downloads keep the verbatim pass-through and cache keys they have always used, so a V2 client on a V2 upstream never depends on the probe. A translated V2 entry carries no package size or hash, because the V3 documents do not publish them and the client reads the bytes through the `src` URL. Known limit: V2 feed paging (`<link rel="next">`) is not followed, so a version list or registration synthesized from a V2 upstream holds only the first page the feed returns and can be truncated for a package with many versions.

- **The legacy V2 feed of a virtual NuGet repository now answers from every member, not just the hosted ones** (#4021). `v2_odata` resolved the virtual's member list and then discarded it (`let (repo_ids, _members)`), and `v2_download` had no remote-member arm at all, so a Chocolatey or `nuget.exe` client behind a virtual repository saw only what hosted members published — a remote member's packages were neither listed nor downloadable, whichever protocol that member speaks. The feed now merges each authorized remote member's entries in configured priority order, deduped case-insensitively by `(id, version)` with earlier members winning, so a hosted member's copy of a coordinate beats a remote member's — the same "local wins" rule the V3 registration merge applies (#3980) — and bounded at the 500 rows the hosted half already caps at. An unreachable member is logged and skipped rather than emptying the whole feed. Downloads go through the same member walk the V3 flat-container route uses, now shared by both routes, so the legacy route inherits its configured priority order, its caller-authorized member set (a member the caller cannot read directly stays invisible) and its rule that a member refusing a package it holds is terminal rather than a reason to fall through to the next member.

- **Promotion and approval copies now carry the source artifact's `origin` instead of re-deriving one for the target repository** (#4152). `artifacts.origin` (#4050) records where an artifact's bytes came from and is immutable once written, but the three copy paths that move content between repositories — single promote, bulk promote and approval-execute — inserted the copy with no `origin` at all, so migration 227's `artifacts_origin_fill` trigger derived a fresh document from the **target** repo and stamped `{"v":1,"kind":"hosted","repository_key":"<target>"}` on it. Promotion is the path most content takes into a serving repository, so the upstream that actually supplied proxied, mirrored or migrated bytes was erased at exactly the hop where it matters: a lower-trust source shadowing a higher-trust one — the attack `origin` exists to make visible — became invisible the moment the artifact was promoted, and `origin ->> 'upstream_url'` (the indexed "which artifacts did this upstream supply?" incident query) stopped naming the copy. All three paths now read the source row's recorded document and write it verbatim onto the copy; the fill trigger already honours an explicitly supplied origin and derives only when the column is NULL, so no schema change was needed and the derivation for a genuine upload is untouched. Copies keep the repository key of first arrival rather than being re-stamped for each hop. Existing rows are not rewritten — `artifacts_origin_immutable` forbids it, and a copy already stamped `hosted` stays that way.

- **`CONDA_ATTESTATION_REQUIRE_VERIFIED` now actually gates CEP-27 conda attestations: the upload path cryptographically verifies Sigstore bundles and fails closed** (#4155, #4048). The flag was parsed fail-closed by default and printed in the startup configuration dump, but it was read at no decision point, and the live attestation endpoint still ran the pre-#4048 shape check — which required a top-level `_type` a Sigstore bundle does not carry, so it rejected every genuine CEP-27 bundle and accepted only the unsigned in-toto Statement, the exact inversion of the advertised posture. The endpoint now runs `verify_conda_bundle` — DSSE signature, Fulcio certificate chain, Rekor inclusion proof and Signed Entry Timestamp, OIDC issuer allowlist, then the CEP-27 statement policy on the signed payload — against a SHA-256 the server streams out of storage and computes itself, persists the verdict next to the stored attestation under the `attestation_verification` metadata key, and when the flag is on (the default) refuses any attestation that does not verify, storing nothing. Only an explicit operator opt-out (`CONDA_ATTESTATION_REQUIRE_VERIFIED=false`) accepts an unverified attestation, and then the failed verification record is stored with it so the gap stays auditable.

- **Eight concurrent anonymous Composer package lookups can no longer deadlock the buffered-metadata proxy path for every format** (#4162). This is the Composer instance of the #4145 hazard: `resolve_v1_provider_metadata` — the v1 provider fallback a proxied Composer repository runs whenever the direct `p2/...` metadata fetch 404s — reserved 128 MiB (`LARGE_METADATA_MAX_BYTES`) of the process-wide buffered-metadata byte budget for the upstream's root `packages.json` and then, while still holding it, took a SECOND untimed reservation from the SAME budget for each `provider-includes` index and again for the final per-package document. The shipped default budget is 1 GiB — exactly eight worst-case buffers — so eight concurrent requests reserved all of it and then each waited for bytes only the others could release, until the 120 s global request timeout or a client disconnect dropped them. The fallback is anonymously reachable on any public remote Composer repository and needs no credentials or setup, and the stall is of the *shared* buffered-metadata path (RPM repodata, npm packuments, the PyPI simple index, Debian `dists`), not just Composer; a lowered `AK_PROXY_METADATA_BUDGET_BYTES` makes it cheaper still. The reservation is taken before the proxy cache lookup, so neither a cache hit nor a negative-cached 404 avoided it. Each fetch is now scoped so its permit is released before the next reservation is requested — a request holds at most one slice of the budget at a time and its peak reservation falls from 256 MiB to 128 MiB — while the discovery walk, the documents it fetches and everything Composer serves are unchanged. A source pin keeps every fetch in the fallback scoped that way.

- **Artifact label writes now need the repository `write` action; visibility alone no longer authorizes them** (#4193). `PUT /api/v1/artifacts/{id}/labels`, `POST /api/v1/artifacts/{id}/labels/{key}` and `DELETE /api/v1/artifacts/{id}/labels/{key}` checked the `write:artifacts` token scope, which every interactive session passes, and the artifact visibility gate, which answers read visibility only: it let every signed-in user through on a public repository and asked a member of a private one for `read`. Any signed-in user with no grant on a public repository, and any read-only member of a private one, could therefore rewrite or delete the labels on its artifacts, and every label change re-evaluates the sync policies that decide what replicates to peers. The three routes now also pass the deny-by-default `require_repo_action(.., "write", ..)` gate the SBOM mutations adopted for GHSA-ww52-pmcg-f53c, and answer 403 to a caller without the action. Removing a label asks for `write`, not `delete`, matching the token scope label operations already carry (#2989) and the `PUT`, which can replace the whole set. Global admins, `developer` and `repository-owner` members and fine-grained `write` grants are unaffected, and so are reads: a public repository's labels stay listable by any signed-in user, and a missing artifact is still a 404.

- **Inbound W3C trace context is adopted only from trusted-proxy peers once `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` is set** (#4195). The `http_request` span adopted an inbound `traceparent`/`tracestate` from any client (#4030), so under the default `parentbased_always_on` sampler a caller could send `sampled=00` to keep its own requests out of tracing, and under `parentbased_always_off` or `parentbased_traceidratio` an untrusted `sampled=01` forced export of traces the sampler would have dropped. The span now consults the header only when the TCP peer falls inside `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`, the list that already decides whether `X-Forwarded-For` is believed; any other peer starts a fresh root trace. The correlation-ID fallback from `traceparent` is unchanged. With the list empty the header is still accepted from every client, so existing deployments keep joined traces, and startup logs a warning when that combines with one of the two samplers a client can force.

- **A personal API token created with a `repo_selector` is now confined to it** (#4219). `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens` had no `repo_selector` field and ignored unknown fields, so the selector the web UI sends when a user scopes a personal token was dropped and the token was minted unrestricted, with no error. The endpoint now accepts `repo_selector`, stores it where service-account tokens store theirs, and the same authentication path enforces it: the token reaches only the repositories the selector matches that its owner can already reach. A selector that would resolve as unrestricted (empty, unparseable, or with a misspelled criterion) is refused with 400, and so is any other unknown field in the request.

  **Operator note:** personal tokens created before this release with a repository selector were issued **unrestricted**, and nothing about them records the scope that was asked for. Review personal tokens minted through the web UI's Access Tokens page with a repository scope, and rotate them.

- **A repository-restricted API token can no longer mint a token without that restriction** (#4225). Every token-mint endpoint (`POST /api/v1/auth/tokens`, `/users/{id}/tokens`, `/users/me/tokens`, `/profile/access-tokens` and `/service-accounts/{id}/tokens`) checked the new token's permission scopes against the presenting credential but not its repository scope, so a token restricted by `repo_selector` or `repository_ids` could mint a sibling with no repository restriction in one call. A token minted by a repository-restricted credential (or by a session exchanged from one) now inherits that credential's repositories, stored as a `match_repos` selector so it is never widened by a later repository deletion; the credential may not name its own `repo_selector` or `repository_ids` for the new token (403), and a credential whose restriction currently matches no repository cannot mint at all. Interactive sessions and unrestricted tokens mint exactly as before. Repository-scoped tokens (`/repositories/{key}/tokens`) were already confined to a repository the caller's credential can reach.

  **Operator note:** tokens minted through a repository-restricted token before this release may be unrestricted. Tokens a token minted carry no marker of it; review tokens created by automation that authenticates with a restricted token, and rotate them.

- **A token's repository restriction no longer fails open when its stored selector cannot be read, or when a mint request misspells a field** (#4226). At authentication a stored `repo_selector` that did not parse was read as empty, which means unrestricted, and service-account token creation stored the selector as given. A stored selector that does not parse, or that carries a criterion the server does not know, now grants no repository at all and is logged at `warn` with the token id; `POST /api/v1/service-accounts/{id}/tokens` validates `repo_selector` with the same rules as personal tokens and refuses an empty `repository_ids`, both with 400. The token-mint requests of `/users/{id}/tokens`, `/users/me/tokens`, `/profile/access-tokens`, `/service-accounts/{id}/tokens` and `/repositories/{key}/tokens` now refuse unknown fields with 400 instead of ignoring them, so a misspelled `repo_selector` can no longer mint an unrestricted token; malformed bodies on these endpoints are now 400 rather than 422.

  **Operator note:** a service-account token whose stored selector misspelled a criterion was broader than written (unrestricted, if every criterion was misspelled) and now reaches no repository. Its holder sees 404s for repositories it used to reach; re-mint it with a corrected selector.

- **Repository-scoped API tokens no longer become unrestricted when every repository they name is deleted** (#4228, #4271, #4270). The `api_token_repositories` rows that pin a token to explicit repositories cascade away with a repository deletion, and a token with no rows was treated as unrestricted — so deleting the one repository a CI token could reach silently widened it to the whole instance. Tokens now carry an explicit `repository_restricted` marker (backfilled, and stamped by a trigger whenever a pin row is written); a restricted token whose allow-list empties out denies every repository instead of falling open. Deleting repositories can now only narrow a token, never widen it. Repository tokens that had already lost every repository before the upgrade are recovered from the `API_TOKEN_CREATED` audit trail and marked restricted too; a service-account token minted with an explicit `repository_ids` list whose repositories were all deleted before the upgrade cannot be told apart from a never-restricted one and should be reviewed and revoked by an administrator.

- **npm and Maven virtual repositories no longer serve hosted-member artifacts that the member's scan policy blocks** (#4286). The npm virtual tarball path (`npm_local_fetch`) discarded every error from the gated exact-path lookup, including the scan-policy 403 and the quarantine 409. It then served whatever its `{package}/%/{filename}` pattern lookup found after checking quarantine only. Hosted npm tarballs are stored at `{package}/{version}/{filename}`, which only the pattern lookup finds, so a tarball a `block_unscanned`, `block_on_fail` or `max_severity` policy refused on the direct hosted route was served through any virtual repository that listed that hosted repository as a member. Only a genuine miss (404) now falls through to the pattern lookup. The row it finds is served through the same gated helper, so quarantine and the scan policy both apply.

  The same review found three related Maven gaps, fixed here too. The virtual member closure discarded the gated lookup's refusal in the same way. It then fell through to the storage-direct fallback, which checked only quarantine on the requested primary's own row and applied the scan policy to the Gate-2 anchor. When a newer primary in the same GAV passed the policy, the blocked jar's bytes were served. That fallback now applies the full gate to the primary's own row. Finally, a `-SNAPSHOT` alias resolved to its timestamped artifact with no download gate at all, on the direct hosted route and through a virtual repository. It now passes the same quarantine and scan-policy gate as an exact-path hit.

- **A credential from the CI OIDC exchange can no longer mint an API token for its service account** (#4314). `POST /api/v1/profile/access-tokens`, `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens` and `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/tokens` now return 403 when the caller is a CI OIDC service account (`auth_provider = ci`), whichever provider type issued the credential. Before this, a pull-only, non-renewable `kubernetes` credential, or a GitHub/GitLab pipeline credential, could mint a `read:artifacts` API token that, under the default token policy, never expires, turning a short-lived credential into a permanent one. A pipeline that needs a longer-lived token should exchange a fresh CI token per job; an administrator can still issue a token for a CI account through the admin endpoints.

- **WASM plugin runtime updated to wasmtime 36.0.16** (#4332; RUSTSEC-2026-0314, RUSTSEC-2026-0316). A WASM plugin guest could allocate past its host-call fuel limit through dynamic record lifting, or panic the host through a filesystem datetime overflow in WASI. Both are fixed upstream in 36.0.16; no configuration change is needed.

- **RPM virtual repositories' repodata now lists only the members the caller may read** (#4346, #3323). `repomd.xml`, `primary.xml.gz`, `filelists.xml.gz` and `other.xml.gz` of a virtual RPM repository were built from every member, so any caller who could read the virtual, including an anonymous caller of a public virtual, could read the names, versions, SHA-256 digests and file lists of packages in private and internal members (package bytes were already protected). The member walk is now caller-authorized like every other format's; the render cache is keyed by the virtual, the metadata root and the caller's authorized member set, so callers with different visibility never share a document, each set renders byte-identically and `repomd.xml.asc` signs exactly the document that caller is served. Each virtual root keeps at most four member-set renders.

  Attaching an `internal` repository to a virtual now needs a read grant on it (or instance admin), as for a `private` one (#3813): a delegated admin of a virtual could otherwise re-export any internal repository through it, anonymously if the virtual was public. The refusal is a 403.

- **WASM plugin runtime updated to wasmtime 36.0.17** (#4361; RUSTSEC-2026-0321, RUSTSEC-2026-0322, RUSTSEC-2026-0323). A WASM plugin guest could get around its fuel limit through WASI preview 0 `poll_oneoff`, make the host allocate excessive memory when it had no stdio, or read uninitialized host memory through `fd_readdir`. All three are fixed upstream in 36.0.17; no configuration change is needed.

- **The promotion-history endpoint now enforces repository read access** (#4418). `GET /api/v1/promotion/repositories/{key}/promotion-history` only required a logged-in caller, so any authenticated user could read the promotion and rejection history of any repository, including private ones: artifact paths, the counterpart repository's key, rejection reasons, who promoted, and policy results. It now takes the same existence-hiding read gate as the other repository read endpoints (a caller who cannot read the repository, or whose token is scoped away from it, gets the same 404 as for a repository that does not exist), and the key of a counterpart repository the caller cannot read is returned as an empty string, matching the redaction the per-artifact `last_promotion` field already applies.

- **Generic, chunked and multipart uploads now refuse remote and virtual repositories** (#4420). The native format routes already rejected writes to a remote (proxy) or virtual repository, but `POST /api/v1/uploads` (chunked sessions), the generic `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{path}` and both multipart `POST` upload routes did not, so a user with write access could plant an artifact in a remote repository that shadowed the upstream it proxies, without it ever being fetched from that upstream (for example a chunked `.deb` into a remote Debian repository got a full catalog row). These paths now answer exactly like the native routes: 405 for a remote repository and 400 for a virtual one, before any session row is opened or any byte is staged. A chunked session staged against such a repository before this change can no longer be completed either: the completion is refused with the same status and the session is failed.

- **The generic download route no longer serves around scan-on-proxy: while a repository scans, a proxied file of an enforced format is refused there** (#4442, part of #4097). `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/download/*path`, which also answers on `/general/{key}/*path` and backs the web UI's download button, streamed a Remote repository's proxy-cache or upstream bytes with no scan gate, for every format. The format routes (`/npm`, `/pypi`, `/cargo`, `/maven`, `/ivy`, `/nuget`, `/vscode` and `/v2`) gate those same bytes, from the same proxy cache, so a package they refused with `403` could be downloaded here. Because the buffered gate commits upstream bytes to the cache before it decides (#4365), a refused pull even left them warm for this route. The route cannot run the gate itself: the gate grades the package coordinate each format route parses from its own request shape, and npm and Cargo even fetch from a source their own metadata names, none of which this route has a parser for. So when a Remote repository of an enforced format has `scan_on_proxy` on, the route now answers `403` with `{"error": "scan_on_proxy_route_required", "file": ..., "handler": ...}` before any routing-rule read, cache read or upstream request, and `handler` names the format handler whose route serves the file through the gate (`sbt` is mounted at `/ivy`, `oci` at `/v2`). A Virtual repository refuses the same way, on this route and on `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts/*path` (which serves a Virtual member's bytes through the same member walk), when a Remote member the caller may read scans under the stricter-of-two rule, while a hosted member that owns the exact path is still served. An unreadable `scan_on_proxy` flag answers `503` instead of streaming unscanned.

  **Upgrade note: this is a deliberate behaviour change for repositories that scan on proxy.** It applies under every `proxy_scan_action`, `record_only` included, because that mode promises every pull is scanned and recorded, which this route cannot do. It applies to every path and to `HEAD`, which therefore no longer costs an upstream request, and it is stricter than the Maven route for POMs, `.xml` metadata and checksums: fetch those through the format route. A client that downloaded proxied files of such a repository through this route, the web UI's download button included, now receives the `403` and should use the format route. Files stored in the repository itself (`artifacts` rows) are served as before behind its download gate, and formats that do not enforce scan-on-proxy, or repositories with it off, are unaffected.

- **An OCI image deleted by digest no longer comes back after a restart** (#4450). `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<digest>` removed every tag and index row for the digest but soft-deleted only the `artifacts` row at the digest path, so the tag's own row (`v2/<image>/manifests/<tag>`) stayed live. On the next start, the OCI migration reindex took that row for a never-indexed migrated manifest and re-registered the tag, its child refs and its `oci_manifests` record: an image an operator had deleted, for example a compromised one, was pullable again after any restart or rollout. A delete by digest now soft-deletes every manifest row of that image name whose bytes are that digest (other image names in the repository keep theirs, #4466), tag rows included, in the same transaction as the index unwind (a failure rolls both back; the soft-delete error used to be dropped). The startup reindex also skips a live manifest row when the same manifest was deleted by digest after that row was last written, so a row left behind by an older replica during a rolling upgrade is not revived either, when the image was also pushed by digest. Deleting by tag name is unchanged, and a child manifest still listed by another tagged index stays. An image pushed only by tag and deleted by digest before the upgrade, or by a not-yet-upgraded replica during the rollout, leaves no marker either; the reindex now repairs only rows the migration worker imported (#4465), so such an image stays deleted unless it was itself a migration import.

- **The API no longer returns a Remote's upstream credentials when they are embedded in `upstream_url`** (#4452). A Remote created with `https://user:password@host/...` had the URL echoed back verbatim, password included, by the create response, `GET /api/v1/repositories`, `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}` and the update response, so any caller with read access to repository metadata could read a live upstream secret. These responses now render the URL with the userinfo removed and report a new boolean `upstream_url_has_credentials` (additive field) so a client can still tell that credentials are configured. The same redaction now applies to the `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/test-upstream` response, to `origin.upstream_url` on the artifact detail responses (the origin record of a proxied artifact is derived from the repository's upstream URL), to origin-policy violation messages returned by promotion and approval and saved in their `policy_result`, to `upstream_url` / `index_upstream_url` values in audit-entry details, and to the proxy, PyPI, npm, OCI and curation-sync log lines and error messages that printed the raw upstream URL. Writes are unchanged: a URL with userinfo is still accepted on create, still stored as given, and the credentials are still sent upstream as HTTP Basic auth, so existing Remotes keep authenticating.

  **Upgrade note:** this release stops *returning* the credentials but does not remove the copies already stored. Besides `repositories.upstream_url`, they remain at rest (lowercased) in the `origin` record of every artifact already proxied through such a Remote (`artifacts.origin` and its migration-230 index), and in promotion / approval `policy_result` records saved before this release whose origin-policy violations quoted the URL. Cleaning those copies is tracked in #4463. If a Remote embeds credentials in its URL, rotate the secret at the upstream and put the new one in the dedicated upstream-auth fields (`upstream_auth_type` / `upstream_username` / `upstream_password` on create, or `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/upstream-auth`), which are stored encrypted and never returned. Because `upstream_url` cannot be changed through the update API, removing the old credentials from the URL itself means recreating the Remote with a credential-free URL.

- **Artifact origin records and the proxy-cache catalogue no longer keep the credentials of a Remote whose upstream URL embeds `user:password@`** (#4463). The origin trigger copied the Remote's `upstream_url`, userinfo included, into `artifacts.origin` of every artifact proxied through it, and the upstream index from migration 230 held the same value. The proxy-cache catalogue recorded the credentialed fetch URL too.
  - The origin normalizer strips the userinfo. This applies to the SQL `ak_normalize_upstream_url` and its Rust mirror, which a test now pins to each other.
  - The fill trigger now also normalizes an explicitly supplied origin, and a new trigger strips `proxy_cache_artifacts.upstream_url` on every write. The database is therefore the single enforcement point, including for a replica still running the previous release during a rolling upgrade.
  - Migration 271 rewrites the stored values in 5000-row batches. While it runs, the immutability trigger admits only an `upstream_url` change to its normalized form.
  - A Remote's upstream URL containing whitespace or control characters is now refused with 400 on create and update. Such URLs were accepted and authenticated, but kept their credentials at rest.

  This also fixes origin policies: `allowed_upstreams` never admitted, and `denied_upstreams` never denied, an artifact proxied through a credentialed Remote, because the stored value carried the credentials and the policy entry did not. Both now match the credential-free URL.

  Operator note: the Remote's own `upstream_url` still holds the credentials, because the proxy authenticates from it. On pre-release builds, policy results saved before #4462 may also still quote them. Move the secret to the Remote's encrypted upstream-auth fields (recreate the Remote with a credential-free URL) and rotate it.

- **Deleting an OCI manifest by digest no longer deletes the same manifest under other image names in the repository** (#4466). `DELETE /v2/<repo>/<image>/manifests/<digest>` removed the digest's tags under every image name in the repository, so deleting `xa@<digest>` also removed `xb:v1` when both pointed at the same manifest, and since the #4450 fix the tag rows of the other names were soft-deleted too, so the loss survived a restart. In the distribution spec `<name>` is `<repo>/<image>`, so the delete now removes only `<image>`'s tags and `<image>`'s manifest rows (canonical and migrated source-layout paths); the same digest stays pullable under every other image name. The manifest's shared records (index edges, blob references, the referrers subject edge and its `oci_manifests` row) still go only when no tag of any image name in the repository points at the digest. The startup reindex's "deleted by digest" guard is scoped the same way, so a delete under one image name never stops the repair of another. Pulling `<image>@<digest>` after the delete is scoped to the image name the same way (#4525): it answers `404` under the deleted name and keeps resolving under the others.

- **The release-target read endpoint now enforces repository read access** (#4473). `GET /api/v1/promotion/repositories/{key}/release-target` only required a logged-in caller, so any authenticated user could read which release repository a staging repository is linked to (key and id), and its 400 "only available for staging repositories" revealed the type of a repository the caller could not read. It now takes the same existence-hiding read gate as promotion history (#4418): a caller who cannot read the repository, or whose token is scoped away from it, gets 404 before the type check. When the caller can read the staging repository but not the linked release repository, the response still reports `linked: true` but returns its key and id as null.

- **The stock `docker-compose.yml` no longer publishes Postgres, OpenSearch, Trivy or OpenSCAP on every host interface** (#4480). A `ports:` entry without an address binds `0.0.0.0` (and bypasses firewalld/ufw on Docker), so a default `docker compose up -d` on a host with a routable address exposed Postgres with its fixed `registry`/`registry` login on 30432 and OpenSearch, which runs with its security plugin disabled, on 9200. The backend reaches all four on the compose network and needs none of these ports. Postgres and OpenSearch are now published on `127.0.0.1` only, which keeps the documented host-side development flow (`docker compose up -d postgres opensearch`, then `cargo run`) working, and Trivy and OpenSCAP are no longer published, with a commented loopback opt-in for debugging. Only Caddy (30080/30443) is reachable from other machines by default. Anyone who relied on reaching these services from another host must now publish them explicitly.

- **A repository the caller cannot read now answers exactly like one that does not exist** (Closes #4498). The REST read endpoints that hide a private repository's existence (`GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}`, its `artifacts`, `artifacts/{path}`, `download/{path}`, `versions/{path}` and `storage` sub-resources, `GET /api/v1/promotion/repositories/{key}/promotion-history` and `release-target`, and the other reads gated the same way) refused an unreadable repository with `Repository '<key>' not found`, while a key that names no repository answered `Repository not found`. The two 404s had the same status but different bodies, so an anonymous caller or a user without a grant could tell that a private repository exists. Both now return the same body, `{"code":"NOT_FOUND","message":"Repository not found"}`.

- **A rejected `S3_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT` or `AZURE_STORAGE_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT` no longer writes its credentials to the log** (#4503). A public endpoint that carries `user:password@` is refused at startup, but the error printed the value verbatim, so the credentials it was refused for ended up in the fatal startup error (primary backend) or the `Additional ... storage backend skipped` WARN (secondary backend). The value is now shown with everything between `scheme://` and its last `@` replaced by `***` (for example `http://***@192.168.42.150:32613`), whatever the reason it was rejected. This also covers a password pasted without percent-encoding that contains `/`, `?`, `#` or `\`, which ends the URL's authority early. Rotate any credentials that were logged this way.

- **Origin policies now gate content a Remote repository serves from its proxy cache or upstream** (Closes #4506). A scan policy's `origin` predicates (`allowed_upstreams`, `denied_upstreams`, `allowed_repositories`, `denied_repositories`, `allowed_kinds`) were evaluated only against an `artifacts` row's recorded origin. Remote fetches for Generic, Maven, npm and the other proxied formats write a `proxy_cache_artifacts` row and no `artifacts` row, so an upstream deny policy did not stop those downloads, and `allowed_kinds` naming `proxy` could never be satisfied (#4161). Content a Remote serves now has the origin `{"kind": "proxy", "repository_key": <remote key>, "upstream_url": <the remote's configured upstream, normalized>}`, the same document an `artifacts` row in that Remote records, and the policies that apply to the Remote (its own and global ones) are evaluated against it before the proxy cache is read or the upstream is contacted. A refused download answers `403 Artifact download is blocked by the repository's scan policy`, as a blocked hosted download does, including for entries cached before the policy was attached, for presigned-redirect fast paths. A virtual repository does not serve the refused content from such a member either.

  **Upgrade note.** A policy whose origin predicates a Remote's content does not satisfy now blocks that Remote, metadata included. In particular a global policy with `allowed_upstreams` that does not list a Remote's upstream, or with `allowed_kinds` that does not include `proxy`, now refuses every download from that Remote. Review global origin policies before upgrading.

- **CI OIDC token exchange now refuses an assertion whose `nbf` (not before) is in the future** (#4511). `POST /api/v1/auth/ci/token` checked the signature, `iss`, `aud` and `exp` of an exchanged CI token but not `nbf`, so a token that was not valid yet was accepted. This applied to every provider type (`gitlab`, `github`, `generic`, `kubernetes`) and both key sources. The claim is now checked with the same 60-second clock-skew leeway as `exp`: a token whose `nbf` is further in the future is refused with 401, and ordinary clock skew between the CI issuer and Artifact Keeper is still tolerated. Tokens without an `nbf` claim are unaffected.

- **Scan-on-proxy fails closed on an unreadable config, decides cache key and scannability once per request, and refuses ambiguous upstream paths** (#4513, #4365). Four hardening fixes from the scan-on-proxy reviews:

  - An unreadable `scan_on_proxy` configuration now answers a retryable `503` on every enforced format's Remote download (Maven, Gradle, sbt, npm, PyPI, Cargo, NuGet, VS Code, OCI manifests) and every Virtual walk. Before, a direct Remote pull read a database error as "scanning off" and streamed the package unscanned. Maven curation now derives the package from the cache-normalized path, so a trailing `/` no longer skips a curation rule.
  - VS Code gallery asset types are matched ignoring case and fetched and cached under their canonical spelling. Only display metadata (manifest, details, changelog, license, icons, `.vsixmanifest`, signature, language-pack translations) streams unscanned; the package is always scanned, and any other asset type is `404` while the repository scans on proxy. Before, a re-capitalised package asset type streamed the `.vsix` unscanned.
  - One helper now returns each request's proxy-cache key and scan decision from the same normalized path, for Maven, sbt, NuGet, npm, PyPI, Cargo and VS Code. Cache keys for well-formed paths are unchanged, so no warm entry is orphaned.
  - Ambiguous proxied paths are refused with `400` before any upstream request. On the npm, PyPI and Cargo download routes, the VS Code gallery routes and the generic download route's Remote arm (Maven, sbt and NuGet already did this), a client path containing any `?`, `#`, `;`, `\`, control character or stray `%` is refused, so `x.tgz?versionId=abc` can no longer smuggle a query to the upstream. For every format, a relative upstream path ProxyService builds is also refused if its path part holds such a character or a trailing space; queries the handlers append themselves (Ansible, Conan search, OCI `tags/list`) and absolute URLs a handler builds or takes from an upstream index (which keep their own guards) are unaffected, as are npm's `%2F` and Go's `!`-escaping.

- **Conda channel responses to authenticated requests are marked `Cache-Control: private` instead of `public`** (#4555). `repodata.json`, `channeldata.json`, the shards and the other channel documents were sent with `public, max-age=60` even when the request carried credentials, so a shared cache in front of the registry could store a private channel's index, or a virtual channel's index as merged for one caller's member access, and serve it to the next requester of the same URL. Any conda response to a request with an `Authorization` header or a session cookie now has the `public` directive replaced by `private`; anonymous responses to public channels are unchanged, and the token-in-URL routes keep `private, no-store`.

- **A virtual conda channel no longer lets a remote member shadow a package name a hosted member owns** (#4555). The virtual merge took records from remote members first and kept the first writer per filename, so an upstream that published `acme-core 99.0` sat next to the internal `acme-core 1.0` in the merged `repodata.json` and won the solve: the textbook dependency-confusion attack, and the gap the name-shadowing guard already closes for npm, PyPI, Cargo, RubyGems and Hex. Once any local or staging member of the virtual has published a name, remote members now contribute no records under that name in any subdir, `channeldata.json` drops their entry for it, and a download of such a file through the virtual is not proxied upstream. Ownership is read from every member regardless of the caller's access, and a database error fails the request instead of merging unguarded.

- **Download tickets now carry the repository restriction of the credential that minted them, and redeeming a valid ticket works again** (#4588, GHSA-2mfv-xg68-gq4p). `POST /api/v1/auth/ticket` stored only the user, so a redeemed ticket was rebuilt from the user account with access to every repository the user could reach. A token restricted to some repositories could therefore mint a ticket for a repository outside its restriction. This was latent: the user lookup at redemption selected a fixed column list that no longer matched the user model, so it failed and every ticket was treated as anonymous. That also broke the web UI's `?ticket=` downloads and streams and the Terraform provider mirror's ticketed archive URLs (#3588). In addition, a path-bound ticket was compared against the nest-stripped request path on `/api/v1/...` routes, so it could not match there. All three are fixed together. A ticket now records the minting credential's repository restriction (migration 286), and redemption restores it, so a ticket never reads more than its minter could. The user lookup reads the whole row. The bound path is compared with the full request path. Minting a ticket now requires the `read:artifacts` token scope, which interactive sessions always have. Tickets minted before the upgrade carry no recorded restriction and are refused. They expire within minutes, so a client only has to mint a new one.

- **Image build specs no longer accept a pip requirement containing a line break** (#4588, GHSA-59mx-6fq9-pp9p). The pip requirement pattern allowed `\s` inside the extras bracket and around version comparators, and `\s` also matches `\n` and `\r`. Each requirement is written into the generated Containerfile's `RUN pip install` line, and the Containerfile parser ends an instruction at an unescaped newline, so a requirement such as `foo[a\nRUN ...]` added its own instruction to the build. That bypassed `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_ALLOW_RUN=false`. Reaching it needs permission to start an image build, which is administrators only unless `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_ADMIN_ONLY=false`. The pattern now allows only spaces and tabs as blanks, and every package spec, for every package manager, is refused with 400 when it contains a control character other than a tab.

- **Eight REST mutation endpoints now check the caller's action on the repository, not only that it can see or reach it** (#4588, GHSA-mvmh-g8wm-r3cp). Each of these stopped at a gate that does not authorize an interactive session: a token scope check (which a session always passes), the tenant gate (a no-op on a public repository, and satisfied by any grant on a private one, read-only included), or authentication alone. Any signed-in user could therefore make these changes on a public repository, and so could a read-only member of a private one:
  - `PUT /api/v1/promotion/repositories/{key}/release-target` (relink or unlink where release promotions land) now needs read access to the staging repository, the `write:repositories` token scope and the repository `admin` action on it, and a release repository the caller cannot read is answered like a missing one. It previously checked nothing beyond a token scope, on private staging repositories too.
  - `POST /api/v1/promotion/repositories/{key}/artifacts/{id}/reject` now needs the promotion capability (an administrator, or a `promote:artifacts` token) and the promotion tenant gate. A caller who cannot read the staging repository gets 404 for every artifact id, so the endpoint is no longer an existence oracle. It previously checked nothing.
  - `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/labels` and `POST`/`DELETE .../labels/{label_key}` (labels select repositories into sync policies) now need the repository `write` action and the `write:repositories` token scope.
  - `GET`/`POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/email-subscriptions` and `DELETE .../email-subscriptions/{id}` now need the repository `admin` action. Listing exposed recipient addresses, and creating a subscription made the instance send mail to arbitrary addresses.
  - `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/image-builds` and `.../image-builds/render`, when `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_ADMIN_ONLY=false`, now need the repository `write` action and the `write:artifacts` token scope.
  - `PUT /api/v1/builds/{id}` and `POST /api/v1/builds/{id}/artifacts` are now limited to the build's creator and administrators, and creating or changing a build needs the `write:artifacts` token scope. Migration 285 adds `builds.created_by`. Builds created before the upgrade have no recorded creator and can only be changed by an administrator.
  - `POST /api/v1/peers/{id}/connections/probe` is now admin-only, like the other mutating peer routes. It previously did not read the caller's identity.
  - `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/security/proxy-scans/rescan` now needs the repository `write` action.

  Refusals answer 403, except where the caller cannot read the repository, which answers 404. Global administrators, `repository-owner` members and fine-grained grants carrying the named action are unaffected. A `developer` member keeps label writes, image builds and rescans, but now needs the repository `admin` action for email subscriptions and the release-target link. `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/test-upstream`, the ninth endpoint in the advisory, was already fixed on this line before this change.

- **Changing a repository's scan configuration now requires the `write:repositories` token scope** (#4588, GHSA-gvhj-8vg9-358g). `PUT /api/v1/repositories/{key}/security` checked the tenant gate and the repository `admin` action but not the presenting token's action scope, so an API token minted with only `read:artifacts` by a user who is a repository admin could turn scanning off, lower the severity threshold or switch the proxy scan action to record-only. The sibling repository-configuration endpoints (cache TTL, npm scope policy, cache invalidation, egress proxy) already required `write:repositories`. This one now does too, and answers 403 to a token without it. Interactive sessions and tokens carrying `write:repositories` are unaffected.

- **Slow or stalled uploads can no longer hold every global request slot, and health and readiness probes are never shed** (#4588, GHSA-9f9r-c4w8-rjv9). Upload and download routes (Git LFS, OCI blobs, the repository artifact routes, `/api/v1/uploads`, Incus/LXC) are exempt from the `GLOBAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECS` wall-clock timeout (#3263). Nothing else limited how long a client could take to send a body. A user with write access to one Git LFS repository could open 512 uploads, send the headers and one byte on each, and hold all of `GLOBAL_MAX_CONCURRENCY`'s request slots for as long as the sockets stayed open. Every other request, including `/health` and `/ready`, was then refused with 503, so an orchestrator would also restart or drain the replica. Git LFS also buffered each object (up to 2 GB) in memory before the handler ran. Four changes:
  - An upload body that delivers fewer than `UPLOAD_MIN_PROGRESS_BYTES` (default 16384) during an `UPLOAD_PROGRESS_WINDOW_SECS` window (default 60) spent waiting for data is aborted with `408 Request Timeout`. This is a progress floor, not an idle timeout, so trickling one byte at a time does not keep a request open. Time the server spends on its own work does not count.
  - A principal (an authenticated user, or a client address when anonymous) may have at most `UPLOAD_MAX_IN_FLIGHT_PER_PRINCIPAL` uploads (default 64) in flight on the native-format routes, the repository artifact routes and `/api/v1/uploads`. Further uploads get `429` with `Retry-After`.
  - `/health`, `/healthz`, `/ready`, `/readyz` and `/livez` bypass the global concurrency limit.
  - Git LFS object uploads stream to the upload scratch disk (`AK_UPLOAD_STAGING_DIR`, or `$STORAGE_PATH/.incoming`) while being hashed, then stream into storage, instead of being buffered in memory. The 2 GB per-object limit is unchanged.

  Each setting accepts `0` to turn its limit off. The scratch-disk sizing guide (`docs/operations/upload-scratch-disk.md`) now lists Git LFS uploads and documents these limits. OCI `/v2` uploads get the progress deadline but not the per-principal cap.

- **A remote repository's upstream credentials are now sent only to its configured upstream's origin, not to hosts named by index metadata** (#4588, GHSA-24rf-2gv2-j47c). Package index metadata can name download locations by absolute URL: a PyPI simple-index `href`, a Helm `index.yaml` `urls` entry, the Cargo `config.json` `dl` template, a Composer `dist.url`, a Terraform `download_url`. The shared upstream fetchers attached the remote's configured Basic or Bearer credentials to whatever URL they were given. An upstream index that is compromised, or that serves content an attacker controls, could therefore point a download at a host of its choosing and receive the credentials, over plain HTTP if it named an `http://` URL. Any client that could trigger the download could cause this, including an anonymous one on a public remote. The buffered, streaming, conditional-revalidation and ETag-probe fetchers and the JSON POST path now attach credentials only when the request URL has the same scheme, host and port as the remote's `upstream_url` or its `index_upstream_url` override. Any other URL is still fetched, but without credentials, and a sampled `security` warning is logged. OCI bearer-realm handling (GHSA-78h6-3wp8-2542, `oci_trusted_bearer_realms`) is unchanged. **A credentialed remote whose upstream serves files from a different host than its index, and needs the same credentials there, will now get 401/403 from that host.** For a Cargo registry with split index and download hosts, set `index_upstream_url` to the index and `upstream_url` to the download host, so that both are configured origins.

## [1.10.0] - 2026-09-20

### Added

- **Container repositories can build images server-side from a structured spec, and any pushed image can be inspected down to the Dockerfile that produced it** (#4034, #4024, #4062). `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/image-builds` queues a build from a spec — an allowlisted base image, ordered package groups each naming its manager (`apt`, `dnf`, `microdnf`, `yum`, `apk`, `pip`, `conda`, so a UBI or Alpine base installs with the tool it actually ships), env, labels, user and workdir — and the server renders a deterministic Containerfile, drives `buildctl` against a rootless BuildKit daemon with `attest:provenance=mode=max`, and pushes the result back into the repository **as the requesting user** through a short-lived API token that is revoked when the build ends. `multistage: true` installs the pip groups in a builder stage and copies only the installed packages into the final image. Status, the pushed digest and the log (capped at 1 MiB) land on the new `image_builds` row (migration 221); a semaphore bounds concurrency and a wall-clock timeout stops runaways. `POST …/image-builds/render` is the dry run the console previews, and `GET …/image-inspect?image=&reference=` describes a pushed image from the registry's own storage — platforms, config, layers, history and, for images carrying a `mode=max` provenance attestation, the actual Dockerfile. `GET …/image-builds/base-info?image=` tells the console what the registry knows about a base image stored here — platform, user, pip/conda presence and the system package manager its own build history ran — so the wizard offers only the managers that fit.

  **Off until configured, administrators only by default, and never a user-authored Dockerfile unless an administrator says so.** Nothing runs until `AK_BUILDKIT_ADDR` and `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_PUSH_REGISTRY` are set; `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_ADMIN_ONLY` (default `true`) restricts building to administrators, otherwise repository write access decides. Every spec field is validated against a shell-safe grammar per manager before anything renders, system-package groups must name the `user` the image runs as afterwards, raw `RUN` lines need `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_ALLOW_RUN`, and a whole-Dockerfile spec needs `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_ALLOW_DOCKERFILE` — with it on, every `FROM` still has to sit under `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_BASE_ALLOWLIST`. `AK_IMAGE_BUILD_PIP_INDEX_URL` pins every generated `pip install` to one index (this instance's PyPI proxy, typically). The backend image gains `buildctl` from `moby/buildkit:v0.33.0`; the daemon is a separate rootless Deployment the backend talks to over TCP, not a sidecar.

- **Every published release digest is now verified after the fact for a build-provenance attestation and a cosign signature, and the check can be rehearsed** (#3519). #3518 made a failed provenance push a red merge job, but nothing re-asked the registry whether the published digest actually carries the predicate. The `verify-published` job now runs `scripts/ci/audit-published-attestations.sh`, which resolves each tag to its digest, requires a `slsa.dev/provenance/v1` attestation via `gh attestation verify` and delegates the signature question to the existing #3559 post-publish signature check, and fails the release path if either is missing. A `published-attestations` mode on the Release Gate Rehearsal workflow exercises the gate against an already-published tag in pass, wrong-digest and wrong-owner scenarios, each asserting its own expected outcome, so the gate is demonstrated both passing and refusing. The script doubles as the one-off audit of digests published while the attestation steps were soft (`audit-published-attestations.sh latest 1.9.0 1.8.2 1.8.1`).

- **A SAML configuration can be addressed by an operator-chosen `slug`, so rebuilding a deployment no longer changes the ACS URL registered at the IdP** (#2583, #3865). The SAML ACS and login URLs embed `saml_configs.id`, which defaults to `gen_random_uuid()`. Any redeploy that wipes the database therefore minted a new id, and the Assertion Consumer Service URL had to be re-pasted into the identity provider by hand — there was no way to pin it, and operators were driving Terraform `null_resource` API calls purely to read the UUID back out and feed it into the SAML module. Migration 218 adds a nullable, validated `slug` (`^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9_-]*$`, at most 64 characters, `UNIQUE`), settable through `POST`/`PUT /api/v1/admin/sso/saml` and returned by every SAML admin read; `GET /api/v1/auth/sso/saml/{id}/login` and `POST /api/v1/auth/sso/saml/{id}/acs` now accept either the UUID or the slug in that segment. The segment is parsed as a UUID first, so resolution for an existing deployment is byte-for-byte what it was, and a slug that would parse as a UUID is refused at write time rather than being silently shadowed. The `AssertionConsumerServiceURL` bound into the outbound AuthnRequest and the `Destination`/`Recipient` binding checked on the callback are both derived from the *resolved* segment the request arrived on, so the two sides agree whichever form the IdP is configured with — including a mixed setup — while an assertion bound to one form is still refused at the other. Slug resolution is an exact match: the value is constrained to a single lowercase spelling, so the uniqueness the database enforces and the equality the ACS lookup performs are the same comparison, and `/saml/Okta/acs` is a 404 rather than a second URL answering for `okta`. Relatedly, a duplicate `name` or `slug` on create/update is now a `409 Conflict` naming the value instead of the `500` that `create_saml` and `update_saml` produced for every database error. `docs/sso-saml.md` documents the slug form, the rules, and what to do with an existing UUID-addressed provider.

  **Nothing that works today changes, and the migration cannot fail on existing data.** `saml_configs.id` remains the primary key and remains what `sso_sessions.provider_id`, `groups.external_provider_id`, the audit log and every `/api/v1/admin/sso/saml/{id}` endpoint use; the admin CRUD routes are deliberately still UUID-only. Migration 218 adds the column nullable and backfills nothing, so every existing configuration keeps exactly its current ACS URL and has no slug until an operator sets one — which is also why the new `UNIQUE` constraint has no pre-existing rows to conflict with, and why this migration has no failure mode on a populated table (Postgres treats NULLs as distinct, so any number of configurations may stay un-slugged). Duplicates can therefore only be introduced afterwards, through the admin API, where they are refused with a 409 before anything is written. Adopting a slug is a two-step operator action with no flag day: set the slug, then repoint the IdP when convenient, because both URLs resolve the whole time. The `use_absolute_acs_url` flag and the trusted-base rule for it (`AK_EXTERNAL_URL` only, never a request header) are unchanged.

- **The first-boot admin password can be preset from an environment variable or a mounted secret file, so an unattended deployment never has to read a generated password out of the container** (#2803). On first boot the backend generated a random admin password and wrote it to `$STORAGE_PATH/admin.password`; the only way to obtain it was `docker exec`/`kubectl exec` into the running container and `cat` the file. That is a human step in the middle of what Helm, Terraform and CI-provisioned environments do unattended, and those deployments already have a secret channel of their own — so the practical workarounds were `ADMIN_PASSWORD`, which also clears `must_change_password` and hands out a permanent credential, or scraping the file out of a pod. `INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD` and `INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE` now supply that initial credential directly. `INITIAL_ADMIN_PASSWORD_FILE` is the form a real deployment should use: a value in the plain variable is readable by anything that can see the process environment (`docker inspect`, the pod spec, `/proc/<pid>/environ`), while a mounted secret file is not. The pair follows the `*_FILE` convention this codebase already uses for `DEPENDENCY_TRACK_API_KEY_FILE` (#2084), including its precedence — the direct value wins when both are set, contents are trimmed, and a blank variable, empty path, missing file or whitespace-only file all fall through to the generated password rather than seeding an empty one. The seeded account is still flagged `must_change_password`, so the setup gate stays armed and the preset value is a single-use bootstrap credential, not a standing one; `ADMIN_PASSWORD` keeps its precedence and its existing "this is the final password" semantics unchanged. The preset value is held to the same `PASSWORD_*` policy as any user-chosen password, plus the well-known-default list, and a violation aborts startup naming the rule but never the value — silently seeding a weak admin is the outcome the feature exists to prevent. It is never logged (the creation line names the variable, not the password; `ARTIFACT_KEEPER_LOG_ADMIN_PASSWORD` cannot echo it) and never written to `admin.password`, because copying it into the storage volume would spread the secret a `_FILE` mount exists to keep out of it; the credential-carrying struct deliberately has no `Debug`. Consequently the "password file missing, regenerating" recovery path is skipped while a preset is configured: no file was ever written, the plaintext is not lost, and regenerating would invalidate the credential the deployment still holds on every restart. The two DB-backed provisioning tests -- this one and #3723's -- now run on a database created and migrated for the test alone (`testing::try_isolated_pool`, #3796): `provision_admin_user` picks any local admin with `LIMIT 1`, so on the shared unit-test database, which hundreds of other tests seed admins into, neither could be made order-independent and both sat behind `#[ignore]`. The `CREATE DATABASE` costs about two seconds per test and the database is dropped when the test ends, panicking included.

  **Upgrade note — nothing changes for a deployment that does not set the new variables, and they only ever apply while the admin account is being created.** The whole mechanism sits on the create branch of `provision_admin_user`: once an admin row exists the variables are ignored, so a restart with the variable still set cannot reset a password the operator deliberately changed, and a leaked variable cannot become permanent access. `SKIP_ADMIN_PROVISIONING=true` still short-circuits ahead of everything and is unchanged, as are `AK_GUEST_ACCESS_ENABLED` and the `?fallback=local` recovery route. Setting a value too weak for the configured policy is a hard startup failure rather than a warning, so validate it in staging before rolling it out; the strictness is entirely under the operator's control through the existing `PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH` / `PASSWORD_MIN_STRENGTH` settings.

- **A CI gate now fails any new migration that would block writes on a hot table, and a runbook documents the online shapes that replace them** (#3864, #2524, PF-008 of the million-artifact epic #2516). At one million artifacts a migration that takes a table-level lock is an outage, not a deploy step, and nothing in the repository enforced the epic's `Online upgrades` release gate (upload/download SLOs within 2x baseline while a large index or backfill deploys). An audit of all 199 files in `backend/migrations/` found 47 statements across 34 of them that block writes on a table holding one row per artifact, download or scan: 27 non-concurrent index builds (`SHARE`, writers blocked for the whole build), 8 `ADD CONSTRAINT`s validated in the same statement that adds them (`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, reads blocked too), 8 whole-table backfill `UPDATE`/`DELETE`s in a single transaction and 4 `ALTER COLUMN … TYPE` rewrites — the worst single file being `176_artifacts_search_vector.sql`, which recomputes `to_tsvector` for every live artifact row in one statement and then builds a GIN index over the result. They were not careless: `sqlx::migrate!` wraps every migration in a transaction and PostgreSQL rejects `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` inside one, so until now there was no way to build an index online from a migration at all, and three files (`106`, `108`, `110`) say exactly that and hand the operator an out-of-band recipe instead. `backend/src/migration_safety.rs` is the enforcement, in the same shape as the repository's other invariant gates (`ci_test_surface`, `tests/streaming_invariant.rs`) and in the library for the same reason — `--lib` runs in every CI Rust-test job, so the gate cannot fall out of CI's `--test` allowlist. It classifies every statement in every migration against the seven blocking patterns, restricted to the 16 tables in `HOT_TABLES` whose row count tracks the workload model in #2516, and requires the result to equal a 42-entry allowlist exactly: a new offender fails the build with the statement, its lock and the online rewrite that replaces it, and a stale entry fails too, so the inventory cannot rot. Two companion checks make the escape hatch usable rather than a new footgun — `CONCURRENTLY` requires a `-- no-transaction` first line (sqlx tests it with `starts_with`, so a blank line above it silently loses the exemption and the migration fails on the operator's database), and a `-- no-transaction` migration must contain exactly **one** statement, because sqlx applies a migration with `conn.execute(&sql)` and no bind parameters, which is the simple query protocol, and PostgreSQL puts a multi-statement simple query in an implicit transaction block; measured against `postgres:16-alpine`, `DROP INDEX IF EXISTS i; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY i …` in one batch still fails with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block`. `docs/operations/online-migrations.md` (new) is the runbook: the exact lock each statement takes, the five rewrites (concurrent index build, `NOT VALID` + `VALIDATE`, `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` + `ADD CONSTRAINT … USING INDEX`, resumable keyset-batched backfill, add-column-and-swap instead of `ALTER COLUMN … TYPE`), and preflight/progress/postflight queries including finding the `pg_stat_activity` row holding the lock and the `pg_index WHERE NOT indisvalid` sweep for indexes left behind by a cancelled concurrent build.

  **Nothing changes at runtime and no migration is edited.** Migrations that have run on production databases must not be modified, so all 47 statements go on the allowlist with the reason each is grandfathered; the gate governs new migrations only. The one correction worth recording is documentary: `106`, `108` and `110` describe their non-concurrent index build as taking `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, which is `SHARE` in fact — readers are fine, writers are not — and those files are history and stay as they are. The GC and lifecycle half of PF-008 (unbounded candidate `fetch_all`s and object-store deletes held open across a database transaction, `storage_gc_service.rs`) is untouched here and remains open on #2524.

- **A Cargo Remote repository can hold newly published crate versions behind the same publish-age gate npm, PyPI and VS Code already use, closing the fast-burn Rust supply-chain window** (#3480, contributed by [@cazlo](https://github.com/cazlo) in #3483). The gate supported npm, PyPI and VS Code from upstream publish timestamps and Go from first-seen observations; Cargo was explicitly outside the capability matrix, so an administrator could not apply a cooldown to a Cargo Remote at all. The 2026-08-20 `arrayref` / `append-only-vec` compromise is the shape of the problem: the malicious `proc-macro1 1.0.107` build dependency was resolvable for 51 minutes before deletion, and `arrayref 0.3.10` for 1h27m, all of it inside a window a minimum-age policy would have covered.
