Disable it with `PATCH /api/v1/repositories/{key}` and `{"quarantine_enabled": false}`, and enable the policy on the hosted repository the content lands in instead. Nothing changes for `local` and `staging` repositories, and the global `QUARANTINE_ENABLED` / `QUARANTINE_DURATION_MINUTES` defaults are untouched.

- **On-demand curation now runs for `poetry`, `jupyter`, `yarn` and `pnpm` staging repositories, not only for `pypi` and `npm`** (#3787). The curation sweep decided whether a staging repository is ingested on demand by comparing its raw format label with `"pypi"`/`"npm"`, while the proxy seam enqueues every PyPI-handled and npm-handled package under the family label. Alias-format staging repositories therefore never had their pending rows evaluated — no attestation verification, no publisher/popularity/typosquat rules, and the rows stayed pending forever — and the publisher extractor likewise returned nothing for them. Both sites now resolve the format to its family through the same mapping the popularity source already uses (`poetry`/`jupyter` → `pypi`, `yarn`/`pnpm` → `npm`; `conda` is deliberately not PyPI), so a JupyterLab-extensions staging repository is curated exactly like a PyPI one.

- **The storage-stats recompute no longer fails the whole tick when a repository is deleted while it runs** (#3957). `recompute_all` takes a per-repository snapshot and then upserts one `repository_storage_stats` row per repository; a repository deleted in between made that insert violate `repository_storage_stats_repository_id_fkey`, so one concurrent deletion aborted the recompute and left `instance_storage_stats` stale until the next tick — and made any DB-backed test that recomputes while a parallel test drops its fixture repository intermittently fail. The upsert now selects from `repositories` instead of a bare `VALUES` list (and the per-prefix OCI root-row upsert filters the same way), so a vanished repository is skipped atomically rather than raising; skipping is correct because the prune step in the same function removes the footprint for repositories that no longer have one, and the rows cascade away with the repository itself.

- **The per-boot OIDC env reconcile keeps `attribute_mapping` keys the `OIDC_*` environment never set, instead of erasing them on every restart** (#3507). The reconcile applied the handful of keys it derives from `OIDC_*` with wholesale-replace semantics, so `groups_claim`, `username_claim` and `email_claim` set through `PUT /api/v1/admin/sso/oidc/{id}` were discarded on the next boot with nothing in the log — the documented remedy for an IdP that publishes group membership under a non-default claim name (GitLab's `groups_direct`) silently did not survive a redeploy. The reconcile now builds a *complete* desired mapping with explicit ownership: a key the environment currently supplies is written, a key the environment supplied on an earlier boot and no longer supplies is removed (so deleting a variable still undoes it), and a key the environment never set is preserved. Which keys the environment last owned is recorded in the mapping itself under `env_owned_keys`, bounded to the keys the bootstrap can actually derive, so a hand-edited value cannot turn it into a delete list for admin-only keys such as `fetch_userinfo_groups`. Whenever the reconcile does replace or remove a stored value for a key it owns, it now logs a WARN naming the key and both values, so a discard is never silent.

  `OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP` is deliberately exempt and stays env-definitive exactly as #3420/#3439 made it: `admin_group` is owned by the environment whether or not the variable is set and whether or not the row carries an ownership record, so unsetting the variable and redeploying still revokes group-based admin elevation — an elevation rule must not outlive the variable that granted it, not even for one boot.

  **Upgrade note.** Rows written before this change carry no ownership record, so the first boot after upgrading treats the environment as owning only what it currently sets. A `groups_claim`/`username_claim`/`email_claim`/`redirect_uri` value that used to be reset on every boot now persists instead: if you were relying on the reset to clear a stale value, set the matching `OIDC_*` variable to the value you want (or unset it once *after* this release, which records the removal). Provider rows the environment manages also gain an `env_owned_keys` array in `attribute_mapping`, visible in `GET /api/v1/admin/sso/oidc`; it is reconcile bookkeeping, not a claim mapping, and is rewritten on every boot.

- **Migrated Docker/OCI manifests are recorded exactly as a native `docker push` records them, and re-running a migration repairs a repository imported before the fix** (#3533, #3536). The importer wrote a Docker/OCI manifest's `artifacts` row through the version-less generic fallback — path `<repo_key>/<image>/<tag>/manifest.json`, name `manifest`, no version, `application/octet-stream` — plus one spurious row per layer/config blob, so the UI's flat listing and docker-tags panel, the generic download endpoint and search all rendered a migrated image differently from a pushed one, and a migrated multi-arch child manifest enumerated as its own item was counted twice by the catalog size sum. The manifest row is now written by the same `upsert_manifest_artifact` the live manifest-PUT path and the referenced-content walk use (`v2/<image>/manifests/<reference>`, `<image>:<reference>`, the reference as version, the body's own media type, config + layer sizes), blobs produce no `artifacts` row at all (they live in `oci_blobs`, as on push), and every format the OCI handler serves (`podman`, `buildx`, `oras`, `wasm_oci`, `helm_oci`) takes this path, not only `docker`/`oci`. A repository migrated before this fix is repaired by re-running the migration: a legacy-shaped row no longer counts as a duplicate of the canonical one, and it is soft-deleted (the ordinary artifact delete, so the usage ledger and GC follow) when the canonical row lands, together with the per-blob rows. A source export that lists two different manifests for one `<image>:<reference>` — Artifactory's `manifest.json` and `list.manifest.json` under one tag folder — now fails that item naming both source paths and digests instead of letting the last one silently win the tag, and an over-long manifest `mediaType` falls back to the canonical media type for the manifest's class instead of aborting the item with a database error. Non-OCI formats are untouched: their stored content type stays `application/octet-stream`, as before. Contributed by @xinnj.

- **A proxied multi-arch tag's packages-catalog size is the image size, not 0 or a few kilobytes of JSON** (#3601). An image index carries no `config` or `layers` of its own, so its size is the sum over the child manifests recorded for it. On a `docker push` the children are uploaded first and that sum is meaningful; on a **proxy** the order is reversed -- the index is fetched by tag and each platform's manifest by digest afterwards -- so the sum the index's own catalog write could compute was over nothing, and `library/alpine:3.19` pulled through a Remote repository was listed at `0` bytes. Nothing corrected it later: a warm proxy cache serves the tag without re-entering the caching path, so the row only moved once the cached tag expired, and even then the sum was wrong in kind -- the `artifacts` rows written for a proxied child manifest recorded the **manifest body length** rather than `config.size + layers[].size`, which is a few kilobytes for an image that is tens of megabytes. Proxied manifest rows now record the image size, the same meaning the push path (`upsert_manifest_artifact`) and the migration importer (#3536) already record and the meaning both readers of that column want (`index_child_artifact_size_sum`, and `fetch_index_child_sizes` behind the Docker tags panel's `total_size_bytes`); and recording a proxied child now re-sizes the catalog row of any parent index that references it, so the tag converges on the full image size as the platforms arrive. Both fetch orders are covered -- children after the index (re-sized from the child's side) and children already cached when the index is recorded (summed by the index's own write) -- and they agree. The push path's semantics are unchanged: a hosted single-arch push still records `config.size + layers[].size` exactly.

  **Upgrade note -- this changes numbers that are already displayed, and only for images pulled through a Remote repository after the upgrade.** There is no backfill: a tag sitting in a warm proxy cache keeps its existing row until the cached tag expires and is re-fetched, or until its platform manifests are pulled again. The re-sizing is deliberately raise-only and never creates a catalog row, so a child manifest cannot publish an index the scan gate has not already agreed to advertise (#3611) and a tag that has since moved to another manifest is not re-sized from the old one's children. `artifacts.size_bytes` for a proxied manifest row is now the aggregate image size rather than the body length, which is what every other writer of that column already means and what the storage-accounting exclusion for `oci-manifests/%` keys already assumes (#3286); a Remote repository with a configured quota therefore measures a cached image at its real weight instead of at the size of its manifest JSON.

- **The keyless CI token exchange no longer needs the admin password to bootstrap, and the token it mints no longer outlives the assertion it was bought with** (#3548, #3820). `POST /api/v1/auth/ci/token` required a `provider_id` in the request body — the UUID of a `ci_oidc_providers` row, server-generated by `gen_random_uuid()` and published by exactly one endpoint, the admin-only `GET /api/v1/admin/ci-oidc`. A pipeline therefore had to log in as `admin` and read the UUID back out before it could perform the exchange, so the "no static secrets" flow began by using the most privileged credential in the system. Baking the UUID into CI configuration works only for a long-lived instance; an ephemeral or preview environment creates the provider row with the environment and has nothing to bake. The provider is now resolved from the assertion itself: the `iss` claim is read out of the **unverified** token, matched (ignoring a trailing slash, the same normalisation the discovery fetch already applies) against the `issuer_url` of the enabled `ci_oidc_providers` rows, and the unchanged full verification — JWKS signature, `aud`, exact `iss`, then the identity-mapping claim filters — runs against the row that matched. Nothing is trusted from the peeked claims; a forged `iss` selects a provider whose JWKS then refuses the signature, which is the same answer as before. Separately, the minted access token was stamped with the full configured `JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN_EXPIRY_MINUTES` (30 minutes by default) no matter how little life the presented assertion had left. This was the one credential-exchange arm #3625 left uncapped — Conan `users/authenticate` and all three OCI `/v2/token` arms cap at the presented credential's expiry — and the argument for leaving it out depended on a downstream endpoint's behaviour (the minted token is not accepted as a CI OIDC assertion, so there is no renewal loop) rather than on this endpoint's own reasoning. It now caps through the same `cap_access_expiry` path, so every arm that exchanges a presented credential is monotonically non-increasing in lifetime for the same stated reason.

  `provider_id` is still accepted, so a caller written against the old shape keeps working unchanged. It is now optional (and the body as a whole is optional — send no body at all), it is checked against the assertion's `iss` and a disagreement is a `400` that names both issuers rather than the verifier's generic "validation failed", and it is the documented answer when an instance runs two enabled providers on one issuer. `ci_oidc_providers` has no `UNIQUE` constraint on `issuer_url`, so that is possible: the tie is broken on the audience the assertion declares, and if that still leaves a choice the request is refused with a `400` asking for `provider_id` instead of guessing which configuration an operator meant. A disabled provider is invisible to issuer resolution, and an issuer nobody has configured is a `404`. A body that was *sent* and is malformed is a `400`, not a silently dropped `provider_id`.

  **Upgrade note — no request that worked before now fails, but a CI token can come back shorter-lived.** The `provider_id` override keeps the pre-existing request shape valid; the only requests whose status changes were already failing (a `provider_id` naming a provider the assertion was not issued for returned `401` from the verifier and now returns `400` before it). The expiry cap is the visible change: CI assertions are deliberately short-lived — GitLab `id_tokens` and GitHub Actions OIDC tokens are commonly valid for five to fifteen minutes — so where the exchange used to return a 30-minute bearer it now returns one expiring with the assertion. `expires_in` has always reported the real lifetime and still does, so a client that honours it needs no change; a pipeline that hard-codes a renewal interval instead should re-exchange on `expires_in`. Re-exchanging is the fix in every case, and it is what the endpoint's own documentation already tells a pipeline running longer than one token's window to do.

- **A Go virtual repository's `@v/list` now collates every member the caller may read, so a hosted fork no longer erases the upstream's version history** (#833, #3857). Publishing one hotfix build of a module to a hosted member of a virtual Go repository made every upstream version of that module disappear from `GET /go/{repo}/{module}/@v/list`: the listing unioned the non-Remote members' artifact rows and, if that union was non-empty, returned it *without consulting the Remote members at all*. That is strictly worse than first-hit-by-priority — it was local-absolute — and it broke exactly the workflow the request describes, publishing a temporary fork of an upstream library through the coordinate developers already resolve. It also left the repository self-contradictory: `.info`, `.mod` and `.zip` walk every member and already fell through to a Remote member for a module a hosted member owns, so the document said one thing and the endpoint it indexes served another. `@v/list` is now the union over the members the caller may read — the non-Remote members' rows, then each Remote member's upstream list — deduplicated keeping the first occurrence, in the order the resolver walks them.

  **This widens the listing, not what the repository serves.** Every version now listed was already downloadable through the same virtual repository; `.info`, `.mod`, `.zip` and `@latest` are untouched and stay first-hit, because each is a single document and two members cannot both supply one file. That is also why this is not a dependency-confusion widening of the kind PyPI's `tracks` declaration (#1600) exists to prevent: no bytes become reachable that were not reachable before. Precedence is unchanged and is where the hotfix actually wins — a version carried by BOTH a hosted member and the upstream still resolves to the hosted member's bytes, because the resolvers consult member artifact rows before falling through to a Remote member. Member visibility is unchanged and enforced: the member set comes from the same caller-authorized helper the listing already used (#3323), resolved once and reused for both halves, so a member the caller cannot read contributes no versions and the collated document is no existence oracle over it.

  Remote members are fanned out concurrently in priority-ordered batches of at most 16, matching the maven and `collect_virtual_metadata` merges, so a cold listing costs roughly the slowest member per batch rather than the sum. **A member that errors, times out, or returns a body this build cannot decode is skipped and logged; the listing is served from the members that answered.** One dead remote taking a whole listing down would be worse than the feature is worth. The skip cannot be reported in the response — `@v/list` is a bare newline-separated list and the `go` toolchain reads every non-empty line as a version, so there is no comment syntax to carry a warning — and the server log naming the member and module is the only channel. Each Remote member's contribution is still age-gate filtered under that member's own policy (#2264).

  **Upgrade note — no configuration, and one cosmetic difference.** This is the same unflagged repair npm received for the identical defect (#2844): collated listings are already the default for npm, maven, PyPI, cargo, conda, cran, helm, hex, rubygems, conan, NuGet, composer, Swift and OCI tags, and Go was the outlier, so no `collation_mode` switch was added for it alone. The change is additive — every version listed before is still listed, and nothing a `go get` previously resolved stops resolving. The one observable difference is that a virtual with a single Remote member now serves the rebuilt document without the upstream's trailing newline, matching what the same endpoint already served for a hosted member; the `go` client skips blank lines and is indifferent. Formats whose listing is a *signed* document — Alpine's `APKINDEX.tar.gz`, Debian's `Release`/`Packages` — are deliberately still first-hit, since merging them invalidates the upstream signature and needs a re-signing strategy; `pub` and HuggingFace listings are likewise unchanged.

- **VS Code gallery gateway: scan-on-proxy now actually gates VSIX delivery, the exact-version age-gate decision is memoised, and upstream gallery documents are parsed leniently** (#3254, #3255, #3256). Follow-ups from the review of the Open VSX gateway (#3253), none of them a regression that PR introduced. `ScanConfigService::is_proxy_scan_enabled` is per-repository and format-agnostic, but `proxy_gallery_asset` never consulted it, so an operator who enabled scan-on-proxy for a `vscode` remote saw the toggle accepted and nothing happen — on the highest-consequence artifact this gateway serves, since a VSIX executes inside the developer's editor with filesystem access. The extension package now goes through the same buffer → digest → `gate_proxy_scan_serve` severity gate npm (`serve_tarball`) and PyPI (`serve_file`) use, while the gallery's display assets (icon, manifest, details/README, changelog) stay on the streaming path: they are rendered, never executed, and buffering each of them would cost a digest and a verdict lookup per extension tile for no security value. On the availability side, every gated asset serve issued its own uncached `extensionquery` POST, so one extension page cost five identical upstream queries — collapsed to one by a 60-second memo of the ALLOW decision keyed on `(repository, package, version, targetPlatform)`, invalidated on every age-gate policy write and every review approve/reject/reopen. Only the ALLOW outcome is memoised: a withheld coordinate must keep reaching the shared seam, which is what records the review request and what makes a reopened review re-block on the very next pull, so the "no warm-cache bypass" ordering and its test are unchanged. The gallery's share of the shared 1 GiB buffered-metadata budget drops from an assumed 32× the wire cap to a documented 6× (wire buffer + parsed `serde_json` tree + serialized response), which takes one in-flight query from 64 MiB to 12 MiB and the concurrent-query ceiling from 16 to 85, and the reservation is now bounded by a 5-second `tokio::time::timeout` that sheds 503 + `Retry-After` rather than queueing — gallery reads are reachable anonymously on a public Remote and are not behind the rate limiter, so an unbounded wait made them a queueing surface for npm packuments, PyPI simple indexes, Debian `Packages` and RPM `repomd` alike. `gallery_upstream`'s `SELECT is_public` is resolved once per request and threaded through the sub-queries instead of re-running on each upstream round-trip. Finally, three parsing gaps: a request `targetPlatform` must now be one of VS Code's documented values (400 otherwise) so one artifact cannot occupy an unbounded family of permanently-immutable cache entries, while an upstream document keeps the looser charset check so a platform Open VSX adds before AK knows about it does not 502 a whole query; an extension carrying no `versions` array is a legitimate flag-conditional shape rather than a malformed document, and the age-gate filter now distinguishes "had no versions array" (kept) from "all versions filtered out" (dropped); a version-skeleton entry missing its `version` field is skipped instead of failing the whole document, so one nonconforming sibling can no longer 404 a legitimate, correctly-aged extension. `TotalCount` is now left alone — it is a cross-page total, so subtracting a page-local removal count was an approximation by construction and `saturating_sub` turned it into a wrong answer for adapters that report the page length there; a slightly-high total is how every filtered gallery behaves and what clients already tolerate.

  **Upgrade note — scan-on-proxy now actually gates VSIX delivery on `vscode` remotes.** A repository that already has `scan_on_proxy` enabled was silently serving proxied extension packages unscanned; after upgrading, those pulls are gated. Under the default `fail_open` action a package with no verdict yet is served with a loud `X-AK-Scan: pending` header while the scan runs, and a package with a cached vulnerable verdict is refused with 403; under `fail_closed`, an inconclusive scan — including a VSIX over the 200 MiB proxy-scan byte cap — answers 423 rather than serving unscanned bytes. The gated path is buffered rather than streamed, so a large extension is held in memory for the length of the scan; repositories that have not enabled scan-on-proxy are untouched and keep streaming exactly as before. The other consequence to know about is the new 400 on an unrecognised `targetPlatform`: a client asking for a platform outside VS Code's documented set (or a non-canonical spelling such as `LINUX-X64`, which is now normalised rather than given its own cache entry) gets a 400 instead of a proxied fetch.

- **#3556: RPM, conda, OCI inline-scan and generic-Remote proxy fetches now classify their cache entries against the repository's real format, so immutable content stops expiring every five minutes.** `proxy_helpers::build_remote_repo` synthesizes the upstream `Repository` a proxy fetch runs against and hardcodes `RepositoryFormat::Generic`, which has no `cache_classifier` arm — so every path reaching it fell to the conservative 5-minute mutable default, including content the real format's classifier marks `Immutable`. A version-pinned `.rpm`, a createrepo `repodata/<sha256>-primary.xml.gz`, a `.conda`/`.tar.bz2` package, a digest-addressed layer staged for the inline image scan, and any format's artifact fetched through the generic `/download/*path` route were therefore re-fetched from upstream forever. Two format-carrying helper siblings were added (`proxy_fetch_streaming_with_disposition_and_format`, `proxy_fetch_capped_with_format`) and the five sites moved onto them, each after checking that the path the cache is actually keyed on is the format-relative coordinate that format's classifier rules were written against. The generic download route resolves the repository's own format rather than taking a constant, and deliberately keeps the conservative classification when a routing rule has rewritten the path — a rewritten path is an upstream shape, not a format coordinate, and misclassifying a mutable path as immutable serves a stale body forever (`cache_classifier::evaluate` short-circuits `Immutable` without consulting `expires_at`), while the opposite mistake only costs one revalidation per TTL window. Each site gained a regression test that reads the cache sidecar and asserts the TTL that was WRITTEN — a classifier-level test passes with this bug fully intact — alongside a mutable negative control in the same fixture (`repomd.xml`, a conda channel document, a tag manifest, `maven-metadata.xml`). Continues #2312/#3206 (OCI) and #3459 (Maven/Gradle/sbt).

- **#3749: an upstream `410 Gone` during proxy revalidation is now negative-cached like a 404 instead of pinning the stale copy forever.** `validate_upstream_status` mapped 410 to `BadGateway`, a transient class, and the refill path's stale-if-error arm excludes only 404 — so when a stale entry was revalidated and the upstream answered 410 to both the conditional `HEAD` and the refill `GET`, the deleted object kept being served from cache indefinitely, with no TTL to age out of and no revalidation that could ever correct it, while the identical 404 case surfaced within the negative-cache TTL. 410 now joins 404 in the shared status classifier, so a gone upstream object is negative-cached and stops being served after `NEGATIVE_CACHE_TTL_SECS`. Found during the #3747 audit.

- **#3836: the OCI virtual-repository negative cache no longer records a throttled or failing upstream as "this does not exist".** `write_negative_cache` on the proxy path is gated on `AppError::NotFound`, so only a definitive upstream 404 becomes a negative — the invariant #3756/#3760 established after the revalidation incident. The virtual resolution path had no such gate: any empty member walk was cached, so a member upstream answering 429 or 5xx made the blob or manifest unresolvable for the whole negative window, and #3527 could only contain the damage by clamping the configurable TTL. The upstream status is now threaded out of `try_upstream_fetch_with_accept` (and read from the member blob fetch) to the resolvers, which record a negative only when every member gave a definitive answer. A definitive 404 is still negative-cached, so the fan-out bound #1348 added is unchanged.

- **`npm audit signatures` sent every attestation lookup upstream, every time** (#3764). `npm audit signatures`, and any `npm install` that checks provenance, asks the registry one question per resolved package version — `GET /npm/{repo}/-/npm/v1/attestations/{pkg}@{ver}` — and almost no published npm version carries a provenance attestation, so the upstream registry answers `404` to nearly all of them. Relaying that `404` is correct and unchanged: it is the registry's own answer, and an Artifact Keeper that invented attestations would be the real bug. What was wrong is that the answer was never memoised. `npm_meta_upstream_bytes`, which backs the whole `/-/` meta namespace for Remote and Virtual repositories, issued an unconditional upstream `GET` on every call with no cache read, no cache write and no TTL — so a CI fleet re-resolving one dependency graph asked the same few thousand distinct questions tens of thousands of times a day, each repeat also holding a slot against `GLOBAL_MAX_CONCURRENCY` and paying the repo-resolve and permission queries in front of it. In one observed day of proxy traffic these lookups were 17.8% of all requests and 94% of all 404s, at ~67 identical questions per distinct URI; caching them removes ~98.5% of those upstream round trips at a 24-hour TTL and ~88.8% at one hour. A negative cache now sits in front of that fetch, and its scope is deliberately narrow on five axes, because the `/-/` namespace as a whole is not cacheable. It applies to **`/-/npm/v1/attestations/*` and nothing else** — `/-/whoami` and `/-/npm/v1/user` are per-principal, `/-/v1/search` is query-dependent and the audit endpoints are request-body dependent, so caching the meta namespace wholesale would be a security bug rather than an optimisation. It stores **negative answers only** (`404`, `410`), which npm's prohibition on republishing a version makes stable facts; a `200` is a real provenance bundle and is never stored, so an attestation published after the first lookup is served the moment upstream has it, and `401`/`403`/`429`/`5xx` are credential-dependent or transient and would turn a blip into a TTL-long outage. It is keyed on the **answering member repository**, not the repository named in the URL: a Virtual repo resolves `/-/*` against the members this caller is authorized to read (#3323), so the authorization walk still runs on every request and can only reach entries for members the caller may use, while two Virtual repos sharing a member correctly share one entry — the upstream URL is folded into the key as well, so repointing a repository's upstream is never answered from the previous upstream's entry. It **steps aside entirely when a repository's npm scope policy is active**, because an active policy rewrites meta bodies per repository (#2424, #2551) and a cached body would have to be policy-specific rather than merely policy-keyed; that path is byte-for-byte unchanged. And it stores **status and body together**, so a cached `404` replays as a `404` rather than as an empty `200`, which npm treats very differently. The cache is in-process and per-replica with no invalidation path, so a wrong entry cannot be flushed short of a process restart and would be visible on one replica only — which is why the default window is an hour rather than a day. Entry count and per-body size are both capped, so neither a large dependency graph nor a broken upstream's error page can grow it without bound. `NPM_ATTESTATION_NEGATIVE_CACHE_TTL_SECS` (default 3600) bounds how long an attestation added after publish stays invisible. An hour rather than a day because this cache fronts *any* upstream, not just registry.npmjs.org: a lazily-warming Verdaccio/Nexus/Artifactory mirror answers `404` for a package it has simply not fetched yet, and holding that for a day would fail a provenance-gated pipeline with no lever to clear it — the failure teams answer by switching the gate off. An hour keeps ~88.8% of the saved round trips against ~98.5% for a day. Raise it if you proxy npm directly, and `NPM_ATTESTATION_NEGATIVE_CACHE_ENABLED=false` — or a zero TTL — turns it off. A new `ak_npm_attestation_cache_lookups_total{repository,result}` counter reports `hit`, `miss_stored`, `miss_uncacheable` and `error`; it is deliberately separate from `ak_proxy_cache_lookups_total`, whose every call site is the artifact proxy cache, so existing dashboards keep measuring what they measured before. This has been the behaviour since the `/-/` meta route was introduced in #1885 (first released in 1.2.1); before that, attestation requests were not proxied at all.

- **Concurrent Maven uploads of the same path no longer surface a UNIQUE-constraint violation as a `500`** (#3587). The upload handler checked for an existing row and then `INSERT`ed, so under upload pressure two requests for one path could both observe no row and both insert; the loser's `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "artifacts_repository_id_path_key"` reached the client as `500 Internal Server Error` on a perfectly ordinary SNAPSHOT republish. The insert is now an `ON CONFLICT (repository_id, path) DO UPDATE` upsert, refreshing sha1/md5 in lockstep with sha256 exactly as the shared `ArtifactService` upload path already did, and the preflight hard-`DELETE` that made the window wider is gone. A coordinate the classifier calls immutable is not silently overwritten by the upsert: the update is conditional, so a racing second publisher of a release coordinate gets the same `409` the duplicate check would have given it (#3839).

- **JetBrains multipart plugin publishes no longer corrupt the plugin zip** (#3848). `extract_plugin_from_multipart` parsed the envelope by converting the whole body with `String::from_utf8_lossy` and then indexing the *original* byte slice with offsets taken from that copy. A plugin is a zip, so the body is never valid UTF-8: every invalid sequence becomes a three-byte U+FFFD, shifting every later offset, and for an invalid-UTF-8 body the `Cow` is a separate allocation whose pointers bear no relation to the body at all. In practice a real (binary) plugin drove the offsets past the end of the body and **panicked** the request; where it did not, the fallback stored the *lossy* bytes and the SHA-256 was computed over that corruption, so nothing detected it at upload, at download, or in any integrity check. Parsing is now delegated to `multer`, which works on bytes end to end — the shape `nuget.rs` and `swift.rs` (#3595 / #3847) already use — bounded by `max_upload_size_bytes`, and a missing `boundary=`, a missing or duplicated `file`/`plugin` part, or a truncated body is a `400` rather than a silent partial store. The raw-upload path (`X-Plugin-Name` / `X-Plugin-Version`) was never affected. **Plugins already published through the multipart path are corrupt on disk and cannot be repaired from what was stored — they must be republished.**

- **An authenticated Terraform provider mirror now hands Terraform ticketed archive URLs, so `terraform init` no longer fails with `401` at the download step** (#3588). Terraform's Network Mirror Protocol states that Terraform does **not** send the configured credentials when it retrieves the archives whose URLs appear in the "list available installation packages" response, and tells a mirror that must protect those archives to provide "cryptographically secure, user-specific, and time-limited URLs" instead. Artifact Keeper advertised a bare relative URL, so `index.json` and `<version>.json` succeeded with credentials and the archive `GET` that followed them was refused. The `<version>.json` document now carries a single-use download ticket per platform, minted for the caller who fetched the document, bound to exactly that archive path and valid for ten minutes — the existing `?ticket=` credential the format routes already accept for reads. An anonymous caller reading a public mirror still gets the plain relative URL, unchanged.

- **The web UI's artifact upload is no longer refused with `403 ... must send the X-Requested-With header`** (#3592). The #3065 CSRF contract accepted exactly one proof that a cookie-authenticated mutation came from our own origin — the `X-Requested-With` header — and the web UI's upload posts `multipart/form-data` through `fetch()` without it, so the one operation the upload tab exists to perform was refused and the error told the user to switch to an API token. The contract now also accepts the browser's own `Sec-Fetch-Site: same-origin` (or `none`) declaration. That is a forbidden request header: only the user agent sets it and page script cannot override it, so it proves exactly what the custom header proves. Nothing is weakened — a `cross-site` post (the vector the contract exists to stop), a `same-site` sibling origin, and a browser that sends no Fetch Metadata at all must all still present `X-Requested-With`, and token/Basic-authenticated clients were never in scope.

- **A Maven PUT now takes snapshot mutability from `cache_classifier`, so a resolved unique snapshot can no longer be silently overwritten** (#3839). The native Maven upload path decided for itself whether a coordinate is mutable, keying on `coords.version.contains("SNAPSHOT")`, while `classify_maven` deliberately classifies a *resolved unique* snapshot leaf (`probe-6.0-20260827.132833-10.jar`) as `Immutable` and matches the `-SNAPSHOT` token on the path **component** rather than as a substring. The two halves of the system therefore disagreed twice over: a timestamped snapshot artifact — a filename that names exactly one deployment, which a build may already have resolved and pinned — could be replaced with different bytes and got `201`, and a version that merely *contains* the token (`1.0-SNAPSHOT-rc1`) was a snapshot to the handler and a release to the classifier. The handler now asks the classifier (`maven_coordinate_is_republishable`, sharing the component-wise SNAPSHOT test of #3554 and the unique-snapshot exemption of #3459) and answers `409 Conflict` for an immutable coordinate. The #3295 behaviour is preserved exactly: a **non-unique** snapshot (`app-1.0-SNAPSHOT.jar`, or an Ivy-layout `mylib.jar` under a `-SNAPSHOT` directory) is still republished in place.

- **`HEAD` on an uncached remote OCI blob larger than 8 MiB reported 404 while the matching `GET` returned 200** (#3605). The remote-blob `HEAD` path ran its upstream fetch through the buffered metadata helper, whose 8 MiB cap made any larger uncached layer look absent — so clients that head-before-pull (`skopeo`, `containerd`) saw the blob as missing while the same request as a `GET` streamed it fine. The `HEAD` path now reuses the streaming upstream fetch the `GET` path already uses and answers with the headers that fetch would advertise (`Content-Length`, `Docker-Content-Digest`, content coding) and an empty body; the upstream read is lazy and never polled, so `HEAD` transfers nothing. A regression test drives a 9 MiB uncached layer through `handle_head_blob` against a direct remote repository and asserts 200 + headers + empty body, the exact shape that previously 404'd.

- **A Nexus migration walks its source once instead of re-walking it per page, and a finished migration job's counters and report now describe what it really did** (#3590, #3512). `NexusClient::list_artifacts` started from `continuationToken = None` on every call, so serving the page at `offset` re-fetched pages `1..N` to get there: N pages cost N(N+1)/2 upstream requests, every earlier component was re-read on every page, and the whole migration was O(n²) in the number of components -- which is why a repository roughly 2.2x larger took roughly 14x longer, and why a large, actively-written repository could look indistinguishable from a hang while the worker did a great deal of real, invisible work. The client now keeps a continuation-token cursor per repository, so the forward walk the migration worker performs costs one request per upstream page; a caller that seeks to an arbitrary offset still gets the documented slice, by walking and discarding what precedes it, and the Artifactory client is untouched. A run that enumerated repositories but moved no per-item counter at all -- the "false-positive clean completion" that reported `status: completed`, `failed_items: 0` and `completed_items: 0` after migrating nothing -- now records a warning in `error_summary`, which `GET /api/v1/migrations/{id}` already returns, alongside a WARN log; `migration_jobs.status` gains no new value, because migration 020's CHECK constraint admits none and `completed_with_errors` (migration 207) already means something else. Separately, the migration report's `total_bytes_transferred` is now summed from `migration_items` -- the same cumulative source as the report's item counts -- instead of `migration_jobs.transferred_bytes`, which the worker publishes per run: a 60-artifact job paused and resumed reported `migrated: 60` next to the byte total of only the 43 artifacts its second run moved. A dry run, which writes no `migration_items`, now reports 0 bytes alongside the 0 item counts it already reported, rather than being the one field in the report describing hypothetical work. The skip path's counters and the enumerated `total_items` denominator (#3378, #3510) already reached the job row and the SSE stream, so a re-run of already-migrated content moves `skipped_items` as the reporter expected; `total_items` is a running total published per listing page, exact only once enumeration ends, and that is now documented on the field itself. Thanks to @ZVilusinsky, whose end-to-end evaluation write-up of Artifact Keeper as a Nexus replacement diagnosed both root causes from the source and measured the super-linear runtime.

- **A tagged image pulled through an OCI Virtual repository never reached the packages catalog, for the request shape every Docker client actually issues** (#3602). #3731 gave the Virtual path the resolving member's own manifest caching, so a pull through a Virtual leaves the member's `oci_tags` row, its `manifest_blob_refs` and its `artifacts` rows -- but the catalog row still landed only when the bytes came from upstream on the `GET` itself. Docker and containerd pull a tag as `HEAD /manifests/<tag>` followed by `GET /manifests/<digest>`, and in that shape the `HEAD` is the cold fetch and the `GET` is a local hit on the member, so the catalog write never ran: `docker pull <host>/<virtual>/library/redis:7.2-alpine` succeeded, the member showed the image in the repository artifact listing, and the Packages page and `/v2/_catalog` stayed empty -- exactly the one-Virtual-over-several-Remotes topology #3441 was reported against. It is the same gap #3707 closed on the direct Remote path, which the Virtual arm never got. A `GET` by digest through a Virtual whose resolving member is a Remote now indexes every tag that member's `oci_tags` maps to the digest, in the member's context and on the serve side of the scan gate, exactly as the direct Remote arm orders it. Ownership is unchanged and deliberate: the cache belongs to the resolving MEMBER -- where the blobs already land, where a direct pull of that member would have cached it, and where every other virtual proxy path puts it (`resolve_virtual_download` fetches a Remote member through the member's own repository record) -- so the Virtual still stores nothing of its own and the same image reachable through several Virtuals produces one set of rows, not one per Virtual. The write is the idempotent upsert the direct path already performs (`artifacts` is `UNIQUE(repository_id, path)`, `packages` `UNIQUE(repository_id, name)`), so a later direct pull of the member converges on the rows the Virtual wrote instead of duplicating them, and members stay filtered by what the caller may read (#3163) -- nothing is published on behalf of a member the caller could not have pulled from directly. A bare `HEAD` still publishes nothing (#3611), a digest with no tag row (`docker pull image@sha256:...`, a multi-arch index's child manifests) still indexes nothing, and hosted members are unchanged. No backfill: an image already pulled through a Virtual appears in the catalog after its next pull once the member's cached tag has been re-resolved, or immediately on the next `GET` by digest. A multi-arch index's catalog row is sized exactly as the direct path sizes it, which is still the lower bound #3601 tracks; this change neither improves nor worsens it.

- **A Debian remote repository now streams `.deb` package content published under `dists/`, instead of 502ing past the 128 MiB buffered-metadata ceiling** (#3596). Not every APT repository uses the `pool/` layout: Proxmox and other vendor mirrors publish binaries next to their index, at `dists/{dist}/{component}/binary-{arch}/{pkg}.deb`. Those requests land on the Debian proxy's `dists/` catch-all, which is written for index documents — it reads the whole body into memory so the index can be parsed and verified against the signed `Release`, bounded at `LARGE_METADATA_MAX_BYTES` (128 MiB) so a hostile upstream cannot OOM the pod. A package larger than that ceiling aborted the buffered read and surfaced as `502 Bad Gateway`, which `apt` reports as a generic connection failure after its own retries; the reporter hit it on a ~220 MiB `pve-firmware`. The catch-all now makes the metadata-vs-content decision explicitly (`dists_path_is_package_content`: a `.deb`, `.udeb` or `.ddeb` leaf is content, everything else is an index) and routes content onto the same streaming primitive the `pool/` download, Cargo crates, npm tarballs and OCI layers already use, so the body is teed to the client and the proxy cache without ever being resident. The ceiling is deliberately NOT raised — that would only move the failure, at 128 MiB+ of heap per concurrent download. Everything ahead of the fetch is unchanged: the #2460 distribution/component/architecture allowlist, the by-hash architecture cross-check, epoch invalidation, and the cache key, so a package already cached by the buffered path stays addressable and the second client is still served warm from cache. Index files (`Packages*`, `Sources*`, `Translation-*`, `Contents-*`, dep11, `by-hash/`) keep the bounded buffered path they need.

  **Upgrade note — no configuration change, and no cache invalidation is required.** Virtual Debian repositories are not covered: their `dists/` walk (`try_virtual_dists`) still buffers at the same ceiling, because it has to try members in priority order and fall through on a 404; a virtual repository over a member using this layout still 502s for an oversized package and is tracked separately. `Range` requests are unchanged — the Debian proxy has never honoured them for cached or uncached content, so an `apt` ranged retry gets a full `200` and restarts the transfer rather than resuming it.

- **A collection published to a hosted Ansible repository now advertises the dependency map from its own `MANIFEST.json`** (#3600). `ansible-galaxy collection publish` sends a multipart body of `file` and `sha256` and nothing else, and the upload path populated `collection_json` only from an optional `collection`/`metadata` part that the native client never sends, so every natively-published collection stored `collection_json: null`. `GET /api/v3/collections/{ns}/{name}/versions/{version}/` reads its dependency map from `collection_json.dependencies` and therefore reported `"dependencies": {}` -- "declares no dependencies" -- for every one of them, so `ansible-galaxy collection install` silently resolved none of a hosted collection's transitive dependencies. The upload path now reads `MANIFEST.json`'s `collection_info` out of the staged tarball before it is streamed to storage and records it as `collection_json`, which also captures the `description`, `license`, `tags`, `repository` and `authors` the same object carries; an optional client-sent metadata part still overlays the keys it actually provides, so those clients are unaffected. The read is bounded through `util::bounded_archive` (total decompressed-byte budget, entry-count cap, and a 1 MiB per-entry cap for the manifest) because it decodes an attacker-supplied archive on the upload path, and it is best-effort: an unreadable archive, an absent `MANIFEST.json`, or a malformed manifest is logged and the publish proceeds, since the upload contract has never required a well-formed collection archive. Remote repositories are unaffected -- their dependency map comes from the upstream document and was already carried across faithfully.

  **Upgrade note: collections published before this release keep the empty dependency map.** The fix records metadata at publish time and does not rewrite existing rows, so a collection that needs its dependencies advertised must be re-published (the tarballs are still in storage, so a backfill that re-reads `MANIFEST.json` for existing rows is possible and is filed separately).

- **Listing an S3 bucket no longer fails wholesale when the endpoint returns a list body the S3 client cannot parse, which unbroke browse, the storage tree and proxy-cache enumeration on Alibaba Cloud OSS** (#3593). Against an `*.aliyuncs.com` endpoint every LIST came back `Generic S3 error: Got invalid list response: unexpected \`Event::Eof\``: OSS's `ListObjectsV2` body is valid XML that `object_store` 0.13's strict `serde` deserialiser rejects, and one rejected page fails the whole listing. Direct GET/PUT were unaffected, so an OSS-backed deployment served artifacts correctly while the web UI showed every repository as empty (`storage/tree`, `/api/v1/tree` and the cached-artifact half of the artifact list all return zero children), proxy repositories could not see their own cache and refetched upstream on every request, and a completed migration looked like it had imported nothing. There is no released `object_store` to upgrade to -- 0.14.2 is current and carries no OSS handling -- so `S3Backend::list` now parses the response itself when the crate cannot: an `ObjectStore` LIST that fails with that error shape is retried as a hand-rolled `ListObjectsV2` request over the same REST API, read by a tolerant event-walking parser that ignores the XML declaration, accepts elements in any order, tolerates unknown siblings, strips namespace prefixes and recovers keys from a body that is outright truncated. The request is built the same way the existing ranged `UploadPartCopy` is (#3164) -- URL shape from `object_store`'s own presigner so path-style, virtual-hosted and custom endpoints keep working, SigV4-signed per call against the store's credential chain so IRSA and container credentials are unaffected -- and it follows continuation tokens, so a bucket over 1000 keys lists in full. Keys are returned byte-exact, including any leading or trailing space, and an `<Error>` document is surfaced as a failure rather than as an empty listing. Nothing needs configuring: the fallback engages off the error itself, latching per process so the doomed attempt is paid at most once, and `S3_PROVIDER=oss` (or an `*.aliyuncs.com` endpoint) skips even that first probe. Every other provider is untouched -- the `object_store` path stays the only one they use, and transport, auth and not-found errors still propagate immediately instead of being retried.

- **OCI blob commits succeed on Alibaba Cloud OSS, which could not run a Docker/OCI registry at all** (#3594). Committing a blob upload renames the staged object to its content-addressed key, and that rename is a server-side `CopyObject`, which `object_store` issues with the AWS header `x-amz-copy-source`. OSS honours only `x-oss-copy-source` and ignores the AWS spelling, so the request degenerated into a PUT with no source and came back `404 NoSuchKey` naming the *source* staging key -- every `PUT /v2/<name>/blobs/uploads/<uuid>?digest=...` 500'd with `BLOB_UPLOAD_UNKNOWN`, for every layer, with no workaround short of moving OCI repositories to the filesystem backend. `object_store` 0.13 and 0.14 expose no per-call header override, so there is nothing to configure around it; when the backend is talking to OSS, `S3Backend::copy` now performs the commit as a streaming PUT -- read the source back through `get_stream` and write it to the destination through `put_stream` -- instead of a server-side copy. That is the same bounded multipart writer every upload already uses, with the same abort-on-cancellation cleanup, and the destination still only becomes visible at `CompleteMultipartUpload`, so an interrupted commit leaves an existing object untouched exactly as the server-side path did. The cost is one extra egress round trip per copied object, paid only on OSS: every other provider keeps the native `CopyObject` and the multipart `UploadPartCopy` above the single-copy ceiling (#3164), both unchanged. The routing is in the storage backend rather than in the OCI handler, so the proxy-cache staging commit and any future caller are covered by the same fix. Maven, npm, generic and the rest were never affected -- they PUT the body directly and never go through CopyObject.

  **Upgrade note -- a new optional setting, `S3_PROVIDER`.** It pins the provider dialect and is documented in `.env.example`. Leave it unset on AWS S3, MinIO, Ceph RGW, R2, Huawei OBS and anything else that matches AWS's wire behaviour; unset is also correct for Alibaba Cloud OSS itself, because an `*.aliyuncs.com` `S3_ENDPOINT` is detected automatically (host match, so a bucket or path that merely contains the string does not trip it). Set `S3_PROVIDER=oss` (aliases `aliyun`, `alibaba`) only for an OSS-compatible gateway published on some other hostname, and `S3_PROVIDER=aws` (alias `generic`) to force the plain S3 dialect on an `aliyuncs.com` endpoint that does honour the AWS headers. An unrecognised value warns and falls back to endpoint detection rather than failing startup, so a typo cannot take a running deployment down. No existing deployment changes behaviour by upgrading.

- **OCI blob-upload tests no longer contend for one another's cleanup-journal row, which made `completion_with_unknown_length_empty_final_put_skips_zero_byte_part` fail intermittently in CI** (#3529). Six tests in `oci_blob_upload_streaming_tests` completed a blob under bytes a sibling test also completed (`b"hello world"` in four, the empty blob in two). `oci_upload_cleanup_keys.storage_key` is `UNIQUE` across the whole database and `blob_storage_key` is content-addressed, so those tests shared a single cleanup-journal row: the second `register_oci_upload_cleanup_key` hit `ON CONFLICT (storage_key)` and got the first test's row id back. Whichever push committed first deleted that row inside its `oci_blobs` transaction (the #3187 guard) and then tore its fixture down, dropping the `oci_blobs` row that was the slower push's only evidence a peer had won — so the slower push saw its journal row gone with nothing referencing the key, which in production means a cleanup sweep reaped the object, and correctly answered `503 BLOB_UPLOAD_INVALID` "blob storage was being reclaimed concurrently; retry the upload". The failure surfaced on whatever unrelated PR happened to be in CI at the time. Those six tests now take a new `test_db_helpers::oci_blob_digest_serial_lock` — a Postgres *session* advisory lock, the same shape as `blob_gc_serial_lock` (#1660) and `oci_reindex_serial_lock` (#3402), which serializes across `cargo nextest`'s process-per-test parallelism — so only one of them runs its push → assert → teardown critical section at a time. Test-only change; no production code and no assertion was touched.

- **`repository_usage_ledger` can be backfilled after a database restore, so the storage headline stops undercounting** (#3650). `/api/v1/admin/stats.total_storage_bytes` sums `repository_usage_ledger` (#3134), and that ledger is maintained exclusively by migration 182's row-level triggers -- which a restore from backup never fires, because the restore inserts rows rather than writing them through the application. The headline then reflected only what the instance had written *since* the restore and could understate the real catalogue by orders of magnitude, with no supported path back short of manual SQL. A new admin-only `POST /api/v1/admin/storage/ledger/backfill` recomputes every repository's ledger row from the authoritative source tables using the migration-182 rules verbatim (`artifacts` excluding soft-deleted rows and `proxy-cache/%` keys, every `proxy_cache_artifacts` row, every `oci_blobs` row) and returns per-repository before/after plus the corrected headline. It is an absolute recompute, so it is idempotent: on a healthy instance it reports zero drift. The API documentation now also states that `proxy_storage_bytes` is a *breakdown of* `total_storage_bytes` rather than a disjoint bucket -- the schema description had been attached to the neighbouring `proxy_artifact_count`, which unlike the byte figure genuinely is disjoint -- so a dashboard that adds the two double-counts the cache.

  **Upgrade note.** Instances whose database was restored from a backup (or otherwise loaded by any route that bypasses the triggers) should run `POST /api/v1/admin/storage/ledger/backfill` once after the restore to correct the storage headline. It is safe to run at any time and on any instance. It is also safe to run `/storage-gc` before the backfill: neither the storage-GC nor the blob-GC orphan rule reads the ledger at any point -- they test `artifacts`, `oci_tags`, `oci_blobs`, `oci_manifest_refs` and `manifest_blob_refs` only -- so an unreconciled ledger cannot make a live blob look unreferenced.

- **OCI objects orphaned by a repository delete are now reclaimed instead of leaking forever** (#3733). Deleting a Docker/OCI repository deliberately leaves its `oci-manifests/<digest>` and `oci-blobs/<digest>` objects on storage: they are content-addressed and can be shared cross-repo through `oci_tags` / `oci_manifest_refs` / `oci_blobs` / `manifest_blob_refs`, so the delete purge's `artifacts`-only exclusivity guard cannot prove any of them unreferenced and deleting one would destroy a manifest or layer another repository still serves (#1598). Reclaiming them is GC's job -- but the same delete CASCADEs away exactly the rows GC scans from (`artifacts` for manifests, `oci_blobs` for blobs), so an object that *was* this repository's alone became undiscoverable at the instant it became reclaimable, and no number of subsequent GC cycles could find it. The delete path now records the repository's committed OCI object keys into a durable candidate set (`oci_gc_candidates`, migration 219) before the cascade, and the storage-GC sweep consumes each recorded key: still referenced by some surviving repository and the row is dropped with the object untouched; referenced by nothing on that backend and the object is deleted. The reference test spans every table that can make an OCI object reachable, not just the two the ordinary scans start from, so a manifest reachable only through a tag or an image-index edge is still protected. Rows never outlive their sweep, so the set stays bounded by the deletion rate; a recorded candidate waits out the same 24-hour grace window blob GC uses before its object can be deleted, because it is the one GC input with no row to lock against an in-flight push.

- **The Swift publish endpoint now stores the `source-archive` part of the multipart request instead of the whole envelope** (#3595). `PUT /swift/{repo}/{scope}/{name}/{version}` took the entire request body as the source archive, but `swift package-registry publish` sends an SE-0292 `multipart/form-data` envelope whose required `source-archive` part carries the zip. Everything published with the official SwiftPM client therefore had the multipart boundary, part headers and the trailing parts stored as if they were the archive: `GET .../{version}.zip` returned a body starting with `--<boundary>` rather than `PK\x03\x04`, and `swift package resolve` failed with "extra bytes at beginning or within zipfile". The corruption was invisible to checksum verification because `checksum_sha256` — the value echoed as the release-metadata `checksum` and the download `Digest` header — was computed over the same wrong bytes. A multipart body is now parsed with `multer` (the parser the nuget push path already uses) driven straight off the request-body stream; only the `source-archive` part is stored, hashed and scanned for `Package.swift`, and the optional `metadata` part is persisted so the release-metadata endpoint's `metadata` object is no longer always `{}`. The handler no longer buffers the upload at all: it took `body: Bytes`, so a publish held the whole request — up to `MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE`, 10 GB by default — on the heap per concurrent request, and the archive part is now spooled to a bounded scratch file and streamed into storage (`stage_stream_content_addressed` + `put_artifact_stream`, the #1608 primitives), with `MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE` enforced mid-stream as a 413. Only the optional `metadata` part is read into memory, under a 1 MiB cap. A request with no `source-archive` part, more than one, a truncated body, or a `multipart/form-data` content type with no boundary is rejected with 400. A raw `PUT ... Content-Type: application/zip` upload (non-SwiftPM tooling) is unchanged: the whole body still is the archive.

  **Upgrade note — every Swift release published through this endpoint with a multipart client must be republished.** The stored object is the envelope and its recorded checksum matches the envelope, so nothing detects the corruption automatically and existing releases stay unusable until they are published again. Because registry releases are immutable, republishing means deleting the affected release and publishing it anew. The archive bytes are still present inside each stored envelope, so an offline backfill that re-parses those objects and rewrites the blob and checksum is feasible for any release whose bytes have not been trimmed; it is not part of this change. The two signature parts (`source-archive-signature`, `metadata-signature`) are still not persisted — no endpoint serves them and no trust policy verifies them — but their presence is now recorded on the release row rather than discarded without trace.

- **Virtual repositories now aggregate their members' content in the Packages page and the Docker grouped tag view** (#3532). A virtual repository owns no catalog rows of its own — a push to it routes to a hosted member, and a proxied pull caches into a remote one — but two listing views filtered by the virtual repository's own key or id instead of expanding to its members, so both came back empty while the flat artifact listing (which already expands) showed the same content. `GET /api/v1/packages?repository_key=<virtual>` filtered `packages` by the virtual repository's key, and `GET /api/v1/repositories/<virtual>/artifacts?group_by=docker_tag` filtered `oci_tags` by its id. Both now expand to the priority-ordered members the caller may read — the grouped view reusing `fetch_virtual_members` plus the same grant and token-scope member filter the flat listing applies (#3163), so aggregation still cannot disclose a private member's tags — and de-duplicate a `(name, tag)` or package present in several members onto the highest-priority one, matching the flat listing's `DISTINCT ON (path)` shadowing contract. Aggregated rows report the virtual repository's key rather than the owning member's, as the artifacts page already does, and `GET /api/v1/packages/{id}?repository_key=<virtual>` reports the virtual key when the package belongs to one of that repository's members so the detail view matches the listing it was opened from. Only the shadowing member may be one that still has the manifest: the grouped view's de-duplication tests `artifacts.is_deleted = false` inside the `DISTINCT ON` subquery, the same place the flat listing tests it, because electing a member whose `oci_tags` row has no live `artifacts` row and only then joining would have dropped the tag from both the page and `?count=exact` while a lower-priority member still served it. Member expansion remains single-level, as it is on every other listing path: a virtual repository nested inside another still contributes nothing, unchanged by this fix. No API shape or permission changes, and a non-virtual repository's listings are byte-for-byte as before.

- **The checksum-refresh re-upload test now runs against a repository whose re-uploads are actually accepted, and CI's quarantine of it is lifted** (#3617, #3494). `search_checksum_sha1_md5_tests::test_reupload_refreshes_all_three_checksums` re-uploaded changed bytes to the same coordinate in a plain Generic repository and expected the `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE` upsert to refresh sha256/sha1/md5; that coordinate is version-immutable, so the second upload was refused with `Conflict("Artifact version already exists and is immutable")` and the case was quarantined behind a `--skip` in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. The immutability check is not new — it dates to the first backend commit, predating the test — so the test never passed; it was `#[ignore]`d and its target was one of the 44 integration targets CI never executed (#3494). The upsert is nevertheless live code: a Generic/Mlmodel repository that opted into first-class versioning (#2367) skips both the live-overwrite check and the release-immutability backstop, so its HEAD row is refreshed in place on every re-upload. The case now runs there, keeping the checksum-refresh coverage it was written for, and a sibling case pins the default contract — the re-upload is refused and all three stored checksums still describe the original bytes. No production code changed; the suite is fully green and moved out of the quarantined-case CI step into the main integration step.

- **Proxy cache hits are now recorded, so a proxy-only repository no longer reports zero downloads while serving continuous traffic** (#3649). `proxy_download_statistics` is the sibling of `download_statistics` for pull-through serves (proxy-cached content deliberately has no `artifacts` row, #1278/#1280), and #3446 wired the recorder into nine formats but explicitly DEFERRED fourteen others — alpine, chef, cocoapods, composer, conan, conda, gitlfs, jetbrains, pub, rpm, sbt, swift, terraform and vscode each carried an `UNRECORDED-PROXY-SERVE` deferral marker on their Remote download arm. Those arms served upstream *and* proxy-cached bytes and counted neither, so on those formats a re-pull of an already-cached artifact returned 200 and refreshed `last_accessed_at` without producing a stats row, and the Downloads figure read 0 no matter how heavily the proxy was used. Every one of those arms now calls `proxy_helpers::record_proxy_download` after the fetch resolves, keyed on the proxy-cache path the fetch commits under; because the streaming helpers answer a warm cache HIT and a cold MISS through the same call, recording once covers both. PyPI additionally counted a cache hit only when it was *streamed*: the #1555 presigned-redirect fast path returned a 307 to the signed cache object and returned before the recorder, so on an S3-backed deployment with presigned downloads enabled every warm hit was invisible — a redirect is now counted at issue time, the same rule `local_fetch_or_redirect` already applies on the hosted side, as are the last-known-good wheels the PyPI download age gate substitutes. The existing guarantees are unchanged: a HEAD still never counts (it serves no body), an OCI blob still never counts (a Docker pull is counted once at the manifest), repository metadata is not a download, and the write stays best-effort — a failure is logged at `debug` and never surfaced to the client.

  **Upgrade note — historical traffic cannot be recovered, and the counters will step up.** The source tables hold no history of the serves that were never recorded, so past values can only be fabricated, not recomputed; nothing is backfilled. After upgrading, `proxy_download_count` (on `GET /api/v1/admin/stats`, the per-repository storage breakdown, and the daily download trend) starts moving on repositories of those fourteen formats that previously read 0, and on every format it now also moves for warm cache hits served as presigned redirects. A trend series that spans the upgrade therefore shows a one-day step; it is a measurement correction, not new traffic. Nothing about artifact delivery changes — this was a reporting gap, not a serving defect.

  **Still out of scope, deliberately: `download_statistics` remains keyed on `artifact_id` and therefore cannot capture proxy traffic at all.** Proxied content never creates an `artifacts` row (#1278/#1280), so the `NOT NULL` `artifact_id` foreign key structurally excludes it — which is exactly why the separate `proxy_download_statistics` table exists (#2270). Consumers reading only `download_count` will still see zero on an all-proxy deployment and must add `proxy_download_count`; the two are disjoint by design and must not be summed with a repository's `proxy_storage_bytes`-style totals. Changing that keying is a schema change and belongs in its own issue, not here. A Remote member reached *through a virtual repository* also stays uncounted, as decided in #1278/#2260 (`resolve_virtual_download_streaming` records the local-member winner only); counting those safely needs a decision about the two-phase member fan-out, which probes members that may lose to a higher-priority candidate.

- **The OCI storage-stats regression test now pins the deliberate manifest exclusion instead of a stale double-count, and CI's quarantine of it is lifted** (#3618, #3494, #3286). `storage_stats_tests::oci_layer_bytes_are_counted` stored a 512-byte `oci-manifests/%` `artifacts` row plus a 4096-byte `oci_blobs` layer and asserted `physical_bytes == 4608`; the aggregate reported 4096, so the case was quarantined behind a `--skip` in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`. The aggregate is right and the expectation was stale: an image manifest's `artifacts.size_bytes` holds `oci_v2::manifest_total_size` (config plus the sum of `layers[].size`, i.e. the aggregate image size), not the stored manifest object, so #3390 excluded `oci-manifests/%` from `REPO_OBJECT_UNION_SQL` after unioning both sources reported 3097 GB against 1.14 TiB of real bucket usage. The test predates that change and had never run (it is `#[ignore]`d, and its target was one of the 44 integration targets CI never executed). The fixture now sizes the manifest row the way the push path does and asserts the layer is counted exactly once, so the case guards the #3286 double-count rather than inviting its return. No production behaviour changed; the suite is fully green and moved out of the quarantined-case CI step into the main integration step. The manifest JSON bytes themselves remain uncounted — a deliberate, bounded undercount (~0.01% of a real footprint; no column holds a manifest's true object size), now stated on the `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/storage` response schema so operators reading the figure know what it omits.

- **OCI/Docker blob `GET` now honours a single HTTP `Range` request across hosted, virtual and pull-through paths** (#3586). A client that retried an interrupted layer download with `Range: bytes=...` always got the full object back with `200 OK` — the OCI Distribution Spec's resumable-pull use case (`skopeo`, container runtimes resuming behind a flaky link) was therefore impossible. The hosted/CAS-hit, virtual-local-member and Remote pull-through serve paths now answer `206 Partial Content` with the exact `Content-Range` window, sliced at chunk boundaries from the existing streaming read (never buffered), `416` with `Content-Range: bytes */total` for an unsatisfiable range, and advertise `Accept-Ranges: bytes` on `GET` and `HEAD` where the full length is known. Remote cold-cache streaming still tees the complete object into the proxy cache; only the client-facing stream is sliced, so a partial request can never poison the cache. If the upstream does not advertise a total length, the response remains a full `200`. A syntactically valid multi-range header degrades to the full `200` (a valid server choice per RFC 7233). Regression tests drive explicit, suffix and unsatisfiable ranges through hosted CAS and both cold/warm Remote pull-through paths.

- **The Conan middleware integration test still pinned the pre-#1808 404 for an unauthenticated request naming an unknown repository, and was quarantined out of CI** (#3616). `conan_error_paths_tests::test_1046_unknown_repo_no_auth_returns_404` asserted that an anonymous `GET /conan/{unknown}/v2/ping` returns 404. That was the middleware's behaviour when #1046 wrote the test in May 2026, but #1808 (fixed in #1812, June 2026) deliberately retired it: an existing *private* repository answers an anonymous caller with 401 + `WWW-Authenticate`, so a key naming no repository answering 404 let anyone enumerate private repository names by status alone. `repo_visibility_middleware` now answers both with the byte-identical 401, and `/conan` is mounted under that same middleware as every other native format — so the test, not the handler, was the stale side, and the suite had never run in CI to catch it (#3494). **No production behaviour changes here; this is a test and CI-wiring correction only.** The case is rewritten as `test_1808_unknown_repo_no_auth_matches_private_401`, which compares the unknown-key response against an existing-private one and requires the status *and* body to match rather than merely asserting some 401 — that equality is what closing the oracle actually requires. The authenticated side is untouched and still pinned by `test_990_upload_to_nonexistent_repo_returns_404` (a valid credential plus an unknown key gets the existence-hiding 404 of GHSA-fv45-mwhh-q23r). The `--skip` quarantine is removed from `.github/workflows/ci.yml` and `conan_error_paths_tests` moves to the fully-green integration step, so all 8 cases now run on every push.

  **Operator note for anyone who read the old 404 as a contract.** Pointing a Conan remote at a repository key that does not exist returns 401, not 404, and has since 1.2.1 (#1812) — as it does for a private repository the caller may not see, which is the point. The Conan client dispatches on the status code and ignores the `WWW-Authenticate` challenge, so `conan install` against a typo'd remote prompts for credentials three times before failing (`Too many failed login attempts`) and under `core:non_interactive=True` fails immediately with `Conan interactive mode disabled` rather than a "not found". Check the remote URL's repository key first when you see either message.

- **A cancelled migration was logged "Migration paused by user"** (#3498). `spawn_migration_worker` builds a `CancellationToken` that nothing in production retains a handle to, and no production path fires it — the real cancel is a database write (`cancel_migration` sets `status = 'cancelled'`) the worker observes through `is_paused`, which matches `'paused'` and `'cancelled'` alike. So the worker's `if self.cancel_token.is_cancelled()` was always false for an operator stop and every genuine cancel took the `else` arm and logged a pause, making the two states an operator most needs to tell apart when diagnosing a stopped migration indistinguishable in the logs. It was cosmetic to the job row (already written `cancelled` synchronously by the cancel handler), so the reproduction asserts on the log line. The worker now re-reads the status it can actually observe and logs the transition that happened — cancel, pause, or the job row having been deleted mid-run — and the finalize-guard exit likewise names the observed status instead of the ambiguous "Migration paused or cancelled before finalization", which also covered a deleted row. The in-process token arm still writes the terminal status, since an in-process cancel is otherwise unrecorded.

- **Cargo dependency scanning works again: a `Cargo.toml` no longer scans as having no dependencies at all** (#3699, #3690). `DependencyScanner::parse_cargo` read the manifest with `content.parse::<toml::Value>()`. In `toml` 0.8 that was the document parser; `toml` 1.0 repointed `impl FromStr for Value` at the *value-expression* parser, so the same line kept compiling and started returning `Err` for every real manifest, and the surrounding `if let Ok(..)` swallowed the error — every `Cargo.toml` scanned reported **zero** crates.io dependencies, with nothing in the logs to say so. The parser is now `toml::from_str::<toml::Value>` (the document parser under both versions) and a parse failure is logged at debug instead of being discarded. A regression test scans a whole manifest — `[package]` header, `[dependencies]`, `[dev-dependencies]`, `[build-dependencies]` — and asserts on the names and versions it yields, so a parser that silently returns nothing cannot pass it again.

- **A singleton job that lost its scheduler lease mid-run kept running against a lease another replica now holds** (#3502). #3084 added a lease-loss `CancellationToken` to the claim-renewal machinery — cancelled the moment a heartbeat reports "ownership lost" — precisely so a long-running singleton job stops its side effects when another replica has legitimately taken the work over. No `SchedulerLease` consumer could observe it, because `SchedulerLease::spawn_renewal` discarded the token. The three scheduled jobs that heartbeat *because their cycles can outlive the fixed TTL* — the lifecycle-policy sweep (destructive: it deletes artifacts and frees bytes), the curation upstream sync, and the bootstrap OpenSearch reindex — were exactly the ones that could lose a lease mid-run, log `claim renewal stopped because ownership was lost`, and then finish the whole cycle anyway, concurrently with the new owner's. `SchedulerLease` now exposes `spawn_renewal_with_cancellation`, and each of the three jobs observes the token between items: the lifecycle cycle stops between policies, the curation sweep stops between staging repos, and the reindex stops between batches (restoring the index refresh interval and surfacing the abort as an error rather than a clean finish). Renewal *errors* still never cancel the token — the claim is held until its TTL lapses — and the operator-invoked variants of these jobs (manual sync trigger, admin reindex) are unchanged: they are not lease-guarded, so there is no lease to lose. The scheduled storage-GC tick is a fourth, explicitly named call site: #3503 had just put the *whole* tick — including the destructive blob sweep — under a single lease, so a tick that lost the lease mid-run kept deleting blobs while the replica that now legitimately owned the occurrence began its own sweep. The tick now hands its lease-loss token to the follow-on, which abandons each remaining workload at its boundary (blob-GC mark, blob-GC sweep, post-GC storage-stats recompute) rather than racing the new owner. The independent 4-hourly storage-stats refresh keeps the token-less variant on purpose and now says why at the call site: it is a single indivisible, read-only, idempotent recompute with no per-item boundary at which an abort could take effect.

- **A Nexus migration no longer fails a large transfer on the clock, or a whole item on a transient source blip** (#3569). `NexusClient` built its HTTP client with a single `timeout()`, which in reqwest covers reading the response body: any artifact whose download took longer than `timeout_secs` (default 30) was killed mid-body and surfaced as `error decoding response body`, so the largest artifact a migration could move depended on the throughput between the two instances rather than on any configured limit, and the same job succeeded or failed run to run while the error pointed at deserialization. Nothing in the client retried either, so a source restart, a 502 from a proxy in front of Nexus, or a 429 under load permanently failed whatever item was in flight — an Artifactory source in the same situation retried, because `ArtifactoryClient` already had `RetryConfig`. The client now bounds the connect and per-read phases instead (`connect_timeout_secs`, default 10; `timeout_secs` becomes the per-read stall bound, so a slow but healthy download survives and a dead connection still fails fast), and retries 5xx, 429 and connect/read timeouts with the same `RetryConfig` the Artifactory client uses. Only the request and response-header phase is retried: a body that dies mid-stream is not re-issued, since the caller is already consuming chunks, and item-level retry stays the caller's job. A `Retry-After` on a 429 is honoured but clamped to `max_delay_ms` (30 s) and multiplied saturatingly, so a rate-limiting proxy answering `Retry-After: 3600` delays a transfer by 30 s rather than an hour and an absurd header value cannot overflow the arithmetic; a cancelled migration ends a retry backoff instead of sleeping through it, so a cancel no longer has to outlast a 30 s wait; and the retry warnings redact the source URL before logging it — `source_connections.url` is accepted with `user:pass@` userinfo, which would otherwise have been written to the log on the first 503 (#2926). The callers that buffer a whole body (`get`, `download_artifact`) keep a total ceiling on the request (`buffered_timeout_secs`, default 300), because `read_timeout` restarts on every chunk and would let a source dribbling one byte per read hold a worker and a growing allocation indefinitely. The streaming download the migration worker uses carries no such ceiling, so a large artifact is still allowed to take as long as it takes.
