Before upgrading, either `UPDATE users SET must_change_password = false WHERE username = 'admin'` (takes effect on the next request) or set `SKIP_ADMIN_PROVISIONING=true` and restart; the latter is the right long-term setting for a deployment whose admins all come from SSO.

- **A chart hosted in a Helm repository could not be consumed as a subchart dependency** (#3680, #3720). The generated `index.yaml` advertised every chart URL as a root-relative path (`/helm/{repo}/charts/{file}`), a form helm's two download code paths read differently: `helm install`/`helm pull` resolve it against the host root and work, but `helm dependency update` joins it onto the repository URL, doubling the path (`.../helm/{repo}/helm/{repo}/charts/...`) into a 404 — so any chart in an Artifact Keeper repository installed fine directly yet broke every umbrella chart that pinned it under `dependencies:`. Advertised URLs are now **relative** (`charts/{file}`), which is what ChartMuseum emits and what both helm paths resolve against the repository URL the client configured. The hosted, remote-proxy and virtual index paths all advertise through the one helper that changed, so all three surfaces move together.

- **An OCI Remote repository kept serving an expired mutable tag from local storage without asking upstream** (#3712). The manifest handlers resolve a reference through `oci_tags` first, and for a Remote repository that row is written by the cold proxy pull and carries no freshness of its own — so once a tag had been pulled once, every later `HEAD`/`GET /v2/<repo>/<image>/manifests/<tag>` resolved the tag to the digest it was cached with, read `oci-manifests/<digest>` from the repository's own storage and returned before ever reaching the proxy layer, which is the only place the cache TTL, the conditional revalidation and the stale-if-error fallback live. A tag re-pointed upstream (`:latest` re-pushed, a rolling `:1` tag) therefore kept resolving to the old digest for as long as the local copy existed, no upstream request was ever made, and the UI's "expired …, will re-fetch on next download" was not true for this path: Docker and containerd issue `HEAD` by tag then `GET` by the returned digest, so the stale digest was pinned end to end. For a Remote repository and a tag reference, the tag row is now trusted only while the proxy-cache entry for `v2/<image>/manifests/<tag>` is within its TTL — the same sidecar the cold pull wrote, so the repository's `cache_ttl_secs` override and the mutable-path default apply unchanged. Past it, the tag is re-fetched through the proxy layer (ETag revalidation, single-flight, stale-if-error included), the re-fetched manifest is re-cached and `oci_tags` follows the digest, and the response is served from local storage through the unchanged quarantine and scan gates with the same `Docker-Content-Digest`, `Content-Type` and `Content-Length` headers as before. A `GET` whose revalidation re-fetched the tag also indexes the packages-catalog row after the scan gate, the way a cold pull does — an upsert, so a manifest cached by a pull the gate refused is indexed by the next re-fetch that passes it, whether or not the digest moved. When upstream cannot be reached and the proxy cache holds nothing to fall back on, the cached copy is still served rather than failing the pull. The same applies, deliberately, to a tag that has been **deleted upstream**: the revalidation gets a 404 (negative-cached for 45 s by the proxy layer), the `oci_tags` row is kept and the cached manifest keeps being served — unlike the cold path, which answers `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` for a tag that was never cached — so a retracted tag stays pullable from the mirror until its cached copy is removed. Digest references are immutable and are not revalidated. Hosted repositories are untouched. A **Virtual** repository fronting a Remote member resolves tags through the member's `oci_tags` rows in `resolve_virtual_manifest` and is covered by #3725 below.

  **Upgrade note:** a warm pull by tag on a Remote OCI repository now makes one upstream request per tag once its cache TTL (`cache_ttl_secs`, default 300 s for tags) has elapsed — single-flighted across concurrent pulls, and when the upstream returned an `ETag` the probe is a conditional request whose 304 extends the entry without a re-download. If the upstream is unreachable the cached copy is still served, but only after the upstream attempt fails — so an offline or seeded-once mirror will see slower pulls (the upstream connect timeout) for tags more than an hour past their TTL, the stale-if-error grace; raise `cache_ttl_secs` on that repository to keep them local. On object-store backends (S3/GCS/Azure) the freshness probe adds one metadata `HEAD` per warm pull by tag. The same now applies to a Virtual repository fronting a Remote member (#3725, below).

- **An OCI Virtual repository fronting a Remote member kept serving the member's expired mutable tag without revalidating it** (#3725). #3712's fix revalidates an expired tag on the direct Remote `HEAD`/`GET /v2/<repo>/<image>/manifests/<tag>` path, but a Virtual repository resolves a tag through its members' `oci_tags` rows in `resolve_virtual_manifest`, which read the row and served `oci-manifests/<digest>` from the member's storage with no freshness check — and the revalidation helper returned early for anything but a direct Remote. So a tag re-pointed upstream resolved to its new digest through the member's own key (one upstream request) yet kept resolving to the old digest through the Virtual (no upstream request) for as long as the member's local copy existed — #3712's symptom one hop up. When the Virtual walk lands on a Remote member's tag row, that row is now put through the same revalidation in the member's context — the member's `cache_ttl_secs`, its `v2/<image>/manifests/<tag>` proxy-cache sidecar, its storage — before it is trusted; a moved tag is re-fetched and re-cached under the member and the Virtual serves the re-read row through its unchanged member-order walk and scan gates. Within TTL nothing changes (no upstream request, the cached digest); when upstream is unreachable the member's cached copy is still served rather than failing the pull or falling through to the next member. Hosted members and digest references are untouched.

- **Pulling an image through an OCI Virtual repository left no tag, artifact or package on the Remote member it was fetched from** (#3731). A Virtual repository stores nothing itself, so what a pull through it should leave behind is exactly what a direct pull of the member leaves: the `oci_tags` row, the `artifacts` rows and the packages-catalog row on the member. It left none of them. `resolve_virtual_manifest` fetched a member's miss through the generic proxy cache and the Virtual `HEAD`/`GET` arms served the bytes straight back, never running the member's manifest caching, its catalog write or its download count — so the pull succeeded with the right digest, the member never learned the tag, the Packages page and `/v2/_catalog` never showed the image, the pull was not counted, and every later pull through the Virtual resolved the same way instead of from the member's local copy. A Remote member is now resolved the way its own key resolves it: a miss is fetched through the member's Remote path and cached under the member (tag row, refs, artifacts), a `GET` whose bytes came from upstream — a cold fetch, or a #3725 revalidation that re-fetched a moved tag — indexes the member's catalog row on the serve side of the scan gate as the direct cold path does (a bare `HEAD` still indexes nothing, #3611), and the pull is counted against the member (#3446). The next pull through the Virtual is a local hit on the member. Digest references are still verified against the requested digest before anything is cached, member order and the caller-authorization filter are unchanged, hosted members are unchanged, and the Virtual still stores nothing. The Virtual `HEAD`/`GET` arms also now run the member's quarantine gate — a manifest quarantined or rejected in the member answers through the Virtual exactly as it does through the member's own key (previously it was served regardless, a gap this fix would otherwise have made reachable from every Virtual pull, since it is what starts writing the member's `artifacts` rows). The Docker pull shape (`HEAD` by tag then `GET` by digest) leaves the tag row and artifacts on the member; its catalog row is #3707's, which lands on the same warm path.

- **A tagged image pulled through an OCI Remote repository by Docker or containerd never appeared in the packages catalog** (#3707). #3599 indexes a proxied package on `GET /v2/<repo>/<image>/manifests/<tag>`, deliberately not on `HEAD` (a bare, ungated HEAD must not publish catalog rows, #3611) and not for digest references (a digest names no version). But Docker CLI and containerd pull a tag as `HEAD /manifests/<tag>` followed by `GET /manifests/<digest>` -- there is no GET by tag in the flow -- so the HEAD cached the manifest and wrote the tag row, the GET served it from local storage, and nothing in the pull reached the catalog: `docker pull <host>/dockerhub-proxy/library/busybox:1.38.0` succeeded and the Packages page stayed empty. On a Remote repository, a `GET` by digest served from local storage now indexes every tag that `oci_tags` maps to that digest, after the scan gate has agreed to serve -- the same ordering as the cold path. The tag→digest row the preceding HEAD wrote is what licenses the write; a HEAD alone still publishes nothing, and a digest with no tag row (`docker pull image@sha256:...`, an index's child manifests) still indexes nothing. The write is the same idempotent upsert a GET by tag performs.

- **A repository reachable only through a fine-grained permission grant listed none of its webhooks** (#3702). `GET /api/v1/webhooks` scopes a non-admin's listing to webhooks they created plus webhooks attached to a repository they hold a `role_assignments` row for, and never consulted the `permissions` table — so a user or group whose access came from `POST /api/v1/permissions` (on the repository, or inherited from its owning project) got an empty listing, while `GET /api/v1/webhooks/{id}` on one of those very rows answered normally, because the per-webhook authorization runs through `user_can_access_repo`, which has honoured both authz stores since #2472. The listing predicate now carries a third arm that resolves the grant, so the two agree wherever the repository read gate does. Two residuals are deliberately untouched: `GET /api/v1/webhooks/{id}` and its delivery listing still authorize on the tenant-only gate, so a `{write}`-only grant holder can fetch a webhook by id that no longer appears in the list (narrower listing than fetch is the safe direction), and the pre-existing `role_assignments` arms remain action-blind, the global one still admitting every webhook in the instance. Same class as #3697 in search; the `created_by` and `role_assignments` arms are unchanged, mutations are untouched, and admins were never affected.

  The new arm requires the `read` **action**, not merely the existence of a grant. `permissions_grant_exists_for` is only the tenant half of the repository read gate (`actions <> '{}'`); the gate is that fragment *plus* `check_repository_action(.., "read", ..)`, and `write` does not imply `read` — so ORing the bare fragment in would have handed a publish-only CI principal every webhook URL, event filter and secret digest on a repository the read gate refuses it, which is exactly what `RepoAccess::TenantOnly`'s contract forbids fronting (#3331). It is also a set-driven `JOIN` rather than a correlated `EXISTS`: correlated, the fragment's project subquery is re-run once per repository row, measured at 56–315 ms per call at 10k repositories, and this predicate runs twice per request (page + count). A DB-backed matrix over every grant shape asserts that every repository the arm admits also passes `user_can_access_repo(.., READ)`.

- **A scan cancelled by its wall-clock budget leaked its workspace directory permanently** (#3565). The inline proxy scan path races the whole scanner future against a wall-clock budget, but workspace cleanup was an explicit call placed *after* the scan in each of the filesystem scanners, so when the budget expired the future was dropped before control ever reached that line and the directory survived. Nothing else reaped it — the janitor service reaps stale `scans` rows in Postgres, not files on disk — and each timed-out attempt staged a *fresh* directory rather than reusing one, so an instance whose scans time out regularly (a CPU-, IO- or memory-starved one, exactly the kind that times out repeatedly) accumulated staged artifact bytes and, for archive formats, entire extracted trees on its dedicated fixed-size scan-workspace volume until it filled. The workspace is now owned by an RAII guard from the moment the directory exists until the scan ends, so it is removed on every exit path — cancellation included — rather than only the ones a caller remembers. The guard also owns the CycloneDX BOM sidecar that Grype writes *beside* the scanned tree (it must stay outside it, or the next catalog would include our own output) and the local OCI layout directory the image scan stages, both of which were previously unlinked only after their scan returned.

  Three details make that hold in practice. Cleanup on the completion path keeps the existing asynchronous removal, including its recursive pre-chmod, but disarms the guard only once removal has actually finished — `chmod` and `remove_dir_all` are themselves cancellation points, and disarming before them would leave a cancelled cleanup with nothing behind it. The failure path now cleans up through the same guard instead of recomputing the path, so no exit removes a workspace twice. And archive extraction, which runs on a blocking task that dropping the future does not cancel, now checks a cancellation flag once per entry: without it the extractor simply rebuilt the tree it had already unpacked — measured at 19,513 of 20,000 entries restored after removal — because both unpackers recreate each entry's parent directory. The check is what keeps the tree from coming back; because nothing synchronises the extractor with the removal, at most one entry can still land after it, which a second removal pass makes unlikely rather than impossible.

  Removal on the cancellation path runs on a dedicated thread rather than inline, so unlinking a tree that can reach the 2 GiB / 200,000-entry extraction cap on a network-backed volume does not stall the runtime worker unwinding the timed-out request. A plain OS thread rather than a runtime task, because guards are also dropped en masse when the process shuts down — a runtime handle is still current then, but `spawn_blocking` accepts the task and discards it unrun, which would leak one workspace per in-flight scan per restart. That thread also runs an owner-`rwX` pre-pass that widens each directory before reading it, so a tree carrying directories the runtime UID cannot traverse (`d--x--S---`, as `tar` lands kernel-module directories) is removed rather than left behind — including when one such directory is nested inside another, which a `walkdir`-driven pass cannot reach. One sidecar is still not covered: Grype's `registry:` pull mode has no scan workspace at all and writes its BOM under `<scan-workspace>/grype-bom/<uuid>.json`, which is still unlinked only when that scan returns.

- **Charts pushed to a hosted Helm repository never appeared on the Packages page** (#3531). The Helm upload handler wrote the `artifacts` row and regenerated `index.yaml` but never registered the chart in the package catalog that the Packages page and `GET /api/v1/packages` read, so a chart was visible under Artifacts, servable with `helm pull`, and absent from the one view meant to list what a repository holds — while a chart *migrated* from Artifactory (which has indexed Helm since #2676) did appear, so the same chart showed up or not depending on how it arrived. The upload path now records the chart through the same `PackageService` write every other format uses, keyed on the `Chart.yaml` name and version (never the filename) and carrying the chart's description; the write is an upsert, so re-pushing is safe, and like every other format's catalog write it cannot fail the publish. **Upgrade note:** nothing backfills the catalog — the admin reindex endpoint rebuilds the search index, not `packages` — so charts pushed before this release stay off the Packages page until they are pushed again.

- **A Go client never routed `go.sum` verification through a GOPROXY repository** (#3642). Before sending any checksum-database traffic through a proxy, the toolchain probes `$GOPROXY/sumdb/<host>/supported` and treats anything but a 200 as "this proxy cannot proxy the sumdb", falling back to a direct connection to `sum.golang.org`. That path is a capability handshake the proxy answers about itself, not an endpoint of the checksum database, so forwarding it upstream returned the upstream's natural 404 and every `go` client silently bypassed the instance for `lookup/` and `tile/` requests: the existing sumdb handlers only ever answered hand-made requests, hosts without direct egress could download modules but not verify them, and checksum lookups were neither cached nor visible in the instance's logs. `supported` is now answered locally with an empty 200 — after the same host allowlist check as every other sumdb path — so the toolchain proxies its checksum lookups through the repository as configured.

- **`npm audit` through a Remote npm repository reported "found 0 vulnerabilities" for dependency trees with known-vulnerable packages** (#3644). npm sends the bulk-advisory and quick-audit POSTs with `Content-Encoding: gzip`, and nothing in the stack decompressed a request body — the `tower-http` compression features are response-side only — so both handlers received gzip bytes where they expected JSON and forwarded them upstream still compressed, labelled `application/json` with no `Content-Encoding`. Upstream rejected the body, the failure branch answered with an empty advisory set and HTTP 200, and npm rendered that as a clean audit: any CI job running `npm audit` through the registry had no vulnerability coverage and no signal that coverage was missing. Both audit routes now decode `gzip`/`x-gzip` and `deflate` request bodies before anything inspects or forwards them, with the decoded size capped at 16 MiB (the same ceiling as the upstream-response read) so a few KiB of compressed upload cannot become an unbounded allocation. A body that does not decode as its declared encoding is a 400 and an encoding that is not supported is a 415 — an audit that could not be performed is now an error, never an empty all-clear.

- **`GET /api/v1/users` returned service accounts with no way to identify or exclude them, so no client could build a working permission picker** (#3634). Service accounts are rows in `users`, so the admin user listing returned them mixed in with people — while `POST /api/v1/permissions` rejects exactly those rows when they are submitted as `principal_type: "user"`, with `400 principal_id <uuid> does not exist as a user`. The two endpoints contradicted each other and gave clients nothing to reconcile them with: `list_users` read `is_service_account` out of the database and then dropped it in `AdminUserResponse`, and `ListUsersQuery` offered no filter, so a caller could neither tell the two kinds of principal apart nor ask the server for one of them. The practical result was that granting a service account repository access — the documented remedy when its token gets `403 You do not have permission to perform this action on this repository`, since token scopes only narrow and never grant — could not be driven from the user list at all. `AdminUserResponse` now carries `is_service_account`, and `ListUsersQuery` accepts an optional `is_service_account` filter applied with the same NULL-passthrough shape as the existing `is_active` / `is_admin` filters. The `validate_principal` guard from #2503 is unchanged and still authoritative; what changed is that clients can now see what it will accept.

  The filter is deliberately opt-in rather than a blanket server-side exclusion: filtering the audit actor list by a service account is legitimate (CI is often the actor under investigation) and so is group membership for one, so an absent filter keeps the historical unfiltered listing and only a caller that asks gets people-only. It is applied to **both** statements `list_users` runs — the page query and the pagination count — because filtering one and not the other makes `total` count rows that `items` excludes, overshooting `total_pages` and growing a phantom trailing page; the two `WHERE` clauses are held byte-identical and a unit test compares them, since that drift cannot be caught without a database otherwise. Note the three filters are all `Option<bool>` and therefore type-identical at the bind site, so a transposed bind would compile silently and filter the wrong column.

  Consumers still have to opt in. In artifact-keeper-web five admin screens read this endpoint — the permissions principal picker, the users list, the group member picker, the audit actor filter and the age-gate approver picker — and four of them have no other source for the distinction; the picker is fixed page-locally in artifact-keeper-web#823, the rest wait on an SDK release carrying this field.

- **A service account could not be granted access through a project, leaving project-managed deployments with no grant channel for it at all** (#3683, #3700). `POST /api/v1/projects/{id}/members` refused `principal_type: "service_account"` outright — `valid_principal_type` accepted only `user | group`, even though its own doc comment claimed to match the principal domain `PermissionService::query_actions` resolves, which has matched `principal_type IN ('user','service_account')` since #2499/#2433. So the read plane happily resolved a `service_account` grant on a `project` target while the write plane refused to create one. A service account is created with no role and no grant, and token scopes only ever *narrow* — they never confer — so with the project endpoint closed and the shipped web UI able to emit only `principal_type: "user"` (rejected for a service-account row by the #2503 correspondence guard, listing half fixed in #3634/#3635), an operator who manages access by project had no way to give the account anything. Every push then failed the repository gate exactly as reported: `denied: You do not have access to this repository` from `docker push`, `403 FORBIDDEN` from a generic `PUT`. Enforcement was never the defect — the deny was `user_can_access_repo` correctly answering "no" because no row named the account. `valid_principal_type` now accepts `service_account` as well. This is not a 1.8.x regression: the gap dates to #2483 (v1.6.0).

  The #2503 mistype guard is untouched. `add_project_member` calls `PermissionService::validate_principal` immediately after the type allowlist, so the `principal_type`/`principal_id` correspondence is still checked against the database: `service_account` naming a person's id is still a 400, and so is `user` naming a service account's id. Widening the allowlist only stops refusing a grant the resolver already honours.

  **Workaround without upgrading**, on any 1.6+ build — grant the service account directly, with the right principal type, on the endpoint that already accepts it:

  ```
  curl -X POST $AK/api/v1/permissions \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer <admin token>" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
    -d '{"principal_type":"service_account","principal_id":"<sa uuid>",
         "target_type":"repository","target_id":"<repo uuid>","actions":["read","write"]}'
  ```

  Adding the service account to a group that holds the grant works too. Note this is the API, not the UI: the web form still submits `principal_type: "user"`, and that half is tracked in artifact-keeper-web — this release does not change it.

  **"Admin permissions don't work either" is a different, deliberate behaviour, not this bug.** A token minted without the `admin` (or `*`) scope is demoted to a non-admin principal by `with_scope_gated_admin` even when the account itself is an admin — that is GHSA-vvc3-h39c-mrq5's scope gate working as designed, and it is why an admin-owned service account with a `read`/`write`-only token is still denied. Mint the token with the `admin` scope if you want admin authority through it, or, better, grant the account the actions it needs and leave the token narrow.

- **Global search ignored every fine-grained permission grant, so a repository a user could download from returned no search hits** (#3697). `resolve_visible_repos` — the accessible-repository set behind every `/api/v1/search*` endpoint (`/quick`, `/advanced`, `/checksum`, `/suggest`, `/trending`, `/recent`) — built the caller's visible set from `role_assignments` alone. The `permissions` table, the target of `POST /api/v1/permissions` and of project membership, was never consulted, so a user whose only access to a private repository came from a grant — group-principal, direct-user, service-account, or inherited from the owning project — got an empty result set from search while `GET /api/v1/repositories` listed the repository and direct downloads by path worked. Nothing indicated the results were incomplete; the repository simply did not exist as far as search was concerned. Present since v1.2.0-rc.1 (#829): the resolver was correct when written and was never updated when `permissions` became a second visibility source in v1.2.3 (#2049). Surfaced while investigating #3681, which it does not otherwise explain — search denies a direct-user grant identically, so it does not match that report's working control.

  The resolver now resolves both stores. The new arm is deliberately **narrower** than the shared `permissions_grant_exists_for` fragment: that fragment is only the *tenant* half of the repository read gate (`actions <> '{}'` — does this principal hold any grant at all), and the gate also runs `check_repository_action` with the `read` action, which `write` does not imply. Search returns a private repository's artifact inventory — names, paths, versions, sizes, and through `/api/v1/search/checksum` sha256 digests — so admitting any non-empty grant would have let a publish-only principal holding `{"actions":["write"]}` enumerate all of it while `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}` still answered 404. The arm therefore requires a grant carrying `read` or `admin`, which makes it a subset of what the read gate admits: such a rule satisfies the tenant half and forces `check_repository_action`'s rule branch, which the same rule then satisfies.

  **Where search now sits.** `GET /api/v1/repositories` and the resolver's pre-existing `role_assignments` arm are both tenant-only and action-blind, and neither is changed here. So search is now strictly narrower than the repository listing (a `{write}`-only grant lists the repository but does not search it) and still wider than the read gate, with the entire remaining gap being that untouched `role_assignments` arm. That arm is wider than a single missing `read`: a *global* role assignment (`repository_id IS NULL`) with a role carrying no permissions makes every repository searchable while the read gate denies each one, and a role that does carry `read` still searches a repository on which an applicable `{write}`-only rule makes the read gate refuse — both exactly as before this release. Closing that gap would narrow existing behaviour and belongs to its own change.

  For performance the arm is expressed as a set-driven join from `permissions` into `repositories` rather than as a correlated `EXISTS` over every repository row. The correlated form re-ran the fragment's project subquery once per repository, so its cost tracked the instance's repository count rather than the caller's access: measured on a 10,000-repository instance it added 18.6 ms to every search request from every non-admin caller, including callers holding two grants, against a 1.2 ms baseline. The join form is 1.8 ms for that caller. Because the arm is no longer the verbatim shared fragment, two DB-backed tests pin it: one asserts set equality against a reference query built from the real `permissions_grant_exists_for` plus the read term over a matrix of every grant shape, and one asserts that every repository the arm yields passes `user_can_access_repo(.., READ)`.

  **Upgrade note:** search result sets will grow for users holding `permissions` grants that carry `read` or `admin`. Grants that omit both — a `{write}`-only publisher, say — do not become searchable, so no principal gains visibility of artifact contents that `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}` would refuse it. API-token repository scope is unchanged and is still intersected after visibility is resolved.

### Security

- **An anonymous `docker pull` told the caller whether a private repository exists** (#3730). On `/v2`, every read handler resolved the repository before checking visibility, so a credential-less caller got the `401` + `WWW-Authenticate` bearer challenge for a private repository but `404 NAME_UNKNOWN` for a key naming no repository at all — the existence oracle #1808 closed on the native format routes, still open on the docker-pull path one hop before the gates #3716 and #3717 unify for authenticated callers. Guessing a key and reading the status answered "is this a private repository?" for anyone who could reach the registry. Anonymous reads (`GET`/`HEAD` manifests, blobs, `tags/list`, referrers) now ask only whether the key is a *public* repository: a private repository and a missing key leave by the same branch with the byte-identical challenge, so the two are indistinguishable before authentication. Public repositories keep their anonymous 200/404 (their existence is not secret), authenticated callers keep the #3716 existence-hiding `404 NAME_UNKNOWN` pair, a saturated pool still sheds its retryable 503, and `/v2/` and `/v2/_catalog` are unchanged. One configuration is carved out: under Docker-mirror mode (`AK_DEFAULT_DOCKER_MIRROR_REPO`, opt-in and off by default) a missing key is re-resolved to the mirror repository before the visibility decision, so with a public mirror the 401/404 difference remains — that deployment deliberately serves arbitrary keys from upstream, so the key space is no longer this registry's.

  **Upgrade note:** an anonymous probe of a nonexistent repository on `/v2` now answers `401` with the bearer challenge instead of `404 NAME_UNKNOWN`, so `docker pull` of a typo'd or deleted name prompts for login rather than reporting the repository as missing; the real `404` follows once the client authenticates. Scripts that treat a `/v2` `401` as fatal should retry with credentials, as the Docker/OCI token handshake already does.

- **A crafted sdist made the PyPI upload route decompress a tar extension record in full before any size cap ran, and the same walk was unbudgeted in four other format extractors** (#3672). #3526 (backup restore) and #3662 (scanner) each fixed one instance of the same defect: `tar` consumes GNU LongName (`L`), GNU LongLink (`K`) and PAX (`x`) extension records *inside* `entries().next()`, via `EntryFields::read_all`, so a bound placed on the entry the iterator yields — the `PKG-INFO` `take()` on the pypi path, or nothing at all on the others — runs after the record has already been inflated and held in memory. Because the inflation is driven by what the record declares rather than by the bytes on the wire, a tarball of a few hundred kilobytes was hundreds of megabytes of resident memory per request. Six tar walks still built `tar::Archive` directly on the gzip decoder; each now wraps the decoded stream in the shared ingest budget (`util::bounded_archive::budgeted`, the placement `HelmHandler` and the conda/protobuf handlers already used), so every record type — and the bodies of entries skipped on the way to the metadata file — is bounded by `MAX_INGEST_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` (128 MiB by default). The client-reachable site is `PypiHandler::extract_sdist_metadata_reader`, reached by any publisher through `POST` upload (`validate_upload_file`); a breach there is now **rejected with `400` and a fixed message** (`Source distribution expands beyond the decompression budget; refusing suspected decompression bomb`) rather than treated as "no metadata" and stored — a stored bomb would make every later walk of it (serve, scan, `parse_metadata`) pay the budget again — and that validation walk now runs under the same ingest-extraction permit (`with_ingest_extraction_async`, 8 global / 4 per repository by default) as the helm, protobuf, conda and rubygems uploads, so concurrent sdist uploads cannot each inflate to the budget at once. Other unparseable sdists are still passed through as before. The remaining four wrapped sites — `NpmHandler::extract_package_json`, `CargoHandler::extract_cargo_toml`, `AlpineHandler::extract_pkginfo`, `ProtobufHandler::extract_buf_yaml`/`validate_bundle` — are reached only through the admin format-test route (`FormatHandler::parse_metadata`/`validate`); their upload handlers already used budgeted or capped readers, so those wraps are defence in depth. The other `tar::Archive::new` sites walk a buffer that was already size-capped before the tar reader saw it (the apk control segment, the conda `info-*.tar.zst`, the Helm lint checker) or an archive the server built itself (the backup artifact count), and are unchanged.

  **Upgrade note:** the 128 MiB ceiling now applies to the decompressed bytes an sdist, npm tarball, crate, apk or protobuf bundle yields *before* its metadata file is reached (`PKG-INFO`, `package/package.json`, `Cargo.toml`, `.PKGINFO`, `buf.yaml` / the first `.proto`). A legitimate archive that large is unusual, and the cap is the same one Helm, Debian, RubyGems and the other formats have honoured since #2556; raise `MAX_INGEST_DECOMPRESSED_BYTES` if an archive this size is refused, and note that a PyPI sdist upload refused for this reason now fails with `400` instead of being accepted.

- **A NUL byte in a JSON body field still reached Postgres as a 500 on five routes — one of them the unauthenticated SSO code exchange** (#3713). #3673 closed the query string at the middleware and the login `username` at its field, and its audit found the body-side carriers that remained: `code` on `POST /api/v1/auth/sso/exchange`, bound into `DELETE FROM sso_exchange_codes WHERE code = $1` on a route that needs no credential and carries no rate limiter, so a `\u0000` escape in it was an anonymous `500 INTERNAL_ERROR` plus a pool checkout and a Postgres `ERROR` line where the same request without it is a 401; and, for any logged-in user, the six text fields of `POST /api/v1/builds` (`name`, `agent`, `vcs_url`, `vcs_revision`, `vcs_branch`, `vcs_message`) and — found in review, not in the issue — the four text fields of each entry on `POST /api/v1/builds/{id}/artifacts` (`module_name`, `name`, `path`, `checksum_sha256`), the API-token `name` on `POST /api/v1/auth/tokens`, and the download-ticket `purpose` on `POST /api/v1/auth/ticket` — whose sibling `resource_path` already refused every byte below 0x20 with a 400. Each of those fields now carries the `deserialize_nul_free_string` hook #3673 introduced (an `Option<String>` twin, `deserialize_nul_free_opt_string`, covers the six optional ones), so a NUL is refused at deserialization and the answer is the `Json` extractor's ordinary `400 VALIDATION_ERROR` envelope, before the handler and before any query runs. The refusal names only the offending byte and is identical whether or not the value would have matched a row, so it is no oracle; a body without a NUL is parsed exactly as before, and an absent optional field still defaults to `null`.

  **Upgrade note:** this changes observable status codes. The SSO and builds handlers were still on `axum::Json`, whose rejections are a 422 (malformed body) or a 415 (wrong or missing `Content-Type`) with a plain-text body; both modules now use the crate's `Json`, whose `map_json_rejection` turns *every* rejection into the documented envelope. A client that matched `422` or `415` from `POST /api/v1/auth/sso/exchange`, `POST /api/v1/auth/sso/ldap/{id}/login`, `POST /api/v1/builds`, `PUT /api/v1/builds/{id}` or `POST /api/v1/builds/{id}/artifacts` now receives `400` with the `{"code":"VALIDATION_ERROR"}` envelope — the same answer every other handler has given since #1368. 413 does not move: neither mount carries a body limit.

  This closes the four sites the audit measured plus the artifacts sibling, not the class. A generic answer — the hook on every bound `String` field, or a `Json<T>` rejection layer that walks string values — is the structural fix and remains open; the per-field hook is the shape #3673 chose because a body is a stream and binary uploads must not be scanned. The `Authorization: Basic` username reaches the same `WHERE username = $1` bind but the middleware collapses the driver error into the 401 the control gets — no 500, no oracle, one wasted pool checkout — and is deliberately left as documented.

- **A native-format read of a private repository answered 403 when the repository carried any ACL rule and 404 when it did not, disclosing both its existence and that it is governed by an ACL** (#3524). `repo_visibility_middleware` has two deny paths for an authenticated caller holding no grant on a PRIVATE repository, and they answered differently based on something the caller has no business learning: if any fine-grained rule existed against the repository — for any principal, including a completely unrelated one — the read arm returned `403 You do not have permission to perform this action on this repository`, while a rules-less private repository and a key naming no repository at all both returned `404 Repository not found`. A 403 therefore told an ungranted caller that the repository exists *and* that an ACL governs it, on every native format route (`/maven/...`, `/npm/...`, `/pypi/...`, ...). This is the same oracle class the middleware already closes elsewhere: its no-repo branch mirrors the private-repo 401 byte-for-byte for anonymous callers (#1808) and answers a valid credential with the existence-hiding 404 (GHSA-fv45-mwhh-q23r), and the REST gate is uniform — `require_visible` returns `NotFound` for every denial. The native-format read arm diverged; the OCI `/v2` read gate carries the same construct and is tracked separately (#3716).

  That arm now returns the same `404 Repository not found` as the rules-less branch immediately below it, so all three cases are byte-identical in status, content type and body. The branch is reachable only for private repositories — the read action on a public repository short-circuits through the `public_read_satisfies_acl` baseline (#2329) before any ACL check — so public repositories, members of either kind of private repository, and anonymous callers (still `401` + `WWW-Authenticate`, #508/#1808) are all unaffected. Writes and deletes are deliberately unchanged and still answer `403`: a caller issuing a `PUT` has generally already read the repository, so the more useful answer there is the permission denial. The denial is still logged server-side with the repository and user id, so an operator can tell "no such repository" from "a repository you may not see" even though the wire cannot.

  **Upgrade note:** this changes an observable status code. A client or script that distinguishes `403` from `404` on a native-format `GET`/`HEAD` against a private repository will now see `404` where it previously saw `403` whenever the repository carries any fine-grained permission rule. Treat both as "not accessible"; a `403` on these routes now means only a token-scope refusal (#504) or a denied write. Both of those still answer `403` for an existing repository and `404` for a missing key, so the repository-existence half of the oracle remains reachable by a repository-scoped token (#3717) or by switching to a write method — the latter deliberately, per #3524.

- **`docker pull` of a private repository answered `403 DENIED` when the repository carried any ACL rule and `404 NAME_UNKNOWN` when it did not, disclosing both its existence and that it is governed by an ACL** (#3716). This completes #3524's closure for OCI: `/v2` is mounted outside `repo_visibility_middleware`, so #3709's fix never reached it, and its own read gate (`oci_read_permitted`) consulted `has_any_rules_for_target` on a denial purely to pick the status — `403 DENIED` if any fine-grained rule existed against the repository, for any principal, and `404 NAME_UNKNOWN` otherwise, which is also what a key naming no repository gets. The private-repository read denial now answers that `404 NAME_UNKNOWN` unconditionally, so the ruled, rules-less and no-such-repository cases are identical in status, content type and body, and the rules lookup is gone from the read path. That holds under Docker-mirror mode (`AK_DEFAULT_DOCKER_MIRROR_REPO`) too: there an unknown key is re-resolved to the mirror repository, and the 404 used to echo the mirror's key for an unknown key but the candidate's own key for an existing private one, so the echo alone said which private repositories exist; every read-path 404 now echoes the key the client asked for. Only private repositories reach this branch; public repositories, members, admins, scanner tokens and anonymous callers (still `401` + `WWW-Authenticate`) are unaffected, and pushes and deletes keep `403 DENIED` per #3524.

  **Upgrade note:** a client that distinguishes `403` from `404` on an OCI `GET`/`HEAD` against a private repository now sees `404` where it saw `403` whenever the repository carries a fine-grained rule; a `403 DENIED` on `/v2` now means only a denied write, a token-scope refusal, or a backend-minted scan-pull token used against a repository other than the one it was minted for; the token-scope case still reveals repository existence to a repository-scoped token (#3717).

- **A NUL byte in a query parameter or in the login `username` still reached Postgres as an anonymous 500** (#3673). #3545 and #3665 refuse a `\0` in the request *path*, but the path guard cannot see a query string or a request body, so four anonymously reachable sites survived: `GET /api/v1/search/advanced?name=a%00b` and `?format=a%00b` (both bound verbatim by `build_name_filter`), `GET /api/v1/search/suggest?prefix=a%00b`, and `POST /api/v1/auth/login` with a `\0` in `username` (bound into `WHERE username = $1` before anything else runs, where the identical request without the NUL is a 401). Each cost a pool checkout and a failing query that Postgres rejects at the wire protocol — a trivially craftable request turning into a `500 DATABASE_ERROR` and a Postgres `ERROR` line, on an unauthenticated surface. A fifth carrier, `?cursor=`, surfaced during review and is covered below. `?q=` / `?query=` never produced a 500 — `sanitize_tsquery_lexeme` strips the NUL and the search ran without it — but they do change answer here; see the behaviour note.

  The path guard (`api/middleware/nul_path.rs`) now also refuses a NUL in the **raw query string**, decoded with the same infallible `decode_binary` byte scan and the same `%`-free fast path. That closes every *percent-encoded* query carrier on every surface at once — including parameters added later — rather than the three filters named above, and needs no per-handler code. The refusal keeps the properties #3665 pins for the path half: a 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR` (the OCI distribution-spec envelope on `/v2/`), emitted inside correlation-id so it still carries `X-Correlation-ID`, and byte-identical for a real repository, an unknown one and an unrouted path, so answering before authentication is no existence oracle.

  One query parameter carries its own encoding and is therefore invisible to that boundary: `?cursor=` on the artifact listing is base64 over JSON, so `serde_json` turns a `\u0000` escape inside it into a real `\0` with no percent-escape for the guard to see, and the decoded cursor halves are bound as `after_path` / `after_name` in six listing statements (the flat listing uses only the first half, so a NUL confined to the second half went 200 there and now answers 400 like the rest). Measured on a public repository, anonymously, it was the same 500 (`?cursor=WyJhXHUwMDAwYiIsIiJd` → 500, control `WyJhYiIsIiJd` → 200). `decode_keyset_cursor` now rejects a decoded component containing a NUL, which routes it through the malformed-cursor arm that already answers 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR` — a NUL cursor was never one this server issued, so no client that paginates with a `next_cursor` it was given is affected.

  **Behaviour note.** Unlike the path guard, this one does change the answer for some requests that previously returned 200: a NUL anywhere in a query string is now a 400, including on `?q=` / `?query=`, where `sanitize_tsquery_lexeme` silently stripped the byte and searched without it, and on routes that never read the parameter (`/healthz?x=a%00b`, `/livez?x=a%00b`, an unused tracking parameter beside an otherwise working `?name=` search). None of those could ever return artifact content, and a NUL in a query string has no legitimate meaning on any route, so refusing them is the intended trade rather than a side effect — but a client that was sending one and getting a stripped-value 200 will now see a 400.

  The body site is refused at its own field instead. A body is a stream, so a `Json<T>` layer would have to walk every request's bytes — binary uploads included — to cover one text field; `LoginRequest::username` carries a `#[serde(deserialize_with = ...)]` hook (`extractors::deserialize_nul_free_string`) that rejects a `\0`, which the crate's `Json` extractor renders as the same 400 `VALIDATION_ERROR` envelope as any other malformed body, before the handler and before the query. `password` deliberately has no hook: it is bcrypt-compared, never bound, and `bcrypt` treats a NUL-bearing password as an ordinary distinct password, so hooking it could lock out an account whose stored credential contains one. The search filters need no hook either — they arrive in the query string, which the guard now covers. Deliberately NUL-only in all three places: every other byte a client may legitimately send is routed, decoded and parsed exactly as before.

  The remaining JSON body fields are **not** closed by this change and are tracked in #3713: `POST /api/v1/auth/sso/exchange` binds `code` verbatim on an unauthenticated route that carries no rate limiter, and three lower-tier endpoints (`POST /builds`, the API-token `name`, the download-ticket `purpose`) do the same for any logged-in user. The `Authorization: Basic` carrier reaches the same `WHERE username = $1` bind as the login body, but the middleware collapses the driver error into the same 401 the control gets, so it costs a pool checkout and a Postgres `ERROR` line without a 500 or an oracle; it is noted on #3713 rather than fixed here.

- **41 handler-local error paths returned the raw Postgres/sqlx or IO error in their response body, most of them to unauthenticated callers** (#3667, #3623, #3666, #3545). #3623/#3666 sanitised `handlers::db_err`, the shared mapper. A second, larger group of sites never called it: they hold a *format-specific* error envelope — Git LFS's `{"message": …}`, Connect's `{"code","message"}`, Swift's `application/problem+json`, npm's `{"error": …}`, the promotion result's `message`, Maven's and pub's plain-text 500 — and so built the body themselves with `format!("Database error: {}", e)`. 39 such sites across seven handlers (`gitlfs` 15, `protobuf` 11, `swift` 8, `promotion` 2, `maven`, `npm`, `pub_registry` 1 each) handed the caller whatever the driver said, e.g. `Database error: error returned from database: invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00` from a NUL byte in a client-supplied string, disclosing driver, schema, constraint and query-shape detail. Most of these routes serve public repositories anonymously, so no credentials were needed to elicit one. Two sites of the same class outside the `Database error:` phrasing are fixed with them: `error_helpers::require_signing_key` (reached from the anonymous `repomd.xml.asc` / `repomd.xml.key` / `Release.gpg` metadata-signing endpoints) interpolated the key-lookup failure, and `incus::fs_err`, on the `write:artifacts`-gated Incus upload and finalize paths, interpolated the raw IO error (errno and OS detail). One arm away from that site, `incus::seal_staging_file` formatted the absolute staging path (`<storage_path>/.incoming/…`) into its "staged upload data is missing" 500; the path now goes to the log and the body is fixed text.

  Each site keeps its own envelope — the change is one line per site — and takes its message from a new `handlers::db_err_message`, which logs the raw error server-side exactly as `AppError::into_response` does for `db_err` and returns the same stable text the sanitised envelope carries: `Database operation failed`, or `Database connection pool is saturated, retry shortly` when the pool is saturated, which the existing `db_status` already sheds to 503 + `Retry-After` (#2083). Status codes are untouched; only the body changed. `require_signing_key` keeps #2636's 500-vs-404 split intact — a repository with no key is still a 404 and a key that will not load is still a loud 500, now loud in the log rather than in the response — and `fs_err` still names the operation it failed at (`Failed to create temp file`), which is a fixed internal literal, just not the error. **Upgrade note:** any client or script scraping the old `Database error: ...` or `Failed to load signing key: ...` text off a 500 from these routes must stop; the message is now stable by design.

  A structural gate in the shape of the #3500 one refuses any `.rs` file under `api/handlers`, outside its `#[cfg(test)]` modules, that contains a format string beginning `Database error: {`. It keys on the string literal rather than on `format!(` so a `write!`, a wrapped `format!` or an `AppError::Internal(format!(…))` is caught too. It is a **lint, not a proof**: a site that invents different wording walks past it. Its job is narrower — 39 near-identical sites are exactly what a new handler gets copy-pasted from — and the per-handler tests are the behavioural pin.

- **One remote repository's upstream credentials could be spent by another repository that has none** (#3606). The in-memory OCI bearer-token cache was keyed on `realm`, `service` and `scope` only. That map belongs to the single `UpstreamClient` the process-wide `ProxyService` owns, so it is shared by every Remote repository in the deployment: a repository holding upstream credentials exchanged them for a token against a private registry, and a *different* Remote repository pointed at the same registry — potentially another team's, with no credentials configured at all — produced the identical key on its next pull and was handed that token. It then read whatever the credentialed repository could read, for as long as the entry stayed inside its TTL. The credential itself was never disclosed; the access it grants was. No configuration flag was involved — two Remote repositories against one registry with credentials on one of them is all it took, which is the ordinary shape when one team mirrors a private registry and another mirrors its public subset.

  The cache key now also carries a SHA-256 digest of the credential the token was minted under, so anonymous fetches and each distinct credential occupy separate entries. The digest is keyed on the credential rather than on the repository id deliberately: a token is a function of the credential exchanged for it, so two repositories presenting the *same* credential are entitled to the same token and still share the entry, while keying on repository id alone would lose those hits and would additionally keep serving a token minted under a credential that has since been rotated. Only the digest is ever cached — never the secret — and `None` (which includes a cross-origin realm stripped of credentials by GHSA-78h6-3wp8-2542's origin pinning) hashes to its own bucket, so an uncredentialed exchange can never land on a credentialed entry. Distinct credentials multiply the number of live entries; the bound is unchanged in kind, since entries past their TTL are still evicted on every write and the TTL is still capped at an hour. No configuration or upgrade action is required.

- **`handlers::db_err` returned the raw Postgres/sqlx error string in its 500 body, to unauthenticated callers** (#3623). The shared DB-error mapper that 114 call sites across 21 format handlers reach through `.map_err(super::db_err)?` (rpm, ansible, hex, debian, helm, goproxy, cocoapods, sbt, composer, chef, conan, nuget, cran, alpine, rubygems, terraform, ...) built its response as a plain-text `format!("Database error: {}", e)`, so whatever the driver said went straight back over the wire — e.g. `Database error: error returned from database: invalid byte sequence for encoding "UTF8": 0x00` from a NUL byte in a client-supplied string. These routes serve public repositories anonymously, so no credentials were needed to elicit one, and the message discloses driver, encoding and query-shape detail that a well-behaved 500 should not. This was the coarser half of the leak #3545 closed on the generic routes, which have mapped `AppError::Database` to a sanitized envelope all along.

  `db_err` now delegates to `error_helpers::map_db_err`, the same sanitizer, so every DB failure on these routes answers with the API-wide `{"code":"DATABASE_ERROR","message":"Database operation failed"}` JSON body and the raw text is written only to the server-side `tracing` event `AppError::into_response` already emits. Operators gain visibility rather than lose it: on the old path the non-timeout branch logged nothing at all, so these 114 call sites emit a server-side ERROR for the first time — expect them to become audible during a database outage. The pool-timeout shed is unchanged in behaviour and now shares the same path: a saturated pool is still 503 + `Retry-After: 1`, carrying `POOL_EXHAUSTED` and the actionable "Database connection pool is saturated, retry shortly" message (#2083). Status codes are otherwise untouched; only the body changed. **Upgrade note:** any client or script scraping the old `Database error: ...` prefix off a 500 from these routes must read the JSON `code` field instead. The format-specific error envelopes that build their own body (npm, OCI, Git-LFS, protobuf, swift, ...) do not go through `db_err` and are tracked separately in #3667.

- **Search and listing filters treated a `%`, `_` or `\` in the user's term as a wildcard instead of a literal** (#3557). #3500 closed the sites that assemble a `LIKE` pattern inside SQL (`LIKE $2 || '%'`); a second group builds the pattern in Rust instead — `format!("%{}%", term)` for a `?search=`/`?q=` box, `format!("{}%", prefix)` for the suggest completions, `format!("{}/%", key)` for a directory — and binds it whole to a bare `name ILIKE $2`. The #3500 source gate cannot see that shape: by the time the string reaches SQL it is a single bind with no concatenation to key on, which is why the cohort survived the #998/#1000 escaping wave and the #3492 audit. Unescaped, a `%` typed into a search box matched any run of characters and a `_` any single one, so both the page and the `total` that drives `total_pages` carried rows the caller never asked for; a backslash — Postgres's DEFAULT `LIKE` escape character — quoted the character after it, so an artifact, user, group, build, package or repository whose name contains one could not be found by typing its own name. Every affected site now escapes its term through the shared `escape_like_literal` helper before the `%` is appended, across the admin user/group/build/package listings, the repository and artifact listings (single-repository and virtual), the grouped-Maven catalog listings, the Composer, NuGet and Terraform registry searches, search suggest, and the advanced-search `?name=` filter. The scope is one already-authorized set of rows in every case, so this widened result sets rather than crossing a permission boundary — though on the unauthenticated `GET /api/v1/search/suggest` a single `%` was an enumeration oracle over every artifact name the same caller could already have paged through.

  Search boxes are now a **literal substring search** — the direction the already-escaped sites took — not a wildcard mini-language: a query of `100%` finds the row named `100%`. The one exception is `GET /api/v1/search/advanced`'s `?name=` filter, where `*` remains the wildcard because the code intends it to be; there the term is escaped *first* and the `*` translated afterwards, so `?name=a_b.jar` no longer also returns `axb.jar` while `?name=my-lib*` still wildcards. Two `LIKE ANY($n)` fan-outs (`ArtifactService::list_by_path_prefixes`, `proxy_catalog::paths_under_prefixes`) keep their over-match: they re-check every row exactly in Rust, and each now wraps its pattern in a `like_any_overmatch_accepted` marker function so the exception is a code construct the class gate checks rather than a comment. `curation_service::search_packages` kept a third hand-rolled copy of the escape rule and now routes through the shared helper.

  The SQL-side `ESCAPE '\'` clauses added alongside are **semantically inert** — `\` is already Postgres's default escape character — and are not the behaviour change; they document the helper's contract and are what the structural gates read. The behaviour change is entirely `escape_like_literal`. The #3500 structural gate likewise gains a companion scanner keyed on the Rust literal rather than the SQL text, but it is a **lint, not a proof**: like the #3500 gate it only shows that an escaper is used somewhere in the function owning the `format!`, not that it is used on that particular value, and it does not see a pattern built with `push_str`, `+` or `concat!`. It exists to stop a *new* site in this shape being added with no escaping story at all; the DB-backed behavioural tests are the real regression pin.

- **A percent-encoded NUL in any URL path turned an anonymous request into a 500 from the database driver** (#3622). `%00` in a wildcard path segment is decoded by the router into a literal `\0`, and Postgres rejects that byte at the wire protocol — so a trivially craftable unauthenticated read of a *public* repository cost a connection checkout plus a failing query and answered `500 DATABASE_ERROR`, a cheap pool-amplification and log-noise primitive as well as a coarse implementation-detail leak. #3621 proposes closing the four generic repository-scoped routes at their own path extraction (#3545); the same class also reached the driver through the format-native wildcard routes (`/maven/{key}/*path`, `/rpm/{key}/packages/*path`, `/hex/{key}/tarballs/*path`, `/puppet/{key}/v3/files/*path`, `/ansible/{key}/download/*path`) and through the repository **key** segment itself (`GET /api/v1/repositories/pub%00gen/artifacts/a`, via `get_by_key`).

  With ~40 format handlers on that surface, the fix is a single shared boundary rather than a per-handler check: a global layer inspects the percent-decoded request path and refuses a NUL with a 400 before routing, so every current and future handler is covered at once. It is deliberately NUL-only — no other byte a client may legitimately percent-encode is touched — and Postgres cannot store `0x00` in a `text` column at all, so no persisted artifact path or repository key can contain one and no request that could ever have returned artifact content changes status (a handful of routes the issue lists as "already safe" do move from one refusal to another, e.g. 404 to 400). The check reads **bytes**, not a decoded `String`: `urlencoding::decode` fails on a path whose decoded bytes are not valid UTF-8 anywhere, which would let one stray `%C0%80` hide a `%00` in another segment (`/maven/pub%00key/a%C0%80b`) — the key-decoding visibility middleware would still bind that NUL to a query. A refusal on the `/v2` OCI surface is emitted as the distribution-spec error envelope rather than the REST body, matching #3284.

  The guard covers the **path** only. A NUL in a query parameter or a JSON body still reaches the driver as an anonymous 500 on a few endpoints (`/api/v1/search/advanced?name=`, `?format=`, `/api/v1/search/suggest?prefix=`, `POST /api/v1/auth/login`) — pre-existing behaviour, unchanged either way by this release, and tracked in #3673 for the query/body half of the same class.

- **A crafted archive uploaded to any writable repository made the scanner decompress unbounded data on the server's own time** (#3528). `unpack_tar_limited` tracked its cumulative-byte, per-entry and entry-count ceilings *inside* the entry loop, i.e. after the tar iterator had already yielded — but `tar` consumes GNU LongName (`L`), GNU LongLink (`K`) and PAX (`x`) extension records inside `entries().next()` itself, via `EntryFields::read_all`, which caps only its 128 KiB preallocation and then reads the full size the record declares. A record declaring gigabytes was therefore inflated and allocated before the entry count, the traversal guard or the per-entry copy ran, and none of them ever saw those bytes: the call returned `Ok`, and the function's own doc comment promised a guarantee ("enforced *during* extraction ... aborts mid-stream") the code did not provide. Reproduced at `max_bytes=1024, max_entries=4` against a GNU LongName record: over 400 MiB of RSS growth, and a successful return. The ratio is set by what the record declares, not by the size of the archive, so a few hundred kilobytes of upload is gigabytes of resident memory on the scanner host. The byte budget now wraps the decoded stream before the tar reader sees it — the same placement #3526 gave the backup restore — so every record type, including the bodies of skipped entries (symlinks, devices, `..` members) that `tar` reads and discards to reach the next header and that were never charged either, is bounded by the same `2 GiB` ceiling (`SCAN_MAX_EXTRACTED_BYTES`, unchanged). That ceiling is what an attacker can now make the scanner read, not a proportion of the upload; a proportional budget like the backup path's is a follow-up. The extractor is reached both from hosted uploads (any writable credential) and from the synchronous inline proxy scan, and the inline 30 s budget bounds the *wait*, not the blocking extraction thread, so the reader-level bound is the only thing that stops the inflation on either path. Framing overhead (512-byte headers and padding per entry) now counts against the budget, which at the 200,000-entry cap is at most ~9.5 % of it; a refusal there degrades to the raw-file scan rather than failing the publish.

  Reachable by any authenticated non-admin with **repository write**: the scan runs asynchronously on push (`prepare_pinned` → `extract_archive` → `extract_archive_blocking` → `unpack_tar_limited`), so uploading the archive is the whole attack. The cumulative-byte budget now wraps the *decoded* stream **before** `tar::Archive::new`, using the same `util::bounded_archive` `BudgetReader` that #3526 put under `BackupService::extract_entries` and that the other ~20 extractors in this codebase already use. That placement is what makes the bound complete — it charges entry bodies, extension records, the 512-byte header of every member and the padding between them alike, and no allocation can outrun it because the reader stops supplying bytes at the cap. The per-entry accounting is kept as defence in depth, and a budget breach still surfaces as the existing "suspected decompression bomb" error wherever it is caught. Limits and their environment overrides are unchanged (`MAX_SCAN_EXTRACTED_BYTES`, 2 GiB by default; 200,000 entries), and archives that legitimately carry these records — any path over the 100-char ustar name field — still extract: the budget bounds extension records, it does not reject them.

- **The local login endpoint no longer reveals whether a username exists** (#3504). `POST /api/v1/auth/login` is unauthenticated, and `AppError::Authentication` passes its message straight through to the response body, so the wording of a failed login was visible to anyone. Two arms of `AuthService::authenticate` answered only for usernames that exist and are active: a username belonging to an LDAP/OIDC/SAML account answered `401 {"message":"Use SSO provider to authenticate"}` — one request per candidate, with any password, confirming both the account and its identity source — and an account driven past `account_lockout_threshold` answered `401 {"message":"Account temporarily locked due to too many failed login attempts"}`, which an unknown username can never produce because there is no row to lock. Every credential-level arm — unknown or inactive username, federated account, missing password hash, wrong password, locked account — now returns the identical status and body (the one exception, a corrupt stored hash, is described below), and the username, the auth provider and the lockout state stay in the server log at WARN under the `security` target. This is the same fix, in the same shape, that #3371 applied to the LDAP login endpoint; it was called out as outstanding in that entry.

  All versions through 1.8.2 carry both leaks. No configuration change is needed and no credentials were exposed — what leaked is account existence, not authentication material.

  **The lockout is no longer disclosed to the caller — a deliberate product decision, and the one behaviour change an end user will notice.** A locked account now receives the same `Invalid username or password` as every other failure. The lockout itself is unchanged: it is still enforced, `failed_login_attempts` and `locked_until` are still written exactly as before, and a correct password still authenticates past the lock and clears the counters (#1871). Only the message changed. The trade is deliberate — telling the owner *why* their password is being refused is genuinely useful, but an unknown username has no row to lock and so can never produce that message, which made it a five-request existence check for any account. A user who has genuinely forgotten their password now sees the same message throughout and needs an administrator; operators keep the signal in the security log and, new in this release, in the audit event's `reason` field (`unknown_or_inactive_user`, `federated_account`, `no_password_hash`, `invalid_password`, `account_locked`), so a SIEM can still separate a username sweep from a locked-out user even though the response cannot. **Not verified:** `artifact-keeper-web` and the SDK live in separate repositories and were not checked for code that string-matches the old lockout text to render a "try again later" banner; nothing in this repository parses it.

  **Timing.** The message arms are only half the oracle: on the login path the arms that never reach a stored hash used to return before any bcrypt work, while a wrong password paid the full cost factor. They now substitute the dummy hash `validate_api_token` already keeps for this purpose into the *same* `verify_password(...)?` call the real path runs — one call site for every arm, so the code path, the error type and the status are identical by construction. That matters beyond the mean: `verify_password` sheds to 503 when the auth-concurrency semaphore saturates, and an arm that discarded its result would answer 401 for an absent username while a real account answered 503, which is a one-request oracle in place of the message one. The pad is charged **only** to `POST /api/v1/auth/login`, through a separate `authenticate_for_login` entry point. The shared `AuthService::authenticate` — which the Basic-auth package-manager paths, the OCI `/v2/` probe and the conda path-token handler reach *before* the API-token path, so in an SSO-only deployment every `cargo`/`npm`/`pip` request takes a rejection arm — keeps main's behaviour exactly: it returns without bcrypt, and it emits no log line on those arms. (Both matter. Padding there would put a cost-12 bcrypt in front of machine-to-machine traffic; logging there would write one WARN per package request, at the same target and level as the login signal below, burying it.) A residual sub-millisecond difference remains — the wrong-password arms also run an `UPDATE` — which is the same order as the residual the #3371 entry records and far below what is separable through the login limiter.

  **New setting: a per-source-IP budget for the bcrypt pad.** `RATE_LIMIT_LOGIN_FAILED_PER_IP_PER_WINDOW` (default **30**) over `RATE_LIMIT_LOGIN_FAILED_PER_IP_WINDOW_SECS` (default **300**); `0` disables it and the pad always runs. It exists because the pad hands an anonymous caller a cost-12 bcrypt per request, and the existing login limiter cannot bound that: it is keyed `login:{username}|{ip}`, which is what stops a flood against one identity from locking out others — and which also means an attacker who changes the username on every request gets a fresh bucket each time, leaving only the global backstop (`RATE_LIMIT_LOGIN_GLOBAL_PER_WINDOW`, 8192/60 s) in the way. The new budget accrues against the source IP for each *failed* login whatever username it named.

  **It gates the pad, not the request — it never returns 429 and never refuses a login.** Once an IP has spent its budget, logins from it run *unpadded*: an arm with no usable password hash answers without bcrypt, while any account that has one is still verified normally, so a correct password always authenticates. A successful login does not reset the bucket — being inside a spent one costs a legitimate user nothing, and resetting would void the bound, since on a shared egress ordinary logins would continuously refill an attacker's sweep budget; the window expires on its own. **The honest trade:** an IP that has burned its budget gets the timing oracle back for the rest of the window. That is the price of holding an attacker to at most 30 padded verifies per IP per window without ever shedding a legitimate user — and shedding is not an option here, because behind a reverse proxy that does not set `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS` every user resolves to the proxy's own address, so one attacker would deny login to the entire deployment. (Note `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_PROXY_CIDRS`, which governs whether `X-Forwarded-For` is believed — not `RATE_LIMIT_TRUSTED_CIDRS`, which exempts addresses from rate limiting altogether and would also remove the per-`(username, IP)` brute-force budget.) Raise the budget if a single egress legitimately produces many failed logins per five minutes.

  One arm is **not** unified and is called out rather than hidden: a `users` row whose `password_hash` is not valid bcrypt — an imported account, or a placeholder — makes `verify_password` fail to parse it and answers `500`, not `401`. That is a data-integrity fault rather than a credential decision, it is not attacker-controllable (it requires a row that already exists in that state), and reporting it as a bad password would hide a broken account from the operator who has to fix it.

- **The bundled `grype` scanner is rebuilt from upstream v0.118.0, clearing the backend half of a HIGH gRPC advisory that is blocking every image publish** (#3655, #3465). The scanner-adapter image fails the same gate on the same advisory against its bundled `trivy`, which is pinned by digest from artifact-keeper/trivy and is fixed there (artifact-keeper/trivy#12); publishes resume only once both have landed. `usr/local/bin/grype` in the backend image carried `google.golang.org/grpc v1.82.1`, and CVE-2026-84304 (HIGH, fixed in grpc v1.83.1) was failing Docker Publish's `Security Scan` on `main` — the gate every `merge-*` job depends on — so no image was published from `main` and Release Preflight read NOT READY. The grype source pin moves v0.117.0 → **v0.118.0** (commit `756eb9a2`), which is the newest anchore/grype release and gets the binary to grpc v1.83.0, one patch short of the fix; the remaining patch is applied as an explicit `go get google.golang.org/grpc@v1.83.1` in the build stage, and the compiled binary's Go build info is asserted to record v1.83.1 — a module graph that is bumped but never linked into the artifact clears nothing.

  The same bump **retires** the `golang.org/x/mod` override #3465 added for CVE-2026-56864 / CVE-2026-56865: v0.118.0's own `go.mod` pins x/mod v0.40.0, so the override became a duplicate of a shipped release — "strictly worse than the bump it imitates", in its own words — and the staleness guard it carried is exactly what stopped the build until it was deleted. That is an override reaching its documented end rather than being noticed by hand, and the grpc block replacing it carries the same guard and the same shape of removal condition: the first grype release whose `go.mod` pins grpc ≥ v1.83.1. Unlike x/mod, whose advisories were scoped to `x/mod/sumdb` and were never linked into `cmd/grype`, grpc *is* linked (`grype/internal/file` → `hashicorp/go-getter` → `cloud.google.com/go/storage`), so this is a fixable HIGH in code the shipped binary really contains, not an artifact of Trivy reading Go binaries at module granularity. Upstream `main` already carries the bump (anchore/grype#3686, merged after v0.118.0 was cut), so the override pulls a merged upstream commit forward by one release cycle rather than inventing a pin.

  Two pieces of bookkeeping travel with it. `GO_MIN_PATCH` moves 1.26.6 → **1.27.1**: #3579 moved the stage to `golang:1.27-alpine` but left the floor on the 1.26 line, and because the check is a `sort -V` every 1.27.x cleared it, so the guard against a mirror lagging behind had gone inert. And the five `github.com/docker/docker` suppressions in `.trivyignore` **stay live** — the retry that file asks for on every scanner bump was run and still fails: v0.118.0 pins v28.5.2+incompatible, unchanged, and `go mod edit -require=github.com/docker/docker@v29.3.1+incompatible` still fails with "unknown revision v29.3.1". Nothing operator-facing changes: `grype --version` still prints the upstream tag (now `0.118.0`), the supported DB schema is unchanged, and the recorded `scanner_version` and build-time seeded vulnerability DB are unaffected.

- **A repository-scoped credential was refused on a public repository that the same request served anonymously** (#3648). `repo_visibility_middleware` runs the #504 API-token repository-scope check (`AccessScope::grants`) immediately after the visibility check, and that scope check had no `is_public` bypass. An anonymous caller never reaches it — there is no `AuthExtension` to test — so a public repository was served unconditionally with no credential, while the identical request carrying a token scoped to a *different* repository was answered `403 Token does not have access to this repository`. Presenting a valid credential therefore granted strictly *less* access than presenting none, on exactly the repositories that are readable by everyone. pip renders that 403 as `No matching distribution found`, so the operator sees a resolution failure and nothing pointing at authorization; a scoped `~/.netrc` entry or a single newly-minted scoped token reintroduces it on a deployment where every other token is read-all. The gate now takes the same `public_read_satisfies_acl` baseline the fine-grained ACL arm ~40 lines below it already applies for the same reason (#2329), and that the REST read gate `require_visible` applies as its own unconditional public short-circuit.

  The exemption is **reads only**, and nothing else moved. It is keyed on `action_for_method`, so `GET`/`HEAD`/`OPTIONS` take it and a token scoped to repository A still cannot `PUT`, `POST` or `DELETE` on public repository B, matching `require_repo_write_access` on the REST side; the write path's own `#508` authentication gate runs before this check and is untouched. The one POST that also takes it is `POST /{repo}/gallery/extensionquery`, the VS Code gallery *search* verb — the sole member of `is_anonymous_readable_format_post`, i.e. the POSTs a public repository must serve to an anonymous caller, so it inverted in exactly the same way and the ACL arm below it already classified it as a read. git-lfs `objects/batch` (an upload negotiation) and conan `users/authenticate` (a credential exchange) both answer 401 to an anonymous caller under `#508`, so they have no anonymous baseline to have fallen below and stay scope-gated. Private repositories never take the bypass, so a scoped token reading a private repository outside its scope is refused exactly as before and the existence-hiding behaviour is unchanged.

  The **middleware's decision** is now identical to the anonymous one — the request is admitted on the same terms rather than on a quieter, credential-aware path — which is what the regression test pins. Handlers that require a credential of their own still answer an authenticated caller differently from an anonymous one, as they always have (conan `users/authenticate` is 401 anonymously and 200 with a token, and the JWT it mints inherits the presenting credential's repository allow-list, so the ceiling is preserved). Note also that the "a credential must never grant less than none" justification presumes an anonymous baseline exists: under `AK_GUEST_ACCESS_ENABLED=false` no anonymous caller reaches a format route at all, and there a scoped token gains read on any repository still flagged public from before the policy was set — consistent with `require_visible` and the #2329 ACL arm, which have both had an unconditional public short-circuit all along, and with `coerce_is_public_for_create`, which prevents new public repositories in that mode.

  Three surfaces were left with the old ordering by that change, because each is a separate gate on a separate mount: the OCI `/v2` read gate (`enforce_token_repo_scope`, #2290), the tree browser (`tree_access_allowed`) and the REST artifact gate (`check_artifact_visibility`). All three are brought into line by the #3704 entry above.

- **The same refusal stood on three more surfaces that the middleware fix could not reach: OCI `/v2`, the tree browser, and the REST artifact gate** (#3704, #3648, #3703). Each is a separate gate on a separate mount, and each ran the API-token repository-scope ceiling *before* consulting `is_public`, so a repository-scoped credential was refused a read that the identical request with no credential at all was served.
