On OCI `/v2` — which `routes.rs` nests before `.merge(format_routes)`, outside `repo_visibility_middleware` entirely — `enforce_token_repo_scope` (#2290) ran ~8 lines ahead of the `public_read_satisfies_acl` bypass in `oci_read_permitted` and again at the top of each of the four read handlers, while an anonymous puller carries the `anonymous` sentinel token for which `authenticate_oci_read` returns `None` and the whole claims block is skipped: `docker pull` of a public image answered 200 anonymously and `403 DENIED` with a token scoped elsewhere. `tree_access_allowed` tested `token_allows` before its `is_public` arm, and `check_artifact_visibility` ran the #504 scope check before anything looked at visibility at all — both answering their existence-hiding refusal where the anonymous request got the content. CI tokens are scoped exactly this way (#3548), so the credential most likely to hit this is the one a pipeline uses.

  All three now take the same `public_read_satisfies_acl(is_public, action)` baseline the middleware took in #3648, and **exactly what a scoped token gains on each is what an anonymous caller was already getting**: on `/v2`, `GET`/`HEAD` of a public repository's manifests, blobs and tag lists — a public `docker pull`; on the tree browser, `GET /api/v1/tree` and `GET /api/v1/tree/content` for a public repository, both of which are already served with no credential; on the REST by-id artifact gate, `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}` and its `/metadata` and `/stats` siblings for an artifact in a public repository. Sub-resources that share `check_artifact_visibility` but require a credential of their own (label listing, quality-gate and scan reads) move to the same public-read baseline, which is the one `require_visible` — the canonical REST read gate on the very same repositories — has applied unconditionally all along (#2329).

  **Nothing else moved.** `public_read_satisfies_acl` is `read`-only by construction: `docker push`, manifest `DELETE`, and the artifact-label `PUT`/`POST`/`DELETE` that share the artifact gate all keep enforcing the scope, which matters most on the label routes because `authorize_label_write` checks only the token's *action* scope, leaving that gate as the sole repository ceiling there. `check_artifact_visibility` now takes the calling handler's `action` explicitly rather than assuming one, so each of its fifteen call sites declares whether it reads or mutates. The OCI scan-pull pin (`enforce_scan_pull_scope`, #2093) is a different ceiling and is **not** relaxed — a scan token is minted for exactly one repository key. **`/v2/_catalog` is deliberately excluded** even though it shares the same read decision: it is an *enumeration* surface that answers an anonymous caller with the 401 `WWW-Authenticate` challenge rather than a public-only listing, so it has no anonymous baseline to have fallen below, and the repository-scope ceiling (#2290/#3316) is precisely what stops a bearer restricted to one repository from learning which others exist — the catalog filter re-applies the unexempted ceiling itself. Private repositories never take the bypass on any of the three, so an out-of-scope read of a private repository is refused exactly as before. The tree browser's `test_access_public_out_of_token_scope_denied`, which pinned the inverted behaviour, is flipped rather than deleted. The `AK_GUEST_ACCESS_ENABLED=false` caveat recorded under #3648 applies unchanged here.

- **A repository-scoped API token could tell whether a private repository exists: 403 on an existing one outside its scope, 404 on a key naming none** (#3717, #504, #3524, #3709, #3751). After #3709 every native-format read denial for a private repository answered the existence-hiding `404 Repository not found` — except the #504 token-scope gate in `repo_visibility_middleware`, which runs ahead of the ACL arm and answered `403 Token does not have access to this repository` for an existing private repository outside the token's `allowed_repo_ids`, while the no-repo branch answered 404. The OCI `/v2` read gate (`enforce_token_repo_scope_on_read`) and the REST artifact gate (`check_artifact_visibility`) carried the same split on their own mounts: `403 DENIED` against `404 NAME_UNKNOWN`, and `403 FORBIDDEN` against `404 Artifact not found`. Repository-scoped tokens are self-service, so any user holding one for a repository of their own could probe every other key — 200 (in scope), 403 (exists, private), 404 (does not exist) — and #3648/#3704, which correctly let public repositories through before the gate, sharpened that 403 to mean exactly "private and exists". On all three surfaces a **read** refused by the scope gate on a private repository now answers the response that surface already gives for a missing key, byte for byte: `404 Repository not found` on the native format routes, `404 NAME_UNKNOWN` echoing the client's first path segment on `/v2` — the same segment the unknown-key branch echoes, which matters under `AK_DEFAULT_DOCKER_MIRROR_REPO`, where an unknown key re-resolves to the mirror repository and an echo of the *resolved* key would have named the mirror for a missing key and the candidate itself for a real private one (a public mirror proxies unknown keys upstream, so that divergence is inherent and not addressed at this layer) — `404 Artifact not found` on `GET /api/v1/artifacts/{id}` and the sub-resources that share its gate. "Read" on the native routes is the set the ACL arm already calls a read: `GET`/`HEAD`/`OPTIONS`, the VS Code gallery query, and the two `non_mutating_post` routes — git-lfs `objects/batch` (how an LFS client reads) and conan `users/authenticate` — which stay scope-gated (on a public repository outside the scope they still answer 403, as #3648 decided) but on a private one now take the read-shaped denial rather than the write-shaped 403. The tree browser was already uniform — `authorize_tree_read` and its missing-key lookup build the identical `NotFound` — and is unchanged, as is the #3524/#3709 answer for a caller whose token *is* in scope but who holds no grant.

  **Writes keep the 403**, matching #3524's decision for the ACL arm: `PUT`/`POST`/`DELETE` to a private repository outside the token's scope, `docker push` and manifest `DELETE`, and the artifact-label mutations still answer the scope gate's own 403 — a caller writing has generally already read the repository, and 403 is the more useful answer there. Public repositories are untouched: a scoped token still reads them on the #3648/#3704 baseline, and is still refused a write to them. The three assertions that pinned the old 403s (`test_3648`'s `private_get`, and the `private_scoped` probes of the #3704 OCI and artifact tests) are re-baselined to the 404 rather than deleted, and each surface gains a test comparing the out-of-scope private read against the nonexistent-key read as full `(status, body)` pairs. **Upgrade note:** a client that distinguished 403 from 404 on a *read* of a private repository outside its token's scope — to tell "exists, not scoped" from "no such repository" — now sees 404 for both; that distinction was the disclosure being closed, and the token's scope is visible to its holder through the token-management API. Operators can still tell the two apart server-side: every scope-gate read denial logs `token repository scope denied read; answering the existence-hiding 404` at `info` with `repository_id` and `user_id`, the same fields the ACL read denials log.

## [1.8.2] - 2026-09-01

### Added

- **Silent SSO auto-login support (OIDC `prompt=none` check-sso)** (#3546). Users with a live IdP session (e.g. Keycloak next to other SSO-protected apps) had to click "Sign in with Keycloak" on every fresh visit, while the obvious fix — auto-redirecting to the sole provider — would bounce every *anonymous* visitor to a visible IdP login page they never asked for, and anonymous browsing is a first-class registry state. The backend now supports the invisible middle path the web UI drives (artifact-keeper-web#812): `GET /api/v1/auth/sso/oidc/{id}/login` accepts an optional `prompt=none` forwarded to the authorize URL (only `none` is accepted — anything else is a 400 before any SSO session is created; the explicit sign-in flow without `prompt` is unchanged byte-for-byte), and the OIDC callbacks map the OIDC Core 3.1.2.6 interaction-required error family (`login_required`, `interaction_required`, `consent_required`, `account_selection_required`) — the IdP's expected "no live session" answer to a silent probe — to a clean 307 to `/callback?silent_denied=1` with no error payload, burning the single-use SSO session so the state cannot be replayed. Every other callback error keeps its existing 400/401 behavior, and the CSRF replay defense, provider binding, PKCE, and SSRF posture are untouched. **Operator kill switch:** `OIDC_SILENT_SSO=false` (or `0`) disables the web UI's silent attempt fleet-wide; the flag is advertised as `auth.silent_sso_enabled` in `GET /api/v1/system/config` (default on, display-only — it gates no endpoint, so flipping it can never lock anyone out).

- **A backup archive's integrity check could be switched off by editing the archive** (#3373). #3011 gave every archive a payload checksum and made `restore` verify it before ingesting a row — but the expected value travelled inside the very file it was supposed to authenticate, and `verify_archive_checksum` returned early whenever `manifest.checksum` was empty. Blanking one JSON field disabled the control; deleting `manifest.json` outright disabled it the same way, because `read_manifest` returning `None` skipped the call entirely. That is the case integrity checks exist for: restore sits behind `admin_middleware`, so the caller is already an admin, and what is untrusted is **the archive** — one tampered with at rest, or pulled back from compromised or third-party storage. `ALLOWED_EXPORT_TABLES` necessarily contains `users`, `roles`, `user_roles`, `permission_grants` and `api_tokens`, so a crafted `database/users.json` carrying `is_admin: true` was ingested and the restore reported `errors: []`. Reproduced against a database on the parent commit: the crafted admin row landed and the call returned success.

  The expected digest now lives **outside** the archive. Every completed backup records its payload SHA-256 on the `backups` row (`payload_checksum`, migration 208), and a restore checks the archive it read back against it before anything is ingested. `restore` resolves its archive through a `backups` row and there is no path that ingests a foreign archive, so that row is always available and is not reachable from the archive bytes. An archive rewritten to be internally consistent — new payload, manifest regenerated over it — passes every check that lives inside itself and still fails this one. The archive length already recorded in `size_bytes` is checked first, but only as a cheap pre-filter that refuses the common case without decompressing: gzip tolerates arbitrary trailing bytes, so a tamperer can pad an archive to exactly the recorded length. The digest is what decides.

  Archives captured before this release have no recorded digest and fall back to the checksum in their own manifest, which detects corruption but not tampering; the restore reports which anchor it used (`integrity_anchor`: `recorded`, `manifest` or `waived`) and records it on the audit event. An archive carrying neither is no longer silently accepted: it is refused unless the caller sets `allow_unverified_archive`, which is an explicit, audited operator decision and never waives a checksum that is present and does not match. A restore on either of the weaker anchors also says so in its `errors` list rather than returning a clean-looking empty one, because until you re-run your backups every existing archive is on the `manifest` anchor — which is exactly where the original weakness still lives. **Re-run your backups after upgrading** so their digests are recorded; until then, the guidance in the 1.8.1 notes still applies — restore only archives you produced and can vouch for.

  Two related gaps in the same path close with it. `extract_entries` decompressed an archive with no bound of any kind: measured on the parent commit, a 521,905-byte archive expanded to 536,870,912 bytes (1028x) and was returned in full, and a 6,252,652-byte archive drove a deployed backend to 4.596 GiB resident before it had checked anything about that archive. Extraction is now bounded by entry count and by total decompressed bytes, with the byte budget wrapped around the decoded stream **before** the tar reader sees it — which is the only place it can be complete. `tar` consumes GNU LongName/LongLink and PAX extended headers inside the entry iterator's own `next()`, reading the full size the record declares, so any bound applied to the entries the iterator yields never sees those bytes at all; and `build_backup_tar` emits GNU LongLink for every path over 100 characters (#758), so these records are in ordinary archives, not just crafted ones. Measured through the real entry point at the default limits: a 1,043,854-byte archive declaring a 1 GiB long name took the process to +2118 MiB and returned success with a bound that read only the entries, and is refused at +132 MiB with the budget on the reader. This is the same `util::bounded_archive` budget the other ~20 extractors in the codebase already use.

  The ceiling is `clamp(compressed_len x 100, 32 MiB, 8 GiB)`: the floor so a small legitimate backup is not refused for being small, the ratio so a large one is not refused for being large, and the absolute cap because the length the ratio scales from is one a padded archive can choose. 8 GiB is a ceiling on what this restore path can do at all — it holds the compressed archive and every decompressed entry in memory at once — rather than a policy about backup size; archives beyond it need a streaming restore, not a larger number.

  Entry paths that are absolute or contain `..` are refused at extraction rather than relied on being sanitised downstream. On the filesystem backend `key_to_path` does strip them, and on S3 (`object_store` percent-encodes `.` and `..`) and GCS (`urlencoding::encode`) the key is encoded — but the **Azure** backend interpolates the raw key straight into the blob URL (`blob_url`, `storage/azure.rs`), and URL parsing removes dot segments, so a `..` in a restored artifact key resolves out of the configured container. On that backend this was a live cross-container write, not defence in depth. `tar::Builder` refuses to write such a path, so no archive this product produced contains one.

  Finally, `target_repository_id` was accepted by `POST /api/v1/admin/backups/{id}/restore`, carried on `RestoreOptions`, and read by nothing: a caller who scoped a restore to one repository got a full global ingest of the identity tables and a `200`. It is now refused with a `400` rather than silently ignored.

  Manifest **signing** — the third box on #3373 — is deliberately not in this change. It needs key generation, storage, rotation and a verification trust store, which is a design rather than a patch, and #2466 already owns bundle signing and provenance for the air-gap bundle format; a second scheme invented here would leave the product with two incompatible ways to sign an archive. Signing is what is needed when an archive moves between instances, which is exactly #2466's scope; the recorded digest is what is needed for the threat this issue describes, and that is what ships here.

- **An empty repository-key segment let an unauthenticated caller make the server buffer a whole upload in memory** (#3508). `repo_visibility_middleware` short-circuits when the extracted repository key is empty, and since #3444 that early return handed the request to the format handler with an anonymous `Option<AuthExtension>` inserted. It runs *before* the middleware's own gates, so the #508 write-auth gate — 129 lines further down — never ran for those paths; the handler did, and its extractors evaluate in order, so a body extractor (`Bytes`, `Multipart`) buffered the ENTIRE request body before the handler's in-line `require_auth` could reject it. The 401 the caller finally received was therefore emitted only after the server had read and allocated the upload.

  That is an unauthenticated memory-exhaustion primitive: no credential, no repository, no configuration. The ceiling per request is `MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE` (`MAX_UPLOAD_SIZE`, 10 GiB by default) and the number of them in flight is bounded only by `GLOBAL_MAX_CONCURRENCY` (512 by default). Measured on a build of the parent commit, backend restarted between runs: an idle 37 MiB backend peaked at 1070 MiB for one anonymous 512 MiB `PUT /npm//pkg` and at 7045 MiB for one anonymous 4 GiB request, and the cost is linear in concurrent requests. Every format prefix reaches the branch (`/npm//pkg`, `/maven//`, `/pypi//`, `/cargo//api/v1/crates/new`, `/api/cargo//…`, `/gems//api/v1/gems`, `/conda//upload`, `/debian//upload`, `/lfs//objects/<oid>`, and the rest — 22 of 36 probed prefixes buffered a 64 MiB anonymous body). Two of those deserve separate mention: `POST /conda/t/upload` is a **single-slash** path, so a reverse proxy that collapses `//` does not filter it, and `/lfs/` is in `BYTE_TRANSFER_PREFIXES`, which exempts it from the global request timeout — so that arm can also be drip-fed to hold the allocation open.

  An empty key names no repository — repository keys are non-empty by construction, so no row can ever match and no format route can serve anything there. The middleware now answers that branch itself with the same existence-hiding 404 the no-repo branch produces, instead of running the handler. Nothing reads the body, and the #3443 defect the fall-through was added for stays fixed for the stronger reason that the handler (and its strict `Extension` extractor) is never invoked at all, so there is no unauthenticated 500 and no internal type path in a response. Authorization outcomes on non-empty keys are untouched.

  One key that only *looked* empty is corrected alongside it, because the new 404 would otherwise apply to a real repository: `extract_repo_key` skipped the conda token-channel pair `t/<TOKEN>` whenever a conda path's second segment was `t`, including on two-segment paths like `/conda/t/upload` or `/conda/t/channeldata.json` that are the plain conda routes for a repository whose key is literally `t`. Those requests resolved to an empty key, so the repository got no visibility, token-scope or permission check and the caller's credential was replaced with the anonymous value (they answered 401 to a valid credential on `main`, and 500 before #3444 — they have never worked). The skip now applies only when a segment actually follows the token, which is the only shape a real token channel has. Its sibling `extract_conda_url_token` got the same shape test: it read the third segment of any `/conda/t/...` path as a URL-embedded credential, so an anonymous read of a repository keyed `t` was rejected as an *invalid credential* it never sent. Real token channels (`/conda/t/<TOKEN>/<channel>/…`) are unchanged in both.

- **The `/api/helm` and `/api/cargo` alias routes evaluated authorization against the wrong repository** (#3443, #2941, #3000). Both aliases are mounted (#3392): `/api/helm` for the ChartMuseum `cm-push` plugin, which POSTs to `{host}/api{repo_path}/charts`, and `/api/cargo` for the sparse index the generated cargo config points at. Their paths are therefore `/api/{format}/{repo_key}/...`, but `extract_repo_key` models a format route as `/{format}/{repo_key}/...` and returns the second segment — so `repo_visibility_middleware` was handed the literal `"helm"` or `"cargo"` as the repository key, while axum strips the nest prefix and hands the handler the *third* segment. The middleware checked one repository and the handler served another.

  With no repository named `cargo` or `helm` present, that split fails closed and is only the compatibility defect it was reported as (#3443): nothing resolves, the middleware answers from its no-repo branch — 401 for an anonymous caller, existence-hiding 404 for a valid credential — and both aliases are mounted but unreachable, so `helm cm-push` and `cargo publish` against the generated sparse-index URL still fail. **When a repository whose key is exactly `cargo` or `helm` does exist, the same split is an authorization bypass.** Those are accepted repository keys and they are the names an operator naturally gives a cargo or a Helm repository. Every gate the middleware owns — visibility, API-token repository scope (#504), and the write/delete permission gate (#508 / #2603) — was evaluated against that repository while the handler served the one named in the third segment:

  - with a **public** repository named `cargo`, an anonymous caller read a **private** repository's sparse index (`/api/cargo/{private}/config.json`, `/api/cargo/{private}/ve/ri/{crate}`) and downloaded its `.crate` bytes (`/api/cargo/{private}/api/v1/crates/{name}/{version}/download`);
  - a token scoped (`allowed_repo_ids`) to the repository `cargo` published into any other repository through `PUT /api/cargo/{other}/api/v1/crates/new`;
  - a token scoped to the repository `helm` deleted charts out of any other repository through `DELETE /api/helm/{other}/charts/{name}/{version}`, and `POST /api/helm/{other}/charts` answered `409 already exists` — an existence oracle over repositories the caller cannot see.

  The identical requests on the native `/cargo/{repo}` and `/helm/{repo}` mounts were refused (401/403) throughout; only the alias path lost the ceiling. This is the same family as the `/ext` WASM-proxy bypass (GHSA-9rqp-mgmw-5879) and the raw-segment key of GHSA-fv45-mwhh-q23r: a mount whose repository key is not the second segment, extracted as if it were.

  **Am I affected:** `v1.8.0`, `v1.8.1-rc.1` and `v1.8.1` carry the `/api/{cargo,helm}` mounts; earlier releases have no such route and are not affected. On an affected version, exposure requires a repository whose key is exactly `cargo` or `helm` — `SELECT key, is_public FROM repositories WHERE key IN ('cargo', 'helm');` answers the question, and renaming that repository closes the bypass without upgrading. The anonymous read half additionally requires that repository to be public. Treat any repository-scoped token that has been used against `/api/cargo` or `/api/helm` while such a repository existed as having held its owner's reach over every repository reachable through that alias, for the period it was valid.

  The extraction now skips the `/api` prefix for exactly those two format names, so the visibility, token-scope and permission checks evaluate the same repository key the handler resolves. The predicate enumerates the two aliased formats rather than treating any `/api/{x}` as a format mount: `/api/v1` is the REST API and its second segment is a resource name, not a repository key, and a broad rule would silently reclassify it. The two exceptions already living in the function — the conda `/conda/t/{token}/{channel}/...` token channel and the `/ext/{format_key}/{repo_key}/...` WASM proxy — have the same shape for the same reason. `/api/v1/...`, `/api/packages/...` and the native mounts are unchanged, including a repository literally named `cargo` or `helm`, which resolves correctly on both its native and its alias path.
- **The LDAP login endpoint no longer reveals whether a username exists in the directory** (#3371). `POST /api/v1/auth/sso/ldap/{id}/login` is unauthenticated, and `AppError::Authentication` passes its message straight through to the response body, so the wording of a failed login was visible to anyone. On the search-then-bind path a username with no matching directory entry answered `401 {"message":"User not found in LDAP"}` while an existing username with the wrong password answered `401 {"message":"Invalid credentials"}` — a user-enumeration oracle that needs no credentials and no rate-limit evasion beyond the login limiter: an attacker walks a username list, keeps the accounts the directory confirms, and sprays passwords at a verified target set instead of a guessed one. Every credential-level arm — absent entry, rejected bind, empty input — now returns the identical body, and the username, the base DN and the underlying LDAP error stay in the server log at WARN under the `security` target where operators debugging a user filter still have them.

  Affected: deployments with an LDAP/AD provider configured **and** a service account set (`bind_dn` + `bind_password`), which selects search-then-bind; the direct-bind fallback used when no service account is configured already answered uniformly because both cases fail at the same bind. All versions through 1.8.1 carry the leak. No configuration change is needed and no credentials were exposed — the leak is account existence, not authentication material.

  **Infrastructure failures are deliberately not folded into the generic message.** A connection failure, a failed search and an authentication timeout stay `AppError::Internal` (5xx), so a directory outage still reads as an outage to operators instead of being reported to every user as a bad password; a regression test pins that distinction from the failing side. Two related items are **not** addressed here and are tracked separately: the residual timing difference between the two paths (an absent user short-circuits before the second bind; measured at roughly 1 ms against a same-host directory, with the distributions overlapping), and the same class of oracle on the local login endpoint, where a username belonging to a federated account answers `Use SSO provider to authenticate` and a locked account answers with the lockout message, both only ever for usernames that exist.

- **Every tag `docker-publish.yml` writes is now re-checked, after publish, against a cosign signature over the digest that tag actually resolves to** (#3559). The question behind this was "can we prove the images we ship are signed?", and the honest answer was no — not because they were not signed, but because nothing ever asked. `cosign sign --yes ...@<digest>` is a hard-failing step (#2824, #3496), yet on the happy path it prints `Generating ephemeral keys... / Signing artifact...` and stops, so a green log is not evidence that a signature was pushed anywhere; and the digest it signs is a value the same job computed, so even a check bolted onto that step could only report that the signer signed what the signer was handed. Each of the three merge jobs now starts over from the published TAG, resolves it through the registry exactly as `docker pull` would, and requires a cosign signature over **that** digest before the job may go green. The invariant, stated in the workflow where the next reader will find it: *the bytes a user pulls by tag are the bytes that were signed.*

  Three details are what make it an assertion rather than a formality. The identity is **pinned** — `--certificate-identity-regexp` naming this repository's `docker-publish.yml` on a branch or tag ref, plus `--certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com` — because anyone can sign any public image with Sigstore, so a verify that accepts any identity establishes nothing; `scripts/ci/check-published-image-signature.sh` refuses a pattern that matches every signer rather than passing vacuously. A signature is required to be **a cosign signature**: under cosign v3 a bare `cosign verify` is satisfied by the `attest-build-provenance` DSSE bundle on its own, so an image with provenance and no signature passes a naive check — the gate requires a payload of type `https://sigstore.dev/cosign/sign/v1`. And an **infrastructure** failure is separated from a finding: a registry 5xx or a Fulcio/Rekor outage exits 2 with its own message, a genuinely unverifiable image exits 1. Both fail the job — nothing in this workflow soft-fails (#3496) — but an outage must never read in the log as a tampered image. The published `1.6.1`, which shipped unsigned in the incident that made the cosign step hard-fail in the first place, is the fixture the gate was proven against: it goes red on it and green on every release since.

  The investigation that produced this also corrects the record. A probe of the registry had reported that no published tag carried a signature, based on the legacy `sha256-<digest>.sig` tag scheme and on `/v2/<name>/referrers/<digest>`. Both are dead ends on this registry: cosign 3.x attaches signatures as OCI 1.1 referrers rather than `.sig` tags, and ghcr.io does not implement the referrers API (it answers `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` for every digest, signed or not) — the referrer index lives under the fallback tag `sha256-<digest>`, with no suffix. Asking cosign instead of the tag namespace: **41 of the 42 published backend releases verify, along with `:latest` and `:dev`; the sole exception is `1.6.1`.** The `472` orphan `.sig` tags in the repository are the residue of pre-cosign-3 publishes, not evidence of misdirected signing. Verification instructions in the publish summary were tightened at the same time, from an identity pattern matching any workflow in the organisation to the one workflow permitted to sign.

- **Release binaries are now signed, attested and carry an SBOM — and the release job refuses to publish until it has verified all three** (#3558). The container images have had cosign signatures, an SBOM attestation and build provenance since #3496. The release binaries had none of it: each one shipped with a `<name>.sha256` beside it and nothing else. That file is served from the same place, by the same authority, as the artifact it describes — whoever can replace `artifact-keeper-linux-amd64.tar.gz` on a release can replace `artifact-keeper-linux-amd64.tar.gz.sha256` in the same action — so it detects a corrupted download and is routinely read as detecting a substituted one. There was also no SBOM of any kind for the binaries, while the images had two.

  Each release now carries one `checksums.txt` covering **every** asset, a `checksums.txt.cosign.bundle` holding a cosign keyless signature over it (GitHub OIDC → Fulcio → Rekor, so there is no key material to hold or rotate and the certificate records which workflow, in which repository, at which tag did the signing), build provenance on every archive, SBOM and the manifest, and a per-target `artifact-keeper-<os>-<arch>.cdx.json` CycloneDX SBOM. The per-file `.sha256` files stay — people script against them — and are themselves listed in the signed manifest. `SECURITY.md` has the copy-pasteable verification commands.

  **The verification, not the signing, is the change.** Signing that nobody checks is a ritual, and this project has the receipts: #2824 (a failed cosign step let 1.6.1 ship unsigned, found later by a human), #3496 (six step-level `continue-on-error` meant build provenance had never been proven to attach to any image), and #3559 — filed this week — where `cosign sign` targets a digest that is not what the release tag resolves to, so the step goes green and the shipped image is unverifiable. So `release.yml` verifies, against the exact bytes it is about to upload, resolved at verify time: `cosign verify-blob` against a certificate identity pinned to this repository, this workflow file and this tag; `gh attestation verify` with `--signer-workflow`; and `sha256sum -c` of the manifest against the files on disk. It also refuses a *permissive* pin before it verifies anything — Fulcio is a public CA, and `--certificate-identity-regexp '.*'` satisfies every flag cosign requires while accepting a certificate minted by anyone's workflow.

  All of it runs **before** `Create Release`, which is an ordering rather than a preference. `.github/scripts/assert-release-absent.sh` refuses to run against a tag that already has a release and `softprops/action-gh-release` runs with `overwrite_files: false`, so a partial publish is not recoverable by re-running — it burns an immutable version number, and v1.7.2 is the cautionary tale. Failing before publication costs a re-run of a job that has produced nothing public.

  The SBOM half is embedded rather than merely shipped: binaries are built with `cargo auditable`, so `cargo audit bin artifact-keeper-linux-amd64` asks the binary what is in it instead of trusting that a `.cdx.json` next to a tarball describes it. That needs its own assertion, because the tool that reads it back out fails open — measured with cargo-audit 0.22.2, a binary built with a plain `cargo build` produces `warning: … was not built with 'cargo auditable', the report will be incomplete (1 dependencies recovered)` and **exit code 0**. A job that merely ran `cargo audit bin` could not fail for the reason it was added: drop `auditable` from the build command and CI stays green while every shipped binary is hollow. `scripts/ci/assert-binary-sbom.sh` asserts on the output, and on a floor for the dependency count, so that revert is a red build.

  Both gates live in `scripts/ci/` with self-tests that run on every PR, because the release path executes once per release and cannot be rehearsed without cutting a tag. The suites construct each refusal — checksums that do not match, a missing signature, a valid signature carrying the **wrong** certificate identity, provenance from a different workflow, a missing SBOM — and a Sigstore or GitHub API outage is classified as INFRA (exit 2, "retry") rather than as tampering (exit 1, "something replaced your bytes"), so an outage and an attack do not read alike. Eleven deliberate mutations of the gates were each confirmed to turn the suites red.

  One defect was found and fixed in the process. The certificate identity was built inline with `sed 's/[.^$*+?()[\]{}|\\]/\\&/g'`, which reads as "escape every regex metacharacter" and is a no-op: `\` is not special inside a POSIX bracket expression, so the `]` after it closes the class. `v1.8.2` came through unescaped and every `.` in the "pinned" identity was a wildcard. Nothing exploitable followed from it — Fulcio only ever issues identities that really are `github.com` URLs — but it is exactly the shape this change exists to prevent: a pin that reads as strict, passes every check around it, and is not doing what its name says, because nothing ever asserted on the pattern's text. It is now `scripts/ci/release-identity-regexp.sh`, escaping by allowlist rather than by a blocklist that fails open when its author forgets an entry, and the self-test asserts both the pattern's text and that it refuses `releaseXyml`, `v1X8X2` and `githubXcom`.
- **The Docker Hub mirrors of every published image are now signed, and checked, the same way the ghcr images are** (#3562). `docker-publish.yml` has always copied each published image to Docker Hub, but `cosign sign` was only ever handed the ghcr reference — so `docker.io/artifactkeeper/backend`, `.../openscap` and `.../scanner-adapter` carried no signature on any tag they have ever published. A cosign signature lives in the repository it was pushed to, and that is the whole of the problem: `backend:1.8.1` resolves to the identical `sha256:44e433bc…` on both registries, the ghcr copy verifies, and the Docker Hub copy is unverifiable because the signature is simply not there to find. Anyone who pulls from Docker Hub — which is what the project's own quick-start line tells them to do — has had no way to check what they got.

  Nothing was broken; a whole distribution channel was absent from the controls. That is worth naming, because it is invisible to every check this repository already runs. The signing step is hard-failing (#2824, #3496) and succeeded, because it did exactly what it was asked. `check-supply-chain-soft-fail.sh` asserts that signing steps cannot fail silently, not what they sign. And the tag-anchored gate added in #3559 is a genuine assertion, but it can only assert about the references it is handed, and it was wired with the ghcr tag set — a gate over one of two registries, staying green over the other for the project's entire history. Each merge job now signs the `docker.io` digest alongside the ghcr one and passes both tag sets to the verification gate, and `scripts/ci/check-registry-publish-parity.sh` reads the workflow itself and fails CI if any publish job mirrors to a registry it does not sign and verify, so the absent half cannot quietly return. The pre-fix workflow is the fixture that gate was proven red against, and the live, genuinely unsigned `docker.io/artifactkeeper/backend:1.8.1` is the fixture for the runtime one.

  The signature is made over the **digest**, which is what lets `apply-floating-tags` stay build-free: it re-points `:latest` and `:X.Y` on both registries at a digest the merge jobs already published, uploading nothing, so the signature keeps covering them. Signing by digest is also self-asserting — `imagetools create` copies a manifest list without rewriting it, so if a Docker Hub copy ever produced different content, `cosign sign` would fail immediately on a manifest that is not there rather than attaching a signature to the wrong bytes.

  **One visible change on Docker Hub.** Unlike ghcr.io, Docker Hub implements the OCI referrers API — `/v2/<name>/referrers/<digest>` answers `200` with a real index there and `404 MANIFEST_UNKNOWN` on ghcr — and on Docker Hub that referrer index is also addressable as the `sha256-<digest>` tag. Expect a `sha256-<digest>` tag per signed digest to become visible in the public Docker Hub repositories' tag listings. It is the signature, it is what makes `cosign verify docker.io/artifactkeeper/backend:<version>` work, and it is the accepted cost of the fix.

  **Already-published Docker Hub images are not retro-signed**, for the same reason `1.6.1` is not on the ghcr side. A signature attached today would be produced by a workflow run that did not build those bytes, asserting a relationship between an identity, a commit and an artifact that never existed — provenance fiction, which is the failure mode this whole area exists to prevent. Tags published from the first release carrying this change onward are signed on both registries; earlier Docker Hub tags stay unsigned and are documented as such, and a consumer who needs a verifiable image today can pull the identical bytes from ghcr.io, where they are signed.

  One hardening travelled with the change. The verification gate accepts a registry credential for resolving tags on a private registry, and the token endpoint that credential is presented to is named by a `WWW-Authenticate` header the *registry* sends. ghcr's realm is on `ghcr.io`; Docker Hub's is `auth.docker.io`, a different origin. Putting a `docker.io` reference into an invocation that carries ghcr credentials would therefore have handed a `GITHUB_TOKEN` to Docker's auth server, so the credential is now pinned to the single host it was issued for and public mirrors resolve anonymously.

### Changed

- **`:latest` and the floating `X.Y` tags now move only after the release gate has certified the bytes they name** (#3540). `docker-publish.yml` runs on the tag push, which is necessarily *before* the gate — it is what builds the images the gate tests — so a `type=raw,value=latest` line in a merge job moved `:latest` before any verdict existed. On 1.8.1 the publish finished at 14:59:49 and the release published at 16:17:54: `:latest` named gate-uncertified bytes for 78 minutes on a cut where nothing went wrong. The same three merge jobs are parallel siblings, so a floating tag also moved as soon as *its own* image passed, whatever happened to the other two — the shape that left `backend:1.7.2` and `backend:latest` publicly pullable for hours for a version that was then retired with the gate never run.

  A tag push now publishes only the immutable `:X.Y.Z`. Every floating tag is written by one job that fans in from all three merge jobs, and for the AK-versioned images that job runs only in the post-gate promotion `release.yml` dispatches once the release gate and the GitHub Release have both succeeded. The promotion rebuilds nothing: it re-points `:latest` and `:X.Y` at the manifest-list digest `:X.Y.Z` already names, so the digest is unchanged and the cosign signature and provenance attestation bound to it keep covering it. The release job then asserts that both tags, on ghcr.io and Docker Hub, resolve to the digest the gate tested.

  Which floating tags may move is decided by the published-release set rather than by the tag being pushed: a floating tag may only name a version with a published, non-draft, non-prerelease GitHub Release, and only if that version is newest in the line the tag represents. A backport therefore advances `:1.7` and leaves `:latest` alone, and a version whose images exist but whose release was never published — the 1.7.2/1.7.5 shape — cannot be named by any floating tag at all.

  **The failure mode this creates is deliberate: when the gate fails, `:latest` and `:X.Y` stay on the previous release.** After a failed cut the registry looks like the release did not happen — `:X.Y.Z` exists and is immutable, but nothing an operator pulls by default has changed. That is the intended end state, and it is also the rollback: to move `:latest` back off a bad release that did publish, delete or mark that GitHub Release as a prerelease and re-dispatch the promotion for the previous version. Prereleases keep taking no floating tag, and the standalone recovery dispatch (`-f promote_version=X.Y.Z` with no `promote_floating`) keeps its existing behaviour exactly: mirror ghcr's current state, move nothing.

  The scanner-adapter's own floating line (`X.Y`/`X`/`latest`) gains the sibling barrier but is deliberately still applied at publish time: `:1` is required by `verify-images-published` before the release job runs, and those tags intentionally follow an unchanged-source rebuild that the adapter's exact tag does not (#2391). That gap is recorded on the issue rather than closed here.

### Fixed

- **A re-tagged release version could never pass `resolve-candidate-digest`** (#3640, #3641). The release workflow located the Docker Publish run vouching for the tagged commit with a query hard-filtered to push events, so on a re-cut of an already-published version it could only ever see the push run that image immutability had (correctly, and permanently) refused — while the documented `promote_version` recovery dispatch succeeded invisibly beside it. The resolver now accepts a successful run for the same commit and ref from either a tag push or a promote dispatch, and adoption of already-published bytes is verified rather than assumed: the release hard-refuses unless the commit the published image was built from and the commit being tagged are byte-identical across every input the backend image is built from (`Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `backend/`, `.sqlx/`, the Dockerfile and `.dockerignore`). Nothing changes for a normal cut; a missing or failed publish still blocks the release, and a stale success for a different commit or branch can never vouch for a tag.

- **The embedded-SBOM release gate could not run on any x86_64 target** (#3636). `cargo audit bin` refuses, before opening the file, any binary over a default 100 MiB, and the x86_64 release binaries are over it — 119,661,680 bytes on linux-amd64, 139,272,192 on windows-amd64, against a 104,857,600-byte ceiling. The gate added in #3558 therefore never got an answer it could read on three of the five targets, and correctly refused to score a tool error as a pass, which stopped the first tag attempt at `build-binaries`. The aarch64 legs passed only because they clear the same ceiling by 2.4 MiB.

  Stripping was not the missing step: `[profile.release] strip = true` is already set and `file(1)` reports the shipped binaries `stripped`. The verified aarch64 artifact is stripped and still yields a complete graph, which settles the open question from #3558 on a real release binary rather than a test crate — `.dep-v0` survives stripping. The gate now hands `cargo audit bin` an explicit `MAX_BINARY_SIZE` ceiling (512 MiB) instead of accepting its default.

  It still fails closed, and in more places than before. A binary over the raised ceiling blocks at a named arm that reports which limit was hit rather than falling through to the generic unrecognised-output verdict; a `cargo-audit` without the flag reports INFRA rather than a pass, since the tool is installed unpinned and a tool that cannot be driven has measured nothing; and the arm that matters — a binary built without `cargo auditable`, which `cargo audit bin` reports with a warning and **exit 0** — is untouched. Raising the ceiling in fact strengthens the gate: the real 114 MiB non-auditable binary that previously produced only the size error is now correctly blocked for carrying no embedded dependency data.

- **Docker/OCI images pulled through a proxy never appeared on the Packages page** (#3441). A Remote (or Virtual-over-Remote) Docker repository cached images correctly — `docker pull` worked, and the manifests and blobs showed up under the repository's flat artifact view — but the image itself never appeared as a *package*, while Maven artifacts pulled through the same instance did. The Packages page reads the `packages`/`package_versions` tables via `/api/v1/packages`, not `artifacts`; `handle_put_manifest` learned to populate that catalog so a **pushed** image stopped being "pullable yet invisible", but the proxy path never did. Reproduced live: pulling `library/alpine:3.19` through a Remote repository wrote the expected `artifacts` and `oci_tags` rows and left `SELECT count(*) FROM packages` at zero.

  The reason it never did is worth stating, because the obvious fix does not work. `ProxyService::index_cached_package` is gated by an allow-list (`catalog_indexable_format`) that admits only the Maven family, and that allow-list is deliberate. But widening it would not have fixed this and would have made things worse: `index_cached_package` only ever sees paths that flow through `ProxyService`, and for OCI those are **blobs** — digest-named, versionless, dozens per image. Manifests are cached by `cache_manifest_reference_locally`, which sits outside `ProxyService` on purpose, pinned by an existing source-level test: routing manifests through the proxy cache reintroduces the doubled-prefix bug of #1278, because manifests live in the per-repository storage location while the proxy cache writes to the global `proxy-cache/` backend. So the identity a user recognises — `image:tag` — exists only in the manifest path, and that is where the catalog write now goes, mirroring the push path rather than inventing a second policy.

  **Why this does not fill the catalog with noise**, which is the real question for a multi-manifest format. The write is gated on the reference being a tag, the same rule `handle_put_manifest` already applies. `docker pull nginx:1.27` fetches the index by tag — one row, `nginx` at `1.27` — and then each architecture's child manifest **by digest**; those are not versions anyone chose and produce nothing. `docker pull nginx@sha256:...` names no version either and likewise produces nothing, exactly as a digest-only push does not. A re-pull of the same tag upserts the single row instead of adding to it. The result is one catalog row per image per tag, with the manifests and blobs left in the artifact view where they belong.

  Sizing reuses the two helpers the push path sizes with, and the two manifest classes land in different places — measured rather than assumed. An **image** manifest is sized exactly from its own `config.size + layers[].size`, which the manifest body carries, so a proxied image is right *before* any layer has been fetched — which matters because on a proxy the manifest arrives first. An image **index** carries no config or layers of its own, so its size is the sum over child manifests already cached, and on a proxy that is **0 on the first pull** because the children are fetched after the index. An ordinary re-pull does not fix it — a warm proxy cache serves the tag without re-entering the caching path — and even after the cached tag expires the sum is over the children's recorded artifact sizes, which on the proxy path are manifest body lengths rather than image sizes. So the size shown for a proxied multi-arch tag is a lower bound, not the image's download size. Verified live: a hosted push of a single-arch image records 54 bytes for a 37-byte config plus a 17-byte layer, while a proxied `alpine:3.19` index records 0. Making that number meaningful requires the proxied child-manifest artifact rows to carry image sizes, which changes a shared pre-existing path the docker-tag grouping also reads; it is filed separately rather than smuggled in here. The write is best-effort, like every other write in that function after the manifest body itself: a catalog failure must never fail a pull the client already committed to. Repository visibility is unchanged — `/api/v1/packages` filters both its page and its count query by the caller's repository visibility, and a package row belongs to exactly one repository, so a proxy's new rows are gated by the same clause every other format's already were.

  Three defects found in review of this change ship with it (#3611). **Ordering:** the catalog write originally ran inside the manifest-caching helper, which executes *before* the inline scan gate on the cold proxy pull — so an image the gate refused to serve (`403`/`423` under `scan_on_proxy`) was still advertised on the Packages page and in `/v2/_catalog`, even though its bytes were not deliverable (manifest and blob reads stay blocked). The write now sits with the download counter on the serve side of `maybe_gate_remote_manifest_scan`, so a refused pull advertises nothing; an allowed pull on the same policy still indexes, and both directions are pinned by tests. **HEAD:** the HEAD handler shares the caching helper, so a bare `HEAD` — which is deliberately ungated, matching the direct-Remote HEAD path — also published catalog rows for content the GET path refuses. Relocating the write closes that; HEAD itself stays ungated, because a HEAD serves no bytes and its caller has already passed repository authorization, and changing that contract is a separate decision from this fix. **Tag length:** `packages.version` and `package_versions.version` were `VARCHAR(100)` while the OCI tag grammar allows 128 characters, and the best-effort catalog upsert swallowed the overflow into a warning — a valid 101–128 character tag (CI schemes like `v1.2.3-nightly-<date>-<sha>-<platform>-<branch>` cross 100 routinely) pulled fine and silently never indexed, on the proxy path and the push path alike. Migration 211 widens both columns to the grammar's bound.
- **A Remote Ansible repository advertised no collection versions, so `ansible-galaxy collection install` could resolve nothing** (#3365). `ansible-galaxy` resolves a collection's version entirely from `GET /api/v3/collections/{namespace}/{name}/versions/` before it requests any tarball. That handler queried locally-catalogued artifacts only and had no Remote branch, which for a proxy is empty — so it answered `200` with `{"data": [], "meta": {"count": 0}}` and the client reported `Failed to resolve the requested dependencies map. Could not satisfy the following requirements: * ansible.posix:1.5.1 (direct request)`. The failure named the requirement, so it read as a bad version pin rather than a server that had never asked its upstream. Fetching the same tarball by its full `download/` path already worked (confirmed live against `galaxy.ansible.com`, byte-identical to upstream's declared SHA-256), so serving was fine and only discovery was broken — the Ansible analogue of the Helm index defect in #3448.

  The Remote branch now merges what the upstream publishes over whatever the repository holds locally, advertising every version under this repository's own routes. Locally-held versions win their version string, because the local row is the one the download route resolves before it ever consults upstream and it carries the artifact's real stored filename. The list is walked to completion rather than stopping at the first page: Galaxy clamps `limit` to 100 server-side (a request for `limit=1000` against a 239-version collection returns 100 items and a `links.next`), and a pinned requirement on an older version lives on a later page. The walk re-requests the same path with a growing `offset` instead of following `links.next`, because that link is spelled relative to the upstream **origin** rather than to the configured `upstream_url` — following it would mean issuing a request outside the configured prefix on the say-so of the upstream's own response body, and a private Automation Hub serving Galaxy under an `/api/galaxy/` prefix makes the same point without any malice. Twenty pages is the ceiling and truncation is logged, never silent.

  **When the upstream is unreachable.** With versions held locally those are still served and a warning is logged: an upstream outage must not stop a collection this repository already has from resolving, which is the point of a cache. With nothing held, the upstream's own error is surfaced — `503` for an upstream 5xx, `404` for a definitive upstream 404, `502` for a connect failure — rather than an empty list. An empty `data` is indistinguishable from "this collection has no versions", which is precisely the silent failure being fixed here; reproducing it in the failure path would be the same bug wearing a different hat. The proxy cache already applies RFC 5861 `stale-if-error` to the version document itself, so a warm proxy keeps serving the last good list before this fallback is reached at all.

  `GET .../versions/{version}/` gained the matching Remote branch. It answered `404` for any version a proxy had not already cached, which failed the install one step after the version list resolved it, and it is where the client reads the download URL, the digest it verifies the tarball against, and the dependency map. The upstream's `download_url` is an absolute upstream URL and is **not** forwarded: every advertised URL is rebuilt against this repository's own `download/` route, so the tarball is fetched back through the proxy and the cache, the download accounting and this repository's authorization all still apply to it. Upstream `name`/`version` values that cannot form a single path segment are dropped rather than advertised, on the same reasoning as #3448 — the index must not promise a URL that resolves to something other than the entry it came from.

  `GET .../collections/{namespace}/{name}/` gained the same branch, and it is not cosmetic. When the client has a response cache configured — which it does whenever the server is declared under `[galaxy_server.*]` in `ansible.cfg`, the ordinary enterprise setup and the shape the report describes — `get_collection_versions` reads that route first for the collection's `updated_at` as a cache key, and treats a 404 from it as "no collection found" by returning an empty list. A proxy that served a complete version list therefore still reported no versions. Confirmed live on the patched build: the identical requirements file installs against an ad-hoc `source:` (client cache off) and failed against a configured `[galaxy_server.*]` (client cache on) until this branch existed. Its `href`, `versions_url` and `highest_version.href` are rebuilt against this repository's routes for the same reason as the download URL. Listing a Remote repository's whole collection catalogue is deliberately still local-only: that is a ~30,000-entry upstream enumeration, not a lookup, and no install path reads it.

  The version-metadata document also had to be corrected to the shape the client actually requires, without which the Remote branch would have been useless: `GalaxyAPI.get_collection_version_metadata` indexes `data['namespace']['name']`, `data['collection']['name']`, `data['href']` and `data['metadata']['dependencies']` unconditionally. `namespace` was emitted as a bare string, and `href` was absent entirely, so the client raised `TypeError: string indices must be integers` and aborted with "Unexpected Exception, this is probably a bug" — on **hosted** repositories too, which is why installing from an Artifact Keeper Ansible repository of any type has never worked. One builder now emits that document for both the locally-held and the proxied branch, so the contract does not depend on which copy answered. A related gap is filed separately rather than smuggled in here: the native upload never reads `MANIFEST.json` out of the collection tarball, so a **hosted** collection's real dependency map is still unknown and is emitted as `{}`.

  **Two integrity invariants in that document are now enforced rather than trusted.** The upstream's `artifact.sha256` is the digest `ansible-galaxy` verifies the downloaded tarball against — but it verifies only `if expected_hash:`, so an absent, null, non-string or empty upstream digest, relayed as the empty string, silently disabled the client's verification while this server verified nothing of its own; a poisoned tarball then installed with `rc=0`. Such a version is now **refused with a 502** that names the missing digest, on both the proxied branch and the locally-held branch (a stored row whose `checksum_sha256` is empty is refused the same way): inventing a digest would be worse than passing none, and advertising an unverifiable one is worse still. Separately, the advertised `download_url` and `artifact.filename` are now always the canonical `{namespace}-{name}-{version}.tar.gz` for the coordinate the client asked about, so an upstream that names a **different** collection or version in `artifact.filename` can no longer make this repository's own download route hand back other bytes under the requested version's name — the earlier check confirmed only that the upstream filename was a single addressable path segment, which a substituted-but-well-formed name passes. Both were reproduced end-to-end against a live instance with the real `ansible-galaxy` client before the fix and confirmed closed after, with a legitimate install still succeeding.

- **Two deployments sharing one S3 bucket shared one proxy-cache, and served each other's cached upstream bytes** (#3454). Proxy-cache content is anchored at the bucket ROOT rather than under `S3_PREFIX`, and deliberately so: that anchoring is what makes a prefixed deployment read back the objects it wrote (#3368/#3513). But it also meant the entire namespace was `proxy-cache/<repo_key>/<path>/__content__`, with nothing in the key naming the deployment that produced it. Two Artifact Keeper deployments pointed at the same bucket and separated only by `S3_PREFIX` therefore shared ONE proxy-cache key space. Two repositories that happened to carry the same key — `maven-proxy`, `npm-remote`, whatever the operator called them — addressed the same physical object in both deployments.

  This is not only a cache-efficiency problem. Reproduced live against two deployments on one MinIO bucket with distinct `S3_PREFIX` values, distinct databases and distinct upstreams: a repository keyed `mvn-proxy` in deployment A (upstream serving bytes A) and in deployment B (upstream serving bytes B). Whichever deployment fetched first wrote `proxy-cache/mvn-proxy/org/example/lib/1.0/lib-1.0.jar/__content__`, and the other then served those bytes from its own endpoint — content it never fetched, from an upstream it is not configured to use, retrieved under the other deployment's upstream credentials if that upstream needed any. It is a two-way exchange, not a one-way leak: the last writer wins, so it is equally a cache-poisoning primitive against the other deployment's users. Neither `S3_PREFIX`, nor separate databases, nor separate IAM policies scoped to different artifact prefixes prevented it, because the cache is not addressed through any of them.

  Cache keys now carry a per-deployment scope segment placed INSIDE the reserved namespace — `proxy-cache/<scope>/<repo_key>/<path>/__content__`. Placing it there rather than moving the namespace under `S3_PREFIX` is what keeps the change small and reversible in its effects: `key_is_bucket_root_anchored` still holds so #3368 stays fixed, `is_proxy_cache_key` and every `storage_key NOT LIKE 'proxy-cache/%'` accounting predicate still classify the key correctly, and the IAM `Resource` list operators were told to grant (`arn:aws:s3:::<bucket>/proxy-cache/*`) still covers it — **no policy needs re-cutting**. The scope defaults to the deployment's persistent peer instance id, the `peer_instance_identity` row seeded on first boot: stable across restarts and upgrades, shared by every replica of one deployment (so a horizontally scaled deployment still shares one cache), and not rewritten when `PEER_INSTANCE_NAME` or any other setting changes — keying a cache on a mutable value would orphan the whole cache the first time an operator renamed something. `PROXY_CACHE_SCOPE` overrides it with a legible token for operators who want one; there is deliberately no value that turns scoping off. The backend logs the scope it resolved at startup (`Proxy cache scope: ...`).

  **Upgrade note — what happens to objects already cached.** A key-layout change cannot both isolate and keep addressing the old objects, so this takes the cold-cache path rather than a read-through fallback to the shared layout: falling back would preserve exactly the cross-deployment reads the issue is about. On first start after upgrading, every proxy-cache lookup that derives its key misses once and refetches from upstream, then warms normally — expect a one-off burst of upstream traffic proportional to your working set, and no correctness change: a proxy cache miss is a refetch, not data loss. Nothing becomes unreachable. Reads that resolve a *recorded* key — the `proxy_cache_artifacts.storage_key` the on-demand rescan uses, and the legacy `artifacts` rows whose `storage_key` is a `proxy-cache/...` value — use the string recorded at write time and are unaffected, which is why the scope goes inside the namespace instead of moving it. **No operator action is required.** Objects cached before the upgrade are left where they are; they are no longer read, so they are dead weight in the bucket. Deleting a repository now sweeps both its scoped subtree and the pre-upgrade unscoped one, which reclaims them over time; to reclaim the rest immediately, delete the `proxy-cache/<repo_key>/` trees that have no scope segment — but only once every deployment sharing the bucket has upgraded, since until then you would be deleting a live cache belonging to one of them, and check first for legacy `artifacts` rows pointing into that tree (`SELECT count(*) FROM artifacts WHERE storage_key LIKE 'proxy-cache/%' AND is_deleted = false;`), which do still read from it.

  **Upgrade note — a handful of very long paths flip from served to a hard 400.** The scope segment is charged against the 1024-byte object-store key budget (`MAX_STORAGE_KEY_BYTES`), which is the object store's own hard limit and cannot be raised. The default (peer-instance-UUID) scope adds 37 bytes to every key — `<36-char-uuid>/` — so the longest cacheable upstream path shrinks by that much (fewer for a shorter `PROXY_CACHE_SCOPE` token). A path whose pre-upgrade key was within ~37 bytes of the limit — roughly 947–990 bytes of path depending on the repository key length — now exceeds the budget and is rejected with a `400` (`Proxy cache key exceeds 1024-byte object-store limit`) instead of being cached and served. This affects only pathologically deep coordinates and is deterministic (the same path always 400s, it does not flap); shorten the repository key or set a short `PROXY_CACHE_SCOPE` if you rely on such paths.

  **Sharing a bucket between deployments is now supported.** The previous guidance — that a bucket must be dedicated to one deployment because prefixing does not isolate the cache — no longer applies. `proxy-cache-staging/` stays unscoped: its keys are freshly minted UUIDs that cannot collide, and leaving it alone keeps the single documented lifecycle rule valid.
- **Maven checksum sidecars were cached for 5 minutes, so a build went back to the upstream registry for every checksum it verified** (#3459). Maven and Gradle request a `.sha1`/`.md5` next to every artifact they download. Those requests are served by the checksum branch of the Maven download handler, which proxies them through `proxy_fetch_capped_budgeted` — and that helper synthesized its upstream `Repository` through `build_remote_repo`, which hardcodes `RepositoryFormat::Generic`. `Generic` has no `cache_classifier` arm, so every path it is asked about falls to the conservative `MUTABLE_DEFAULT_TTL_SECS` 5-minute default. The classifier itself was never wrong: `classify(Maven, "foo-1.0.pom.sha1")` already strips the sidecar suffix and returns `Immutable`. It was being handed the wrong format. The result was a `.pom` cached for a decade next to a `.pom.sha1` that expired in five minutes and could never come back different, measured by the reporter at roughly a thousand redundant upstream round-trips per build, every one of them a checksum and every one answered `304 Not Modified`.

  The Maven-family proxy call sites now carry the repository's real format, so a released coordinate's sidecar is cached with the same effectively-infinite lifetime as the coordinate it describes: the direct Remote arm, the Virtual → Remote member arm (the topology in the report), and the ungated streaming arm a primary takes when its upstream publishes no `.sha1`. The sbt/ivy remote download arm had the same defect on the artifacts themselves and is fixed with it — sbt shares Maven's classifier rules, so its released `.jar`s were also being re-fetched every five minutes. `-SNAPSHOT` coordinates are republished in place and deliberately stay on the mutable TTL, as do `maven-metadata.xml` and its sidecars; regression tests pin that direction so this cannot become "cache every checksum forever".

  **The SNAPSHOT rule is corrected in the same change, and it matters most to sbt.** `classify_maven` decided a file under a `-SNAPSHOT` directory was still mutable by looking for the `-SNAPSHOT` token in the **filename** — which only holds for Maven's layout, where the filename repeats the version. Ivy's default pattern, `[organisation]/[module]/[revision]/[type]s/[artifact].[ext]` (what `Resolver.ivyStylePatterns` emits, and a supported sbt setup), keeps the revision in the **directory** only, so `org.example/mylib/1.0.0-SNAPSHOT/jars/mylib.jar` read as a released coordinate. Routing sbt to the real classifier without fixing this would have cached that jar for a decade — and cache freshness short-circuits an immutable entry to *fresh* without consulting its expiry, so a republished snapshot would never have been re-fetched at all. The guard now tests the path **component** and exempts only a filename carrying a resolved unique-snapshot stamp (`-YYYYMMDD.HHMMSS-<build>`), which is strictly more conservative than before in every case. Timestamped snapshots stay immutable, and that direction is pinned by its own test rows. The same correction reaches the release-immutability guards, which ask the same classifier.

  This is the same class as #3206 (OCI layers expiring five minutes after a pull, fixed by #2312 the same way), and `build_remote_repo` is shared, so the `Generic` default is reachable from other formats' proxy paths too. **Five of those sites are genuinely affected and are NOT fixed here**: the RPM package and repodata arms, the conda package arm, the OCI inline-scan blob staging arm, and the generic Remote download route all still cache immutable content for five minutes. They are tracked in #3556 with the per-site analysis, and they need helper siblings this change does not add. They are deliberately not swept in a patch that is already flipping paths from mutable to immutable: that is the direction that serves stale content forever, the sbt SNAPSHOT correction above is what happens when it is done without reading each site, and #3556 records that as the reason. The other format-less call sites carry index/metadata documents, which classify mutable under every arm and so are unaffected today.
- **Read paths matched `LIKE` patterns without escaping the value that becomes the pattern, so a path, a search term or a stored name containing `%`, `_` or `\` returned the wrong rows** (#3500). Six predicates across four sites assembled their `LIKE` *pattern* inside SQL by concatenating an operand — `a.path LIKE $2 || '%'`, `$2 LIKE a.name || '-%'`, `LIKE '%' || $2 || '%'` — and none carried an `ESCAPE` clause. That makes the pattern stop describing the thing it was derived from: `%` and `_` become wildcards, and a backslash — Postgres's DEFAULT `LIKE` escape character — quotes the character after it. This is the read-path half of #3492/#3493, which was the same shape on the Maven delete guards; there the consequence was data loss, here it is wrong rows.

  - **Repository tree listing** (`GET /api/v1/tree`): browsing a folder named `a\b` returned the contents of `ab/` and hid its own, because the pattern `a\b/%` was read as `ab/%`. A folder containing `%` or `_` pulled in sibling folders. Measured against a database and pinned by a regression test that fails in exactly that way on the parent commit.
  - **RubyGems quick gemspec** (`GET /gems/{repo}/quick/Marshal.4.8/{full_name}.gemspec.rz`): a gem whose stored name contains a backslash could not be fetched at all — its own row was filtered out of the candidate set before the exact re-check ran, and the endpoint answered 404. The over-matching direction the report describes is **not** a defect and is now pinned as such: `%`/`_` in a stored name only widen the candidate set, and the handler already re-verifies every candidate exactly in Rust, so a widened match cannot select the wrong gem.
  - **Docker tag search** (`?search=` on the tag listing, both the page and the `?count=exact` total): searching `1_0` also returned `1.0` and `120`, and a tag containing a backslash could not be found by typing it. Both arms now build the filter from one shared fragment so a future change cannot fix the page and leave the count disagreeing with it.
  - **Cargo search** (`GET /cargo/{repo}/api/v1/crates?q=`): the same shape, and **not** in the report — found by sweeping for it. Searching `serde_json` also matched `serdeXjson`, and a bare `%` returned the whole registry, with `meta.total` counting the extras.
  - **Artifact listing** (`GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/artifacts?path_prefix=`, and its `?count=exact` total): the same folder-listing defect as the tree, on the larger endpoint. Its pattern is built in Rust rather than in SQL, so it is a different shape from the four above and was found by review; it is fixed here because it is a folder-browse filter like the tree's, not a free-text search.

  Which escape a site needs is decided by where its pattern operand lives, and that rule is now written down next to the helper. Where the operand is a Rust value — the tree prefix, the artifact-listing prefix, the two search terms — it goes through the existing `escape_like_literal`, matched under `ESCAPE '\'`, so `%`, `_` and `\` are all literal: on a read path over-matching *is* the defect. Where the operand is a SQL expression the Rust helper cannot reach — the RubyGems column — it uses `ESCAPE ''`, the same answer #3493 chose for the Maven guards, which stops a backslash quoting while deliberately leaving `%`/`_` widening (harmless there, because that handler re-verifies every candidate exactly in Rust — pinned by a test that a first-row-wins handler fails). Every search stays a substring search; a positive control on each site pins that escaping did not turn one into an exact match.

  **The escaping, not the clause, is what fixes this.** `ESCAPE '\'` names the character Postgres already uses by default, so on its own it changes nothing: `'ab/x' LIKE 'a\b/' || '%'` is true with and without it, and `_` stays a wildcard either way. It is written explicitly because the rule should be visible at the site, but the fix is `escape_like_literal` on the bound value.

  A structural test scans every `.rs` file under `backend/src` and fails, with the offending file and line, on a SQL-assembled pattern that has no escaping story: it requires an `ESCAPE` clause **and** either `ESCAPE ''` (for an operand derived in SQL, which no Rust helper can reach) or an `escape_like_literal` in the function that owns the predicate. Requiring only the clause would have been useless, since `ESCAPE '\'` is the default; requiring the pair is what makes the gate fail on a site that carries the clause and binds a raw operand. It recognises the operator form (`~~`), `concat()`, `SIMILAR TO`, predicates wrapped across lines, and a second predicate on the same line, and it scopes the clause to the operator it matched so a neighbouring predicate's `ESCAPE` cannot vouch for an unescaped one.

  **What that gate does not prove:** its escaper check is function-scoped, so it shows an escaper is applied somewhere in the owning function, not that it is applied to *this* operand — and it is scoped to the SQL-assembled shape, so it says nothing about patterns built in Rust. The per-site behavioural tests are what prove the fix; the gate's job is narrower, to stop a new site in this shape being added with no escaping story at all.

  **Not swept here**, and tracked in #3557: roughly thirty sites that build their pattern in *Rust* (`format!("%{}%", q)`) for admin and package search listings. Several already escape, several take a pre-escaped value from their caller, and two deliberately over-match and re-check in Rust, so telling a real defect from a correct site needs per-site reading rather than a mechanical pass — and the change would settle a product question about whether a search box is a literal substring search or a wildcard mini-language. The one confirmed live defect in that group, the artifact-listing `path_prefix`, is fixed here rather than deferred.
- **A proxy rescan that could not produce a verdict answered one indistinguishable 503, and inherited a budget sized for a different request entirely** (#3455). `POST /{key}/security/proxy-scans/rescan` re-runs the scanner over bytes already sitting in the proxy cache, and until now every way that could fail to produce a verdict -- no scanner configured on the instance, the scan itself erroring, or the scan not finishing in time -- collapsed to the same `503 Service Unavailable` with the same generic body. An operator staring at that response had no way to tell "go configure a scanner" from "the scanner is broken" from "give it more time and try again"; all three demand a different next step, and the endpoint gave none of them a name.

  The budget half of this was worse than an inconvenience. The scan this endpoint runs shared its 30-second timeout with the inline download-time gate, and that 30 seconds was sized for a specific, narrower problem (#2954): bounding how long a client's `pip install` (or `npm`, or any other package-manager pull) sits waiting on a synchronous scan before the proxy serves or blocks it. A rescan has no such client on the other end -- the only party waiting is the operator who explicitly asked for it -- so there was never a latency budget to protect here, only a borrowed one. On a resource-constrained instance the borrowed budget could genuinely not be enough, and the scanner's cost here is a fixed startup cost -- loading a ~2 GiB vulnerability database and bootstrapping the cataloguer -- that a small artifact does nothing to reduce. CPU starvation is one demonstrated way to get there: measured against the real backend scanner image on a 74-byte input doing no meaningful scan work, wall-clock scan time was 2.84s unconstrained, 7.37s at 0.5 vCPU, 14.88s at 0.25 vCPU, and 34.75s at 0.1 vCPU -- past the old 30-second budget on CPU alone. Burstable instance types that have exhausted their CPU credits, and noisy-neighbour contention on shared tenancy, land exactly there. A separate block-read throttle on local NVMe, with full CPU and memory unconstrained, took the same scan to 21s at 100 MB/s, 27.6s at 75 MB/s, 40.8s at 50 MB/s and 101s at 20 MB/s. That experiment establishes that constrained read bandwidth can exceed the old budget without CPU or memory pressure; it does **not** measure network-attached storage, whose latency and jitter remain untested. The completed 20 MB/s run fits under the new budget's 120-second ceiling (a deployment that needs the full ceiling must run with a global request timeout above it -- see the derivation below). A 1 MB/s run was still incomplete after 129 seconds and was stopped, so it is not a completed worst-case measurement. Memory behaves differently again: it is not a gradual slowdown but a cliff, flat at ~3.5s from 512Mi down to 160Mi and then an OOM kill below that, which surfaces as a *failed* scan rather than a slow one. None of this is an exhaustive account of how a scan can run out of time -- it is what could be reproduced on one machine -- and the point of the discrimination half of this fix is that the endpoint could not tell any of these apart. What the endpoint cannot do is tell any of them apart, which is the other half of this fix: a rescan request that should succeed times out instead, and the only signal was the same undifferentiated 503 every other failure mode produced.

  The response now carries the standard machine-readable `code` field alongside the shared 503: `NO_SCANNER_CONFIGURED` when no scanner is wired up for the instance, `RESCAN_SCAN_FAILED` when the scan ran and errored (the underlying error is logged at `warn!` for an operator to triage, but deliberately not echoed into the response body -- it can name scanner internals the caller can act on none of), and `RESCAN_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` when the scan did not finish in time. The rescan endpoint now gets its own budget, independent of and wider than the inline gate's 30-second file budget, sized for the CPU-starved case above rather than for a `pip install` timeout it was never actually bounding. That budget is **derived from the router-wide request timeout** (`GLOBAL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_SECS`, default 120s) rather than fixed: the rescan route is not exempt from that timeout, the outer clock starts at request arrival while the budget clock starts only after auth, the catalog lookups, the cached-object read and its SHA-256, and a budget equal to the outer timeout therefore always loses the race -- the backstop kills the request first with exactly the undifferentiated timeout 503 this change exists to remove, and `RESCAN_BUDGET_EXCEEDED` is never reachable. A quarter of the outer window (at least one second) is reserved as headroom for that surrounding work, capped at a 120-second ceiling: 90 seconds at the default timeout, the full ceiling when the outer timeout is disabled (`0`) or at least 160 seconds.

  Widening the budget on its own would have let a repeatedly-timing-out rescan stack multiple scanner subprocesses against the same repository, so the per-repository cooldown between rescans moves from 30 seconds to 120 seconds to match: the cooldown must be at least as long as the widest budget a rescan can run under (the ceiling above), or a second rescan could be claimed and start while the first is still consuming CPU.
