The cooldown claim runs **before** the cached object is read and hashed, not after: the claim is the only thing bounding how many of these up-to-200 MiB scan buffers are in flight at once, so a rescan rejected by the cooldown is rejected before it costs a storage `GET`, a 200 MiB heap buffer, or a SHA-256 -- and an object that then turns out to be unreadable releases the claim again, so a pre-scan storage failure keeps its canonical 404 without consuming the repository's slot. That cooldown is now also released early for the one cause that never did any scanning work at all -- `NO_SCANNER_CONFIGURED` fails before a scan is ever attempted, so it no longer locks the repository out of rescans for the following two minutes on top of failing instantly. A cause that failed after actually starting a scan keeps a cooldown, because this endpoint has no clean way to tell a scan that failed immediately apart from one that failed after paying real scanner cost -- but a *failed* scan's remaining cooldown is capped at the pre-existing 30-second window, since the most common failure here is an absent or misconfigured scanner erroring in milliseconds (the report that opened #3455) and a full two-minute lockout per attempt would make that configure-and-retry loop four times worse; a budget-exceeded scan, which by definition consumed up to its whole budget, keeps the full window. `Retry-After` on the 503 now reflects the genuine remaining cooldown for whichever of these actually applies, rather than the old behaviour of naming the wait only on the budget-exceeded arm (and naming the wrong duration even there, since by the time that response is built the cooldown has typically already run out) and naming no wait at all on the other two, when in fact most of a two-minute cooldown was usually still outstanding. The throttled 429 also now uses the same standard `{code, message}` error envelope (`RESCAN_THROTTLED`) as every other error this endpoint returns, instead of a bespoke `{"error": ...}` shape only it emitted, and its OpenAPI entry documents the body.

  Separately, a scan that is cancelled when its budget expires no longer leaves its scanner subprocess running. `tokio::process::Command` does not kill its child when the future awaiting it is dropped unless told to, and a timed-out scan's future is exactly what gets dropped when `tokio::time::timeout` fires -- so a grype, trivy, or (for OCI image scans) tar/unsquashfs-extracting Incus scan that ran past its budget kept running to completion, unsupervised, on the box whose CPU was already the reason it timed out in the first place. Every timeout-reachable process-spawning scan and cleanup path, including the workspace-permission `chmod`, now sets `kill_on_drop(true)` so a dropped timeout ends the child along with the future that was waiting on it. Widening the rescan budget to 120 seconds without this fix would have let repeated timed-out rescans stack orphaned scanner processes on precisely the CPU-starved instances this change targets.

- **An upstream Rust release turned `main` and every open pull request red with no change of ours** (#3551). Nothing in this repository pinned a compiler. `🦀 Check Rust` installs no toolchain at all — it compiles with whatever `rustc` the self-hosted runner image happens to bake in — and every other Rust job asked for `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable`, which resolves at run time. On 2026-08-24 the runner image picked up Rust 1.98.0 (released 2026-08-20) and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` went from clean to **555 errors**, all `clippy::result_large_err`, all in `backend/src/api/handlers`, all on the one type `http::Response<axum::body::Body>`. Confirmed by A/B on the same unchanged commit: 1.97.0 exits 0, 1.98.0 exits 101 with exactly those 555. Three unrelated pull requests, one of which changes no Rust at all, were red on the identical count, and `CI Complete` gates the merge queue and the release chain.

  `Result<T, Response>` is the axum idiom here: the `Err` payload is not an error description to be rendered later, it *is* the HTTP response about to be returned, so `?` can propagate a fully-built 401/404/409 out of a helper. There is nothing to box. `axum::response::Response` measures 128 bytes, which is exactly clippy's default `large-error-threshold`, so `.clippy.toml` now sets that threshold to **129** — one more than the size of that single type. The lint stays enabled everywhere and keeps a real job: any `Err` variant of 129 bytes or more still fails the build. A unit test pins `size_of::<Response>()` against the threshold, so an axum or compiler upgrade that grows the type fails as one named assertion with both numbers in the message, rather than as hundreds of anonymous lint errors attributed to whoever pushed next.

  The compiler is pinned alongside it, because the lint was the symptom and the floating toolchain was the cause. `rust-toolchain.toml` names an exact version; `rustup` honours it over the `rustup default` that `dtolnay/rust-toolchain` sets, so one line governs CI, local `cargo` runs and contributor machines together, and the six workflow refs are pinned to the same version. Taking a new Rust release is now a pull request that has to go green before it reaches `main` — which is where new lints are meant to be triaged. `scripts/ci/check-toolchain-pin.sh` fails the build if the file and the workflow refs drift apart or if either re-floats, and `--active` (run in `🦀 Check Rust` before anything compiles) asserts the `rustc` that job is really about to use, so a pin that a runner image ignores fails immediately and by name instead of looking like protection it is not providing.

- **Native format routes refused reads a principal was entitled to, and misreported the refusal as a missing member configuration** (#3452, #3387, #3386). Two independent defects on the same request path, reported three times.

  The first is an authorization gate that disagreed with every other gate in the codebase. `repo_visibility_middleware`'s READ arm resolved a non-admin's access from the `permissions` table alone (`check_permission`), while the same middleware's write/delete arm, the ~23 REST read surfaces behind `require_visible`, and the virtual-member filter `try_authorize_virtual_members` all resolve through `check_repository_action` — which additionally honours a `role_assignment` when no fine-grained rule applies to the principal. So writing the FIRST fine-grained rule against a repository, for any principal including a completely unrelated one, silently revoked native-protocol READ for every principal whose grant is a role assignment: the creator auto-grant, `repository-owner`, and the rows migration 172 wrote on upgrade. Reproduced on a clean instance: with an unchanged `developer` role assignment, `GET /maven/{repo}/…/x.pom` went 200 → **403** the moment an unrelated user was granted `read`, while `PUT` to the same path stayed 201 and `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}` stayed 200 — the same principal could write a repository it could not read. The read arm now consults `check_repository_action` as well. This can only widen, never narrow: an applicable rule carrying the action (or `admin`) already satisfied the previous two checks. What is added is `check_repository_action`'s rule in full — **(a)** a role assignment carrying `admin` wins over everything, including an applicable rule; **(b)** otherwise an applicable direct/group/project rule is authoritative for the principals it names; **(c)** otherwise the principal keeps its role capabilities. An applicable `{write}` rule therefore still denies `read` to a `developer`, but **not** to a `repository-owner`: that role carries `admin`, and `check_repository_action` OR-s the admin-role term outside its rule-authoritative `CASE`. The practical consequence, stated because it is easy to miss — **`POST /api/v1/permissions` cannot narrow a repository owner's read on the native routes**, and `repository-owner` is auto-granted to every repository creator. That is not introduced here: the write/delete arm of the same middleware, `require_visible` and `try_authorize_virtual_members` have all resolved through this function since #3331, and `GET /api/v1/artifacts/…/download` already answered 200 for exactly that principal before this change. Revoking an owner means removing the role assignment, not writing a narrower rule. The two cached calls are kept ahead of the canonical query to short-circuit the population that IS named by a rule; note that for the role-assignment principal this change unblocks, `check_permission` returns false every time, so the uncached query does run on their allowed reads too (~0.5 ms cold, ~0 warm).

  The second is the message. A virtual-repository member walk that resolves to zero usable members has two causes — no member rows, or every member removed by caller authorization — and they were reported with three different bodies across two content types: maven answered `text/plain` `Virtual repository has no members`, npm and pypi answered `application/json` `{"code":"NOT_FOUND","message":"Virtual repository has no members"}`, and the download primitive's filtered arm answered `Artifact not found in any member repository`. That divergence broke two things. It left open the existence oracle `resolve_virtual_download`'s own comment claimed to close — only the filtered arm had been changed, so "this virtual is empty" and "this virtual aggregates a repository you may not see" stayed distinguishable. And `has no members` names a *configuration* fault, so an operator whose members are configured correctly re-checks them through the admin API, finds them present, and concludes the member resolver is broken. Every one of these paths (maven, npm, pypi, cargo, composer, and the shared download/metadata primitives) now returns one constant, `Virtual repository has no accessible members`, in the JSON error envelope on every format — including PyPI's two hand-rolled member walks (`serve_file` and the PEP 658 `.metadata` route), which bypass those primitives and were a live oracle of their own. The adjacent "members were visible, the artifact was not there" case keeps its own distinct message — a caller reaching it has already learned a member is visible to it — but that message, too, now renders as the JSON envelope on every format instead of `text/plain` on maven and JSON on pypi. The response body is identical by construction; the two causes remain distinguishable by TIMING (the filtered arm does the member-filter work the empty arm skips, ~2x median), which is structural and pre-existing and is not addressed here. The distinguishing detail moved to the server log, which is where it is safe: the member filter records how many members it dropped and why, and the middleware now states its decision on the existence-hiding 404 for a private repository the caller holds no grant on — previously neither the response nor the log said which of the two it was.

  #3386 ("service user ACL is reset on every update") is the same defect seen from the upgrade side and is closed as a duplicate: no ACL row is lost. Verified live — a redeploy that re-runs migrations leaves `permissions`, `role_assignments` and `user_group_members` byte-for-byte unchanged, `PATCH /api/v1/service-accounts/{id}` writes only `display_name`/`is_active`, and no migration deletes or rewrites any of the three (172 is purely additive). What changed across the upgrade was the evaluation above; recreating the account and reassigning permissions appeared to fix it because that writes an explicit `permissions` row, the one grant shape the old read gate honoured.

  Not changed, deliberately: `POST /api/v1/users/{id}/roles` writes `user_roles`, a table no authorization gate reads, so a user can be reported as holding `developer` with `["read","write"]` and still reach nothing. Wiring it up moves the gate in the fail-open direction with instance-wide blast radius — the table carries no repository scope, `developer` carries `write`, and SSO role mapping rebuilds it on every federated login — so it is documented on both endpoints and pinned by a characterization test, with the decision tracked in #3522. Group grants are unaffected and already work: `permissions` rows with `principal_type = 'group'` resolve through `user_group_members` in every gate.

- **Every partially-successful migration was recorded as a total failure** (#3497). A migration job in which some artifacts transferred and some did not resolves to `completed_with_errors` (`determine_final_status`, since #2457), and `MigrationJobStatus` renders that as the string `completed_with_errors`. The CHECK constraint on `migration_jobs.status` was written in migration 020 and never altered, and it did not list that value — so finalizing a mixed-outcome job raised `new row for relation "migration_jobs" violates check constraint "migration_jobs_status_check"`, the error propagated out of the worker, and the spawn wrapper stamped the job `failed` with the Postgres message in `error_summary`.

  The operator therefore saw a total failure for a run whose transferred artifacts were present and correct, and the one field that exists to say *which* items failed carried a constraint violation instead. The natural response — re-run the whole job — was the wrong one. `completed_with_errors` was also unreachable while `is_terminal_status` already advertised it as a terminal state on the SSE progress stream, so a client waiting for it waited forever. Migration 207 adds the value to the constraint; nothing else changes, and the constraint still rejects any value outside the model's set.

  **Reconciling past runs:** historical rows are deliberately not rewritten, but they are identifiable. `SELECT id, completed_items, failed_items, finished_at FROM migration_jobs WHERE status = 'failed' AND error_summary LIKE '%migration_jobs_status_check%';` lists the jobs that were in fact partial successes; their `completed_items` is the work that really landed. Re-labelling them (`UPDATE ... SET status = 'completed_with_errors', error_summary = NULL`) is safe after upgrading, but is left to the operator rather than done by the migration.

- **A Remote (proxy) Helm repository served an empty `index.yaml`, so `helm pull`, `install` and `upgrade` could not resolve any chart through it** (#3448). `helm` resolves a chart name and version entirely from the repository index before it requests any tarball, and for a Remote repository that index was built only from locally-catalogued artifacts — which for a proxy is empty. `helm repo add` and `helm repo update` both succeeded against `entries: {}`, so the failure presented as "no such chart" rather than as a server problem, while fetching the same tarball by its full path worked (200). Serving was fine; discovery was not. Anything pinning a complete chart URL was unaffected, which is likely why it survived: a Virtual repository with a Remote member already merged its members' upstream indexes, so only a repository pointed straight at an upstream was broken.

  A Remote repository's index is now the upstream's index, merged over whatever the repository holds locally, with every URL rewritten to this repository's own `charts/` route so the client comes back through the proxy for the tarball. The merge prefers the locally-held entry for a `(name, version)` it already has, because that entry carries the artifact's real stored filename — which is what the download route resolves before it consults upstream — and an upstream entry would advertise the `{name}-{version}.tgz` convention instead. That set is exactly what the download route can serve, so the index no longer promises more or less than the repository can deliver.

  When the upstream cannot be reached the answer depends on what is held. With charts held locally they are still served, so an upstream outage cannot break resolution of a chart the repository already has; with nothing held, the upstream's own error is surfaced instead of an empty index, because `entries: {}` is indistinguishable from "the upstream publishes no charts" and would leave `helm repo update` reporting success — the silent failure this issue is about. The status is the upstream's, not a uniform one: an upstream 5xx becomes 503, an upstream 404 (a mistyped `upstream_url`, the most common misconfiguration) stays 404, and a connect/DNS failure is 502 — so the operator can tell an unreachable upstream from a wrong URL from an upstream that is merely down. The proxy cache already applies RFC 5861 `stale-if-error` to the `index.yaml` object itself, so a warm proxy keeps serving the last good upstream index before that fallback is reached.

  Two robustness corrections come with proxying a third party's document. Upstream entries are dropped from the proxied index when their `name`/`version` cannot form a single path segment (`/`, `\`, `?`, `#`, `%`, control characters): the index rebuilds every URL from those attacker-influenced strings, and an entry like `../../../../etc/passwd` produced a still-same-origin URL — the `/helm/{repo}/charts/` prefix is fixed, so no host can be smuggled — that no longer addressed the chart the index had just promised. Percent-encoding was the obvious alternative and was rejected: an encoder aggressive enough to cover `%` also rewrites `+`, moving the URL of every legitimate `1.0.0+build.5` chart. Separately, `urls`, `created`, `digest` and `generated` now default when an upstream omits them; an index is parsed as one document, so previously a single non-conforming entry anywhere in it failed the whole parse and took the entire repository's discovery with it. `name` and `version` are still required, because there is nothing to advertise without them.

  The upstream index fetch is shared with the chart-download path, which resolves real chart URLs out of the same document, and its byte ceiling moves from the 8 MiB default to the large-metadata ceiling. A Helm index is the whole-repository listing — the direct analogue of the PyPI simple-index and npm packument documents already on the larger ceiling — and real upstreams exceed 8 MiB (`charts.bitnami.com`'s is ~26 MiB), which the default would have turned into a 502 for exactly the repositories this fix is for. The fetch now also reserves against the shared buffered-metadata budget (#2665/#2684), which the previous unbudgeted 8 MiB read did not, and that reservation is held across the parse, the merge and the render before riding the response body — the lifetime the RPM repodata proxy already established, so no part of the derived working set (the parsed tree, the chart vector cloned out of it, the rendered document) sits outside it.

  What the budget does and does not bound was measured rather than assumed, because the reservation is sized to the 128 MiB ceiling and not to the body. It therefore admits eight concurrent buffered index requests process-wide and makes further ones wait, which caps peak memory by CONCURRENCY rather than by bytes. Against a 27 MB upstream index on a cold backend, peak RSS above baseline was +1.94 GiB at 16 concurrent index requests, +2.34 GiB at 64 and +2.48 GiB at 256 — a sixteenfold increase in connections for a 28% increase in memory — while a 450 KB index moved it by +0.008 GiB at 64, confirming the cost tracks index size and not connection count. So the total no longer grows with load, but eight admitted requests whose individual working set exceeds its 128 MiB reservation still peak above the 1 GiB budget. Bounding it in bytes would need the whole-request working-set reservation the VS Code gallery path uses, which is a change to the shared budget's contract rather than to this handler, and is deliberately not made here.

  The chart-download path shares that fetch and therefore joins the same budget, having previously been unbudgeted. Its `index.yaml` lookup now waits for a reservation under heavy concurrent metadata load instead of buffering unconditionally; it is the hotter of the two paths, and this is a deliberate trade of tail latency for participation in a bound it was previously outside.

- **The mandatory pre-push checklist named a test command that fails on a clean tree, and `.config/nextest.toml` explained itself with a CI job that no longer exists** (#3479). `CLAUDE.md` told contributors to run a plain single-process `cargo test` for unit tests. Both CI unit-test jobs — Tier 1 and coverage — have run `cargo nextest run --workspace --lib --test-threads 8` for some time, and the difference is load-bearing: nextest gives each test its own process, and a number of unit tests depend on that isolation because they touch process-global state or are serialized only by the `db-serial` groups in `.config/nextest.toml`, which a plain `cargo test` run does not honour. Following the documented command on an unmodified tree produced ten NuGet `*_db_tests` failing with `503 Too many concurrent uploads for this repository` — the process-global per-tenant upload semaphore shedding across tests — and, at the default thread count, a run that did not terminate at all (#3377). Neither has anything to do with the contributor's change, and a checklist that is red for everyone teaches people to ignore red, which is more expensive than the original defect.

  The checklist now names the command CI runs, and documents the environment it needs — `DATABASE_URL`, `AK_TESTS_REQUIRE_DB=1`, `SQLX_OFFLINE`, `JWT_SECRET` — because without `AK_TESTS_REQUIRE_DB=1` every DB-backed test skips and reports success, which is a green run that proved nothing. The Tier 2 entry is corrected alongside it: CI does not run the whole `backend/tests/` tree either, but a fixed list of files' `#[ignore]`d cases, run serially.

  `.config/nextest.toml`'s rationale is re-derived from the current setup. It claimed a single-process `cargo test` unit-test job kept its in-process mutexes working, "which is why that gate stays green while coverage fails". No such job exists, and the premise did not generalize regardless — the `sync_worker` entries have no in-process mutex at all and fail today under a multi-threaded single-process run, so for those the test groups are the only serialization there has ever been. Reading the old comment, a maintainer would have concluded that removing an entry merely degrades one gate; it breaks the unit-test gate outright.

  A `shell-tests` guard now pins the documented command to the one CI invokes, with its own self-test. This defect class — documentation describing a gate configuration that has since moved — is invisible to every other check in the repository, because documentation is not compiled, linted or executed.

- **Proxy-cache content was read at a key nothing ever writes, on both S3 with `S3_PREFIX` set and on the filesystem backend** (#3368, #3463; layout documented for #3454). One storage backend holds two key spaces: artifact bytes, scoped to the deployment (`S3_PREFIX` on S3, `<STORAGE_PATH>/<repo_key>` on filesystem), and proxy-cache content — `proxy-cache/<repo>/<path>/__content__`, its `__cache_meta__.json` sidecar, and `proxy-cache-staging/` write staging — anchored at the shared root. Which scope applied depended on *which handle a caller happened to hold*: `StorageRole::ProxyCache` drops the prefix and is rooted at `STORAGE_PATH`, `StorageRole::ArtifactSource` keeps the prefix and is rooted at the repository's own directory. Every reader of a proxy-cache key therefore had to guess, and a `Remote` repository's `artifacts` row is read through the artifact handle by the local-artifact path of every format. Those reads resolved `<S3_PREFIX>/proxy-cache/...` (S3) or `<STORAGE_PATH>/<repo_key>/proxy-cache/...` (filesystem) — keys no writer produces.

  The result was a structurally guaranteed miss with no error anywhere: `serve_metadata`'s storage read missed and routed into `coordinated_retry_get`, which only re-reads the same key and answers **507 Insufficient Storage** — at a 1:1 ratio with the miss, permanently (#3463) — while the object sat untouched at the shared root; and the PyPI download arm's cache-hit branch missed on every request and re-fetched upstream. With no `S3_PREFIX` the two S3 layouts coincide, which is why the S3 half was invisible on most deployments; the filesystem half needs no configuration at all.

  The scope policy now follows the **key** rather than the handle. `proxy-cache/` and `proxy-cache-staging/` are reserved namespaces anchored at the shared root, applied where each backend picks its scope: `make_full_key` on S3, and `StorageRegistry::backend_for` handing the filesystem handle the global `STORAGE_PATH`. Both handles now address the same object. This fixes the reads for every format at once (npm, Maven, NuGet, Go, Debian, Helm, cargo, OCI and PyPI all record proxy downloads). Reading artifact bytes without their scope (#3171) stays fixed and is pinned by negative controls, including one asserting that a repository still cannot see another repository's hosted files. GCS and Azure register a single shared instance with no per-repository scope and are unaffected. `S3_PREFIX` set to a reserved namespace is now flagged at startup, since the two key spaces would overlap.

  **Am I affected?** Only deployments **upgraded from an older release** are. Current proxy traffic records cached objects in `proxy_cache_artifacts` and never writes a `proxy-cache/` key into `artifacts` (#1278), so on a database created fresh on 1.8.x these read paths are dormant. It is the surviving legacy `artifacts` rows that carry proxy-cache keys, and they are what the affected paths resolve: `SELECT count(*) FROM artifacts WHERE storage_key LIKE 'proxy-cache/%' AND is_deleted = false;` answers the question.

  **No migration and nothing is stranded.** Objects are not moved: the change makes reads target the location the proxy cache has always written to, so existing cached objects become readable again rather than being orphaned. On a prefixed S3 deployment the old miss-recovery left duplicate bodies under `<S3_PREFIX>/proxy-cache/` that no reader consulted; they can be deleted at any time (`aws s3 rm --recursive s3://<bucket>/<S3_PREFIX>/proxy-cache/`).

- **A refetched proxy-cache body is no longer written back through the artifact handle** (#3368, #3147). On a cache miss the PyPI download arm re-fetches upstream and teed the body into storage under the row's key. That refetch already runs through the proxy service's own cache path, which commits the body **and** its `__cache_meta__.json` sidecar under the `CachePersister` contract (#1618 S9) — so the second write added nothing except a body with no sidecar, no #1365 zero-byte guard, no #1051 ETag re-pin, no `proxy_cache_artifacts` row and no quota accounting, racing the proxy's own writer for the same object. Because `is_fresh` falls back to comparing the stored object's size against the sidecar's `size_bytes` when the pinned ETag is multipart-shaped, a same-length out-of-band body kept the entry "fresh" and the redirect path could sign a presigned URL for bytes the sidecar never vouched for. The truncation compensator would also `delete()` the live cache object. The tee is now restricted to keys the artifact handle actually owns. This has been live on every deployment without `S3_PREFIX`; on prefixed ones it landed on the unread shadow path, so anchoring the key layout without this would have made it live everywhere.

- **Neither the storage GC nor the repository-delete purge collects proxy-cache objects any more** (#3368). Both sweeps drive off `artifacts.storage_key` and neither consults `proxy_cache_artifacts`: the GC orphan predicate examines `artifacts`, `oci_tags`, `oci_blobs` and `oci_manifest_refs`, and the repository-delete purge's exclusivity guard (`no other artifacts row shares this key`) asks only about other `artifacts` rows. Proxy-cache keys are derived purely from `(repo_key, path)`, so a soft-deleted — or simply repo-owned — `artifacts` row names the *same* object a live `proxy_cache_artifacts` row points at. Either sweep would have destroyed a live cache entry and left a dangling catalog row whose `size_bytes` only clears on the next fetch. Neither bit before, because the delete was issued against a key nothing had written (`<S3_PREFIX>/proxy-cache/…`, or the per-repository filesystem root) and silently hit nothing; anchoring the layout makes those deletes land, so the exclusions land with it. Proxy-cache objects are reclaimed by `purge_repo_cache` — which the repository-delete path already runs — and by TTL/lifecycle expiry.

  The GC spares the *object* but still hard-deletes the stale *row*, deliberately: that hard-delete is the only reaper of soft-deleted `artifacts` rows in the codebase, so excluding the key from the candidate scan outright would have left those rows unreclaimable. A pass that skips a cache object no longer counts it toward `storage_keys_deleted` or `bytes_freed`, since nothing was reclaimed from storage.

- **A PEP 658 `.whl.metadata` miss on a proxy-cache-backed row no longer pays for a repair that cannot work** (#3463). `coordinated_retry_get` is the repair path for a *locally stored* artifact: it takes a cluster-wide hydration lease, re-reads the same key, and answers 507 if the object is still absent. Nothing local ever writes a `proxy-cache/` key, so on such a row the lease, the second read and an ERROR-level log line bought nothing — one deployment recorded the miss and the 507 exactly 32,681 times each in 24h, without a single coordinated re-read ever succeeding. `serve_metadata` now answers 507 straight away for those rows, which is the signal `serve_virtual_metadata` already recovers from by re-fetching the member's own upstream (the same provenance the wheel download resolves to). To be precise about the scope: this removes wasted work and the ERROR-log volume; it does not add a recovery that was missing, because the caller's own upstream re-fetch was already reached, and re-fetching inside `serve_metadata` as well would duplicate it. #3368 above is what stops the miss happening in the first place. The `#3372` invariant is unchanged — the answer stays 507 and never the 404 that would let virtual resolution fall through to a *different* member — as is a non-`NotFound` storage error, which is still surfaced rather than reinterpreted, and a hosted row, which keeps the hydration repair.

- **The storage layout and the IAM permissions the backend needs are now documented** (#3454). `.env.example` states that `S3_PREFIX` scopes artifact bytes only, lists the `proxy-cache/` and `proxy-cache-staging/` root paths the proxy cache requires, and gives the resource list an IAM policy must cover. A policy scoped to `<S3_PREFIX>/*` alone starts and serves hosted artifacts, then 403s every proxy-cache write, which the cache absorbs by silently re-fetching upstream on every request. The staging-prefix lifecycle-rule recommendation is stated in the same place. This documents the current layout; it does not move cache content under `S3_PREFIX`, and #3454 stays open for that.

- **A paused migration that is resumed and stopped again keeps the record of what it already migrated, and a running dry run reports real progress** (#3510). `process_job` restarts its in-memory counters at zero every time it is entered, while the job row's counters do not — a resumed job still carries the `completed_items`, `skipped_items` and `transferred_bytes` of the pass that was paused. The run-end and interruption publishes added in #3378 wrote those per-run counters to the row *absolutely*, so a job paused at, say, 73 of 100 items and then resumed and paused again before it had re-listed anything had its numerator and its transferred-byte total rewritten to zero — while the transfers they described were still recorded in `migration_items` and still present in the destination, and while the guarded `total_items` held at 100. The row read `0/100` at 0%, which is the same symptom the fix set out to remove, and because `generate_report` takes `summary.total_bytes_transferred` straight off that row, the job's migration report claimed that nothing had been transferred at all.

  Per-run counters are not themselves wrong: `resume_job` deliberately re-lists from offset 0 and re-classifies the earlier pass's work as `skipped`, so once a run has enumerated the whole source its figures are a complete description of the job. The error was publishing them before that point. A run may now only *replace* the row's figures once it has enumerated the whole source; while its view is still partial it may only *advance* them — the three item counters move as a group and only when the run has accounted for at least as many items as the row already claims, `transferred_bytes` never shrinks, and the denominator may grow but not fall back. Replacing stays available at the end of a run because that is what corrects an assessment estimate the content never matched, which is what #3378 asked for; and the `WHERE status NOT IN ('paused','cancelled')` guard on the denominator (#3378) and on the terminal status write (#3380) is unchanged, so a stopped job is still never stamped terminal.

  Two related corrections in the same function:

  - **A running dry run, and a re-run that finds everything already present, now report progress while they run** rather than only in the row they leave behind. The numerator went out once, at the end of the run, while the denominator went out per page, so for its whole running life such a job read `0/N` at 0% and then jumped straight to `N/N` — true of the final row but not of the running migration. The counters are now published at the end of every page as well, alongside the denominator that page already published. Per page rather than per artifact keeps the write rate of an all-skip delta run where it was.

  - **A migration the operator cancels in the moment after starting it is no longer run to completion and stamped `completed`.** `POST /migrations/{id}/start` sets the row to `running` and then spawns the worker as a detached task, so a cancel can land in the window before that task is scheduled. `process_job` opened with an unguarded `update_job_status(Running)` that put the row back to `running`; the guarded finalize then had nothing to protect and stamped the cancelled job `completed`, having migrated every artifact of a migration the operator had cancelled and received a `200 OK` for. The worker now claims the job under the same `WHERE status NOT IN ('paused','cancelled')` guard the finalize carries, and returns without contacting the source if the job was stopped first.

- **A running migration reports a real denominator instead of `N/0` at 0%, and a dry run or an all-duplicate re-run no longer reports `0/N` at 0% either** (#3378). `migration_jobs.total_items` and `total_bytes` were only ever written by `MigrationService::add_migration_items` and `save_assessment`, and the worker calls neither — it inserts each row through its own `add_migration_item`, which tracks the item but never touches the job's totals. Both the REST response and the SSE stream then divided the incrementing processed count by that untouched zero and short-circuited to `0.0`, so every job displayed a correct numerator over a zero total for its entire life and finished the same way. The worker now publishes the totals it enumerates, one update per page of source listings and once more when the run ends, and the two write paths no longer contend for the columns: the assessment's figures are a pre-run estimate that the run overwrites with what the source actually yields (the estimate itself is unaffected in `config.assessment`, which is what `GET /assessment` reads). A running total is the only honest option here, and deliberately so — neither Artifactory's AQL nor the Nexus component API reports a result-set count, which is exactly what the reporter observed about the Nexus paging model, so a total is knowable only by enumerating and any figure produced up front would be invented. The cost is that the percentage can fall back when a new page lands: a finished page of 1000 reads as nearly full until page two arrives and the same work reads as half. It is exact once enumeration ends, which is when it matters most, and the alternative — carrying an "unknown total" through the API for a web UI that has no way to render one — would leave every existing client showing nothing at all. Items the transfer loop skips before writing a `migration_items` row (duplicates, dry runs) still count toward the total, because they are counted in `skipped`/`completed` and the two sides of the fraction have to be drawn from the same population.

  The numerator had the same hole from the other side, which is why the report also covers dry-run executions. The only per-artifact `update_job_progress` sits at the end of the transfer block, and the three arms that `continue` before reaching it — a dry run, an item an earlier pass already completed, and a duplicate already present in the destination — never write anything to the row. A job made entirely of those ran all the way to a terminal status with `completed_items`/`skipped_items` still at the zero they were created with, so `N/0` at 0% simply became `0/N` at 0%: the same stall, and the reason a dry run or a delta re-run that found nothing left to do reported no progress at all. Every exit from `process_job` — a clean finish, an operator pause, a cancel — now publishes the counters and the discovered totals one last time, so the row a stopped or finished job leaves behind describes what the run actually did.

  Three smaller corrections ride along. **The run no longer clears the totals to `(0, 0)` before its first source listing.** The per-page publish is absolute and overwrites whatever it inherits, so clearing bought nothing and cost a window in which a resumed job showed a literal "73/0 items, 0%" — #3378's exact symptom — for as long as the first page fetch took; since #3380 made pause/resume reachable for single-repository jobs at all, that is the normal path rather than a corner. **`update_job_totals` now carries the same `WHERE status NOT IN ('paused','cancelled')` guard `finalize_job_status` has**: a page listing already in flight when the operator stops a job used to land afterwards and leave a dead job advertising a denominator covering work it never processed (`cancelled`, `1000/2000`, 50%) — it never touched `status`, so it could not revive a job, but the figures were fiction. And **a running job no longer reports a full 100%**: because the denominator is published a page ahead of the items in that page, a job that had just drained a full page read `1000/1000` and parked at a hard `100.0` until the next listing arrived, so a client keying on `progress_percent >= 100` would call it finished several pages early and a progress bar would fill and empty repeatedly. The reported share is now held just below full until the job reaches a terminal status, where the totals can no longer grow; `status` remains the authoritative completion signal and the underlying arithmetic is unchanged. That arithmetic now lives in one place, `models::migration::progress_percent`, with `reported_progress_percent` layering the ceiling on top, rather than in three subtly identical copies across the model, the job response and the stream loop — and the terminal-status predicate the stream stops polling on is now the same one the percentage consults, so the two cannot drift. It clamps at 100 because repository-level failures (a source repo missing from the listing, a destination conflict) land in `failed_items` without ever having been enumerated as items, and could otherwise push a job past full.
- **Pausing or cancelling a migration job during its final repository no longer flips it to a terminal status** (#3380). A pause or cancel observed between artifacts returned the same result as a fully drained repository, so when the interruption landed during the final (or only) repository the worker stamped a terminal status and `finished_at` over `paused`/`cancelled`; resume then rejected the job, leaving delete as the only option — for single-repository jobs pause always ended the job. The interruption now propagates distinctly from repository processing, and the terminal write is guarded at the database level (`UPDATE … WHERE status NOT IN ('paused','cancelled')`), so a pause racing the final write cannot be clobbered either. Uninterrupted jobs keep the exact prior behavior.
- **An empty repository-key segment no longer answers 500 with an internal type path** (#3443). `repo_visibility_middleware` returns early when the extracted key is empty — there is no repository to authorize — but it returned *without* inserting the `Option<AuthExtension>` every format handler binds, so axum rejected the request with `500 Missing request extension: Extension<core::option::Option<...AuthExtension>>`. Every format route reached it: `/npm//pkg`, `/pypi//simple/`, `/maven//`, `/lfs//objects/batch` and the rest all answered an unauthenticated 500. The middleware now answers that branch itself with an existence-hiding 404 rather than falling through, so the handler — and the strict extractor that produced the 500 — never runs. (The first version of this fix inserted an anonymous extension and let the handler run; that reintroduced the request body on an unauthorized path and was replaced, see the Security entry for #3508 above.)
- **The two guards that decide whether a Maven `maven-metadata.xml` rollup is still in use now anchor correctly for every stored key** (#3492). Both guards build a directory-prefix `LIKE` pattern *from* a stored key — the storage GC sweep's rollup guard (`ORPHAN_MAVEN_FLAT_PREDICATE_SQL` guard 3) and the collector that lists a repository's flat Maven objects before the repository is deleted — and neither carried an `ESCAPE` clause. Postgres's default `LIKE` escape character is a backslash, so for the subset of keys containing one the pattern no longer described the directory it was derived from: `maven/g/a\b/` became the pattern `maven/g/ab/`. The guards are `NOT EXISTS` tests, so a pattern that misses means "nothing is using this" — and for a rollup whose own subtree is still live, that is the wrong answer in the destructive direction.
- **Deleting a Docker/OCI manifest through the REST artifact API now unwinds the OCI index, and does it in the same transaction as the delete** (#3476). `DELETE /api/v1/repositories/<key>/artifacts/v2/<image>/manifests/<reference>` only flipped `artifacts.is_deleted`. The manifest's `oci_tags`, `oci_manifest_refs`, `manifest_blob_refs` and `oci_manifest_subjects` rows survived, so a "deleted" image was gone from the UI, the artifact listing and quota accounting while `GET /v2/.../manifests/<tag>` still served it, `tags/list` still advertised it and `docker pull` still succeeded. `HEAD` by tag and by digest both answered 200 with a matching `Docker-Content-Digest`, which is the `ErrAlreadyExists` short-circuit containerd-based pushers (`buildx --push`, `nerdctl`, `crane`, `skopeo`) use to skip the upload — so a re-push could not resurrect the row either. The surviving `manifest_blob_refs` are also what `BLOB_PROTECTED_BY_REFS_SQL` consults, so the config and layer blobs stayed permanently unreclaimable by storage GC.

  Both guards now go through one shared fragment, `metadata_rollup_dir_anchor_sql`, which carries `ESCAPE ''`. That makes the invariant the code has always documented — the anchor test can only ever over-*protect* — true for every character rather than only for `%` and `_`. `%` and `_` keep widening the pattern deliberately: over-matching spares a document that could have been reclaimed, which is a recoverable storage leak, while under-matching removes one that is still being served, which is not. Behaviour is unchanged for every key without a backslash, and unchanged for genuinely unreferenced documents, which are still reclaimed. Routing both call sites through the same fragment is also what stops the two delete paths drifting apart again, the divergence behind #3156 and #3197.

  The repository-delete collector is the more consequential of the two: it has no opt-in gate (unlike the sweep, which is behind `MAVEN_FLAT_GC_ENABLED` since #3431), and its whole purpose is to spare a rollup that *another* repository is still serving. On a shared cloud key namespace — the pre-#2624 layout, still selectable with `STORAGE_KEY_SCHEME=flat`, and the layout every object written before #2624 still lives in — deleting one repository could therefore remove a `maven-metadata.xml` a different repository was still serving. Repository-scoped keys (the default since #2624) are not exposed to that cross-repository case, because the directory prefix contains the owning repository's id.

  Regression tests cover both paths, with `%`/`_` fixtures pinning the over-protect direction and positive controls so that genuinely unreferenced documents — including ones whose directory contains a backslash — are still collected. No migration and no data repair: the guards decide what to delete, and nothing needs backfilling.
- **`OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP` is read by the environment bootstrap, and is definitive like every other `OIDC_*` setting** (#3420). The bootstrap read every other documented `OIDC_*` variable but never this one, so the env-managed provider's `attribute_mapping.admin_group` — the key the OIDC callback reads for admin elevation — never followed the variable. Renaming the group in the IdP and updating `OIDC_ADMIN_GROUP` left the stale group elevating, and the login-time env fallback could not cover it because it only engages when the mapping carries no value at all. The variable now flows through both bootstrap paths: creation persists it into the mapping, and the per-boot reconcile applies it to the existing provider.

  Both guards now go through one shared fragment, `metadata_rollup_dir_anchor_sql`, which carries `ESCAPE ''`. That makes the invariant the code has always documented — the anchor test can only ever over-*protect* — true for every character rather than only for `%` and `_`. `%` and `_` keep widening the pattern deliberately: over-matching spares a document that could have been reclaimed, which is a recoverable storage leak, while under-matching removes one that is still being served, which is not. Behaviour is unchanged for every key without a backslash, and unchanged for genuinely unreferenced documents, which are still reclaimed. Routing both call sites through the same fragment is also what stops the two delete paths drifting apart again, the divergence behind #3156 and #3197.
