On a shared cloud key namespace — the pre-#2624 layout, still selectable with `STORAGE_KEY_SCHEME=flat`, and the layout every object written before #2624 still lives in — deleting one repository could therefore remove a `maven-metadata.xml` a different repository was still serving. Repository-scoped keys (the default since #2624) are not exposed to that cross-repository case, because the directory prefix contains the owning repository's id.

  Regression tests cover both paths, with `%`/`_` fixtures pinning the over-protect direction and positive controls so that genuinely unreferenced documents — including ones whose directory contains a backslash — are still collected. No migration and no data repair: the guards decide what to delete, and nothing needs backfilling.

- **The scheduled storage-GC tick no longer runs on every replica at once, and its slowest guard is no longer a full scan of `artifacts` per candidate** (#3384). Each replica's scheduler computes the same cron occurrence independently, so on a multi-replica deployment every replica fired the hourly pass at the same instant and ran the same Maven flat-object orphan scan concurrently — observed in `pg_stat_activity` as several identical copies of that query sharing one `xact_start` and running for 20+ minutes. The pass is now wrapped in the cluster-wide `SchedulerLease` singleton already used for lifecycle-policy execution, under the job name `storage_gc`: exactly one replica runs it per tick, the rest return immediately, and the lease is released at the end of the pass rather than left to lapse. The lease is renewed for as long as the pass runs, so a sweep that outlives the TTL on a large registry does not lose it mid-run. **The on-demand endpoints are deliberately not gated** — `POST /api/v1/admin/storage-gc` and the per-repository panel call the GC service directly and keep working while a scheduled tick holds the lease.

  **This closes part of the tick, not all of it.** The lease covers the artifact-level GC pass only. The OCI blob-GC mark/sweep and the storage-stats recompute that share the same tick still run on every replica — with two replicas, the leased `maven_flat_object_owner` scan drops to one per minute while the un-leased `oci_blobs` scans stay at four to six. A replica that loses the lease now also returns immediately instead of after a two-minute GC, so the un-leased half fires on every replica simultaneously with none of the accidental stagger the slow path used to provide. Extending the coordination over the rest of the tick is tracked in #3503.

  The tick's other cost was one guard. The rollup guard that spares a `maven-metadata.xml` while any live artifact remains under its directory builds its `LIKE` pattern per candidate row, and Postgres only rewrites a `LIKE` into an indexable range scan when the pattern is a plan-time constant — so the guard was a hash anti-join against the entire `artifacts` table, re-evaluated once per candidate, and accounted for essentially the whole run. A partial `gin_trgm_ops` index on `artifacts.storage_key` (`WHERE is_deleted = false`, matching the guard's own filter) turns it into a bitmap index scan with the correlated pattern as an index condition. Measured on a 400,000-row `artifacts` table at the attribution-table size the report describes (136 rows), the candidate scan drops from **54.7s to 151ms** — the un-indexed plan removes 54,400,000 join-filter rows, one full pass over `artifacts` per rollup candidate, so it is quadratic and the gap widens with the candidate count: at 20,000 attribution rows the indexed scan still ran in 2.5s while the un-indexed one had not finished after 52 minutes. The result set is identical — GIN trigram scans are lossy by construction and Postgres always rechecks the real `LIKE` against the heap row — and it composes with the `ESCAPE ''` anchoring from #3492, which still plans as an indexable `~~`.

  **Operator note — this migration briefly blocks writes to `artifacts`.** `sqlx` runs each migration inside a transaction, so `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` cannot be used; the plain build takes a `SHARE` lock on `artifacts` for its duration. Reads are unaffected (`SELECT` takes `ACCESS SHARE`, which is compatible), but uploads across *every* format block until it completes, and it runs at each replica's startup migration — so the stall lands in the middle of a rolling deploy. Measured: 1,492 ms for a 24 MB index over 400k rows, roughly linear in row count, so around 40s at ~10M artifacts and over 3 minutes at ~50M. Size and build time also scale with key length, which is user-influenced (`storage_key` is `varchar(2048)`): at a fixed 20,000 rows, typical Maven keys built in 223 ms / 3.9 MB while max-length high-entropy keys took 5,463 ms / 115 MB. Sites that cannot accept the stall should build the index out of band before upgrading — the migration is `IF NOT EXISTS`, so it then becomes a no-op:

  ```sql
  CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_artifacts_storage_key_trgm
    ON artifacts USING gin (storage_key gin_trgm_ops)
    WHERE is_deleted = false;
  ```

  A second index on `maven_flat_object_owner.storage_key` was proposed with this change and **dropped after measurement**: at 20,000 attribution rows over 400k artifacts the planner did not choose it in the real query (the five-way anti-join estimates a single surviving row, so an ordered index scan is never believed to terminate early), and it made no measurable difference — 2,522 ms with it against 2,468 ms without, `Seq Scan` plus top-N heapsort both ways. It would have cost a write-blocking build and ongoing write amplification for nothing.

  Two smaller items ride along: the block's fixed 120-second startup sleep now uses the same jittered startup delay as every other periodic block in the scheduler, and the tick body moved out of the scheduler closure into `StorageGcService::run_scheduled_tick`, where it is directly testable. Neither the opt-in `MAVEN_FLAT_GC_ENABLED` gate nor the source allowlist from #3431 is touched — both are re-asserted through the leased entry point by regression tests, since this change makes that sweep reach its candidates far more reliably than before.
- **The unit-test suite hung indefinitely under a plain `cargo test` run, and four `read_json_capped` tests failed at lower thread counts** (#3377). `test_configured_proxy_host_is_exempted_from_guard` sets `HTTP_PROXY` — and clears `NO_PROXY`, removing the usual loopback exemption — for the synchronous window in which it builds its own client (#2570). `std::env::set_var` is process-wide, so under the single-process, multi-threaded runner any client another test happened to build inside that window was captured, because reqwest reads the proxy environment at client-build time. Requests those tests aimed at their own loopback listener went to the sibling test's proxy listener instead.

  What that looked like depended on timing. At `--test-threads 8` the proxy listener was already gone, so four `services::http_client::tests::test_read_json_capped_*` failed with `Connection refused` on a port none of them had opened — the shape reported. At the default thread count the proxy listener was still accepting, so the captured request waited for a response that never came while the test's own spawned server task sat in a bare `let _ = server.await` over `listener.accept()`, which cannot return if the connection never arrives: the whole run never terminated. Three further tests were caught through a second consumer of the same variables — the SSRF DNS resolver builds its proxy-host exempt-set from them (#2570), so a resolver constructed inside the window exempts `localhost`, the loopback hard-block those tests assert on stops firing, and an intact security control is reported as broken.

  Every client in the module that talks to a listener the test itself started is now built with `no_proxy()`, which is immune to the environment instead of depending on each call site remembering to take a lock. The three tests that assert the resolver REFUSES a host are built inside the existing `PROXY_ENV_LOCK` window instead, because reqwest's proxy setting cannot undo the resolver's exempt-set and only excluding the window can. Every spawned server task is now joined under a wall-clock bound, so a future miswiring fails with a diagnosis rather than hanging the binary, and a source guard keeps both shapes from returning.

  No CI gate was affected: CI runs `cargo nextest`, which gives each test its own process, so the process-wide variable cannot cross between them. The cost was borne locally, where a contributor's pre-push run either failed on four tests unrelated to their change or never finished at all.

- **Build provenance attestation now fails the publish job instead of being swallowed, and VEX attachment says out loud that it is best-effort** (#3496). Six STEP-level `continue-on-error: true` sat on `docker-publish.yml`'s supply-chain steps: `Generate artifact attestation` on all four published images (backend, OpenSCAP, scanner-adapter, backend-alpine) and `Attach VEX attestations` on the two that carry VEX. Step-level is the worst available shape for a control — unlike job-level it leaves the JOB result `success`, so `needs.<job>.result`, required checks and every downstream gate see green, nothing is written to the run summary, and no annotation is raised. An OIDC token outage, a registry rejection, a rate limit or an `actions/attest-build-provenance` outage was therefore indistinguishable from success, and the only trace was a small icon in a log nobody opens. **Build provenance had consequently never been proven to attach to any published image.** It is the same failure the project already paid for in #2824, where the cosign step failed and 1.6.1 shipped unsigned and was caught only because someone went looking; the four `Sign image with cosign (keyless)` steps have hard-failed since then and were not part of this defect.

  Provenance attestation is a **control** and now hard-fails. That is affordable here for a reason worth stating: the attestation step runs *after* `Apply ghcr tags` and `Copy to Docker Hub`, so hard-failing does not block a publish that would otherwise have happened — the image is already on both registries either way. What it changes is that the missing predicate becomes a red job instead of nothing at all, and the recovery is `Re-run failed jobs`, because every step in these jobs is idempotent by construction (`imagetools create` re-points the SAME digest, `cosign sign` and `attest` are safe to repeat).

  VEX attachment is **best-effort**, and stays so — `docker scout attestation add` depends on an external service and on Docker Hub credentials, and an outage there is not a reason to redden a release. But the decision moved out of the invisible YAML key and into the script, where a reader can see it: failures are collected per file and reported with a `::warning::` annotation and a `$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY` section naming each VEX document that did not attach, and the step still exits 0. `docker-publish.yml` now carries no `continue-on-error` at all.

  `scripts/ci/check-supply-chain-soft-fail.sh` pins the invariant so it cannot come back: no attestation (`actions/attest-*`) or cosign signing/attesting step in `.github/workflows/` may set `continue-on-error` to anything but a literal `false` — an expression that could evaluate true counts as soft — and the publish workflow may carry none on any step or job. It fails rather than passing vacuously if signing and attestation disappear entirely, and it ships with a self-test (`test-check-supply-chain-soft-fail.sh`, wired into the shell-tests job) that asserts each of the shipped shapes is rejected. Run against the pre-fix workflow it reports all six steps by name.

  Two things are deliberately **not** in this change. There is still no post-publish verification that a published digest actually carries the provenance predicate and its signature — `verify-published` probes for tag existence only — and adding an unvalidated `gh attestation verify` hard gate to the tag path would be the same class of mistake as the one being fixed, so it is tracked separately along with a one-off audit of the digests published while the control was soft.
- **The #2609 container-scan publication guard has been failing on `main` since #3122 and running in no CI job at all** (#3437). Two independent defects in the same file, and the guard was worthless for both reasons at once.

  **It was wrong.** `backend/tests/workflow_scan_gate_tests.rs` asserted that *every* `aquasecurity/trivy-action` step in `docker-publish.yml` carries `exit-code: '1'`. #3122 deliberately split the scan into two passes per image — a SARIF **visibility** pass at `exit-code: '0'` that feeds the Security tab at every severity and never blocks, and a table-format **enforcement** pass at `exit-code: '1'` that is the control the `merge-*` jobs depend on — because `trivy-action` runs `unset TRIVY_SEVERITY` for SARIF, so the old single pass discarded its own `CRITICAL,HIGH` filter and blocked every publish from `main` on a LOW (#3121). Three of the guard's four assertions only ever made sense on the enforcement pass, so from #3122 onward it reported the gate as disabled while the gate was in fact working. The guard now models the **pair**: each scanned image must have exactly one visibility pass and exactly one enforcement pass, the enforcement pass must gate on the stated policy (`exit-code: '1'`, `CRITICAL,HIGH`, `ignore-unfixed`, `.trivyignore`, and a non-SARIF format so the filter survives the action), and the visibility pass must not block and must not declare a `severity:` it cannot honour. Pairing is what keeps it non-vacuous: filtering to enforcement steps and checking only those would accept a workflow that had quietly lost its enforcement pass altogether, which is the regression #2609 exists to catch.

  **It never ran.** The file is an integration target under `backend/tests/`, so Tier 1 (`cargo nextest run --workspace --lib`) never compiled it, and Tier 2 runs a fixed 16-name `--test` allowlist that does not include it. The issue's premise that `cargo test --workspace` is the Tier 2 gate and is red is not correct — no job runs that command, so there was no red signal anywhere; a guard against image publishing silently becoming non-blocking was itself silently non-blocking. It now runs in **Tier 1**, as its own step in the unit-test job, with `--no-tests=fail`. Adding it to the Tier 2 allowlist as first suggested would have re-created the defect in a new place: that job invokes `-- --ignored`, every suite in its allowlist is 100% `#[ignore]`d by construction, and these tests are not — the invocation reports `running 0 tests ... 3 filtered out` and exits **0**. Tier 1 is also the right home on the merits: pure YAML parsing, no database, no network, ~25 ms, and it gates every pull request rather than only backend-touching ones.

  The sibling `scripts/ci/check-trivy-gate-severity.sh` (#3122) is deliberately left alone: it covers the same policy from the other side — every *gating* Trivy step in *every* workflow applies the filter it declares — with no Rust compile, and the two together now fail from either direction.

- **The code-duplication gate silently skipped 45% of `backend/src`, so for the repository's largest files it had never been able to fail** (#3495). jscpd defaults to `maxLines: 1000` and `maxSize: "100kb"` and skips a file over **either** limit silently — no error, no warning, no entry in the report — after which the gate reports whatever the remaining files measured. The CI step never overrode those limits, so **152 of 336 `.rs` files under `backend/src` were never analysed, 125 of them not on `.jscpd.json`'s ignore list**, including `services/`, `storage/` and `middleware/` files that the config's own comment goes out of its way to keep in scope. A pull request whose Rust changes landed only in one of them got a duplication verdict computed from an empty file set: with `repositories.rs` and `services/artifact_service.rs` as the entire changed-file list the gate reported `Code Duplication: 0% (no duplicates found)` and passed, having analysed nothing at all. A deliberate 79-line clone injected into `artifact_service.rs` passed the same way.

  (The issue this fixes named three files, on the basis that they exceed both limits. jscpd applies the two limits independently, so the real set is every file over *either* — about 45% of the tree.)

  **Raising the limits alone would have made the gate unusable, which is why the measurement changed too.** `backend/src` is 474k lines, of which 265k — **56%** — are inline `#[cfg(test)]` modules; `repositories.rs` is 26,328 lines with 22,164 of them test code. With the limits raised and nothing else changed the non-ignored tree scores **3.38%** and **23 of the last 44** code-touching commits on `main` would have failed the 3% gate, with 58 of 61 clones in the reported sample sitting entirely inside `#[cfg(test)]`. That is not a duplication problem; it is the gate measuring something it never meant to. `.jscpd.json` already ignores `**/*_test.rs` and `**/tests/**`, and the CI step already drops `_test`/`tests/` paths from the changed-file list — test code is out of scope **by policy**, and inline test modules were out of scope only **by accident**, because the files holding them were too big for jscpd to open. They are now excluded explicitly, by `scripts/ci/jscpd-prepare-sources.py`, which copies each changed source with its top-level `#[cfg(test)]` items removed and keeps a line map so a failure still reports real line numbers. Only **column-0** attributes count as boundaries: an indented `#[cfg(test)]` is inside another item, and treating it as top-level would delete production code — 22 files under `backend/src` have one. With that in place the tree scores **2.27%** and 2 of those 44 commits exceed the threshold, both on genuine production-code clones in `storage_gc_service.rs` and `auth_config_service.rs`.

  **Two silent passes are now failures.** A changed file that jscpd did not analyse — for any reason, not only size — fails the gate with the file named and the reason given, rather than being averaged out of the result; and a run that produces no report at all now fails instead of printing `0% (no duplicates found)`, which is precisely what a whole-file-set skip looked like. A changed-file set where nothing reaches jscpd's 10-line floor is still reported as N/A and passes, because that is the one legitimate omission. The limits live in `.jscpd.json` next to the ignore list, the CI step reads them from there and passes them explicitly, and `scripts/ci/test-jscpd-prepare-sources.sh` (wired into the shell-tests job) pins the preparation step's behaviour from the failing side.

  Two consequences worth stating. Files it now measures may hold pre-existing clones that the PR touching them did not introduce, because the gate's scope is whole changed **files**, not changed lines (#1619). And `oci_v2.rs` stays on the ignore list: that exemption is deliberate and documented (#1704), and is unaffected by this change either way.

- **`release.yml` did not require a Release Preflight, so the guard that would have saved v1.7.5 and v1.7.7 was optional** (#3538). `RELEASING.md` step 1 has said "run the release preflight and get a `READY` before you tag" since #3043, and nothing enforced it: `release.yml` had no dependency of any kind on `release-preflight.yml`. A guard's absence is invisible — only its failure is visible — and the two most expensive incidents in the 1.7.x line were both that shape, together ~46 hours of delay and two permanently burned version numbers. **v1.7.5**: preflight check 4 (#3339) exists precisely to catch an unbumped `docker/scanner-adapter/VERSION`, was merged 2026-08-13, and was simply never run — the Actions API shows zero Release Preflight runs between 2026-08-14T14:19Z and 2026-08-17T13:51Z. **v1.7.7**: the preflight ran and was *right*. Run `32377238021` reported `Docker Publish for HEAD did NOT cleanly publish the manifest — a tag cut WILL stall on the same gate`; two dispatches at 21:22Z reported the follow-up publish's `verdict does not exist yet`; `v1.7.7` was tagged at 21:40:17Z, eighteen minutes later, and that docker-publish concluded `failure` nineteen seconds after the tag push.

  `release.yml` now has a `preflight-evidence` job ahead of `resolve-candidate-digest`, and the `release` job names it too. The rule is one sentence: every Release Preflight run for the commit being tagged must have **completed**, and the newest completed one must have concluded `success` and left a `release-preflight-<sha>` artifact naming that commit. Each clause is load-bearing. An **in-flight** run is a verdict that does not exist yet, so it blocks rather than being read as absent or harmless — that is the v1.7.7 shape exactly, and a concurrent re-run costing a release forty seconds is worth paying to make it impossible. The **newest completed** run decides, not "some green run exists": checks 1, 3 and 4 measure state outside the tree, so the same commit can legitimately go red after being green, and honouring a superseded green would re-import the revoked "the red is cosmetic, promote anyway" reasoning at the level of run selection. And the run must **name the tree it audited**, because the Actions API's `head_sha` is the sha of the ref a run was *dispatched* on, not the sha it checked out; `release-preflight.yml` now computes `git rev-parse HEAD` inside the run and puts it in the artifact name.

  Requiring the evidence rather than re-running the preflight inside `release.yml` is the deliberate choice, and it is not the simpler one. An inline copy could not be stale — but it would run *after* the tag exists, which is after the version number is already spent and the tag is immutable, so it would have moved v1.7.5's red later rather than earlier. The only way to hold a green preflight for commit X is to have run it on X, before tagging; requiring the evidence is what puts the check back in front of the cut. It also keeps one definition of "releasable" instead of two that can drift, and costs two API calls instead of ~40s of duplicated work on every release.

  The preflight's own `exit 1` (NOT READY) / `exit 2` (INFRA) distinction is preserved end to end: a query that could not be answered reports `INFRA` and fails the job, and is never rendered as a pass. A **documented break-glass** exists, per the freeze policy's "skip schedule, never integrity" — this gate predicts whether the chain will stall, it does not certify the bytes, and the three gates that do certify bytes (`resolve-candidate-digest`, `release-gate`, `verify-images-published`) are untouched and still required. The override is a `Preflight-Override: <reason>` trailer in the **annotated tag's own message**: the tag object is immutable under ruleset 19144026, is scoped to exactly one version, cannot be added after the fact, and is readable forever with `git show`, none of which is true of a workflow input or a repository variable. A reason is required (at least 20 characters of one); a trailer without one is refused rather than honoured, and every honoured override prints the verdict it overrode, raises a workflow warning and is written to the run summary.

  **One behaviour change to `release-preflight.sh`'s exit-code contract, stated out loud.** Every check that cannot be measured exits the script immediately, which discarded whatever `problems` the earlier checks had already counted — so a run where check 1 found real forward-port drift *and* a later check hit INFRA reported exit 2, `retryable`, when the true answer was "you are not ready and retrying will not help". **Exit 1 now outranks exit 2**: if a blocking problem has already been counted, an unmeasurable later check yields NOT READY, with the transcript saying which checks did not run so the incomplete audit is not mistaken for a clean sweep. This does not weaken INFRA in the direction that matters — an indeterminate result still never reads as a pass, nothing that used to block stops blocking, and the only conversions are exit-2 → exit-1. Checks only ever add problems, so a verdict reached this way cannot be withdrawn by a check that did not run. The case is real rather than hypothetical: it is what surfaced when #3537's CHANGELOG-reconciliation check landed alongside the ref-awareness cases here, and it is now pinned from both sides — forcing `infra_exit` to always exit 2 fails the new cases, and forcing it to always exit 1 fails five pre-existing INFRA cases, including #3537's own.

  One thing the gate depends on was fixed alongside it. `release-preflight.yml` hardcoded `ref: main` in its checkout, so dispatching it from `release/1.7.x` audited **main's** tree — v1.7.5, v1.7.6 and v1.7.7 each got a `READY` verdict that was a statement about a different branch (#3464). That was corrected on `release/1.7.x` for v1.7.8 and never forward-ported; `main` still had it. The workflow now audits the ref it was dispatched on (with an optional `ref` input), and the verdict line names the ref and sha it evaluated. `scripts/ci/test-assert-preflight-evidence.sh` covers every leg of the new gate from the failing side — no run, in-flight, superseded green, red, evidence naming another commit, both indeterminate paths, and each break-glass outcome — and runs in the `shell-tests` job alongside the preflight's own self-test.

- **Release bookkeeping is now checked by the pipeline instead of by a human days later** (#3537). Four of the last eight releases shipped with wrong or missing notes/CHANGELOG state, and the only automated check asserted two things: that a `## [X.Y.Z]` heading exists and that it has at least one non-empty line under it. A section can exist, be non-empty, and describe a different release. v1.7.1 was cut with no `.github/release-notes/1.7.1.md`; `release.yml`'s "Resolve release notes" step tested `if [ -f "$F" ]`, found nothing, logged a line and fell back to `generate_release_notes: true` — and because auto-notes do not promote the CHANGELOG, eight `[Unreleased]` entries that had already shipped stayed under `[Unreleased]`, one of them telling 1.7.1 operators to act "before upgrading to 1.7.2" when they had been exposed for a week (#3318). A PR merged about five hours after the v1.7.3 tag filed its bullet under `## [1.7.3]`, so those notes claim a fix that release does not contain. The 1.7.5 prep renamed `## [Unreleased]` without opening a fresh one, and four later PRs merged into the released section with no conflict (#3433). The two scanner-CVE fixes that unblocked the v1.8.1 publish were filed under `[Unreleased]` rather than `[1.8.1]`.

  Five things now assert what was previously assumed. A stable `vX.Y.Z` with no curated notes file is **refused** — at the release preflight, a minute in, and again at the step that makes the decision; the `generate_release_notes` fallback survives for prereleases only, which is the only case it was ever meant for. The CHANGELOG's first `## [` heading must be `## [Unreleased]` at release time and not only on PRs, because a release-prep commit can land the 1.7.5 rename without any PR-time run seeing the tree in that state. `.github/release-notes/` may not hold a file for a version with neither a tag nor a Release; `1.7.5.md` was such a file and is removed here. And `scripts/ci/release-preflight.sh` gains a two-way reconciliation: every pending entry's lead issue reference must resolve to a commit in `<previous stable tag>..HEAD`, and every merged PR in that range must be named by some pending entry. Replayed against the v1.7.1 cut, the preflight reports the entry that was left behind and the release-time check refuses the tag outright.

  Two details are load-bearing rather than incidental. The pending section is `## [Unreleased]` **plus** any `## [X.Y.Z]` section newer than the previous stable tag: preflight is step 1 of a release and the CHANGELOG promotion is step 3, so a run made in between sees the same work under a version heading, and reconciling against `[Unreleased]` alone would report every commit in the range as undocumented — 27 false failures against one true one on the v1.7.1 replay. And every check reads **the ref being released**, never `main`. `main` and `release/1.7.x` hold disjoint halves of the 1.7.x curated-notes set — 1.7.6 and 1.7.8 exist only on the branch those releases were cut from, which is the ref `release.yml` reads — so a main-relative check would fail two correct releases and catch nothing extra.

  Reconciliation depends on a convention that is now written down: every CHANGELOG bullet names the issue it closes, and dependency bumps and `chore(release):` commits are the only commit shapes exempt from needing an entry. `### Sponsors` and `### Thank You` bullets credit whoever filed an issue and are not entries. Each new assertion has a self-test that constructs the bad state and proves it red, wired into the `shell-tests` job — including one that extracts the `Resolve release notes` block out of `release.yml` and executes it, so a revert to the silent fallback fails a test rather than passing review.

- **Natively-published npm packages are actually scanned** (#3442). Grype scans of npm packages published directly to a hosted repository returned `0 findings` regardless of what the package contained. The hosted-upload scan path extracts the tarball into a workspace and runs the CVE engine in directory mode, and directory-source cataloging reads `package-lock.json` but not the standalone `package/package.json` that a published npm tarball ships — so the engine cataloged nothing, matched nothing, and reported a `completed` scan with zero findings and no error. "Nothing was assessed" and "the artifact is clean" were the same result. Verified on a hosted `lodash@4.17.11` (1 Critical + 3 High): `completed, findings_count = 0`, `0 cataloged`, against a current CVE database.

  The machinery to fix this already existed and was simply not reachable from this path. The inline proxy gate (#3003/#3004) derives an `ExpectedComponent` from the request coordinate and materializes an ecosystem-native metadata file into the scan workspace so the engine has something to grade; every hosted call site passed `None`. A hosted upload has no request coordinate, but it has the registry's own `artifacts` row, written by the format handler from the publish payload it already validated — so the pin is now built from that. It costs no network call and reuses code already under test. The same `lodash@4.17.11` now reports 7 findings (1 Critical, 3 High, 3 Medium), matching what the engine reports for that coordinate directly; a genuinely clean package still reports zero.

  Scoped deliberately to npm and its handler aliases (`yarn`, `bower`, `pnpm`). Formats the engine already catalogs on its own — Maven jars, PyPI wheels — are untouched, as is every format with no pin defined; PyPI sdists, RubyGems, Cargo and NuGet have the same blindness on the same path and are tracked in #3603 rather than widened into this fix, because each needs either a dedup design decision or a new pin ecosystem, and each carries its own upgrade note. Because the pin is a second catalog entry for the uploaded component, a tarball that also ships a `package-lock.json` or `npm-shrinkwrap.json` naming itself was cataloged up to three times and had each of its findings counted three times (measured: 21 findings / 3 Critical for 7 real CVEs); pinned scans now collapse those duplicates before the counts are taken and before the rows are persisted, so the summary and the finding list cannot disagree. Distinct component versions survive, and unpinned formats keep their previous behavior exactly.

  **Making the verdict a function of the coordinate required hardening four things around the pin, or the fix would have turned into an attacker-controlled false clean (#3604).** The cross-artifact scan-reuse key (`find_reusable_scan`) matched only `(checksum, scan_type)`; once the answer depends on the coordinate, byte-identical uploads under different coordinates collapsed onto one cached verdict, and reuse is consulted before the scan runs, so a publisher with only `write:artifacts` could prime a clean verdict under a throwaway name and have it served for the real vulnerable coordinate — and the reverse, priming a flagged verdict to block good content. Each `scan_results` row now carries the `pin_identity` that produced its verdict (migration 209), and reuse requires `pin_identity IS NOT DISTINCT FROM` the current request's — so a `NULL` (unpinned) verdict matches only another unpinned request and never an npm advisory, and vice versa. The pin, trusted from the `artifacts` row, is now cross-checked against the tarball's own `package/package.json` the same way the proxy serve path already was: a file uploaded to a coordinate it does not actually claim (a text file at `.../handlebars/4.0.11/notes.txt`) is scanned unpinned and recorded `partial`, not graded as that component. The generic artifact endpoint's coordinate derivation now keeps an npm scope with its name (`@babel/traverse/7.23.0/x.tgz` → `@babel/traverse@7.23.0`, not `@babel@traverse`). And an npm upload with no usable version is recorded `partial` rather than as an authoritative complete clean.

### Security

- **The scanner-adapter image shipped vulnerable OpenSSL from its Alpine base** (#3612). `Dockerfile.scanner-adapter` installed its runtime packages with `apk add --no-cache ca-certificates git rpm`, and a comment above that line claimed the `no-cache-filters` cache-bust (#2391) would pull "current package errata" on every build. It cannot: `apk add` resolves only the packages it is given, and `libcrypto3`/`libssl3` arrive inside the `alpine:3.24` base layer, which that line never names. The image therefore shipped whatever OpenSSL the base image was built with — `3.5.7-r0`, carrying CVE-2026-14456 (HIGH, unbounded memory growth in the QUIC server, fixed in `3.5.8-r0`). `docker/Dockerfile.backend.alpine` has been immune since #2391 because it runs `apk upgrade` before installing; the adapter never got that half, and that asymmetry is the whole bug.

  The runtime stage now upgrades the base errata before installing. Both Go binaries in the image — the adapter itself and the bundled trivy — were already clean, and the pinned `ghcr.io/artifact-keeper/trivy` digest needed no rebuild; the finding was entirely in the base layer. Suppression was not an option worth taking: `/.trivyignore` scopes itself to bundled-scanner CVEs, states base OS packages are deliberately not suppressed, and sets the bar at "no fixed version we can BUILD AGAINST exists" — `3.5.8-r0` is published in `v3.24/main`, so the bar is not met.

  Found because the `Security Scan` gate in Docker Publish went red on `main` and hard-gates the whole release chain, which is the gate behaving exactly as intended.

- **`wasmtime` is bumped to 36.0.14, closing RUSTSEC-2026-0269 (filesystem sandbox escape on trailing slashes)** (#3608). The advisory (`GHSA-vqjp-4c8c-hfgg`, CVSS v4 8.8 high) is a `cap-std` symlink-resolution bug reached through `wasmtime-wasi`: a guest given write access to any directory inside its sandbox can reach any filesystem location the host process can, and a guest with read-only access can do the same where a symlink already exists. wasmtime is not incidental here — it is the engine for the **WASM plugin system**, the one place this product deliberately executes code it did not build, so a broken filesystem sandbox is a failure of the exact control that system's threat model rests on. Both workspace pins move together, `wasmtime` and `wasmtime-wasi`, because the two crates must be compiled against each other; a lone `wasmtime-wasi` bump has failed CI here before on a version split. Staying inside 36.x is deliberate: it is the smallest version that satisfies the advisory, while the other patched lines (46.x, 47.x, 48.x) are ten-plus majors of `WasiView`/`WasiCtxView` and component-linker churn — a migration, not a patch. No source change was needed and no API moved.

  **This was not a live escape on a deployed instance, and saying so is the point.** The advisory's precondition is a directory preopened into the guest sandbox, and there is no `preopened_dir` call in the backend: `PluginContext::new` builds the only WASI context in the codebase as `WasiCtxBuilder::new().inherit_stdio().build()`, so a plugin gets `wasi:filesystem` over an empty preopen set and has no descriptor to walk out of. Upstream also notes the specific `cap-std` bug does not affect a Linux kernel after 5.6 with `openat2`, which is a normal container host. **Plugin operators need take no action beyond upgrading, and no plugin needs to be re-reviewed for this.** What the bump buys is that the guarantee is real *before* someone needs it: granting a plugin a scratch directory or a staging path is a one-line, entirely reasonable future change, and on 36.0.13 that line would silently re-arm an 8.8 with no advisory left to notice it. Every released version — `v1.7.0` on 36.0.12 through `v1.8.1` on 36.0.13 — carries an affected pin.

  Lockfile and manifest only; the `wasmtime`, `cranelift`, `pulley`, `wiggle` and `winch` families move as one 36.0.13 to 36.0.14 set and no other crate changes. It also unblocks the repository: `🔒 Security Audit` runs a bare `cargo audit` and `✅ CI Complete` needs it, so this single advisory was failing every open pull request. The remaining `cargo audit` output — `fxhash` and `paste` unmaintained, `anyhow` and `event-listener` unsound, a `chacha20` yank — are warnings that do not fail the job and are deliberately untouched here rather than swept in or suppressed.

### Upgrade note — npm scan results change, and npm promotion gates may start blocking

This is a behavior change with a blast radius outside this repository, so read it before upgrading a deployment that gates on npm scan results.

**Before this release, npm packages published directly to a hosted repository were not being scanned.** They were reported as scanned — `completed`, zero findings, no error — but the CVE engine had nothing to look at and graded nothing. Any promotion rule, quarantine policy, or severity threshold configured against npm has therefore been passing not because the packages were clean but because nothing was examined. **After upgrading, those same packages return their real findings**, and gates that have always passed will begin to fail for artifacts that have not changed. That is the correct outcome — a control that silently passes everything is worse than no control — but it will arrive as a blocked promotion if you are not expecting it.

The change takes effect **at the next scan**, not at upgrade, and only where a scan is actually triggered. Stored results are not rewritten, so previously-scanned artifacts keep their zero-finding rows until they are rescanned. Note that native `npm publish` does not itself trigger a scan — `store_npm_version` writes the `artifacts` row directly and never reaches the scan-on-upload hook, so a package published that way is graded only when a scan is subsequently triggered against it (the admin `POST /repositories/:key/security/scan`, the promotion-time repository scan, or an upload through the generic artifact endpoint, which does scan on upload). Once a scan runs, it grades correctly. A completed zero-finding row is reusable by checksum for 24 hours, so a rescan issued right after upgrading should pass `bypass_dedup: true` to avoid being handed the stale result it is trying to escape.

**To size the blast radius before you upgrade**, list the hosted npm artifacts whose current clean verdict was never actually earned:

```sql
SELECT r.key AS repository, a.name, a.version, s.completed_at
FROM scan_results s
JOIN artifacts a ON a.id = s.artifact_id
JOIN repositories r ON r.id = a.repository_id
WHERE r.format IN ('npm', 'yarn', 'bower', 'pnpm')
  AND r.repo_type IN ('local', 'staging')
  AND s.scan_type = 'grype'
  AND s.status = 'completed'
  AND s.findings_count = 0
  AND a.is_deleted = false
ORDER BY r.key, a.name, a.version;
```

Every row is a package that will be graded for the first time on its next scan. Check those coordinates against your advisory source of choice, or upgrade a staging instance and rescan there, before you decide whether to upgrade with npm gates enabled. If you need to land the upgrade before you have triaged the list, raise the affected repositories' `max_severity` threshold or disable the npm promotion rule for the duration of triage rather than leaving a gate that blocks releases you have not looked at yet — and put the threshold back once you have.

## [1.8.1] - 2026-08-21

### Fixed

- **Storage GC no longer deletes Maven objects whose attribution row an operator wrote, and the flat-object sweep is now opt-in** (#3431, reported by [@ThaSami](https://github.com/ThaSami)). `cleanup_orphan_maven_flat_objects` enumerated its delete candidates **from `maven_flat_object_owner`** and reclaimed every row whose catalog anchors were gone — live, on the hourly scheduled pass. But since #2574/#2585 that same row is what makes a *row-less* legacy object **readable**: it is the last layer of read-time owner resolution, and inserting one is the documented remediation for keys the catalog-only backfill of migrations 163/170 cannot see. For exactly that class — an object whose only catalog record is its owner row — every anchor arm of the sweep's predicate is true by construction and permanently. The row that made the object servable was the row that queued it for deletion: an operator who repaired a fail-closed 404 by attributing the key got a 200 for one hour, and then lost the bytes. The flat key is the only physical copy, and the sweep deleted the attribution row with it, so nothing recorded that the key had ever been hand-attributed.

  Two independent fixes, either of which would have prevented the loss. **(1)** The predicate now reclaims only rows the system itself **wrote and can re-derive** — `primary_row`, `metadata_files`, `derived_checksum`, `metadata_rollup` (migrations 163 and 170) and `write_claim` (the runtime claim path). Those rows are caches over other catalog state, so once the anchors vanish they are stale by definition; an operator-inserted row is a primary record that nothing can reconstruct. It is an **allowlist**, not a denylist, so any value a future code path, an external repair tool, or a hand `INSERT` stamps is protected by default — the failure direction is leaked storage, never lost bytes. `write_claim` stays reclaimable deliberately: an orphaned claim from a crashed first publish is precisely the leftover this sweep exists to collect. **(2)** The sweep is gated behind `MAVEN_FLAT_GC_ENABLED`, mirroring `BLOB_GC_ENABLED`'s "bias to leaking storage over losing data". Unset — the default — it still runs and **reports** what it would reclaim (`maven_flat_objects_gated` on the GC result, plus a log line) but deletes nothing. That gate is the deeper fix: this sweep's entire subject matter is objects *the catalog cannot see*, and on an instance migrated from another registry that absence is the **expected** state of legitimate legacy data — it is why the attribution table exists — so catalog absence alone is not proof of garbage without an operator saying so. The gate is applied in the service, so the per-repository admin GC endpoint, which shares the predicate constant with the scheduled pass, shares the gate too.

  **Operator note.** What was lost: the storage objects for row-less Maven flat keys — GAV-grouped companion files (`.pom`, `.module`, `-sources.jar`), verbatim `maven-metadata.xml`, and checksum/signature sidecars — together with their `maven_flat_object_owner` rows. Hand-attributed keys were the affected class: a key with no owner row was invisible to this sweep, so **attributing a key to repair a 404 is what made it eligible for deletion**, and an untouched broken key was left alone. Deleted objects are **not recoverable** from within Artifact Keeper — the sweep deletes the object first and the attribution row in the same pass, and neither is journalled anywhere; recovery depends entirely on storage-side retention (S3/GCS/Azure object versioning or a bucket lifecycle noncurrent window, a bucket replica, or a filesystem backup), and once the attribution row is gone the database no longer records *which* keys were operator-attributed. The one in-product record of what was taken is the log: each reclaim emits `Storage GC: reclaimed orphaned row-less Maven flat object` at INFO with the `storage_key`, so a backend log with sufficient retention reconstructs the key list to restore from bucket versions. Before upgrading, snapshot `maven_flat_object_owner` (`storage_backend`, `storage_key`, `repository_id`, `source`) — with this fix that snapshot is what identifies the rows now protected. Two upgrade notes: the sweep now **deletes nothing by default**, so anyone relying on it to reclaim genuinely-orphaned Maven storage must set `MAVEN_FLAT_GC_ENABLED=true` (check `maven_flat_objects_gated` first to size the pass); and the 1.7.3 guard rebuild plus the #3385 indexing made this scan *complete* on large attribution tables where it previously timed out, so upgrading to 1.7.3+ **for those fixes** is what activated mass reclaim of hand-repaired data at up to 1000 keys per pass, per replica. v1.7.6 and v1.8.0 both carry the unfixed sweep.
- **Proxied downloads are counted for Docker/OCI, cargo, NuGet, Debian, Helm and Go, and a class guard now stops the next format from shipping uncounted** (#3446). Two functions count a download and they are not interchangeable: `record_download` is keyed on an `artifacts.id` and writes `download_statistics`, while `record_proxy_download` is keyed on `(repository, path)` and writes `proxy_download_statistics`. Proxy-cached content is deliberately not registered in `artifacts` (#1278), so a format calling only the first *looks* instrumented on inspection and records nothing at runtime — the id lookup returns `None`, nothing errors, and the counter never moves. That is precisely how ~19 formats stayed broken behind #3388, which fixed Maven and concluded Maven was the only one. Cargo's Remote arm returned the upstream stream directly and never reached the `record_download` fifteen lines below it; OCI called `record_oci_manifest_download`, which resolves a manifest through `artifacts.storage_key` and silently no-ops for every proxy-cached object, so **every** `docker pull` through a proxy counted zero. Recording is now in place on all six high-traffic proxy formats, keyed on the same proxy-cache path the fetch commits under so the count lands on the catalog row the artifact listing renders (#3388's display half). The unit of a Docker pull is unchanged — counted once at the manifest, never per blob (#2260) — and a HEAD still counts nothing on every path.

  The guard is the part that generalises. `every_proxy_serve_path_records_a_download_or_is_explicitly_exempt` scans every format handler for the primitives that put upstream bytes in front of a client and fails unless each site either records (directly, via the recording `try_remote_or_virtual_download`, or one call hop away — pypi records in the caller of its streaming helper, npm in the callee, and both are correct) or carries a written `UNRECORDED-PROXY-SERVE:` marker stating why. Not counting is sometimes right, so the marker is a greppable token that keeps the judgement in review rather than in an allowlist that drifts. It immediately found a serve path the per-format audit had missed: RPM's catch-all `/rpm/{repo}/*path` route records nothing even though RPM's main download path does. The 14 formats not fixed in this pass (alpine, chef, cocoapods, composer, conan, conda, gitlfs, jetbrains, pub_registry, rpm's catch-all, sbt, swift, terraform, vscode) each carry a marker naming #3446, and a companion test pins that count at 14 so the remaining work can only shrink. Repositories in those formats keep reporting 0 downloads — a reporting gap, not a serving defect; artifacts are served correctly either way.
- **The release-branch gate can now express a maintenance-branch-only change, so it no longer has to be bypassed to cut a release** (#3422). The gate indexes `git patch-id` over main's last 1500 commits and requires an exact match, which is right for catching genuine drift but cannot represent two legitimate shapes — and during the 1.7.6 cut both were waved through with `release-process: approved` four times in one release, which is how a required gate stops meaning anything. A **release prep** (`chore(release): prepare 1.7.6`) bumps `Cargo.toml`, `Cargo.lock`, `**/openapi.rs`, `CHANGELOG.md`, `.github/release-notes/**` and `docker/*/VERSION` for a version that exists *only* on the maintenance branch; there is nothing on main to trace to and there should not be. A **narrowed backport** carries a correct `(cherry picked from commit <sha>)` trailer but a different patch by construction, because hunks that could not apply were resolved away (a guard test depending on scaffolding the branch lacks, a CHANGELOG hunk targeting `[Unreleased]` when the branch needs `[1.7.6]`). Both are now accepted on their own terms: the release prep only when the subject prefix *and* the whole path set qualify, the backport only when the trailer names a sha that is actually on main — and the narrowing is logged as `narrowed backport of <sha>` rather than passed silently. A trailer naming a sha main does not have is now its own distinct failure, since it asserts a provenance that is not there. Everything else still fails exactly as before, and the `release-process: approved` label remains for the genuine remainder. The logic moved out of the workflow into `scripts/ci/check-release-branch-commits.sh` with a self-test (`test-check-release-branch-commits.sh`, wired into CI's shell-tests job), because a gate that only runs on release PRs is far too rare to notice a regression in — the self-test exercises both exemptions from the failing side, so a `chore(release):` commit that also touches source, or a version-file-only commit under another subject, cannot slip through.
- **Every `release/**` branch publishes container images on push, not just `release/1.1.x`** (#3422). `docker-publish.yml`'s push trigger hardcoded a single maintenance branch, so a commit landing on `release/1.7.x` produced no images at all. Preflight check 3 then correctly reported "no Docker Publish run exists for HEAD" (it resolves the run by `head_sha` since #3338), and every 1.7.x cut needed an undocumented manual `workflow_dispatch` first. The trigger is now a `release/**` glob. The one thing in that workflow that keyed on the branch name — the `X.Y-dev` floating alias, hardcoded as `1.1-dev` in eight metadata blocks — is now derived from the branch in `publish-preflight` and exported as an output, so `release/1.7.x` publishes `1.7-dev` exactly as `release/1.1.x` publishes `1.1-dev`, and a new maintenance line gets one the moment it is created with no workflow edit.
- **A release-prep commit can no longer silently strand CHANGELOG entries under an already-released heading** (#3433). `chore(release): prepare 1.7.5` renamed `## [Unreleased]` to `## [1.7.5]` without opening a fresh empty `## [Unreleased]` above it. Every PR branch cut before that rename still anchored its CHANGELOG hunk on the old heading, so the entries merged into the renamed, *already released* section — no conflict, no warning, no signal of any kind. Thirty entries of 1.8.0 work ended up filed under `[1.7.5]`, a version that produced no images and no release object (#3429), and would have shipped undocumented; two were upgrade-affecting (#3286 storage accounting, #3231 Rekor SET verification). `scripts/ci/check-changelog-unreleased.sh` now asserts that the first `## [` heading in `CHANGELOG.md` is exactly `## [Unreleased]` — a repo-state invariant, so it fires on whichever PR reaches CI first rather than depending on who made the change — with a self-test alongside it so the gate cannot rot, both wired into the shell-tests job.

### Changed

- **`RELEASING.md` tells you to check the versioned component source sets before tagging a backport** (#3429, #3340). `v1.7.5` died because a **comment-only** edit to `docker/Dockerfile.scanner-adapter` rode along in a backport: the publish gate treats any change under a versioned component's source set as a source change and refuses to republish an existing exact version tag, so the tag's publish failed — and the ruleset forbids deleting or moving it, so the version was burned. `v1.7.2` died the same way. The cut sequence gains a required step: confirm no change touches `docker/*/VERSION`'s directory or its sibling Dockerfile unless that `VERSION` is bumped in the same change, with the two commands to run. Step 3 also now states *why* the fresh `## [Unreleased]` is mandatory rather than leaving it in parentheses.

### Security

- **`h2` is bumped to 0.4.16, closing RUSTSEC-2026-0258 (unbounded empty DATA frames)** (#3449). `h2` < 0.4.16 accepts and queues empty HTTP/2 DATA frames without limit; if the receiving streams are not actively drained this grows memory without bound, or panics when the accumulated length overflows. It reaches us transitively through `hyper 1.8.1`, `reqwest` and `tonic`, and the path is reachable from the network rather than theoretical: the gRPC listener (`0.0.0.0:9090`, `GRPC_PORT`) is HTTP/2-only h2c and answers before any application-level authentication, `axum` is used with its default `http2` feature so the REST and registry surface serves HTTP/2 as well, and remote/proxy repository fetches negotiate HTTP/2 outbound — so a hostile upstream can aim the same frames at the registry. Upstream rates it low severity, and it is: the frames are empty, so the attacker trades bandwidth for the server's per-frame bookkeeping rather than for payload. The fix costs a two-line lockfile change, which is a poor trade to decline on an unauthenticated listener. Lockfile-only — `hyper`, `reqwest` and `tonic` all accept `^0.4`, so no direct dependency moves and no HTTP stack major bump was needed. **`v1.8.0` and earlier tags carry the vulnerable `h2` 0.4.13**; deployments that expose port 9090 (or terminate `h2` in front of the registry) should take the patch release.

- **The bundled `grype` CLI is built against `golang.org/x/mod` v0.40.0, clearing CVE-2026-56864 and CVE-2026-56865** (#3465). Both are HIGH and both are fixed in x/mod v0.40.0; grype v0.117.0 pins v0.38.0, so `Security Scan` reports `usr/local/bin/grype  Total: 2 (HIGH: 2)` against the backend image and fails. Docker Publish on `main` failed on this for two consecutive runs (32337069636, 32419016885) with every manifest-merge job skipped, so **no images published from `main` between 2026-08-19 and this fix** and the `v1.8.1` tag could not be cut. The same finding burned `v1.7.7` on `release/1.7.x`, where rulesets forbid deleting or moving a tag and the version number was lost.

  Neither lever the `grype-bin` stage already had could reach it. This is a **module**, not the standard library, so the `GO_MIN_PATCH` toolchain floor (#3352) does nothing; and there is no release to bump to — v0.117.0 is the latest anchore/grype release and `main` (`ffbca56`) still pins v0.38.0, with no open or merged PR to move it. Upstream has not made this bump anywhere, which is what makes this an **override** rather than the version bump that clears the same CVE pair in the scanner-adapter's Trivy (upstream v0.74.0 carries x/mod v0.40.0 itself). `docker/Dockerfile.backend` and `docker/Dockerfile.backend.alpine` therefore apply `go get golang.org/x/mod@v0.40.0` after the commit-pin verification and before `go build`, with three build-time guards: the pinned source must still require v0.38.0 (so the tag bump that makes the override redundant is also what stops the build until it is deleted), `go get` must move only the five declared `golang.org/x/*` modules MVS pulls with it, and the compiled binary's Go build info must record v0.40.0 — because that build info is exactly what Trivy reads. `grype --version` still prints `grype 0.117.0` and `Supported DB Schema` is still 6, so `scanner_version` and the DB seeded at build time are unaffected.

  **The vulnerable code was never linked in**, and that is worth recording rather than implying urgency the finding did not have. Both advisories are scoped to `golang.org/x/mod/sumdb` (`Client.Lookup`, GO-2026-6180) and `golang.org/x/mod/sumdb/tlog` (`tileHashReader.ReadHashes`, GO-2026-6179) — the GOSUMDB transparency-log client — and neither package is in grype's build graph: `go mod why golang.org/x/mod/sumdb` answers "main module does not need package", and `go list -deps ./cmd/grype` links only `semver`, `module`, `modfile` and `internal/lazyregexp`, reached via `cmd/grype/cli/commands/internal/jsonschema` → `x/tools/go/packages`. Trivy flags Go binaries at module granularity from the embedded build info and cannot see that, while `govulncheck` would call the binary unaffected. It is fixed at source anyway rather than suppressed in `.trivyignore`, which is reserved for findings with no fix available in a tool we can build.

  This clears the backend image only. The same CVE pair was also reported against `usr/local/bin/trivy` in the scanner-adapter image and is cleared separately by repointing at a Trivy build carrying x/mod v0.40.0; **both were required before `main` could publish again**, and both ship in this release.
- **The scanner-adapter bundles a trivy binary rebuilt on go1.26.7, clearing all 10 HIGHs that were blocking Docker Publish, and the adapter's own Go build now asserts a `GO_MIN_PATCH` floor** (#3352). `docker/Dockerfile.scanner-adapter` pinned `ghcr.io/artifact-keeper/trivy` at the `0.73.0-r2` manifest list, whose binary was compiled on go1.26.5 and carried 10 HIGH findings against `usr/local/bin/trivy`. They are **not** all standard library, and grouping them as such — as the original entry did — hides which lever moves which: **six** are Go stdlib against that go1.26.5 build (CVE-2026-33818, -56853, -56858, -56859, -56860, -56862), **two** are `golang.org/x/net` (CVE-2026-39821 in `x/net/idna`, and CVE-2026-46600), and **two** are `golang.org/x/mod` (CVE-2026-56864, CVE-2026-56865). Only the first six move with a toolchain floor; the other four are modules and move with the source pin. **All ten surfaced at main's gate** — none of them is suppressed in main's `.trivyignore`, and the `x/net` pair that `release/1.7.x` still lists as a live token there is a `# RETIRED:` tombstone on main (#3352, #3309), so 1.7.x's gate saw eight of these where main's saw all ten. The Trivy gate in `docker-publish.yml` runs `severity: CRITICAL,HIGH` with `ignore-unfixed` and `exit-code: 1`, so it failed on every push to main; because the gate is a `needs:` of `merge-scanner-adapter`, no multi-arch manifest was assembled and the whole publish chain stopped. That is why `v1.8.1` could not be tagged on its originally prepped date of 2026-08-19. The pin now names the `0.74.0-r1` manifest list (`sha256:37317c08…`), an in-house build of upstream trivy v0.74.0 on go1.26.7 that picks up `x/mod` v0.40.0. Measured against the same vulnerability DB, the trivy binary goes **10 HIGH → 0** at the gate's settings and **11 → 1** at all severities with no ignorefile, adding nothing; the survivor is `GO-2026-5932` in `x/crypto`, which has no fixed version and is UNKNOWN severity, so it is outside the gate on both filters. Nothing in the backend reads the trivy version string — the adapter probes it at startup — so the move from 0.73.0 to 0.74.0 is contained to this image.

  The second half is the durable part. The adapter's Go stage builds on the floating `golang:1.26-alpine` tag with no floor, an asymmetry with `docker/Dockerfile.backend{,.alpine}` that this file's own comment flagged and said to close "if this adapter ever fails a scan on the same class". It has: `release/1.7.x`'s adapter binary (1.2.3) carries the same six Go-stdlib HIGHs, because a floating tag is only as good as the last rebuild and that image was built before go1.26.6 existed. The same `ARG GO_MIN_PATCH=1.26.6` plus `sort -V` assertion the backend Dockerfiles use is now in the adapter's build stage, so a lagging mirror or a stale builder cache fails the build loudly instead of shipping a vulnerable stdlib silently. On main that has not bitten: the floating tag currently resolves to go1.26.6, so main's adapter binary already scanned clean before this change and still does. **The floor clears no finding on main** — it is purely a regression guard. `docker/scanner-adapter/VERSION` goes to **1.2.7**: the adapter's version space is shared across branches, 1.2.6 is reserved for `release/1.7.x`, and exact version tags are never republished (#3429).

## [1.8.0] - 2026-08-17

### Security

- **A suppressed virtual-PyPI member's cached distribution is no longer served, on either the download or the PEP 658 metadata path** (#3404). The virtual member loop tries local storage first for *every* member, Remote ones included, because Remote-typed repositories legitimately carry `artifacts` rows (direct upload, replication, promotion) and because a distribution and its `.metadata` sidecar must resolve from the same member. But the PEP 708 ownership decision (#1600 / #2311 / #2937) was computed ~50 lines *after* that local-first serve and consulted only by the upstream-fetch branch, so a member the dependency-confusion guard suppresses still answered from its cache. A Case-B distribution — a version only the remote has, for a name a higher-priority local member owns — was therefore correctly hidden from the simple index while remaining downloadable through the same virtual repository, permanently, for any file that member had ever cached. Such rows accumulate through ordinary operation: any request that legitimately resolved the distribution before a local member claimed the name, while the remote was ranked equal-or-higher, or under a since-removed PEP 708 `tracks` declaration, leaves one behind. `uv.lock` and hashed `requirements.txt` pin exact filenames, so a resolution made while the remote was permitted kept succeeding long after an operator re-ranked the members to stop it.

  The decision is now resolved once per request and applied at the *top* of the member loop, so a suppressed Remote member is skipped before any of its bytes, its cache row, or its per-member gates are consulted. `serve_virtual_metadata` carried an independent copy of the same ordering defect and is fixed with it — fixing only the wheel would have left the sidecar describing exactly the distribution the wheel now refuses. Both paths share one `PypiOwnershipGuard`, so they can no longer drift. Unchanged: the #2937 Case-A carve-out (a platform/ABI-distinct wheel of a version the owner already provides still downloads, because the index still lists it), Local/Staging members (never the suppressed side), Remote members the operator ranked equal-or-higher than the owning local, and the #3220 fail-closed download-gate block. The index/download symmetry invariant #2937 states — a distribution the index advertises is downloadable and one it hides 404s on both — now also holds for members with a local row.
- **Content-negotiated PyPI simple indexes declare `Vary: Accept`, and a credentialed caller's index is no longer marked shared-cacheable** (#3406). The simple index is negotiated on `Accept` (PEP 691 JSON vs PEP 503 HTML) and was served `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60` with a body-hash `ETag` but no `Vary`. Under RFC 9110 §12.5.1 a shared cache — a corporate forward proxy, a CDN, nginx, Squid — is then entitled to serve either stored representation to any client and to validate one representation's `ETag` against the other's. `uv` rejects a simple index whose `Content-Type` is not one it accepts, so a mis-served representation is a hard install failure, not a cosmetic one; this is the downstream twin of the defect #3290 fixed in AK's own proxy cache and of the upstream mislabelling #2801 handles.

  Two directives, for two distinct reasons. `Vary: Accept` is now emitted on every negotiated emitter — both simple-index builders, both representations, and the `304` shortcut, which must carry the same cache-key metadata as the `200` it stands in for. Separately, `Cache-Control` is downgraded to `private, max-age=60` when the request carries a credential (`Authorization`, `X-API-Key`, or the `ak_access_token` session cookie), because AK's indexes are caller-dependent: a virtual repository's listing is built from the members the *caller* is authorized to read (#2073 / #3323 / #3399), and a private repository's requires credentials at all. `Vary: Accept` alone would not have addressed that, and `public` is not merely a missing opt-out — under RFC 9111 §3.5 it is the explicit permission that overrides a shared cache's default refusal to store a response to an `Authorization`-bearing request. Anonymous reads of public repositories keep `public, max-age=60` and stay CDN-cacheable, which is the case the 60s TTL exists for. The credential test is shape-based and reuses the middleware's own carrier list, so a fourth carrier cannot be added without this following. Non-negotiated callers of the shared helper (Maven `maven-metadata.xml`, Conda repodata) are deliberately untouched: adding `Vary` there would fragment their caches for no gain.
- **OpenPGP repository-metadata signatures now carry an explicit expiration window, and the signed-Release cache is capped below it** (#1327). Signatures produced by `SigningService::sign_openpgp_detached` / `sign_openpgp_cleartext` had no `SignatureExpirationTime` subpacket, so a signed `InRelease` copied to a mirror stayed indefinitely valid on its face. `apt` does not enforce signature expiry, but mirror-validation tooling does (`debmirror`, `apt-mirror2`, `gpgv --check-quiet`), and an unbounded signature gives those tools nothing to check a stale mirror against. Every on-demand metadata signature now carries a validity window — default **7 days**, matching the cadence official Debian archives re-sign at — configurable via `SIGNATURE_EXPIRY_SECONDS`.

  The in-process signed-Release cache is what makes this safe rather than merely declarative. That cache is keyed by content hash, so a distribution whose `Release` never changes would otherwise keep serving one signature forever, straight past its own stated expiry. Cache entries now carry the instant they were signed and age out at **the signature window minus one hour**, so the registry stops serving an entry strictly before the signature inside it stops verifying, and re-signs on the next request. The expiry/rotation arithmetic lives in pure helpers (`signature_expiry_duration`, `signed_cache_max_age`, `signed_cache_entry_is_fresh`) that are unit-tested without a database or a keyring, including the boundary case and a backwards clock step.

  **Rollover semantics — what happens to already-published metadata:**

  - **Nothing already published becomes unverifiable.** This changes only metadata the registry **re-signs on demand**: Debian `InRelease` and `Release.gpg`, and the live RPM `repomd.xml.asc`. Each is recomputed from current repository content on request, so the client always receives a signature minted well inside its window.
  - **Signatures that are minted once and stored are deliberately excluded.** RPM published `@N` snapshots write `repomd.xml.asc` to storage and never regenerate it — an expiring signature there would silently stop verifying once the window elapsed. Signature expiry is therefore **opt-in per call site** (`SigningService::with_signature_expiry`) rather than a constructor default, so any signing path not explicitly audited for re-signing keeps its previous behaviour. `@N` snapshots continue to verify indefinitely.
  - **No key rotation is involved.** The signing key, its fingerprint, and the published public key are unchanged; only the signature carries a window. Signatures made before this change have no expiration subpacket and remain valid exactly as before — there is no flag day and no re-import.
  - **Clients need to do nothing.** `apt` ignores the subpacket. Mirror-validation tooling gains a stale-mirror check it did not previously have. A mirror that refreshes at least weekly is unaffected; one that has not refreshed in over 7 days will now be reported as carrying an expired signature, which is the intended signal.

  **Upgrade note for operators:** if you mirror an Artifact Keeper Debian repository with tooling that enforces signature expiry, ensure the mirror refreshes more often than `SIGNATURE_EXPIRY_SECONDS` (default 7 days), or raise the window. Air-gapped exports that sit longer than the window between refreshes should set a longer window, or `SIGNATURE_EXPIRY_SECONDS=0` to restore the previous no-expiry behaviour exactly. Values below 7200 or above 31536000 are clamped into that range rather than rejected, so a bad value cannot take the registry down.
- **The OCI `/v2` read path now enforces the token's `read:artifacts` action scope** (#3408). `oci_scopes_grant` is the action ceiling for an API token presented directly to `/v2` (as a Bearer token, or in the Basic password field). It was called at seven sites and every one of them asked for `write:artifacts` or `delete:artifacts`; the pull path asked for nothing. `oci_read_permitted` enforced the scan-token pin and the token's *repository* allow-list, then the admin and public-read bypasses, then the `read` permission — but the token's declared *action* ceiling was never consulted for a read. A token minted with `scopes = ["write:artifacts"]` and nothing else could therefore `docker pull` every repository its owner was permitted to read: the push-only CI publish credential was silently also a read credential.

  A pull now takes the same gate the other six verbs take, in the same shape and the same position — immediately after authentication, so it runs **before** the admin bypass, for the same reason the repository allow-list is documented as binding admins: an action ceiling the principal themselves asked for should bind them regardless of `is_admin`. The refusal is `403` with the OCI `DENIED` envelope naming the missing scope, matching the write gate; a `404` would be indistinguishable from a deleted repository and would tell the operator nothing about their token. It applies to every read verb — manifest `GET`/`HEAD`, blob `GET`/`HEAD`, `tags/list`, `referrers`, and `_catalog`. `Claims.scopes` is deliberately untouched: threading the ceiling there would deliver it by demoting `is_admin` through `with_scope_gated_admin`, which roughly 34 raw handler checks also read, changing what the principal *is* everywhere the resulting `AuthExtension` travels (decided on #3322).

  So that the next `/v2` verb cannot re-open the hole, the property is enforced structurally rather than by a test pinned to the sites fixed here. `authenticate_oci` — the wrapper that returned claims and discarded the scope tuple — is deleted, so a handler cannot acquire the identity without also acquiring the ceiling that governs it; and a class-level test scans this module and fails on any production authentication that is not followed by an `oci_scopes_grant` check naming an `OCI_SCOPE_*` constant, unless the call site carries a written `OCI-SCOPE-EXEMPT` justification. This is the same greppable-exemption shape #3399 and #3331 used.

  **Upgrade note.** This is a fail-closed behaviour change. Affected: any API token presented directly to `/v2` whose scope list omits `read:artifacts` and is neither `*` nor `admin` nor the bare parent `read`, being used to pull — concretely, `write:artifacts`-only CI publish tokens that also `docker pull`. Such a pull now returns `403 DENIED` ("Token does not have required scope: read:artifacts"); the fix is to add `read:artifacts` to the token's scopes. Unaffected: unscoped credentials (JWT login sessions, `docker login` with a password, and any token whose ceiling is absent — `oci_scopes_grant` passes `None` through), tokens carrying `*` or `admin`, scanner pull tokens, anonymous pulls of public repositories, and every write or delete path.
- **REST content paths now require the `read` action, not merely any grant, on a private repository** (#3331). `RepositoryService::user_can_access_repo` answered *"does this principal hold any grant on this repository"* and took no action parameter at all, so every one of its call sites got the same any-grant answer — including the ones that return artifact **bytes**. A principal whose only entitlement on a private repository was `{write}` or `{delete}`, or who held a role carrying no `read`, was therefore served that repository's contents through the REST API while the equivalent OCI `/v2` and native-format reads of the same repository correctly refused. The grant predicate tests only `actions <> '{}'`, and `permissions.actions` is `TEXT[]` rather than an enum, so a rule carrying an unrecognised action string qualified too; the `role_assignments` arm never joined `roles`, so a role's own permissions were never consulted.

  `user_can_access_repo` now takes a required `RepoAccess` argument. `RepoAccess::READ` layers the canonical action choke-point — `PermissionService::check_repository_action`, the same function with the same arguments that the direct `/v2` read gate and `repo_visibility_middleware` call — on top of the unchanged tenant gate, so a repository is readable through REST exactly when a direct read of it succeeds, by construction rather than by assertion. All eleven call sites were classified individually. Six now ask for `read`: the artifact-by-id gate and its label/security/SBOM/quality-gate siblings, `/api/v1/tree/content` (which serves bytes), the repo-scoped SBOM and CVE-history reads, the quarantine reason text, and `require_visible` — which alone fans out to roughly 23 read surfaces including `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}`, artifact listings and downloads, storage trees and storage-usage trees, virtual member listings, and the security, signing, curation, approval, promotion-rule, quality-gate and repository-label reads.

  Five sites deliberately keep the tenant gate and say so in the source with a `TENANT-GATE-ONLY` marker: the REST write/delete gate (whose action half is layered separately and canonically by `require_repo_action(.., "write"/"delete", ..)` — naming `read` there would refuse a legitimate publish-only identity), repo-token management (a visibility bar; the delegation ceiling is enforced per-scope at mint time), cross-tenant promotion and the two curation tenant-ownership gates (tenant identity, not a capability, and enforced independently of the admin flag), and repo-scoped webhook management. Making the parameter required means a new call site cannot inherit the action-blind behaviour by omission, and a structural test scans the whole backend source tree and fails on any `RepoAccess::TenantOnly` that does not carry a written justification — the class-level shape #3399 used for virtual member walks, chosen because a test pinned to the sites fixed here would go green while the next content path re-opened the hole.

  **Who is affected.** Only callers reading a **private** repository, and only those whose grant does not carry `read`. Concretely: a fine-grained `permissions` rule with `actions` of `{write}`, `{delete}`, `{write,delete}`, or any value the action vocabulary does not recognise; and a custom role whose `permissions` array omits `read`. The built-in roles all carry it (`admin`, `developer`, `reader` and `repository-owner` each include `read`), so a default installation sees no change. Public repositories, anonymous reads, global admins, and every write or delete path are unaffected. Publish-only automation identities that were reading through these surfaces will now be refused — that is the intended capability removal, and the fix is to add `read` to the grant. This closes the asymmetry #3323 and #3326 left behind, where the virtual-member path was stricter than a direct REST read of the same member.
- **Virtual-repository reads authorize the member set against the caller across every format** (#3323). The format-route visibility middleware authorizes only the repository named in the URL — the virtual PARENT — while everything a virtual repository aggregates is a separate repository with its own ACL, so an anonymous request to a **public** virtual over **private** members reached each member's content unchecked. The filter existed (`proxy_helpers::authorize_virtual_members`) but was applied on a minority of call sites, and the two shared metadata primitives (`resolve_virtual_metadata`, `collect_virtual_metadata`) took no caller at all, so every one of their callers inherited an unfiltered walk. All content-serving virtual read paths — PyPI simple index (root and per-project), npm packument and version metadata, cargo sparse index, Helm `index.yaml`, NuGet V2/V3 search, registration and version indexes, Conda repodata/channeldata, CRAN `PACKAGES`, Hex names/versions/package, RubyGems spec indexes and quick gemspecs, Conan search/revisions/package listings, Composer `packages.json` and p1/p2 metadata, Pub package and version info, Swift release listing and metadata, Go `@v/list` and `@v/*.info`, Debian `Release`/`InRelease`/`Packages`, Alpine `APKINDEX`, Maven root listing, and the Hugging Face `ETag`/`X-Repo-Commit` resolution — now resolve members through one shared helper, `proxy_helpers::authorized_virtual_members`, which is `fetch` composed with the same caller predicate a direct read of that member would apply. The two primitives now REQUIRE a caller, so their remaining callers cannot regress silently, and a structural test scans every format handler and fails on any raw member walk that neither authorizes nor carries an explicit `UNFILTERED-ENFORCEMENT` marker. Enforcement walks — the OCI scan-verdict deny-set, the PEP 708 isolation and shadowing guards, priority maps, cache invalidation and cycle detection — are deliberately left unfiltered, because narrowing a deny-set or a shadowing decision by caller visibility would let a caller who cannot see a member escape that member's gate.

  Three caller-INDEPENDENT caches sat in front of documents that are now caller-dependent, which would have moved the leak rather than closed it: the npm computed-packument cache, the cargo in-process sparse-index cache, and the Maven virtual `maven-metadata.xml` merge cache. Each is now used only when the aggregated document cannot vary by caller — that is, when every member is public, the exact condition under which the authorized member set is identical for anonymous and authenticated callers. A virtual repository with a private member computes per request; all-public virtuals keep their cache.

  Not included: the RPM `repodata` walk (`repomd.xml` and friends). Its document is rendered once and cached per virtual repository id, and `repomd.xml.asc` is a detached signature over the rendered bytes, so a per-caller document breaks both the shared cache and the reproducible-signature invariant (#2636). It carries an explicit `UNFILTERED-DEFERRED` marker in the source and remains tracked on #3323 pending a cache re-keying design.
- Unrecognised scanner severity tokens now classify as `high` instead of `info`, so ungraded findings fail closed at severity gates (#3306).
