Aliases collapse exactly as handler resolution does (`gradle`→`maven`, every OCI alias→`oci`, `lxc`→`incus`), which is the granularity `format_handlers` is keyed by and the granularity the enablement gate reads.
- **Publishing a Flutter package to a hosted Pub repository works** (#3058). `PubSpec` modelled dependency values as strings, but Pub allows a dependency value to be either a version string or a mapping — for SDK, git, path and hosted dependencies. Every Flutter package declares `flutter: {sdk: flutter}`, so `serde_yaml` rejected the pubspec outright with `dependencies.flutter: invalid type: map, expected a string`, and the extraction helper turned that into the `400` publishers saw on the multipart upload step while step 1 of the flow succeeded. Both dependency maps are now typed as `serde_json::Value` so every dependency form round-trips, mirroring how the cargo handler already solves the identical problem. Remote and virtual Pub repositories are unaffected: proxied metadata is passed through as raw JSON with only `archive_url` rewritten.
- **OCI pushes to classic Helm repositories are rejected** (#3150). An OCI Distribution request against a repository whose format is not backed by the OCI handler now returns `400 UNSUPPORTED` before any write; `helm_oci` and the other OCI-backed formats keep working. Repositories already affected produce a valid `index.yaml` again, because legacy OCI manifest rows are excluded from classic Helm index generation rather than migrated destructively.
- **Docker lifecycle retention counts versions per image, and ages tags by last push** (#2998, #3026). Docker manifest artifacts encode `image:tag` in `artifacts.name`, so the `max_versions` query treated every tag as its own one-item partition and never pruned anything; valid tag-shaped references are now partitioned by image name, preserving registry ports, while `image:sha256:<digest>` references stay distinct full-name partitions so multi-architecture child manifests — which can be stored by digest with no `oci_tags` row — are not grouped together. Separately, `max_age_days` aged a tag by the path-keyed artifact row's original `created_at`, so a moving tag such as `latest` looked 91 days old even though it had just been re-pushed to a fresh digest; live OCI tag-backed manifests are now aged by `oci_tags.updated_at`, which is refreshed on every successful manifest `PUT`, with `artifacts.created_at` retained as the fallback for non-OCI artifacts and unmatched legacy rows, and the same expression used for the preview and the deletion queries.
- **OIDC and SAML users with no directory email address get distinct synthetic addresses** (#3119, #3167). An OIDC provider is not obliged to release an `email` claim, and both claim-extraction paths defaulted a missing one to `""`. `users.email` is `UNIQUE NOT NULL`, so a deployment whose IdP does not release `email` could onboard exactly **one** federated user and then failed everyone else on `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "users_email_key"`. The address is now derived per subject — a sanitized prefix of the subject for operator recognizability plus a SHA-256 fingerprint of the raw subject, so distinct subjects stay distinct despite lossy sanitization, bounded inside `VARCHAR(255)` — under `.invalid`, reserved by RFC 2606, so it can never resolve or collide with a real mailbox. A claim that is present but blank is treated as missing. The SAML path had a narrower relative: it computed its `{username}@unknown` placeholder from the *pre-uniquification* username while inserting the uniquified one, so two distinct NameIDs whose username attribute happens to match got distinct usernames (`alice`, `alice_1`) and the **identical** placeholder address, and the second person could not log in at all. The SAML placeholder is now keyed on the NameID, which is already what the account row is stored and looked up by, so the synthetic address is unique and stable in exactly the cases the account is. Keying it on the username would have been worse than the original bug: the username attribute is self-settable at any IdP that maps it from a user-editable directory field, which would turn an availability defect into a targeted one. Both federated paths now share one derivation, and the addresses shipped for OIDC are unchanged byte for byte. `unknown` is also a resolvable TLD, so the old placeholder could collide with a real mailbox rather than merely with another placeholder.
- **Service-account grants show who they empower** (#2826). Permission list and get responses joined `users` only for `principal_type = 'user'`, so a service account's grant returned `principal_name: null`, and create and update hard-coded both display-name fields to null. The join is now keyed by the `users` primary key for every principal type, matching how permission enforcement itself resolves the row, and create and update return the same hydrated response out of the single statement that writes the row, so the display fields cost no second query and cannot drift from the list and get shape. It is deliberately **not** guarded on `is_service_account`: migration 057 introduced that column in February 2026 but `principal_type = 'service_account'` was not honoured by any resolver until #2499 in July, so in that window the only way to grant a service account fine-grained access was `principal_type = 'user'` plus the account's `users.id`. No migration re-types those rows and the enforcement path still matches them by bare `principal_id` — they are live, enforced grants today, and a type-guarded join rendered exactly those rows nameless, hiding from admins who a still-effective grant empowers. A guardless join keyed on the primary key can never attach the wrong name, only a missing one.
- **Backups never report success when artifact bytes are missing** (#3170, #3171). The backup path collected artifact bytes with `if let Ok(content) = self.storage.get(&key).await`, so a failed read was discarded: not counted, not logged, not in the manifest, not in the job status. The job reported `completed` with `artifact_count=0` and the restore reported `errors=[]` — the worst failure a backup can have, because it is discovered only at restore time when there is no recourse. Every read failure is now logged at `warn` with the key and the underlying error, counted into the manifest's new `artifacts_unreadable` field (`#[serde(default)]`, so existing archives still deserialize), and **fails the job** with a message naming the affected keys unless partial backups were explicitly opted into. The archive and manifest are still written before the job fails — partial data plus a recorded miss count is strictly more useful than discarding both, and the manifest is what lets the restore path refuse the archive later. Restore now reads the manifest and records an error when it declares unreadable artifacts, so a restore can never report `errors=[]` over a known-incomplete archive.
- **`POST /admin/backups/{id}/execute` reports a failed run on the backup, not as a `500`** (#3327). The trigger endpoint called `BackupService::execute`, whose `Err` for a failed run propagated straight through `Result<Json<_>>`, so a run that ended `failed` answered `500 {"code":"INTERNAL_ERROR","message":"Internal server error"}` — and the message #3170 composes for precisely this moment, naming every artifact object whose bytes could not be read, was written to `backups.error_message` and the server log and then discarded at the HTTP boundary. An operator triggering a backup got a bare 500 with no way to learn why. A run that reaches a terminal state has already recorded its own outcome on the backup row; that is a fact about the backup, not about the request, which was understood and carried out. The endpoint now answers with the `BackupResponse` it documents: `200` with `status: "failed"` and `error_message` carrying the cause, or `status: "completed"` for a clean run. **Clients must read `status`, not just the HTTP code** — nothing became quieter, the failure now reaches the caller instead of only the log, and `409` (another backup in progress), `404` and `500` (the run could not be started, or its outcome could not be recorded) are unchanged. `BackupService::execute` keeps its `Err`-on-failed-run shape for the scheduler, whose `backup_schedule_runs` bookkeeping depends on it; the new `execute_run` is what reports an outcome rather than reacting to one. This does not change which bytes a backup captures: on filesystem deployments artifact bytes are still missed for the reason tracked in #2863, and the miss is still reported, now on the resource the operator is looking at.
- **Objects larger than 5 GiB are copied server-side instead of through the application** (#3164). `S3Backend::copy` fell back to `get_stream` + `put_stream` above the 5 GiB single-copy limit, so every byte of a multi-gigabyte object came back through the backend and was re-uploaded. The integrity check was worse than the restream: it ran *after* `CompleteMultipartUpload` had already published the destination, so on a mismatch the corrupt bytes were already live — and it compared the tap hasher against the writer's hasher, two SHA-256s of the same in-process byte stream, so it was structurally unable to detect a transfer that diverged from the source at all. Copies now use one ranged `UploadPartCopy` per 5 GiB slice, as the S3 API requires above the single-copy ceiling; no payload byte passes through the application, and the destination only becomes visible at completion, after every part copied successfully — the same publish-is-the-last-step atomicity the ≤5 GiB native copy gives, which is the property the staging-key proxy-cache publish relies on. Failures abort the multipart upload and leave an existing destination untouched. The ranged call is hand-rolled against the S3 REST API because `object_store` 0.13 only exposes the un-ranged variant, but it is signed with that crate's own public SigV4 signer and the store's own credential chain, so static keys, IRSA, ECS/EKS container credentials and session tokens all keep working.
- **Multi-gigabyte S3 transfers are no longer capped by a 30-second client timeout** (#3180). `object_store`'s default request timeout applies "from when the request starts connecting until the response body has finished" — a cap on total transfer duration, not a stall detector — and it was never overridden. Two operations on the OCI blob-finalize path routinely exceed it for a multi-gigabyte layer: draining each upload part is a single HTTP request whose whole body must arrive inside the window, and promoting the finalized object onto its digest key is one `CopyObject` that S3 holds open for the entire server-side copy. Both surfaced as exactly-30-second stalls. The client is now split the way the GCS backend already splits its own, for the same reason: a control-plane store for head, exists, list, delete, multipart-create and presign keeps a short cliff so a wedged endpoint still fails fast, while a bulk store for gets, puts, part uploads, multipart completion and server-side copy gets a much longer ceiling. Azure already avoided a total timeout on bulk transfer, so S3 was the last backend applying a control-plane cliff to payload movement.
- **The scanner-adapter is handed a registry URL reachable from its own container** (#3169). The backend reused grype's host fallback, which defaults to `http://localhost:8080` when nothing is configured. That is correct only for grype, which execs inside the backend container — the scanner-adapter is a separate container that itself listens on `:8080`, so trivy inside it dialled its own Go server and got `404 page not found` on `GET /v2/`, then reported `unable to find the specified image`. No shipped configuration set a registry host, so the documented enable path in `docker-compose.yml` could never produce a working image scan. Resolution order is now the new dedicated override, then the explicitly configured grype chain (byte-identical to before), and otherwise: when the adapter host is non-loopback — i.e. it cannot share this network namespace — the backend advertises its own route-facing address with its bind port and logs the substitution, while a loopback adapter keeps the historical fallback for local development. A derivation failure also degrades to the historical fallback, so this is never a new failure mode. The commented compose block also mounted the trivy **server's** root-owned cache volume into the adapter, which runs as UID 1001, producing the reported `permission denied` on `fanal.db`.
- **`/health` and `/healthz` no longer fan out to live dependency probes on every request** (#3127). Both are declared at the router root, outside the `/api/v1` nest, so none of the rate-limit layers apply — and every request performed three uncached probes: a real service-account **directory bind** through a freshly constructed LDAP service, an OpenSearch `cluster_health()` query, and a Trivy probe over a brand-new HTTP client, where every client build does a blocking file read of the custom CA bundle on the async runtime when that variable is set. The LDAP leg is the sharpest: an unauthenticated request storm becomes a directory-connection storm capable of exhausting server-side connection limits or tripping the directory's own lockout and throttling counters — a dependency-side outage triggered from an anonymous endpoint. Measured against the real handler with counting stub servers, ten sequential requests produced ten binds and ten probes each, and 25 concurrent requests produced 25. All three now sit behind their own TTL cache at the same 5-second window the storage probe already used; the same load produces one of each, and the Trivy probes share one connection pool.
- **The Maven repository-delete path spares checksum sidecars and rollup documents another repository is still serving** (#3160, #3188, #3156, #3197). Four distinct gaps in the same purge list, all on cloud backends where the flat `maven/{path}` key space is shared between repositories — filesystem backends isolate each repository's key space and are unaffected. First, both `NOT EXISTS` guards tested the candidate key verbatim, and nothing ever references a checksum or signature sidecar *by name* (a parent artifact's `files[]` lists the companion, never the companion's `.sha1`), so both guards always missed on a sidecar — and in a `NOT EXISTS` guard a miss means DELETE. Deleting repository A therefore destroyed `<companion>.sha1` while repository B's live parent artifact was still serving `<companion>`, leaving B publishing an artifact whose checksum sidecar 404s: a warning under Maven's default `checksumPolicy=warn`, a **hard build failure** under `checksumPolicy=fail` or Gradle dependency verification. Each guard now runs a second time against the sidecar-stripped key, establishing the invariant that *a sidecar is spared whenever its base object is spared*. Second, three of those guards matched only the snake_case `files[]` key spelling while the affected rows record the companion under camelCase `storageKey` and the read path deliberately accepts both — protecting legacy rows on deployments upgraded through the version that wrote that spelling. Third, the repository-delete collector never grew the `maven-metadata.xml` anchor the storage-GC predicate has carried since #2668, so it destroyed a rollup document — the file the Maven layout defines for version-range resolution and the `LATEST`/`RELEASE` markers — along with its checksums, while GC would have spared it. All the new arms mirror the guards they shadow exactly apart from the stripped key, because any condition present on one and absent from the other re-creates the same bug for the rows it excludes.
- **The OCI cleanup-journal sweep can no longer delete a blob that was re-pushed underneath it** (#3085, #3187). The sweeps re-checked blob liveness when they claimed a key and again at the guarded row `DELETE` — but that `DELETE` runs *after* the storage object is already gone, and nothing consulted liveness immediately before the destructive delete. A push that commits an `oci_blobs` row for the same storage key during the sweep's walk lost its bytes: the pre-delete hook extended the claim lease without checking liveness, the object was deleted, and the guarded row `DELETE` then correctly refused to remove the journal row because `oci_blobs` now referenced the key — it saved the row, not the data, leaving a live row pointing at bytes that no longer exist. A claimed batch is up to 1,000 rows walked sequentially against an object store, so the window is the whole batch walk rather than an instant. The first fix re-asserted the full liveness predicate inside the same atomic lease-renewal `UPDATE`, which narrows the window but cannot close it — that `UPDATE` locks the journal row only for the duration of one autocommit statement, and the obvious repair does not transfer, because a racing push **INSERTs a new** `oci_blobs` row rather than conflicting onto an existing one, so there is nothing there to lock. The window is now genuinely closed with a two-phase tombstone: the push participates by taking the journal row lock at commit time, so no interleaving of a push and a sweep can leave the storage object deleted *and* an `oci_blobs` row referencing it. The trade is stated plainly: a push that loses the race is refused with a retryable `503` rather than silently succeeding.
- **The startup warning claiming permission enforcement is inactive is removed** (#3185). Every boot with at least one row in `permissions` logged that rules "are stored but not consulted during request authorization". That was inert text left in place after the enforcement work landed, and it misled operators about their security posture. Enforcement is genuinely active on both paths — `repo_visibility_middleware` gates native-protocol writes through `PermissionService::check_repository_action` deny-by-default and reads through the rules lookup plus `check_permission`, the REST path calls the same function, and `/api/v1/system/config` already reported `permissions.enforcement_enabled: true`, directly contradicting the warning. The message is replaced by a regression test that pins the enforcement it denied, so the two cannot drift apart again.

### Performance

- Health probes for LDAP, OpenSearch and Trivy are TTL-cached, collapsing an unbounded per-request fan-out on `/health` to one probe per dependency per window (#3127).
- npm packument responses revalidate with `304` instead of re-sending tens of megabytes per metadata request (#3052).
- Objects over 5 GiB are copied server-side rather than restreamed through the application (#3164).

### CI / Release Assurance

- **The release preflight refuses to tag when a version-pinned image would collide.** `v1.7.2` was tagged with `docker/scanner-adapter/VERSION` still at `1.2.2` while the go-git fix had re-pinned the bundled trivy base image inside `docker/Dockerfile.scanner-adapter`. Exact version tags are never republished, so the tag's `Docker Publish` refused the collision — which skipped every remaining multi-arch manifest, left `resolve-candidate-digest` with nothing to pin, and stalled the entire release chain on a tag that, being immutable, had to be deleted by hand. Nothing caught it earlier because the exact-tag check is only evaluated on a clean `refs/tags/v*` ref: `Docker Publish` passed on `main` for the **same commit**, and an `-rc.N` tag would have passed too, so the defect was reachable only at the one moment it is most expensive to find. `release-preflight.sh` now reads each component's pinned `VERSION`, asks the registry whether that exact tag is already published, and if it is, compares the published index's `org.opencontainers.image.revision` annotation against the very paths the publish job diffs. Changed sources block the cut and name the file to bump; an unchanged-source rebuild still passes, because re-pointing the floating tags for base-image errata is legitimate. A registry it cannot read reports `INFRA` (exit 2) — neither a pass nor a failure — the same distinction check 3 learned in #3308. The adapter moves to **1.2.3**; the scanner-adapter is the only component in this repo tagged from a checked-in `VERSION` file, and the check is a list so the second one is a one-line addition. Both directions are covered in `test-release-preflight.sh` (#3339).
- **Releases are cut from a release candidate first.** `RELEASING.md` now records that `vX.Y.Z-rc.N` should be tagged and the full chain allowed to complete before the real tag. v1.7.0 was cut this way and needed four candidates — rc.1, rc.2 and rc.3 all failed; v1.7.1 and v1.7.2 went straight to a real tag, and v1.7.2 left a dead one. This is safe because the repository ruleset applies tag immutability to `refs/tags/v*` but excludes `v*-rc*`, `v*-beta*` and `v*-alpha*`, so candidates are deletable and re-cuttable while releases are not. The runbook also notes what a candidate does *not* cover, since some publish logic keys on a clean `refs/tags/v*` ref (#3339).
- **Backend integration tests gate pull requests.** `🔗 Backend Integration Tests` ran only on pushes to `main` and `release/*`, and `ci-complete` treated the resulting skip as a pass — so a PR could break every integration test and still show all-green, with the breakage appearing only after merge on a push whose failure blocks nothing and notifies nobody. The suite now also runs on backend-touching PRs, classified from the same changed-file listing the docs-only gate already fetches, and it **fails open to running** (if the classifier job dies the suite runs anyway) while `ci-complete` **fails closed** (a skipped integration job on a backend-touching PR is now a hard failure). Docs-only PRs, version-bump-only release PRs and PRs touching no backend path still pass on a skip (#3124).
- **The container build and smoke chain runs on pull requests.** `detect-changes` carried `if: github.event_name == 'push'` directly under a section header reading "CONTAINER BUILDS (PR only)"; the header was the aspiration and the `if` was the behaviour, so the image builds and the smoke suite reported `skipped` on every PR and `ci-complete` passed the skip. The path filter supports `pull_request` natively, so dropping the `if` is the whole fix; push behaviour is unchanged. `ci.yml` itself is added to the backend filter, so a change to this gate exercises the gate — which is also how the hole went unnoticed, since the jobs were never observed *not* running (#3166).
- **The container CVE gate honours its declared `CRITICAL,HIGH` severity.** The gate declared `CRITICAL,HIGH` but failed on a fixable CVE of any severity, because the scanning action unsets the severity filter whenever the SARIF format is selected and severity limiting is not explicitly requested. Replaying the composite action against the real trivy binary reproduced a publication blocked by 17 findings whose maximum severity score was 6.3, none of them CRITICAL or HIGH. Scanning is now split from gating: one pass for visibility at all severities, one that gates. Both directions are proven — MEDIUM/LOW-only findings pass, and a build carrying fixable HIGHs still fails (#3122).
- **The shared-cargo-registry mutation flake is fixed and coverage build failures are no longer masked** (#3154). Rust jobs intermittently died one to two and a half minutes into their build with one of three signatures — a vendored C header truncated mid-read, a spawn failure because the child's working directory had been deleted, or a missing dep-info file whose listed sources had vanished — on commits whose sibling jobs built identically. The runner pods point `CARGO_HOME` at a hostPath volume shared by up to six concurrent runner pods, and two things treated that registry as private mutable state: the caching action tar-extracts over the live shared copy at job start and, on save, deletes and prunes the registry down to the saving job's own package set; and cargo re-extracts whatever goes missing under a lock that protects extraction against other extractions but not against sibling pods' deletions. At least six failed jobs in one week were attributable to this class, and every instance cleared on rerun — which is exactly the pattern that teaches people to ignore red.
- **Two cluster-wide test assertions no longer flake against concurrent suites.** The storage-GC footprint test asserted before/after deltas over cluster-wide `oci_blobs` totals while other suites delete rows from the same table, and under nextest fail-fast one flake cancelled roughly 1,500 other tests per occurrence; it now asserts exact equalities scoped to its own seeded digests — strictly stronger than the old `>=` deltas — while still executing the unscoped production report under race-free absolute lower bounds (#3129). The two empty-set `COALESCE(SUM(…), 0)` tests in the admin handler emptied a table inside a rolled-back transaction and then aggregated globally, which is not isolated under READ COMMITTED — any row a concurrent test commits between the `DELETE` and the `SELECT` is visible — and this took down `Backend Unit Tests` on an unrelated PR; both now scope the aggregate to a freshly generated repository UUID that is never inserted, which the foreign key guarantees stays empty (#3277).
- **`config.rs` tests no longer leak `DATABASE_URL` process-wide** (#3191). Those tests drive configuration parsing by writing environment variables through `std::env::set_var`, which mutates the whole process; `cargo test` runs the entire suite in one process across many threads, so while a config test held the sentinel `postgresql://127.0.0.1:1/testdb`, every DB-backed test that happened to start in that window failed with `Connection refused`. Saving and restoring the previous value and taking a module-local mutex do not help — the racing reader is a test on another thread that never takes it, and restoring promptly narrows the window without closing it. A test-only thread-local environment overlay now makes those writes visible only to the calling thread, so there is no window to lose; production code is untouched, since the non-test build still imports `std::env`. Postgres was never down — this was a false-signal bug.
- **The library test build is restored after parallel-merge signature drift** (#3214). `cargo test --lib` stopped compiling on `main`, blocking every Rust job: one PR added a second call site for a NuGet download helper in a test module while another added a parameter to that helper and updated only the pre-existing call site. Each PR was green against its own base and the merged tree was never rebuilt.
- **`release-preflight.sh` blocks on a measured-red Docker Publish instead of reporting READY** (#3308). The script measured the failing publish, printed `main's last Docker Publish did NOT cleanly publish the manifest -- a tag cut will likely stall the same way`, and then printed `READY: no blocking problems. Safe to cut the tag.` in the same run: the check called `warn`, which does not increment the problem count, where it needed `bad`. Three outcomes are now kept deliberately distinct, because *"I did not look"*, *"I could not look"* and *"I looked and it is red"* are different claims — not measured is a note and does not block, a failed query exits `2` as an infrastructure result rather than a readiness verdict, and a measured-red publish exits `1` as **NOT READY**. `PREFLIGHT_ALLOW_RED_PUBLISH=1` is a separately named human override rather than a reuse of `PREFLIGHT_SKIP_DOCKER_HEALTH`. The gating was backwards in a way this incident proves: the check that was already hard — that `main` is a superset of every `release/*` branch's `.trivyignore` — is only a **proxy** for "will Security Scan pass" and detects exactly one cause, and #3307 affected `main` and the release branches equally, so it passed clean while the release was definitively blocked. `scripts/ci/test-release-preflight.sh` covers all five outcomes against a stubbed `gh` and runs in `release-preflight.yml` ahead of the real check; restoring the single `warn` turns two of its cases red while the green-path case still passes.

## [1.7.1] - 2026-08-07

A maintenance release. The headline is that the bundled Trivy scanner is now built and hardened in-house, which clears a HIGH advisory that no upstream Trivy release fixes yet and had been blocking the release pipeline. Alongside it: NuGet remote-repository search now actually reaches the upstream feed, a scan-gate evaluation bug that could let a blocked artifact through is closed, and a cluster of Maven, PyPI, OIDC and multi-replica correctness fixes.

### Upgrade note — proxy downloads may start being blocked

The repository age gate is now genuinely enforced on **npm, PyPI and Go proxy downloads**. It was configurable before but silently did not apply to those formats, so a repository with an age gate configured was not actually gating them. After upgrading, package downloads that are younger than the configured `min_age_days` will return `451` where they previously succeeded.

**Am I affected?** Only if you have the age gate enabled on a remote/proxy repository serving npm, PyPI or Go. Check with `GET /api/v1/repositories/{key}/age-gate` (admin only as of this release). If you were relying on the previous non-enforcement, either raise the threshold or disable the gate before upgrading. The `451` body carries `min_age_days` so blocked callers can see the policy that stopped them.

### Security

- **The bundled Trivy scanner is now built in-house from pinned upstream source.** The scanner-adapter image vendored `ghcr.io/aquasecurity/trivy:0.73.0`, whose bundled `oras-go v2.6.1` carries CVE-2026-50163 (HIGH). Upstream merged the fix on `main` but has not released it, and 0.73.0 remains the latest release, so there was no upstream tag to move to. The scanner is now built from the same upstream v0.73.0 source with a pinned Go toolchain and one documented dependency override, on a hardened UBI 9 base, in [artifact-keeper/trivy](https://github.com/artifact-keeper/trivy) — with its own blocking CVE gate, DISA STIG evaluation and build verification. The shipped binary also now carries its licence, NOTICE and modification record, which the runtime previously omitted.
- **Scan gates are evaluated across all scanners, not just the most recent result** (#3138). A repository scanned by more than one scanner had its download gate decided by whichever row was newest, so an `OpenSCAP` result registering last could leave the severity gate inert for npm, PyPI, Maven and generic downloads.
- **Age-gate policy is enforced on npm, PyPI and Go proxy downloads**, and the age-gate config read endpoint now requires admin (#2264) rather than returning gate posture to any authenticated caller with read scope.
- **OIDC outbound responses are size-capped** (userinfo, token, discovery and JWKS), so a hostile or malfunctioning identity provider cannot exhaust memory through an unbounded response body.

### Added

- System stats now report proxy-cache storage consumption and artifact count.

### Fixed

- **NuGet remote repositories now proxy search to the upstream feed.** A remote repository advertised `SearchQueryService` in its service index but answered every query from the local database, so a proxy repository with nothing cached returned zero results — "No packages found" in Visual Studio — while `dotnet restore` against the same repository worked. Search now reaches upstream, rewrites result URLs back through the proxy, and degrades to local results rather than erroring if the upstream feed offers no search.
- **Per-repository storage-GC estimates work again.** The web UI's per-repository storage panel called `POST /api/v1/repositories/{key}/storage-gc` for its "reclaimable now" figure, but only the instance-wide route existed, so every estimate returned 404.
- **Maven catalog versions are derived from the GAV path** on the generic and chunked upload paths, and migration 192 no longer aborts startup on a UNIQUE violation when a package has two broken catalog rows and one candidate version.
- **PyPI proxying**: an upstream `<base href>` on a proxied Simple index no longer re-anchors rewritten download URLs onto the upstream origin; PEP 658 `core-metadata` is advertised for wheels so installers can skip downloading whole wheels to resolve; the PEP 691 `versions` array is ordered by PEP 440 rather than byte order; invalid PEP 440 local versions are rejected instead of silently mangled; and an advertised-but-unavailable metadata file now falls back instead of failing the install.
- **OCI**: a manifest pushed by digest is verified against that digest rather than accepted with a mismatch, and cross-repository blob mount (`?mount=&from=`) is implemented so a client can mount an existing layer instead of re-uploading it.
- **Proxy-cache redirects are gated on the object actually existing.** `local_fetch_or_redirect` passed a hardcoded `cache_is_fresh = true`, so an `artifacts` row alone was enough to sign a presigned redirect without consulting the object store. An object deleted out of band — a lifecycle rule expiring proxy-cache entries by age, for instance — produced a dead 302 that 404s at the object store, past any fallback the server controls, and kept serving dead redirects until repaired by hand. A miss now falls through to the buffered read and repopulates the cache.
- **Multi-replica background jobs** claim their remaining cluster-work items, so replicas no longer duplicate or drop work.
- **Scheduled backups claim one durable run per due occurrence** (#2219): multi-replica schedulers no longer create duplicate archives for the same schedule tick. Long runs renew their token-fenced claim, and run finalization plus advancement of the unchanged schedule occurrence is transactional. A schedule whose cron expression has no further occurrence is now disabled with a warning instead of being left permanently due, where it consumed a due-schedule slot and could starve other schedules.
- **Password-expiry notifications are claimed before SMTP** (#2219): concurrent replicas no longer email the same password-version warning in one scheduler tick. Failed attempts observe a retry delay, stale account/password candidates are rejected at claim time, and usernames are escaped in HTML mail.
- **Generic chunked uploads take a completion lease before finalizing** (#2219): a duplicate `complete` no longer re-checksums, re-copies, and re-upserts the same session, and a failed storage copy no longer leaves a session marked `completed` with no artifact. `cancel` can no longer delete the temp file out from under a live committer, and the expired-session reaper claims its cancels instead of racing them. Chunk uploads are rejected once a session is committing, and a `complete` that fails its authorization re-check releases the lease so the session stays retryable.
- **Incus chunked finalize takes an exclusive lease** (#2219): concurrent `complete` requests can no longer both append the final request body to the staging file and spawn two finalizers, and a reclaim after a crashed append truncates the unrecorded tail instead of double-appending it. Chunk uploads to a session that is already finalizing are rejected with `409` instead of appending to the file being checksummed. The stale-session reaper skips sessions with a live finalize lease.
- **OCI cleanup-journal sweeps claim keys before deleting storage objects** (#2219): concurrent GC ticks no longer issue the same destructive object delete, a failed delete releases the claim with the error recorded for retry, and dry runs stay read-only.
- **Health monitoring, lifecycle execution, and the OpenSearch bootstrap reindex are cluster-leased** (#2219): the health monitor's `consecutive_failures` counter has a single writer, due lifecycle policies execute once per cycle instead of once per replica, and a fresh multi-replica deployment starts one full reindex rather than one per replica. Long-running leases heartbeat while their owner is alive.
- **Curation sync honors `curation_sync_interval_secs`** (#2219): the configured interval was read and discarded, so every enabled staging repository re-fetched upstream metadata on every five-minute tick. Repositories now record `curation_last_synced_at` after a successful fetch-and-evaluate and are skipped until their interval elapses (60s floor); the manual single-repository sync trigger still runs immediately.
- Probe endpoints (`/health`, `/healthz`, `/ready`, `/readyz`, `/livez`) no longer emit a per-request log line, which had buried real request logs under Kubernetes polling. A non-success probe response is still logged. Set `LOG_PROBE_REQUESTS=1` to restore the previous behavior.
- The hardened backend image includes `xz`, which Incus `.tar.xz` extraction requires.

### Performance

- Repository listing reads storage totals from the usage ledger instead of computing a live `SUM`.

## [1.7.0] - 2026-07-31

A supply-chain-enforcement and release-assurance release closing the 1.7.0 milestone. The headline is that scan and curation policy now *block at serve time*: an inline scan-and-block gate rejects vulnerable artifacts on download across proxy and hosted repositories (PyPI, npm, Docker/OCI) and the virtual repos that aggregate them, while a new typed curation engine adds publisher-trust and popularity/typo-squat rules — including Unicode-confusable (homoglyph) and affix detection — that stop suspect packages before they reach a client. Underneath the features, the release re-architects the release pipeline into a real assurance gate (blocking security suite, DTF gate against the candidate digest, promote-by-digest, dispatch-rehearsable dry runs), makes the repository usage ledger authoritative to enable O(1) quota admission, and lands a broad performance pass (keyset pagination, GIN-indexed full-text search, off-hot-path side effects). It also closes a cluster of token, refresh, and federated-admin authorization gaps (several with GHSA advisories) and a deep set of cloud-storage, migration, and native-format fidelity fixes.

### Sponsors

Thank you to our sponsors for supporting ongoing development of Artifact Keeper.

**Backers**

- Ash A. ([@dragonpaw](https://github.com/dragonpaw))
- Gabriel Rodriguez ([@injectedfusion](https://github.com/injectedfusion))

[Become a sponsor](https://github.com/sponsors/artifact-keeper) to support the project and get your name listed here.

### Thank You

Huge thanks to the external contributors and issue reporters who shaped this release:
